### 1.13 AI—at the Intersection of Computer Science and Data Science

When a baby first opens its eyes, does it “see” its parent’s faces? Does it understand any notion of a face or even a simple shape? Babies must “learn” the world around them. That’s what artificial intelligence (AI) technology called machine learning does. It observes massive amounts of data and learns from it. AI technologies are being used to play games, implement computer-vision applications, enable self-driving cars, enable robots to learn to perform new tasks, diagnose medical conditions, translate speech to other languages in near real-time, create chatbots that can respond smoothly and accurately to arbitrary questions after being trained on massive text databases called **large language models**, and much more. Who’d have guessed just a few years ago that artificially intelligent self-driving cars would be allowed on our roads—or even become common?

#### 1.13.1 Artificial Intelligence (AI)

Two definitions of **artificial intelligence (AI)**^([99](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_99a),[100](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_100a)) are:

*   “a branch of computer science dealing with the simulation of intelligent behavior in computers” and

*   “the capability of a machine to imitate intelligent human behavior.”

[99](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_99). “artificial intelligence.” [Merriam-Webster.com](http://Merriam-Webster.com). Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/artificial%20intelligence`](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/artificial%20intelligence).

[100](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_100). “Artificial intelligence.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence).

The term AI was coined by John McCarthy in 1956\. AI-based systems now permeate our daily lives. Examples include computer vision, speech recognition, natural language translation, recommender systems (such as Amazon recommending products you might like or Netflix recommending shows and movies you might like), automated game-playing systems, self-driving cars, and more recent remarkable tools like

*   chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity that converse almost indistinguishably from conversing with humans,

*   image generators like OpenAI’s Dall-E (now integrated into ChatGPT), Google’s Imagen (integrated into Gemini), Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Adobe’s Firefly and many more that create original images from text descriptions, and

*   video generators like OpenAI’s Sora, Adobe’s Firefly Video, Google’s Veo 2, Meta’s MovieGen and Runway’s Gen-3 Alpha that create original video from text descriptions.

For many decades, AI has been a field with problems and no solutions. That’s because once a problem is solved, people say, “Well, that’s not intelligence; it’s just a computer program that tells the computer exactly what to do.” However, with AI techniques like machine learning ([Section 1.13.4](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev2sec30)) and deep learning ([Section 1.13.5](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev2sec31)), we’re not pre-programming solutions to specific problems. Instead, we’re having computers solve problems by learning from data—typically, lots of it. Many of the most interesting and challenging problems are being pursued with deep learning.

#### 1.13.2 Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)

The ultimate goal of AI is **artificial general intelligence (AGI)**^([101](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_101a)) that, like a human, can understand, learn and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks without needing extra training—basically, an AI that can “carry out any task that humans are capable of.”^([102](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_102a)) Experts disagree on when or if artificial general intelligence might become a reality—from 2025^([103](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_103a)) to the 2030s^([104](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_104a)) to 2300 or never.^([105](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_105a))

Several AI milestones have captured people’s attention and imagination, made the general public start thinking that AI is real and made businesses think about commercializing it:

*   In a 1997 match between **IBM’s DeepBlue** computer system and chess Grandmaster Gary Kasparov, DeepBlue became the first computer to beat a reigning world chess champion under tournament conditions.^([106](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_106a)) IBM loaded DeepBlue with hundreds of thousands of grandmaster chess games. DeepBlue could use brute force to evaluate up to 200 million moves per second!^([107](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_107a)) This is big data at work. IBM received the $100,000 Carnegie Mellon University Fredkin Prize, offered in 1980 to the creators of the first computer to beat a world chess champion.^([108](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_108a))

#### 1.13.4 Machine Learning

**Machine learning** is “a subfield of artificial intelligence that gives computers the ability to learn without explicitly being programmed.”^([117](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_117a)) Machine learning typically uses predefined algorithms to build models that learn from training data. Those models can then be used to make predictions.^([118](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_118a)) For example, given labeled training data that contains legitimate e-mails and junk (also called spam) e-mails, a machine-learning model can learn from the training data, then be used to classify e-mails it has never “seen” as junk or not junk. E-mail apps like Microsoft’s Outlook and Google’s Gmail use techniques like this to move junk emails out of your inbox.

[117](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_117). Sara Brown “Machine learning, explained.” April 21, 2021\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/machine-learning-explained`](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/machine-learning-explained).

[118](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_118). “Machine learning.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning).

#### 1.13.5 Deep Learning

**Deep learning** is a subset of machine learning that involves building artificial neural networks, which “attempt to simulate the network of neurons that make up a human brain so that the computer will be able to learn things and make decisions in a human-like manner.”^([119](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_119a)) The term “deep” comes from the number of software “layers” in an artificial neural network—the more layers, the deeper the network. The network learns more from its training data as it proceeds through the network layers.^([120](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_120a)) The availability of big data, significant processor power, faster Internet speeds and advancements in parallel computing hardware and software are making it possible for more organizations and individuals to pursue resource-intensive deep-learning solutions that are producing impressive results in computer vision, speech recognition, speech synthesis and newer generative AI applications ([Section 1.14](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev1sec14)).

[119](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_119). Jason Brownlee, “What is deep learning?” November 16, 2023\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-is-deep-learning/`](https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-is-deep-learning/).

[120](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_120). “Deep learning.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning).

#### 1.13.6 Reinforcement Learning

**Reinforcement learning**^([121](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_121a),[122](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_122a)) is a subset of machine learning in which algorithms learn from their environment, similar to how humans learn—for example, a video game enthusiast learning a new game or a baby learning to walk or recognize its parents. The algorithm implements an agent that learns by trying to perform a task, receiving feedback about success or failure, making adjustments then trying again. The goal is to maximize the reward. The agent receives a positive reward for doing something right and a negative reward (a punishment) for doing something wrong. The agent uses this information to determine the next action to perform and must try to maximize the reward.

### 1.14 Generative AI

**Generative AI (genAI)** describes algorithms that can generate new content—including text, images, audio and video—based on prompts provided by a user as input.^([123](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_123a),[124](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_124a),[125](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_125a))

[123](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_123). “What Is Generative AI?” McKinsey & Company, April 2, 2024\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/mckinsey-explainers/what-is-generative-ai`](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/mckinsey-explainers/what-is-generative-ai).

[124](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_124). “Generative artificial intelligence.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence).

[125](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_125). Hannah Wren, “A Beginner’s Guide to Generative AI for Business,” Zendesk, October 22, 2024\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.zendesk.com/blog/generative-ai-guide/`](https://www.zendesk.com/blog/generative-ai-guide/).

##### GenAI Chatbots

OpenAI’s **ChatGPT**, Google’s **Gemini**, Anthropic’s **Claude** and **Perplexity** are AI-based chatbots you can converse with using natural language.^([126](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_126a)) For example, you could prompt it with text like:

*   “Tell me about the history of the Java programming language.”

*   “Who coined the term Metaverse?”

*   “Summarize the article at” followed by a link to the article.

[126](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_126). “Introducing ChatGPT.” November 30, 2022\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt`](https://openai.com/blog/chatgpt).

Each chatbot then responds with answers that look and feel as if they were generated by a human.

##### Multimodal Chatbots

When genAIs were first introduced, they typically received a text prompt and generated a specific type of output, such as text or an image. Many genAI chatbots are now multi-modal, enabling them to understand text, images, audio and even video inputs and use them to generate outputs combining text, images, audio and video. For example, you can prompt genAIs with a speech audio file and instructions asking them to transcribe the speech to text, display the transcription, analyze its sentiment (positive, negative or neutral), translate it to another spoken language and synthesize speech in that other language—and even create images and videos from the generated text! These capabilities were out of reach even to the most sophisticated developers just a few years ago. Today, they’re available to the general public.

##### Turing Test

When you converse with ChatGPT and similar tools, it may seem like you’re chatting with another person. In 1950, Alan Turing proposed the **imitation game**—now known as the **Turing test**—as a way to determine whether a computer exhibits truly intelligent behavior.^([127](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_127a)) In it, three computer terminals would be hidden from one another, with two people operating terminals via text-based inputs and the third being computer-operated. One person would ask text-based questions that would be sent to the other two terminals. The second person and the computer would send text responses. If the person asking the questions could not determine whether the answers came from the other person or the computer, then the computer would be considered to have exhibited intelligent behavior.

[127](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_127). “Turing test.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_test`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_test).

##### Things GenAIs Can Do

We prompted ChatGPT, asking for a list of all the types of things generative AIs can generate.^([128](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_128a)) We then asked it to summarize its lengthy response:

*   **Text**—Articles, essays, stories, poems, lyrics, code, summaries, marketing copy, academic writing, emails, and instructional guides.

*   **Visual/images**—Digital illustrations, concept art, character design, photo-realistic images, logos, branding elements, infographics and AI-enhanced graphics.

*   **Audio**—AI-composed music, sound effects, ambient audio, text-to-speech, narration, voice cloning and synthesized speech.

*   **Video**—AI-generated animations, explainer videos, video synthesis from text, deepfake videos and virtual characters.

*   **3D**—3D models for games, simulations, virtual reality, digital sculptures, animations and special effects.

*   **Code and software**—Automated code generation, programming assistance, chat-bots, virtual assistants, automation scripts and machine-learning algorithms.

*   **Interactive**—Chatbot conversations, dynamic storytelling, personalized quizzes, surveys, interactive website and educational tools.

*   **Data-related**—AI-generated data analysis, reports, visualizations, graphs, charts, tables and synthetic datasets.

*   **Educational**—Study guides, lesson plans, quizzes, textbook sections, tutorials and interactive learning exercises.

*   **Multimodal**—AI-generated videos with narration and graphics, interactive simulations, and virtual environments combining text, visuals and user interaction.

*   **Art and creative**—Digital comics, graphic novels, mixed media art, style-transfer artwork, custom merchandise designs and AI-generated screenplays.

*   **Miscellaneous**—AI-generated recipes, fitness plans, daily affirmations, product names, slogans, personalized recommendations and legal document templates.

[128](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_128). *ChatGPT* response to “Give me a list of all the types of things generative AIs can generate.” October 26, 2024\. [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com). We edited the response.

These capabilities make content creation accessible to everyone.

##### Large Language Models (LLMs)

A **large language model (LLM)**^([129](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_129a),[130](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_130a),[131](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_131a)) is an AI that understands and can generate natural language. The term “large” comes from the fact that LLMs are implemented as artificial neural networks (or neural nets) with billions, and even trillions, of parameters. LLMs are trained on massive amounts of text—articles, books, the Internet, code and more. As neural nets learn, they tune parameters, attempting to produce better results. The parameters neural nets learn help LLMs understand and generate language patterns.

[129](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_129). “[Large Language Model](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev3sec52).” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model).

[130](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_130). Sean Michael Kerner, “[Large Language Model (LLM)](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev3sec52),” TechTarget. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/large-language-model-LLM`](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/large-language-model-LLM).

[131](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_131). Adrian Tam, “What Are Large Language Models?” Machine Learning Mastery, July 20, 2023\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-are-large-language-models/`](https://machinelearningmastery.com/what-are-large-language-models/).

LLMs can generate text that’s indistinguishable from human writing. Some continue to learn and adapt, improving their effectiveness over time. They’re great at natural language tasks like translation, classification, summarization, answering questions, sentiment analysis, creative writing, and more. They’re also great at generating code, explaining code, finding errors in code, refactoring code and more.

##### Transformers

A **transformer**^([132](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_132a),[133](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_133a),[134](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_134a)) is a neural network that processes sequential data, like text. It can understand and recognize relationships between even distant words in a sentence. Transformers also recognize the relative importance of words. Many LLMs use **generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs)**^([135](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_135a)) that are trained on massive amounts of text using several artificial intelligence techniques.^([136](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_136a)) There are other techniques, like Google’s **Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)**, which is geared to natural language understanding (NLU; introduced in [Section 1.14](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev1sec14)).^([137](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_137a))

##### Self-Attention

**Self-attention**^([138](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_138a),[139](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_139a)) is a key aspect of transformers, which are used in natural language processing. When trying to understand a word in a sentence, the context provided by surrounding words plays a significant role in determining its meaning. For example:

*   The word “good” typically is positive, but when preceded by “not,” the context becomes negative.

*   The word “bank” could refer to a financial institution or the side of a river, depending on whether it’s paired with words like “loan” or “river.”^([140](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_140a)) Instructors like to use books that are accompanied by a “test bank,” which helps them create quizzes.

*   Similarly, a phrase like “break the ice” shifts from its literal interpretation to a metaphorical one when used in contexts related to social interactions.^([140](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_140a))

[138](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_138). Ashish Vaswani et al, “Attention Is All You Need,” arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.03762 (2017). Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762`](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

[139](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_139). “Attention (Machine Learning).” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_(machine_learning)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attention_(machine_learning)).

[140](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_140). *ChatGPT* response to “Provide examples in which the context provided by surrounding words plays a significant role in determining a word’s meaning in a sentence.” October 26, 2024\. [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com). We edited the response.

Transformers leverage self-attention to analyze each word in relation to the others around it. Since not all words contribute equally to the meaning of a sentence, self-attention assigns different weights to words, focusing more on the most relevant ones. Unlike humans, transformers can process and analyze vast numbers of words simultaneously, making connections between them to better grasp their overall meaning.

##### Tokens, Context and Context Windows

A **token**^([141](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_141a)) is the unit of processing in language models. Tokens can be words, parts of words or punctuation. Tokenization converts tokens to numerical values models can process. A token’s **context** is a sequence of tokens that comes before (and sometimes after) a word or phrase. Understanding the context helps models generate more accurate responses. A **context window**^([142](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_142a)) is the maximum number of tokens (input and output combined) a model can consider at once. The larger the context window is, the more context there is to your conversation with a genAI, the more relevant and coherent its responses will be, and the greater the cost to generate a useful response. This is why genAIs’ free tiers often have smaller context windows or allow fewer queries in a given time period.

[141](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_141). Microsoft. “Understanding Tokens.” Microsoft Learn, May 20, 2024. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/ai/conceptual/understanding-tokens`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/ai/conceptual/understanding-tokens).

[142](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_142). IBM Research. “Why Larger LLM Context Windows Are All the Rage.” IBM Research Blog, July 24, 2024\. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://research.ibm.com/blog/larger-context-window`](https://research.ibm.com/blog/larger-context-window).

GenAI chatbot context window sizes vary tremendously. For the four we use extensively—OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude and Perplexity—the context window sizes range from a low of 8,000 tokens for ChatGPT’s free version^([143](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_143a)) to a high of 1,000,000 tokens for Gemini’s paid version.^([144](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_144a))

[143](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_143). *ChatGPT* response to “What’s your context window size?” February 15, 2025\. [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com).

[144](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_144). “Gemini Advanced.” Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://gemini.google/advanced`](https://gemini.google/advanced).

##### Prompts and Prompt Engineering

**Prompt engineering** is the process of designing prompts to obtain the best responses. Outside [Chapter 19](#ch19.xhtml_ch19), many of the book’s sections end with Generative AI exercises in which we focus on prompt engineering to help you interact effectively with genAI tools. Think of this as learning a new and different type of programming language. With prompt engineering, you craft precise instructions or queries to guide genAIs in producing the required responses.

When you prompt genAIs, be sure to:

*   **Include “Java” in your prompt** when you ask genAIs to write Java code or answer questions about Java features. Also, **ask them to write Java code using the latest Java idioms** based on the Java version you’re using.

*   **Keep track of your prompts and the quality of their results.** This is crucial for learning what works and what doesn’t. This will also help you identify the nuances of different genAI platforms. **You’ll build a repertoire of valuable prompts and anticipated results.**

*   **Experiment with multiple genAIs**—including new ones as they appear—and compare the results to understand their varying capabilities.

*   **Experiment with different prompting strategies** to see which ones help you achieve your desired outcomes. Different programming challenges can require different prompting strategies.

*   **Tune your prompt and try again if the genAIs’ results are not satisfactory.** Better prompts produce better results. Some genAIs dig deeper into the subject matter.

When prompting some genAIs, pressing *Enter* (or *Return*) submits your prompt immediately. For others, you must explicitly press (or select) a button to submit the prompt. **To move the cursor to a new line without submitting the prompt**, use

```
Shift + Enter
```

or

```
Shift + Return
```

When we ask you to provide Java code to the genAIs as part of a prompt in [Chapters 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02) and higher, we recommend that you copy and paste the code from Java source-code files. **Most genAIs also allow you to upload one or more files**, but this is sometimes a feature provided only for paid subscribers.

It takes lots of experience to learn how to create great prompts. Various online guides to help you build better prompts, and you can even ask the genAIs themselves to tune your prompts. **OpenAI provides a nice prompt engineering guide** at

[Click here to view code image](#ch01_images.xhtml_f0040-01)

```
https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-engineering
```

and an **extensive set of sample prompts** at

[Click here to view code image](#ch01_images.xhtml_f0040-02)

```
https://platform.openai.com/docs/examples
```

##### Generative AI Anecdotes

During November and December of 2023, we would ask ChatGPT to perform tasks for which it previously generated detailed responses. Rather than detailed responses, it was lazy and provided steps telling us how to perform the tasks ourselves. Some researchers proposed the “winter break hypothesis,”^([145](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_145a)) speculating that ChatGPT learned to do less work at that time of year because people in the west tend to do less around the holiday season.

[145](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_145). Edwards, Benj. “As ChatGPT gets “lazy,” people test “winter break hypothesis” as the cause." December 11, 2023\. Accessed October 13, 2024. [`https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2023/12/is-chatgpt-becoming-lazier-because-its-december-people-run-tests-to-find-out/`](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2023/12/is-chatgpt-becoming-lazier-because-its-december-people-run-tests-to-find-out/).

Though powerful, genAI chatbots sometimes make errors or even “**hallucinate**,”^([146](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_146a)) confidently presenting incorrect information as facts. As one example of an error, we asked several genAIs, “What do these Java statements output?” and fed them five simple statements that display the following three lines of asterisks:

```
****
*****
******
```

[146](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_146). “Hallucination (artificial intelligence).” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallucination_(artificial_intelligence)).

The typical genAI response was:

```
***************
```

or to display one asterisk per line vertically.

Around August 2024, someone discovered that asking ChatGPT’s voice mode, “How many R’s are in strawberry?” yielded the incorrect spoken response, “There are two R’s in strawberry.”^([147](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_147a),[148](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_148a)) Interestingly, entering the same question as a text prompt yielded the correct answer, “There are three R’s in strawberry.” On March 30, 2025, we repeated this experiment with ChatGPT’s voice mode, and it once again said, “There are two R’s in strawberry.” We said, “No. There are three R’s in strawberry.” The ChatGPT voice came back and said, “Let’s see: S-T-R-A-W-B-E-R-R-Y. You’re right, there are three R’s!”

[147](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_147). Kit Eaton, “How Many R’s in Strawberry? This AI Can’t Tell You,” Inc., August 28, 2024\. Accessed March 1, 2023\. [`https://www.inc.com/kit-eaton/how-many-rs-in-strawberry-this-ai-cant-tell-you.html`](https://www.inc.com/kit-eaton/how-many-rs-in-strawberry-this-ai-cant-tell-you.html).

[148](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_148). We tried this in March 2025, and ChatGPT voice mode still gives the wrong answer.

One example of hallucinating is that GenAIs have been known to make up court cases. You might research this with the following prompt, “Give me citations for court cases in which judges reprimanded lawyers for citing non-existent court cases generated by AIs.”

Another example of hallucinating comes from our experience in the early days of ChatGPT. We wanted to experiment with its ability to create text-based content. We asked it to write definitions of various computing terms and to provide four references for each—one of which we required to be Wikipedia. In general, it produced nice definitions and gave a direct link to the correct Wikipedia page. Without fail, however, the other three references we requested were completely fabricated—fake names, fake quotes, fake websites, and sometimes real websites but pages that did not exist. Though they are much better now than in their early days, you should always verify the information genAIs provide. Also, data on the Internet can have biases. When genAIs are trained, they might pick up those biases. We discuss these issues in Exercise 1.23 and in a section in [Chapter 19](#ch19.xhtml_ch19).

##### Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Natural Language Understanding (NLU)^([149](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_149a))

[149](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_149). *Claude* response to “Please write a paragraph explaining what natural language processing and natural language understanding are and how they’re fundamental to generative AI.” February 18, 2024\. [`https://claude.ai`](https://claude.ai). We edited the response.

**Natural language processing (NLP)** and **natural language understanding (NLU)** are two key technologies that enable genAIs to interact with human language. NLP focuses on how computers process and analyze human language—breaking down text into meaningful pieces like words, sentences and relationships between them.^([150](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_150a)) Think of NLP as the system that helps computers read and make sense of text, much like how you’re currently reading and processing these words.

[150](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_150). The phrase “red brick factory” illustrates why natural language is such a challenging subject. Is a “red brick factory” a factory that makes red bricks? Is it a red factory that makes bricks of any color? Is it a factory built of red bricks that makes products of any type? In today’s music world, it could even be a rock band’s name or the name of a game on your smartphone.

NLU helps computers understand the meaning and context of language, not just the individual words. For example, when you ask a genAI, “What’s the weather like?” then ask, “Should I bring an umbrella?”, the genAI uses NLU to recognize that your second question is related to the weather and that you’re asking about rain protection.

NLP and NLU form the foundation for generative AI to understand your prompts and generate human-like responses. Without them, interacting with generative AI would be like trying to converse with someone who knows all the words in a language but doesn't understand how they fit together or what they actually mean.

### 1.15 Wrap-Up

This chapter introduced terminology and concepts that lay the groundwork for the Java programming capabilities you’ll learn throughout the book. We discussed Moore’s Law, noting that the steady stream of dramatic improvements it so accurately predicted for decades seems to be ending. As a result, hardware designers have shifted to multi-core architectures, which you’ll program with the multithreading techniques we discuss in [Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18), [Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads](#ch18.xhtml_ch18). We introduced Java and encouraged you to avoid reinventing the wheel when developing new software by using preexisting software components from the Java API and open-source Java libraries.

We briefly reviewed object orientation and the notions of classes, objects, interfaces, inheritance and polymorphism, providing the groundwork for the objects-natural case studies in [Chapters 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02)–[7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07) and [11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11) and our detailed treatment of object-oriented programming in [Chapters 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)–[9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09).

We discussed a typical Java program-development environment in the context of the Java Development Kit (JDK) then used its tools to test-drive a Java program to prepare you to run the book’s example programs and original programs you’ll write. You can also run our programs with a Java integrated development environment (IDE)—we provide test-drives for several popular IDEs at [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5).

We discussed the Internet, the web, the cloud and the Internet of Things (IoT). We introduced the Metaverse and key associated technologies—blockchain, cryptocurrencies, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), Web3, augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR) and mixed reality. We considered various software development technologies, including refactoring, design patterns, software development kits (SDKs), version control systems (VCS), agile software development, test-driven development (TDD), microservices and containerization.

We introduced big data analytics, then discussed big data and various data sizes, from megabytes to exabytes. Finally, we introduced artificial intelligence (AI)—an intersection between computer science and data science—presenting various AI milestones and brief overviews of several AI technologies, including artificial general intelligence (AGI), machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning and generative AI, which you’ll use throughout this book to leverage your Java learning experience. In this chapter’s end-of-chapter exercises, you’ll begin using generative AI to enhance your Java learning experience. In [Chapter 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02), you’ll begin programming in Java.

#### Special Section: Generative AI Exercises

For each of the following questions, try multiple genAIs to determine which performs best. Always verify the results. Keep in mind that they sometimes make mistakes and even hallucinate, creating unreliable information.

**1.1** ***(2010 “Flash Crash”)*** An example of the consequences of our dependency on computers was the so-called “flash crash,” which occurred on May 6, 2010, when the U.S. stock market fell precipitously in minutes, wiping out over one trillion dollars of investments—then recovering in minutes. Use genAIs to investigate the causes of this crash and discuss the issues it raises.

**1.4** ***(Same Question, Different Answer)*** Prompt genAIs, asking why when you ask them the same question seconds, minutes, hours, days or more later, they often return significantly different responses each time.

for a tutorial on its multimodal capabilities for working with text, images, audio and video (if any). Ask it to suggest the kinds of multimodal apps you can build.

for a tutorial on its multimodal capabilities for working with text, images, audio and video (if any). Ask it to suggest the kinds of multimodal apps you can build.

```
https://claude.ai
```

for a tutorial on its multimodal capabilities for working with text, images, audio and video (if any). Ask it to suggest the kinds of multimodal apps you can build.

```
https://www.perplexity.ai/
```

for a tutorial on its multimodal capabilities for working with text, images, audio and video (if any). Ask it to suggest the kinds of multimodal apps you can build.

**1.9** ***(GenAI Job Opportunities)*** Prompt genAIs asking what you should do to prepare for a career in generative AI and what kinds of new job opportunities generative AI is creating.

**1.10** ***(Technical Innovations and Jobs)*** Some people are concerned that genAIs will eliminate jobs. Prompt genAIs for examples of other major technical innovations—such as the Internet, Google Search and others—that eliminated some jobs but also created new ones.

**1.11** ***(Verify Generative AI Responses)*** Prompt genAIs, asking why they sometimes hallucinate and to provide best practices on how to detect and deal with this problem.

**1.12** ***(Funny Generative AI Anecdotes)*** Prompt genAIs for a list of funny generative AI anecdotes.

**1.13** ***(Free Generative AIs)*** Prompt genAIs to list free genAIs or ones that have a free tier and/or a free trial.

**1.14** ***(Video Generation)*** Some genAI services with limited free video generation include:

*   Synthesia.io ([`https://synthesia.io`](https://synthesia.io)) lets you create up to three minutes of video per month, using nine avatars and various AI voices in 130+ languages.

*   Invideo AI ([`https://invideo.io`](https://invideo.io)) lets you create up to 10 minutes of video per week. Based on your text inputs, it can autogenerate scripts, video clips, subtitles, background music, and transitions.

*   Pictory AI ([`https://pictory.ai`](https://pictory.ai)) offers a free trial for three five-minute videos.

*   Adobe Firefly ([`https://firefly.adobe.com`](https://firefly.adobe.com)) offers free monthly credits.

Prompt generative AIs to give you links to demos produced by each service. Try and comment on these demos.

**1.15** ***(Free Text-to-Speech Services)*** Two popular services are:

*   Google Cloud’s Text-to-Speech offers one million free characters per month for their WaveNet (natural-sounding) voices and four million free characters per month for their standard voices.

*   Amazon Polly’s free tier allows five million characters per month using their standard voices and one million characters per month using their neural (natural-sounding) voices for the first 12 months.

Prompt generative AIs to give you links to demos produced by each service. Try and comment on these demos.

**1.16** ***(Detecting AI Generated Content)*** Prompt generative AIs to find free tools and tools with free tiers or free trials for detecting AI-generated content. This is a difficult problem and the reported results are often wrong. Comment on the ethics of using these tools.

**1.17** ***(Ethics)*** Prompt generative AIs to write tutorials on ethics in AI and list the ethical issues of using generative AI.

**1.18** ***(Negatives)*** Prompt generative AIs to list AI negatives.

**1.19** ***(Regulation)*** Prompt generative AIs to write tutorials on government regulation of AIs. These cans vary by state or country.

**1.20** ***(Safety)*** Prompt generative AIs to write tutorials on AI safety.

**1.21** ***(IQ Test)*** Prompt generative AIs to list the types of questions that might appear on IQ tests.

**1.22** ***(Anecdote: Decisions at the Speed of Light)*** During the United States Civil War, the telegraph was used for near real-time communication.^([151](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_151a)) There’s an anecdote attributed to Abraham Lincoln in which one of his young lieutenants excitedly tells him that they’re wiring the battlefields with telegraph capabilities. The lieutenant tells the president he’ll be able to make decisions with the speed of light. The older and wiser Lincoln responds to the lieutenant that he’ll also be able to make *wrong* decisions with the speed of light.

[151](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_151). “Civil War Signals,” Accessed June 24, 2024\. [`https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/resources/everyone/digital-media-center/video-audio/general/civil-war-signals-transcript.pdf`](https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/resources/everyone/digital-media-center/video-audio/general/civil-war-signals-transcript.pdf).

We asked generative AIs to track down this anecdote. Here’s what ChatGPT said: “The quote you are referring to is often attributed to Abraham Lincoln regarding the use of the telegraph during the Civil War. However, it appears to be a paraphrasing rather than a direct quote from Lincoln. The idea is that the rapid communication provided by the telegraph allowed for quicker decision-making, but also meant that wrong decisions could be disseminated just as quickly. Here is the commonly referenced paraphrased idea: 'With the advent of the telegraph, wrong decisions could now be transmitted at the speed of light.' This reflects Lincoln's awareness of how new technology, like the telegraph, could impact the speed and consequences of decision-making during the Civil War. The telegraph was indeed a critical tool for communication and coordination in that era, and while it had many benefits, it also meant that mistakes could be communicated and acted upon much more quickly than before.”^([152](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_152a))

[152](#ch01.xhtml_fn1_152). OpenAI ChatGPT 4o, Accessed June 24, 2024\. [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com).

Generative AI is a relatively new technology with many ramifications that must be carefully considered. One of its advantages over the Lincoln telegraph anecdote is that it offers many possibilities for improving decision quality. Prompt generative AIs for how they can help you improve decision quality.

**1.23** ***(Issues with Generative AI: Biases)*** Data on the Internet has lots of biases and that data is being used to train genAI large language models. So, when the models are trained, there is a chance they’ll pick up those biases. Prompt genAIs, asking what they do to avoid picking up biases from the training data.

**1.24** ***(Issues with Generative AI: Copyright Issues)*** Prompt genAIs, asking how they ensure the images they create are original and do not violate copyrights.

**1.25** ***(AI Agents)*** Prompt genAIs, asking what an AI agent is and to give several prominent examples of them.

**1.26** ***(Humans in the Loop)*** Prompt genAIs, asking about the importance of keeping humans “in the loop” when using genAI results, especially in business-critical and mission-critical situations.

## 2

## Intro to Java Programming

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this chapter, you’ll:

*   Write, compile and run Java programs.

*   Use input and output statements.

*   Declare, initialize and use variables of primitive types.

*   Use arithmetic operators.

*   Understand the precedence of arithmetic operators.

*   Write decision-making statements.

*   Use relational and equality operators to form conditions.

*   Use generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience.

*   Begin appreciating the “objects-natural” learning approach by conveniently creating and using powerful objects of the Java API’s `String` class before you learn to code your own custom classes in later chapters.

Outline

### 2.1 Introduction

This chapter introduces Java programming. We begin with simple programs that output messages on the screen. We then present a program that inputs (that is, reads) two numbers from a user, calculates their sum and displays the result. You’ll perform arithmetic calculations and save their results for later use. The last example demonstrates decision-making by comparing two numbers then displays messages showing the comparison results. Throughout the chapter, you’ll use generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. You’ll use the JDK’s command-line tools to compile and run this chapter’s programs. If you prefer to use an integrated development environment (IDE), see our Test-Drives of popular IDEs at

```
https://deitel.com/javafp5
```

##### The “Objects-Natural” Learning Approach

In your programs throughout this book, you’ll create and use many objects of preexisting carefully developed and tested classes that enable you to perform significant tasks with minimal code, even in the book’s earliest chapters. These classes typically come from:

*   the Java Application Programming Interface (Java API), and

*   free third-party libraries created by the massive open-source communities that have developed around key programming languages.

To help you appreciate this programming style even in the book’s introductory chapters, you’ll conveniently create and use powerful objects of preexisting Java API classes without yet knowing how to create custom Java classes. We call this the objects-natural approach. In this chapter’s final example, you’ll begin by creating and using `String` objects. Then, in [Chapters 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)–[9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), you’ll craft valuable custom classes for your own use and for reuse by other programmers.

### 2.2 Your First Program in Java: Printing a Line of Text

Consider a simple program that displays a line of text. [Figure 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01) shows the program followed by a box that displays its output. We use line numbers for instructional purposes—they’re not part of the program. This example illustrates several important features. We’ll see that line 7 performs the program’s key action—displaying the text `"Welcome to Java Programming!"` on the screen.

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0049-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.1: Welcome1.java
 2   // Text-printing program.
 3
 4   public class Welcome1 {
 5      // main method begins program execution
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.println("Welcome to Java Programming!");
 8      } // end method main
 9   } // end class Welcome1
```

```
Welcome to Java Programming!
```

**Fig. 2.1** | Text-printing program.

##### Commenting Your Programs

We insert **comments** to document programs and improve their readability. The compiler ignores comments, so they do not cause the computer to perform any action when you run the program. By convention, we begin every program with a comment indicating the figure number and the program’s filename to help you find the file in the book’s `examples` folder (discussed in the Before You Begin section). The comment in line 1 indicates that you can find `Welcome1.java` in the `examples/ch02/fig02_01` folder. This comment begins with **`//`**, indicating it’s an **end-of-line comment** that terminates at the end of the line. Such comments need not begin a line; they also can begin in the middle of a line and continue until the end (as in lines 5, 8 and 9). By our convention, line 2 is a comment describing the program’s purpose.

Java also has **traditional comments** that you can spread over several lines, as in

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0049-02)

```
/* This is a traditional comment. It
   can be split over multiple lines */
```

These begin with the delimiter **/*** and end with ***/**. The compiler ignores all text between the delimiters. Some organizations require programmers to start every source-code file with a multiline comment, including the program’s purpose, the programmer’s name, and the date and time the programmer last modified the program.

##### Javadoc Comments

A third comment type, called a **Javadoc comment**, is delimited by **`/**`** and **`*/`**. The compiler ignores all text between the delimiters. Javadoc comments enable you to embed program documentation directly in your programs and are preferred in industry. The **`javadoc`** **utility program**^([1](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_1a),[2](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_2a)) (part of the JDK) reads Javadoc comments and uses them to prepare program documentation that’s viewed in a web browser. We use `//` comments throughout our code to save space.

[1](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_1). “How to Write Doc Comments for the Javadoc Tool.” Accessed May 17, 2024\. [`https://oracle.com/technical-resources/articles/java/javadoc-tool.html`](https://oracle.com/technical-resources/articles/java/javadoc-tool.html).

[2](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_2). “The `javadoc` Command.” Accessed September 21, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/javadoc.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/javadoc.html).

##### Syntax Errors

Forgetting a comment delimiter is a **syntax error**—such errors occur when the compiler encounters code that violates Java’s language rules (that is, its syntax). These rules are similar to natural-language grammar rules specifying sentence structure, such as those in English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, etc. Syntax errors are also called **compilation errors** because they’re detected by the compiler. A program must compile without errors before you can execute it to perform its job.

##### Using Blank Lines

Blank lines (like line 3), space characters and tabs—known as **whitespace**—can make programs easier to read. The compiler ignores whitespace.

##### Declaring a Class

Line 4 begins class `Welcome1`’s **class declaration**. Every program consists of at least one class that you declare. The **`class`** **keyword** introduces a class declaration and is immediately followed by the **class name** (`Welcome1`). **Keywords** are reserved for use by Java. Each is spelled with all lowercase letters. Most classes we declare begin with the **`public`** **keyword**. You’ll learn more about `public` and non-`public` classes in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08). The following table shows the complete keywords list:

| Keywords |
| --- |
| `abstract` | `assert` | `boolean` | `break` | `byte` |
| `case` | `catch` | `char` | `class` | `continue` |
| `default` | `do` | `double` | `else` | `enum` |
| `extends` | `final` | `finally` | `float` | `for` |
| `if` | `implements` | `import` | `instanceof` | `int` |
| `interface` | `long` | `native` | `new` | `package` |
| `private` | `protected` | `public` | `return` | `short` |
| `static` | `strictfp` | `super` | `switch` | `synchronized` |
| `this` | `throw` | `throws` | `transient` | `try` |
| `void` | `volatile` | `while` | `_ (underscore)` |  |
| **Contextual keywords (reserved for use in certain program contexts)** |
| `exports` | `module` | `non-sealed` | `open` | `opens` |
| `permits` | `provides` | `record` | `requires` | `sealed` |
| `to` | `transitive` | `uses` | `var` | `when` |
| `with` | `yield` |  |  |  |
| **Reserved keywords not currently used by the language** |
| `const` | `goto` |  |  |  |

##### Filename for a `public` Class

A `public` class must be placed in a file with a filename of the form *ClassName*`.java`, so `Welcome1` is stored in the file `Welcome1.java`. A compilation error occurs if a `public` class’s filename differs from the class name (in spelling or capitalization) followed by `.java`.

##### Class Names and Identifiers

By convention, every word in a class-name identifier begins with an uppercase letter. For example, the name `DollarAmount` starts its first word (`Dollar`) with an uppercase `D` and its second word (`Amount`) with an uppercase `A`. This naming convention is known as **camel case** because the uppercase letters stand out like a camel’s humps.

A class name is an **identifier**—a series of characters consisting of letters, digits, underscores (`_`) and dollar signs (`$`) that does not begin with a digit and does not contain spaces. Some valid identifiers are `Welcome1`, `$value`, `_value`, `m_inputField1` and `button7`. The name `7button` is invalid because it begins with a digit, and the name `input field` is invalid because it contains a space. Java is **case sensitive**—uppercase and lowercase letters are distinct—so `value` and `Value` are different valid identifiers.

##### Class Body

A **left brace** (**`{`** at the end of line 4) begins the **class declaration body**. A corresponding **right brace** (**`}`** at line 9) must end each class declaration.

Lines 5–8 are indented. You should indent the entire body of each class declaration one “level” between the braces. This convention emphasizes the class’s structure and makes it easier to read. We use three spaces to form an indent level—many programmers prefer two or four spaces. Whatever you choose, use it consistently. IDEs typically indent code for you, using four-space indents by default. The *Tab* key may also be used to indent code. You can configure each IDE to specify the number of spaces inserted when you press *Tab*.

It’s a syntax error if braces do not occur in matching pairs. To prevent this error, when you enter an opening left brace (`{`), immediately enter the closing right brace (`}`). Then, put the cursor between the braces and indent to begin entering the body. In most IDEs, when you enter the opening left brace (`{`), the IDE adds the closing brace, moves the cursor between the braces and indents for you.

##### Declaring a Method

Line 6 is the starting point of every program. The **parentheses** after the identifier `main` indicate that it’s a program building block called a method. Class declarations normally contain one or more methods. One method must be called `main` and must be defined as in line 6; otherwise, the program will not execute.^([3](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_3a))

[3](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_3). At the time of this writing, a preview feature called “instance `main`” simplifies line 6 to `void main() {`.

Methods perform tasks and can return information when they complete their tasks. We’ll explain the purpose of keyword `static` in [Section 8.2.5](#ch08.xhtml_ch08lev2sec8). The **`void`** **keyword** indicates that this method will not return any information. Later, we’ll see methods that return information. For now, mimic `main`’s first line in your programs. [Chapter 6](#ch06.xhtml_ch06) discusses the `String[] args` in parentheses.

The method’s left brace (end of line 6) begins the **method body**. A corresponding right brace (line 8) ends it. You should indent each method’s body one “level” between the braces, as in line 7\. This emphasizes the method’s structure and makes it easier to read.

##### Performing Output with `System.out.println`

Line 7 displays the characters between the double quotation (`"`) marks. The quotation marks are not displayed. Together, the quotation marks and the characters between them are called a **string**, a **character string** or a **string literal**. The compiler does not ignore whitespace characters in strings. Strings in double quotation (`"`) marks may not span multiple lines of code.^([4](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_4a))

[4](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_4). Later, we’ll discuss text blocks for forming multiline strings.

**`System.out`** is the **standard output object**, which is predefined for you. It allows programs to display text in the **command window** where you execute the program:

*   a Command Prompt or Windows PowerShell on Microsoft Windows, or

*   a **terminal** or a **shell** in Linux/macOS.

Many programmers call the command window simply the **command line**.

The **`System.out.println`** **method** displays a line of text. The string in the parentheses in line 7 is the method’s **argument**. When `System.out.println` completes its task, it moves the output cursor (the location where the next character will display) to the beginning of the next line. This is similar to pressing the *Enter* key while entering text in an editor—the cursor moves to the beginning of the next line in the document.

The entire line 7, including the **semicolon** (**`;`**), is called a **statement**. A method typically contains statements that perform its task. Most statements end with a semicolon.

##### Using End-of-Line Comments on Right Braces for Readability

For now, we include an end-of-line comment after a closing brace that ends a method declaration and after a closing brace that ends a class declaration. For example, line 8 indicates the closing brace of the `main` method, and line 9 indicates the closing brace of the `Welcome1` class. We’ll omit such ending comments after this chapter.

#### 2.2.1 Compiling the Program

You can now compile and execute the program. Here, we’ll use the Java Development Kit’s command-line tools. We assume the book’s examples are in your user account’s `Documents` folder in a subfolder named `examples` as discussed in the Before You Begin section.

##### Change to the Correct Folder

First, open a command window (see [Section 1.7](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev1sec7)) and change to the folder where the program is stored. Operating systems typically use the command `cd` to change folders. On Windows, change to the `fig02_01` folder by entering the following command and pressing the *Enter* (or *Return*) key:

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0052-01)

```
cd %userprofile%\Documents\examples\ch02\fig02_01
```

On Linux/macOS, use the following command instead:

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0053-01)

```
cd ~/Documents/examples/ch02/fig02_01
```

##### Compile the `.java` File

To compile the program, enter the following command and press *Enter*:

```
javac Welcome1.java
```

If the program does not contain compilation errors, this command creates `Welcome1`’s **class file** (`Welcome1.class`) containing the platform-independent bytecodes representing the program. When we use the `java` command to execute the program on a given platform, the JVM will translate these bytecodes into instructions understood by the underlying operating system and hardware.

##### Error Messages

When compiling, if you receive the error message “`class Welcome1 is public, should be declared in a file named Welcome1.java`,” either

*   your filename does not match the file’s `public` class name or

*   you misspelled the class name in the compilation command.

Sometimes, it’s helpful to “break” a working program to become familiar with the compiler’s error messages. Though error messages generally give you an idea of what caused them, they do not always state the exact problems in the code. Try removing a semicolon or brace from the program of [Fig. 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01), then recompiling to produce the error messages generated by the omission.

If the compiler reports a syntax error, it may not be on the line that the error message indicates. First, check the line reported in the error message. If you don’t find an error on that line, check several preceding lines. Each compilation error message contains the filename and line number where the error occurred. For example, `Welcome1.java:6` would indicate that an error occurred at line 6 in `Welcome1.java`. The rest of the message would provide information about the error.

Execute the `Welcome1` program by entering the following command and pressing *Enter*:

```

```

Notice that you do not include the`.class` filename extension when running the program. The JVM launches and loads the `Welcome1.class` file, then calls `Welcome1`’s `main` method. Next, line 7 in `main` displays

### 2.3 Modifying Your First Program

In this section, we modify [Fig. 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01)’s example to print text on one line using multiple statements and to print text on several lines using one statement.

##### Displaying a Single Line of Text with Multiple Statements

Class `Welcome2` ([Fig. 2.2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig02)) uses two statements (lines 7–8) to produce the output in [Fig. 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01).

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0054-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.2: Welcome2.java
 2   // Printing a line of text with multiple statements.
 3
 4   public class Welcome2 {
 5      // main method begins program execution
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.print("Welcome to ");
 8         System.out.println("Java Programming!");
 9      } // end method main
10   } // end class Welcome2
```

```
Welcome to Java Programming!
```

**Fig. 2.2** | Printing a line of text with multiple statements.

The program is similar to [Fig. 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01), so we discuss only the changes here. Line 2 is an end-of-line comment stating the purpose of the program. Line 4 begins the `Welcome2` class declaration. Lines 7–8 in the `main` method display one line of text. The first statement uses the **`System.out.print`** method to display a string. Each `print` or `println` statement resumes displaying characters from where the last statement stopped. Unlike `println`, after displaying its argument, `print` does not position the output cursor at the beginning of the next line—the next character the program displays will appear immediately after the last character that `print` displays. So, line 8 positions the first character in its argument (the letter “`J`”) immediately after the last character that line 7 displays (the space character before the string’s closing double-quote character).

##### Displaying Multiple Lines of Text with a Single Statement

A single statement can display multiple lines using **newline characters** (**`\n`**), which position the output cursor at the beginning of the next line. The program in [Fig. 2.3](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig03) outputs four lines of text. Most of the program is identical to those in [Figs. 2.1](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig01) and [2.2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig02).

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0054-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.3: Welcome3.java
 2   // Printing multiple lines of text with a single statement.
 3
 4   public class Welcome3 {
 5      // main method begins program execution
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.println("Welcome\nto\nJava\nProgramming!");
 8      } // end method main
 9   } // end class Welcome3
```

```
Welcome
to
Java
Programming!
```

**Fig. 2.3** | Printing multiple lines of text with a single statement.

Line 7 displays four lines of text. Normally, each character in a string displays as it appears in the double quotes. However, the paired characters `\` and `n` (repeated three times in the statement) do not appear on the screen. The **backslash** (**`\`**) is an **escape character**, which has special meaning to `System.out`’s `print` and `println` methods. When a backslash appears in a string, it’s combined with the next character to form an **escape sequence**—the `\n` escape sequence represents the newline character. When `\n` is encountered in a string being output, the output cursor moves to the beginning of the next line.

The following table describes several escape sequences—for the complete list, refer to the Java Language Specification, Section 3.10.7, Escape Sequences:^([5](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_5a))

[5](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_5). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. Section 3.10.7, “Escape Sequences.” Accessed May 30, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.10.7`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.10.7).

| Escape sequence | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `\n` | Newline. Position the screen cursor at the beginning of the next line. |
| `\t` | Horizontal tab. Move the screen cursor to the next tab stop. |
| `\\` | Backslash. Print a backslash character. |
| `\"` | Double quote. Print a double-quote character. For example,[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0055-02v) 
```
System.out.println("\"in quotes\"");
```

displays `"in quotes"`. |

### 2.4 Displaying Text with `printf`

The **`System.out.printf`** **method** displays formatted data—the “`f`” in `printf` means “formatted.” [Figure 2.4](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig04) uses `printf` to output `"Welcome to"` and `"Java Programming!"` on separate lines.

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0056-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.4: Welcome4.java
 2   // Displaying multiple lines with method System.out.printf.
 3
 4   public class Welcome4 {
 5      // main method begins program execution
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.printf("%s%n%s%n", "Welcome to", "Java Programming!");
 8      } // end method main
 9   } // end class Welcome4
```

```
Welcome to
Java Programming!
```

**Fig. 2.4** | Displaying multiple lines with method `System.out.printf`.

Line 7 calls `System.out.printf` to display the program’s output. The method call specifies three arguments. When a method requires two or more arguments, you place them in a **comma-separated list** with a space after each comma (*`,`*) for readability.

Method `printf`’s first argument is a **format string** that may consist of **fixed text** and **format specifiers**. Fixed text is output by `printf` just as it would be by `print` or `println`. Each format specifier is a placeholder for a value and specifies the type of data to output.

Format specifiers begin with a percent sign (`%`) followed by a character representing the data type. The **`%s`** **format specifier** is a placeholder for a string. The format string in line 7 specifies that `printf` should output two strings, each followed by a newline character. This example substitutes `"Welcome to"` for the first `%s` and `"Java Programming!"` for the second `%s`. The output shows that two lines of text are displayed.

Notice that instead of the newline escape sequence `\n`, which we’ve been using with `System.out.print` and `System.out.println`, we used the **`%n`** **format specifier**, which may appear only in format strings. In later chapters, we’ll present additional details of formatting output with `printf`, and [Appendix B](#appb.xhtml_appb) covers print formatting in more depth.

### 2.5 Another Program: Adding Integers

The program in [Fig. 2.5](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig05) reads (or inputs) two **integers** (whole numbers, such as –22, 7, 0 and 1024) entered by a user, stores them in variables, computes their sum and displays it. In our program outputs, we use bold text to identify user inputs (**`45`** and **`72`** in this example).

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0057-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.5: Addition.java
 2   // Addition program that inputs two numbers then displays their sum.
 3   import java.util.Scanner; // program uses class Scanner
 4
 5   public class Addition {
 6      // main method begins program execution
 7      public static void main(String[] args) {
 8         // create a Scanner to obtain input from the user
 9         Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
10
11         System.out.print("Enter first integer: "); // prompt
12         int number1 = input.nextInt(); // read first number from user
13
14         System.out.print("Enter second integer: "); // prompt
15         int number2 = input.nextInt(); // read second number from user
16
17         int sum = number1 + number2; // add numbers, then store total in sum
18
19         System.out.printf("Sum is %d%n", sum); // display sum
20      } // end method main
21   } // end class Addition
```

```
Enter first integer: 45
Enter second integer: 72
Sum is 117
```

**Fig. 2.5** | Addition program that inputs two numbers then displays their sum.

##### `import` Declarations

A great strength of Java is its rich set of predefined classes that you can reuse rather than “reinventing the wheel.” These classes are grouped into **packages**—named groups of related classes—collectively called the Java Application Programming Interface (Java API).

Line 3 is an **`import`** **declaration** that helps the compiler locate a class used in this program. It indicates that the program uses the predefined `Scanner` class (discussed shortly) from the **`java.util`** **package**. The compiler then ensures that you use the class correctly.

All `import` declarations must appear before you declare a class in the file. Placing an `import` declaration inside or after a class declaration is a syntax error. Forgetting to include an `import` declaration for a class that must be `import`ed results in a compilation error containing a message such as “`cannot find symbol.`” When this occurs, check that you provided the proper `import` declarations and that the names in them are correct, including proper capitalization.

##### Declaring and Creating a `Scanner` to Obtain User Input

You must declare each variable with a name and a type before using it. A **variable’s name** enables the program to access the variable’s value in memory. By convention, variable-name identifiers use the camel-case naming convention with a lowercase first letter—for example, `firstNumber`. A variable name can be any valid identifier—again, a series of characters consisting of letters, digits, underscores (`_`) and dollar signs (`$`) that does not begin with a digit and does not contain spaces. A **variable’s type** specifies what kind of information is stored at that location in memory. Like other statements, declaration statements end with a semicolon (`;`).

Line 9 of `main` is a **variable declaration statement** that specifies the name (`input`) and type (`Scanner`) of a variable used in this program. A **`Scanner`** (package `java.util`) enables a program to read data (such as, numbers and strings) for use in a program. The data can come from many sources, such as the user or a file on disk. Before using a `Scanner`, you must create it and specify the source of the data.

The `=` in line 9’s declaration indicates that `Scanner` variable `input` should be initialized to prepare it for use in the program. The initial value is the result of the expression to the right of the equals sign—`new Scanner(System.in)`. This expression uses the **`new`** **keyword** to create a `Scanner` object that reads characters entered by the user. The **`System.in`** **standard input object** enables programs to read bytes entered by the user. The `Scanner` translates these bytes into types (like `int`) the program can use.

##### Prompting the User for Input

Line 11 uses `System.out.print` to display `"Enter first integer: "`. This **prompt message** directs the user to take a specific action. We use `print` here rather than `println` so that the user’s input appears on the same line as the prompt—the space after the prompt’s colon (`:`) makes the program’s output more readable. Recall from [Section 2.2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec2) that identifiers starting with capital letters typically represent class names. The `System` class is part of the **`java.lang`** **package**, which Java automatically imports into every program. The `java.lang` classes are the only Java API classes that do not require an `import` declaration.

##### Declaring a Variable to Store an Integer and Obtaining One from the User

The variable declaration statement in line 12 declares that `number1` holds data of **type** **`int`**—that is, integer (whole number) values, such as `72`, `–1127` and `0`. The value range for an `int` is –2,147,483,648 to +2,147,483,647\. A program’s `int` values may not contain commas because Java uses them to separate items in lists, such as the arguments to method `System.out.printf` in line 19 of this program. For readability, you can group digits with underscores as a **digit separator**—so `60_000_000` represents the value 60,000,000.

**Types** **`float`** and **`double`** hold real numbers, and **type** **`char`** holds character data. Real numbers contain decimal points, such as `3.4`, `0.0` and `–11.19`. Variables of type `char` represent individual characters, such as

*   a letter (e.g., `A` or `z`),

*   a digit (`0`–`9`),

*   a special character (e.g., `*` or `%`) or

*   an escape sequence (e.g., `\t` for a tab or `\n` for a newline).

The types `int`, `float`, `double` and `char` are **primitive types**. Their names are keywords and must appear in all lowercase letters. The other primitive types are `boolean`, `byte`, `short` and `long`. For a summary of the numeric primitive types’ value ranges, visit the Java Language Specification [Section 4.2](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec2), “Primitive Types and Values.”^([6](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_6a))

[6](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_6). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. [Section 4.2](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec2), “Primitive Types and Values” Accessed May 30, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2).

The `=` in line 12 indicates that `int` variable `number1` should be initialized in its declaration with the result of `input.nextInt()`. This uses the `Scanner` object `input`’s `nextInt` method to obtain an integer from the user. At this point, the program waits for the user to enter a number and press the *Enter* key to submit it to the program.

Our program assumes that the user enters a valid integer value. If not, a logic error will occur, and the program will terminate. [Chapter 10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10), [Exception Handling: A Deeper Look](#ch10.xhtml_ch10), discusses how to make your programs more robust by enabling them to handle such errors. This helps make your program fault-tolerant.

##### Obtaining a Second Integer

Line 14 prompts the user to enter the second integer. Line 15 declares the `int` variable `number2` and initializes it with a second integer read from the user.

##### Using Variables in a Calculation

Line 17 declares the `int` variable `sum` and initializes it with the result of the calculation `number1 + number2`. The `+` operator is a **binary operator** because it has two **operands**—`number1` and `number2`. Portions of statements that contain calculations are called **expressions**. In fact, an expression is any portion of a statement that has a value. The value of the expression `number1 + number2` is their sum. Similarly, the value of the expression `input.nextInt()` (lines 12 and 15) is the integer entered by the user. Place spaces on either side of a binary operator for readability.

##### Displaying the Calculation Result

After the calculation has been performed, line 19 uses method `System.out.printf` to display `sum`’s value. The **`%d`** **format specifier** is a placeholder for an `int` value (`sum`)—the letter `d` stands for “decimal (base 10) integer.” The remaining characters in the format string are all fixed text. So, method `printf` displays `"Sum is "`, followed by `sum`’s value—which replaces `%d`—and a newline.

We could have combined lines 17 and 19 into the single statement

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0059-01)

```
System.out.printf("Sum is %d%n", (number1 + number2));
```

The parentheses around the expression `number1 + number2` are redundant—they’re included to emphasize that the value of the entire expression is output in the position of the `%d` format specifier.

##### Declaring and Initializing Variables in Separate Statements

Each variable must have a value before you use it in a calculation (or other expression). The variable declaration statement in line 12 declares `number1` and initializes it with a value the user enters. Sometimes, you declare a variable in one statement then give it a value in another. For example, line 12 could have been written in two statements as

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0060-03)

```
int number1; // declare the int variable number1
number1 = input.nextInt(); // assign the user's input to number1
```

The first statement declares `number1` but does not initialize it. The second statement uses the **assignment operator** (**`=`**) to assign `number1` the integer entered by the user. You can read this statement as “`number1` gets the value of `input.nextInt()`.” Everything to the right of the `=` is evaluated before the assignment stores the result.

### 2.6 Arithmetic

Many programs perform arithmetic calculations using the **arithmetic operators** summarized in the following table:

| Operation | Operator | Algebraic expression | Java expression |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Addition | `+` | *f* + 7 | `f + 7` |
| Subtraction | `–` | *p* – *c* | `p - c` |
| Multiplication | `*` | *bm* | `b * m` |
| Division | `/` | *x* / *y* or $\frac{x}{y}$ or *x* ÷ *y* | `x / y` |
| Remainder | `%` | *r* mod *s* | `r % s` |

Note the use of various special symbols not used in algebra. The **asterisk** (*) indicates multiplication, and the **percent sign** (**%**) is the **remainder operator**, which we’ll discuss shortly. The arithmetic operators in the table are binary operators—each operates on two operands—e.g., the expression `f + 7` contains the binary operator `+` and the two operands `f` and `7`.

##### Integer Division

**Integer division** yields an integer quotient. For example, the expression `7 / 4` evaluates to `1`, and the expression `17 / 5` evaluates to `3`. Any fractional part in integer division is truncated (that is, discarded)—no rounding occurs.

##### Remainder Operator (`%`)

The remainder operator, `%`, yields the remainder after division—`x % y` yields the remainder after dividing `x` by `y`. Thus, `7 % 4` yields `3`, and `17 % 5` yields `2`. This operator is most commonly used with integer operands but also can be used with other arithmetic types. Popular uses of this operator are to determine whether an integer is even or odd, or whether one number is a multiple of another.

##### Arithmetic Expressions in Straight-Line Form

Arithmetic expressions must be written in **straight-line form** to facilitate entering programs into computers. Thus, expressions such as “`a` divided by `b`” must be written as `a/b` so all constants, variables and operators appear in a straight line. The following algebraic notation is generally not acceptable to compilers:

$\frac{a}{b}$

##### Parentheses for Grouping Subexpressions

Parentheses group terms in Java expressions in the same manner as in algebraic expressions. For example, to multiply `a` times the quantity `b + c`, we write

```
a * (b + c)
```

If an expression contains **nested parentheses**, such as

```
(a * (b + c))
```

the expression in the innermost set of parentheses—`b + c` in this case—evaluates first.

##### Rules of Operator Precedence

Java applies the arithmetic operators in a precise sequence determined by the **rules of operator precedence**, which are generally the same as those followed in algebra:

1.  Multiplication, division and remainder operations are applied first. If an expression contains several such operations, they’re applied from left to right. Multiplication, division and remainder operators have the same level of precedence.

2.  Addition and subtraction operations are applied next. If an expression contains several such operations, the operators are applied from left to right. Addition and subtraction operators have the same level of precedence.

3.  The assignment operator is applied last.

These rules enable Java to apply operators in the correct order.^([7](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_7a)) When we say operators are applied from left to right, we’re referring to their **grouping**. Some group from right to left. The following table summarizes these rules of operator precedence:

[7](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_7). We use simple examples to explain the order of evaluation. Subtle order-of-evaluation issues can occur in more complex expressions. For more information, refer to [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15) of The Java™ Language Specification ([`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html)).

| Operator(s) | Operation(s) | Order of evaluation (precedence) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `*``/``%` | MultiplicationDivisionRemainder | Evaluated first. If there are several operators of this type, they’re evaluated from left to right. |
| `+``-` | AdditionSubtraction | Evaluated next. If there are several operators of this type, they’re evaluated from left to right. |
| `=` | Assignment | Evaluated last. |

You can view the complete operator precedence chart for Java’s operators at

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0062-02)

```
https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/nutsandbolts/
   operators.html
```

### 2.7 Decision Making: Equality and Relational Operators

A condition is an expression that can be **`true`** or **`false`**. The **`if`** **statement** makes a decision based on a condition’s value. You form conditions in `if` statements using the **equality operators** (**`==`** and **`!=`**) and **relational operators** (**`>`**, **`<`**, **`>=`** and **`<=`**) summarized below:

| Algebraic operator | Java equality or relational operator | Sample Java condition | Meaning of condition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Equality operators* |  |
| = | `==` | `x == y` | `x` is equal to `y` |
| ≠ | `!=` | `x != y` | `x` is not equal to `y` |
| *Relational operators* |  |
| > | `>` | `x > y` | `x` is greater than `y` |
| < | `<` | `x < y` | `x` is less than `y` |
| ≥ | `>=` | `x >= y` | `x` is greater than or equal to `y` |
| ≤ | `<=` | `x <= y` | `x` is less than or equal to `y` |

Both equality operators have the same precedence level, which is lower than that of the relational operators. The equality operators group from left to right. The relational operators all have the same precedence level and also group from left to right.

##### Using the `if` Statement

[Figure 2.6](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig06) uses six `if` statements to compare two integers input by the user. If the condition in any of these is `true`, the corresponding body statement executes; otherwise, it is skipped. We use a `Scanner` to input the integers from the user and store them in variables `number1` and `number2`. The program compares the numbers with all six relational and equality operators and displays the results of the comparisons that are `true`. We show three sample outputs for different pairs of values entered by the user.
