Line 10 in class `Comparison`’s `main` method sets up a `Scanner` for reading data from the user. Lines 12–13 prompt the user to enter the first integer, then input the value and store it in the `int` variable `number1`. Lines 15–16 prompt the user to enter the second integer, then input the value and store it in the `int` variable `number2`. Lines 18–20 compare the `number1` and `number2` values to determine whether they’re equal. If so, line 19 displays the numbers separated by ==. The `if` statements starting in lines 22, 26, 30, 34 and 38 compare `number1` and `number2` using the operators `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. For those `if` statements in which the conditions are `true`, the corresponding body statement displays an appropriate line of text showing the condition that evaluated to `true`.

##### Blocks

Each `if` statement in [Fig. 2.6](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig06) contains one body statement that’s indented to enhance readability. IDEs typically do this indentation for you. Also, notice that we’ve enclosed each body statement in a pair of braces, `{ }`, creating a **block**.

You don’t need to use braces around single-statement bodies, but you must include the braces around multiple-statement bodies. You’ll see later that forgetting to enclose multiple-statement bodies in braces leads to errors. To avoid such errors, always enclose an `if` statement’s body statement(s) in braces.

Placing a semicolon immediately after the right parenthesis after the condition in an `if` statement is often a logic error (although not a syntax error). The semicolon (`;`) acts as an **empty statement** (i.e., a statement that does nothing). In this case, the `if` statement performs no action, regardless of whether the condition is `true`. Worse yet, the indented statement that appears to be in the `if` statement’s body always executes—a logic error that typically causes the program to produce incorrect results.

##### Whitespace

Note the use of whitespace in [Fig. 2.6](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig06). The compiler ignores most whitespace, so statements may be split over several lines and spaced according to your preferences without affecting a program’s meaning. Identifiers and strings may not be split. Ideally, statements should be kept small, but this is not always possible.

If you spread a statement over several lines, choose natural breaking points, such as after a comma in a comma-separated list or after an operator in a lengthy expression. When a statement is split across two or more lines, indent all lines after the first by the same amount until the end of the statement.

### 2.8 Objects-Natural Case Study: Creating and Using Objects of the Java API’s `String` Class

Throughout this book, we emphasize using valuable preexisting classes from the Java API and various libraries from the Java open-source community. You’ll focus on knowing what libraries are out there, choosing the ones you’ll need for your applications, creating objects from existing library classes and making those objects exercise their capabilities. By “objects natural,” we mean that you’ll be able to conveniently create and program with powerful objects even before you learn to create your own custom classes in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08).

You’ve already worked with Java objects. You used the `System.out` object to display a program’s output, and you used `Scanner` objects with the `System.in` object to obtain inputs from the user. These encapsulate the mechanisms for output and input. The `System.out` and `System.in` objects are created for you by the `System` class, and you created the `Scanner` objects with the `new` operator. In this section, you’ll create and interact with objects of the Java API’s **`String`** **class**.^([8](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_8a))

[8](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_8). You’ll learn additional `String` capabilities in subsequent chapters. [Chapter 7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07) discusses class `String` in detail, test-driving many more of its methods.

##### Test-Driving Class `String`

Classes cannot execute by themselves. A `Person` object can drive a `Car` object by telling it what to do (go faster, go slower, turn left, turn right, etc.) without knowing how the car’s internal mechanisms work. Similarly, the `main` method can “drive” `String` objects by calling their methods—without knowing how the class is implemented. In this sense, `main` in the following program is referred to as a **driver program**. [Figure 2.7](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig07)’s `main` method test-drives several `String` objects.

[Click here to view code image](#ch02_images.xhtml_f0066-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 2.7: StringTest.java
 2   // String class test program.
 3   public class StringTest {
 4      public static void main(String[] args) {
 5         String s1 = "happy";
 6         String s2 = " birthday";
 7         String s3 = ""; // creates an empty string
 8
 9         // display the Strings and show their lengths
10         System.out.printf("s1: \"%s\"; length: %d%n", s1, s1.length());
11         System.out.printf("s2: \"%s\"; length: %d%n", s2, s2.length());
12         System.out.printf("s3: \"%s\"; length: %d%n%n", s3, s3.length());
13
14         // compare Strings
15         System.out.println("Results of comparing Strings:");
16         System.out.printf("s1.equals(\"happy\"): %b%n", s1.equals("happy"));
17         System.out.printf("s2.equals(s1): %b%n%n", s2.equals(s1));
18
19         // test String method isEmpty
20         System.out.println("Testing s3.isEmpty():");
21
22         if (s3.isEmpty()) {
23            System.out.println("s3 is empty; assigning to s3");
24            s3 = s1 + s2; // assign s3 the result of concatenating s1 and s2
25            System.out.printf("s3: \"%s\"; length: %d%n%n", s3, s3.length());
26         }
27
28         // testing whether Strings start with "ha" or end with "ay"
29         System.out.printf("s1.startsWith(\"ha\"): %b%n",
30            s1.startsWith("ha"));
31         System.out.printf("s2.startsWith(\"ha\"): %b%n",
32            s2.startsWith("ha"));
33         System.out.printf("s1.endsWith(\"ay\"): %b%n", s1.endsWith("ay"));
34         System.out.printf("s2.endsWith(\"ay\"): %b%n", s2.endsWith("ay"));
35      } // end method main
36   } // end class StringTest
```

```
s1: "happy"; length: 5
s2: " birthday"; length: 9
s3: ""; length: 0

Results of comparing Strings:
s1.equals("happy"): true
s2.equals(s1): false

Testing s3.isEmpty():
s3 is empty; assigning to s3
s3: "happy birthday"; length: 14

s1.startsWith("ha"): true
s2.startsWith("ha"): false
s1.endsWith("ay"): false
s2.endsWith("ay"): true
```

**Fig. 2.7** | `String` class test program.

##### Creating `String` Objects

For each string literal, the Java compiler creates an object of the Java API’s `String` class and initializes it with the literal’s characters.^([9](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_9a)) So, lines 5–7 create three `String` objects: `s1` contains `"happy"`, `s2` contains `" birthday"`, and `s3` contains the **empty string (****`""`****)**. When we declare `int` variables, as we did earlier, the compiler knows what `int` is—it’s a primitive type built into Java. Similarly, the compiler understands aspects of the Java API’s `String` class, such as how to create a `String` object from a string literal.

[9](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_9). For most classes, you must create objects of the class using `new`, as you did with class `Scanner` in [Figs. 2.5](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig05) and [2.6](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig06).

Like the `System` class, the `String` class is part of the `java.lang` package, so it’s imported into every program. When packaged properly, classes can be reused by other programmers. This is one of the most significant benefits of working with languages like Java that support object-oriented programming. Such languages have rich libraries of powerful prebuilt classes. For example, you can reuse the Java API’s classes in any program simply by importing them, as we did with the `Scanner` class in [Figs. 2.5](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig05) and [2.6](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig06).

##### `String` Method `length`

Lines 10–12 output each `String` and its length. The `String` class’s **`length`** **method** returns the number of characters stored in a particular `String` object. To call this method for a specific object, you specify the object’s name (`s1`), followed by the **dot operator** (**`.`**), then the method name (`length`) and a set of parentheses. Empty parentheses indicate that `length` does not require additional arguments to perform its task.

##### Comparing `String` Objects

`String`s can be compared with one another for equality using the `String` class’s **`equals`** **method**, which returns `true` or `false`:^([10](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_10a))

*   Line 16 compares `s1`’s contents to the contents of the string literal `"happy"`—these `String`s contain the same characters, so `equals` returns `true`.

*   Line 17 compares `s2`’s contents to `s1`’s contents—these `String`s do not contain the same characters so `equals` returns `false`.

[10](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_10). Note that operator `==` cannot be used to compare the contents of `String` objects. We’ll explain why in the object-oriented programming chapters.

`String` comparisons are case-sensitive.^([11](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_11a)) The `printf` calls in lines 16 and 17 use the **`%b`** **format specifier**, which is a placeholder for the value of a condition. This format specifier causes `printf` to display a condition’s value as the word `"true"` or the word `"false"`.

[11](#ch02.xhtml_fn2_11). In [Chapter 7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07), you’ll see that `String`s perform “lexicographical” comparisons using the numerical values of the characters in each `String`.

##### `String` Method `isEmpty`

Line 22 calls `String`’s **`isEmpty`** **method**, which returns `true` if the `String` is empty—i.e., its length is `0`. The object `s3` was initialized to the empty string (`""`), so it is indeed empty, and the body of the `if` statement will execute.

##### `String` Concatenation

Line 24 assigns a new value to `s3` produced by “adding” the `String`s `s1` and `s2` using the + operator—known as **`String`** **concatenation**. After the assignment, `s3` contains the characters of `s1` followed by the characters of `s2`—that is, `"happy birthday"`. Line 25 outputs `s3`’s contents and length to demonstrate that the `String` concatenation worked correctly.

##### S`tring` Methods `startsWith` and `endsWith`

Lines 29–34 demonstrate **`String`****’s** **`startsWith`** **method** and **`endsWith`** **method**, which return `true` if the `String` starts with or ends with a specified substring, respectively; otherwise, they return `false`. These `String` comparisons are also case-sensitive. Lines 30 and 32 show that `s1` starts with the substring `"ha"`, but `s2` does not. Lines 33 and 34 show that `s1` does not end with `"ay"` but `s2` does.

### 2.9 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you created basic Java programs. We started with programs that displayed messages on the screen using `System.out`’s `print`, `println` and `printf` methods. The addition program used a `Scanner` object to perform input from the user. We discussed the arithmetic operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, and `%`) and how the operator precedence rules determine the order in which Java evaluates operators in an expression. We briefly mentioned other primitive types. You used the `if` statement to make decisions based on conditions formed with the equality (`==` and `!=`) and relational (`<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`) operators.

Finally, we introduced our objects-natural approach to learning Java by creating objects of the powerful Java API class `String` and interacting with them. Throughout the chapter, you used generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience. In subsequent chapters, you’ll create and use many objects of existing classes to accomplish significant tasks with minimal amounts of code. Then, in [Chapters 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)–[9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), you’ll use Java features that enable you to craft valuable custom classes. In the next chapter, we introduce control statements that specify the order in which a program performs its actions.

## Control Statements: Part 1

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this chapter, you’ll:

*   Use the `if` and `if`…`else` selection statements to choose between alternative actions.

*   Use the `while` iteration statement to execute statements in a program repeatedly.

*   Use counter-controlled iteration, sentinel-controlled iteration and nested control statements.

*   Use the compound assignment operators and the increment and decrement operators.

*   Consider the portability of primitive types.

*   Use generative AI to leverage your Java learning experience.

*   Continue our objects-natural approach with a case study on creating and manipulating integers as large as you want them to be.

Outline

### 3.1 Introduction

In this chapter and the next, we present the theory and principles of structured programming. As you’ll see in later chapters, the concepts presented here will be crucial in building classes and manipulating objects.

We discuss the `if` statement in more detail and introduce the `if`…`else` and `while` statements. We introduce the compound assignment operators and the increment and decrement operators. We also consider the portability of Java’s primitive types. Finally, we continue our objects-natural approach with a case study on creating and manipulating super-sized integers that can represent values beyond the limited integer ranges supported by Java’s integer primitive types.

### 3.2 Control Structures

Statements in a program typically execute one after the other in the order they’re written, as you saw in [Chapter 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02). This process is called **sequential execution**. Various Java statements enable you to specify that the next statement to execute is not necessarily the next one in sequence. This is called **transfer of control**.

During the 1960s, it became clear that the indiscriminate use of transfers of control was the root of much difficulty experienced by software development groups. The blame was pointed at the **`goto`** **statement** (used in most programming languages of the time), which allowed you to specify a transfer of control to one of a wide range of destinations in a program.^([1](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_1a))

[1](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_1). Java does not have a `goto` statement; however, `goto` is reserved by Java and should not be used as an identifier in programs. Using it causes a compilation error.

The research of Bohm and Jacopini^([2](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_2a)) demonstrated that programs could be written without any `goto` statements. The challenge for the era’s programmers was to shift their styles to “`goto`-less programming.” The term **structured programming** became almost synonymous with “`goto` elimination.” Not until the 1970s did most programmers start taking structured programming seriously. The results were impressive. Software development groups reported shorter development times, more frequent on-time delivery of systems and more frequent within-budget completion of software projects. The key to these successes was that structured programs were clearer, easier to debug and modify, and more likely to be bug-free in the first place.

[2](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_2). C. Bohm and G. Jacopini, “Flow Diagrams, Turing Machines, and Languages with Only Two Formation Rules,” *Communications of the ACM*, Vol. 9, No. 5, May 1966, pp. 366–371.

Bohm and Jacopini’s work demonstrated that all programs could be written in terms of only three control structures—the sequence structure, the selection structure and the iteration structure. When we introduce Java’s control-structure implementations, we’ll refer to them in the terminology of the *Java Language Specification* as “control statements.”

#### 3.2.1 Sequence Structure

The **sequence structure** is built into Java. Unless directed otherwise, the computer executes Java statements one after the other in the order they’re written—that is, in sequence. The following **UML activity diagram** illustrates a typical sequence structure in which two calculations are performed in order:

![Images](graphics/f0071-01.jpg)

Java lets you have as many actions as you want in sequence. As we’ll soon see, anywhere a single action may be placed, we may place several actions in sequence.

A UML activity diagram models the **workflow** (also called the **activity**) of a portion of a software system. Such workflows may include a portion of an algorithm, like the sequence structure above. Activity diagrams are composed of symbols, such as **action-state symbols** (rectangles with their left and right sides replaced with outward arcs), **diamonds** and **small circles**. These symbols are connected by **transition arrows**, which represent the flow of the activity—that is, the order in which the actions should occur.

Activity diagrams help you develop and represent algorithms. They clearly show how control structures operate. In [Chapters 3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03) and [4](#ch04.xhtml_ch04), we use the UML to show each control statement’s workflow—also called its **flow of control**.

The preceding activity diagram includes two **action states**, each containing an **action expression** specifying a particular action to perform—“add grade to total” or “add 1 to counter.” Other actions might include calculations or input/output operations. The arrows represent transitions, indicating the order in which the actions described by the action states occur. The program that implements the preceding diagram’s activities first adds `grade` to `total`, then adds `1` to `counter`.

The **solid circle** at the top of the activity diagram represents the **initial state**—the beginning of the workflow before the program performs the modeled actions. The **solid circle surrounded by a hollow circle** at the bottom of the diagram represents the **final state**—the end of the workflow after the program performs the modeled actions.

The diagram also includes rectangles with the upper-right corners folded over. These optional **UML notes** (like comments in Java) are explanatory remarks describing the purpose of the diagram’s symbols. Our notes show the Java code associated with each action state. A **dotted line** connects each note with the element it describes. Activity diagrams usually do not show the corresponding Java code. We show it here to illustrate how the diagram relates to Java code. For more information on the UML, visit [`https://uml.org`](https://uml.org).

#### 3.2.2 Selection Statements

Java has three types of **selection statements** (discussed in this chapter and [Chapter 4](#ch04.xhtml_ch04)). The `if` statement ([Section 3.3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec3)) either performs (selects) an action if a condition is `true` or skips it if the condition is `false`. The `if`…`else` statement ([Section 3.4](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec4)) performs an action if a condition is `true` and performs a different action if the condition is `false`. The `switch` statement ([Section 4.8](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec8)) performs one of several actions depending on the value of an expression.

The `if` statement is called a **single-selection statement** because it selects or ignores a single action (or, as we’ll soon see, a single group of actions). The `if`…`else` statement is called a **double-selection statement** because it selects between two different actions (or groups of actions). The `switch` statement is called a **multiple-selection statement** because it selects among many different actions (or groups of actions).

#### 3.2.3 Iteration Statements

Java provides four **iteration statements**—also called **repetition** or **looping statements**—for performing statements repeatedly while a **loop-continuation condition** is `true`. The iteration statements are `while` ([Section 3.5](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec5)), `for` ([Section 4.3](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec3)), `do`…`while` ([Section 4.7](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec7)), and enhanced `for` ([Section 6.13](#ch06.xhtml_ch06lev1sec13)). The `while` and `for` statements perform the action (or group of actions) in their bodies zero or more times—if the loop-continuation condition is initially `false`, the action (or group of actions) will not execute. The `do`…`while` statement performs the action (or group of actions) in its body one or more times.

##### Keywords

The words `if`, `else`, `switch`, `while`, `do` and `for` are Java keywords. We showed the complete list of Java keywords in [Section 2.2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec2). You can also find them in the *Java Language Specification*, [Section 3.9](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec9), “Keywords.”^([3](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_3a))

[3](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_3). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. [Section 3.9](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec9), “Keywords.” Accessed May 21, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.9`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-3.html#jls-3.9).

#### 3.2.4 Summary of Control Statements

Java has only three kinds of control structures, which we refer to as control statements from this point forward:

*   the sequence statement,

*   selection statements (three types) and

*   iteration statements (four types).

We can model each control statement as an activity diagram containing initial and final states representing a control statement’s entry and exit points. **Single-entry/single-exit control statements** make it easy to build programs by connecting the exit point of one to the entry point of the next—that is, **control-statement stacking**. The only one other way in which control statements may be connected is **control-statement nesting** in which one control statement appears inside another.

### 3.3 `if` Single-Selection Statement

We briefly introduced `if` single-selection statement in [Section 2.7](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec7). Programs use selection statements to choose among alternative courses of action. For example, suppose a passing grade on an exam is 60\. The following `if` statement determines whether the condition `grade >= 60` is `true`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0073-01)

```
if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}
```

If so, the statement prints `"Passed"`; otherwise, the condition is `false`, and the output statement is ignored and the next statement in sequence (if any) executes. Indenting the second line is optional but recommended for clarity.

##### `boolean` Primitive Type

In [Section 2.7](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec7), you created conditions using the relational and equality operators. A Java condition must evaluate to **`true`** or **`false`**—each is a Java keyword. Java provides the **`boolean`** **primitive type** for variables that can store only `true` or `false` values.

##### UML Activity Diagram for an `if` Statement

The following diagram illustrates the single-selection `if` statement’s flow of control:

![Images](graphics/f0073-02.jpg)

This figure contains an activity diagram’s most important symbol—the diamond, or **decision symbol**, which indicates a decision is to be made. The workflow continues along a path determined by the symbol’s associated **guard conditions**, which can be true or false. Each transition arrow emerging from a decision symbol has a guard condition specified in square brackets next to the arrow. If a guard condition is true, the workflow enters the action state to which the transition arrow points. In this diagram, if the grade is greater than or equal to 60, the program prints “Passed,” then transitions to the activity’s final state. If the grade is less than 60, the program transitions to the final state without printing a message. The `if` statement is a single-entry/single-exit control statement.

### 3.4 `if…else` Double-Selection Statement

The `if` single-selection statement performs an indicated action only when the condition is `true`. The **`if`****…****`else`** **double-selection statement** allows you to specify an action to perform when the condition is `true` and another action when the condition is `false`. For example, the following `if`…`else` statement prints `"Passed"` if the student’s grade is greater than or equal to 60; otherwise, it prints `"Failed"`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0074-01)

```
if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}
else {
   System.out.println("Failed");
}
```

In either case, after printing occurs, the next statement in sequence (if any) executes. The `if` and `else` bodies are both indented equally. For readability, you should consistently apply your indentation convention throughout your programs. If there are several indentation levels, each should be indented with the same additional amount of space. We prefer three-space indents. IDEs typically auto-indent the code for you.

##### UML Activity Diagram for an `if`…`else` Statement

The following diagram illustrates the flow of control in the preceding `if`…`else` statement:

![Images](graphics/f0074-02.jpg)

Once again, the UML activity diagram begins with the initial state, contains transition arrows, a decision and action states, and ends with a final state.

#### 3.4.1 Nested `if`…`else` Statements

You can test multiple cases by placing `if`…`else` statements inside `if`…`else` statements to create **nested** **`if`****…****`else`** **statements**. The following nested `if`…`else` prints `A` for grades greater than or equal to 90, `B` for grades 80 to 89, `C` for grades 70 to 79, `D` for grades 60 to 69 and `F` for all other grades. We use shading to highlight the nesting:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0075-01)

```
 if (grade >= 90) {                         
    System.out.println("A");                
 }                                          
 else {                                     
    if (grade >= 80) {                      
       System.out.println("B");             
    }                                       
    else {                                  
       if (grade >= 70) {                   
          System.out.println("C");          
       }                                    
       else {                               
          if (grade >= 60) {                
             System.out.println("D");       
          }                                 
          else {                            
             System.out.println("F");       
          }                                 
       }                                    
    }                                       
 } 
```

If `grade` is greater than or equal to 90, the first four conditions in the nested `if`…`else` statement are `true`. However, only the first `if` part’s statement executes—the `else` part of the “outermost” `if`…`else` statement is skipped.

Most programmers prefer to write the preceding nested `if`…`else` statement as

```
if (grade >= 90) {
   System.out.println("A");
}
else if (grade >= 80) {
   System.out.println("B");
}
else if (grade >= 70) {
   System.out.println("C");
}
else if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("D");
}
else {
   System.out.println("F");
}
```

The latter form avoids deep indentation to the right, which often leaves little room on a line of source code, forcing lines to be split and making the code less readable. In a nested `if`…`else` statement, ensure that you test for all possible cases.

#### 3.4.2 Blocks

The `if` statement expects only one statement in its body. To include several statements in an `if`’s or `else`’s body, you must enclose the statements in braces (`{` and `}`). Recall from [Section 2.7](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec7) that statements in braces form a block. You can place a block anywhere in a method where you can place a single statement. We always enclose control statement bodies in braces. This avoids a logic error called the “dangling-`else`” problem.

The following example includes a multi-statement block in an `if`…`else` statement’s `else` part:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0076-01)

```
if (grade >= 60) {
   System.out.println("Passed");
}
else {
   System.out.println("Failed");
   System.out.println("You must take this course again");
}
```

If `grade` is less than 60, both statements in the `else`’s body execute, displaying:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0076-02)

```
Failed
You must take this course again
```

The braces surrounding the two statements in the `else` clause are important. Without the braces, the statement

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0076-03)

```
System.out.println("You must take this course again");
```

would be outside the `else`’s body and `"You must take this course again"` would print even for passing `grade`s—a logic error.

##### Syntax Errors and Logic Errors

The compiler catches syntax errors, such as when one brace in a block is left out of the program. A logic error, such as an incorrect calculation, has its effect at execution time. A **fatal logic error** causes a program to fail and terminate prematurely. A **nonfatal logic error** allows a program to continue executing but causes it to produce incorrect results.

##### Empty Statement

Just as a block can be placed anywhere a single statement can be placed, it’s also possible to have an empty statement. Recall from [Section 2.7](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec7) that the empty statement is represented by placing a semicolon (`;`) where a statement would normally be.

Placing a semicolon after the condition in an `if` or `if`…`else` statement leads to a logic error in single-selection `if` statements and a syntax error in double-selection `if`…`else` statements (when the `if`-part contains an actual body statement).

#### 3.4.3 Conditional Operator (`?:`)

The **conditional operator** (**`?:`**) can be used in place of simple `if`…`else` statements. The conditional operator is the only **ternary operator**—it takes three operands. Together, the operands and the `?:` symbol form a **conditional expression**. For example, the following statement prints the value of `println`’s conditional-expression argument:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0077-02)

```
System.out.println(grade >= 60 ? "Passed" : "Failed");
```

*   The operand to the left of the question mark (`?`)—grade >= 60—is a condition that evaluates to `true` or `false`.

*   The operand between the question mark (`?`) and the colon (`:`)—`"Passed"`—is the conditional expression’s value if the condition is `true`.

*   The operand after the colon (`:`)—`"Failed"`—is the conditional expression’s value if the condition is `false`.

The conditional expression in this statement evaluates to `"Passed"` if `grade >= 60` is `true` or `"Failed"` if it’s `false`. Thus, this statement with the conditional operator is essentially the same as the `if`…`else` statement shown at the beginning of [Section 3.4](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec4). The conditional operator’s precedence is low, so it’s usually placed in parentheses.

### 3.5 `while` Iteration Statement

An iteration statement specifies that a program should repeat an action while some condition remains `true`. Consider a program segment that uses the **`while`** **iteration statement** to find the first power of 3 larger than 50\. After this code executes, `product` contains the result:

```
int product = 3;
while (product <= 50) {
   product = 3 * product;
}
```

First, we initialize `product` to `3`. Then, the `while` statement executes as follows:

1.  The program tests the condition `product <= 50`, which is `true` because `product` is `3`. The body statement multiplies `product` by `3` and assigns the result (`9`) to `product`. The loop’s first iteration is now complete.

2.  The program tests the condition again—it’s `true` because `product` is now `9`. The body sets `product` to `27`. The loop’s second iteration is now complete.

3.  The program tests the condition again—it’s `true` because `product` is now `27`. The body sets `product` to `81`. The loop’s third iteration is now complete.

4.  The program tests the condition again—it’s finally `false` because `product` is now 81, which is not less than or equal to `50`, so the loop terminates.

Variable `product` now contains `81`—the first power of 3 greater than 50\. The `while` statement’s body may be a single statement or a block.

##### UML Activity Diagram for a `while` Statement

The following UML activity diagram illustrates the preceding `while`’s flow of control:

![Images](graphics/f0078-01.jpg)

This diagram introduces the **UML’s merge symbol**. The UML represents both the merge symbol and the decision symbol as diamonds. The merge symbol joins two flows of activity into one. In this diagram, the merge symbol joins the transitions from the initial state and from the action state, so they both flow into the decision that determines whether the loop should begin (or continue) executing.

The decision and merge symbols can be distinguished by the number of “incoming” and “outgoing” transition arrows:

*   A decision symbol has one transition arrow pointing to the diamond and two or more pointing from it to indicate possible transitions. Each transition arrow pointing from a decision symbol has a guard condition next to it.

*   A merge symbol has two or more transition arrows pointing to the diamond and only one pointing from it to indicate multiple activity flows merging to continue the activity. A merge’s transition arrows do not have guard conditions.

The diagram clearly shows the `while` statement’s iteration. The transition arrow emerging from the action state points back to the merge, from which program flow transitions back to the decision tested at the beginning of each iteration. The `while` statement executes until the guard condition “product <= 50” becomes false, and thus the guard condition “product > 50” becomes true. Then, the `while` statement reaches its final state, and the program continues with the next statement in sequence.

### 3.6 Counter-Controlled Iteration

Let’s solve two variations of a problem that averages student grades. Consider the following problem statement:

A class of ten students took a quiz. The grades (integers in the range 0–100) for this quiz are available to you. Determine the class average on the quiz.

The class average is the sum of the grades divided by the number of students. The program for solving this problem must input each grade, keep track of the total of all grades input, perform the averaging calculation and print the result. We use **counter-controlled iteration** to input the grades one at a time. This technique uses a variable called a **counter** (or **control variable**) to control the number of times statements will execute. Counter-controlled iteration is also called **definite iteration** because the number of iterations is known before the loop executes. In this example, iteration terminates when the counter exceeds 10\. This section presents the Java program ([Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01)) to implement the algorithm.

#### 3.6.1 Implementing the Algorithm

In [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01), class `ClassAverage`’s `main` method allows the user to enter 10 grades, then calculates and displays the average.

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0080-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 3.1: ClassAverage.java
 2   // Solving the class-average problem using counter-controlled iteration.
 3   import java.util.Scanner; // program uses class Scanner
 4
 5   public class ClassAverage {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // create Scanner to obtain user input
 8         Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
 9
10         // initialization phase
11         int total = 0;  // initialize sum of grades entered by the user
12         int gradeCounter = 1; // initialize grade # to be entered next
13
14         // processing phase uses counter-controlled iteration
15         while (gradeCounter <= 10) { // loop 10 times
16            System.out.print("Enter grade: "); // prompt for next grade
17            int grade = input.nextInt(); // input the grade
18            total = total + grade; // add grade to total
19            gradeCounter = gradeCounter + 1; // increment counter by 1
20         }
21
22         // termination phase
23         int average = total / 10; // integer division yields integer result
24
25         // display total and average of grades
26         System.out.printf("%nTotal of all 10 grades is %d%n", total);
27         System.out.printf("Class average is %d%n", average);
28      }
29   }
```

```
Enter grade: 67
Enter grade: 78
Enter grade: 89
Enter grade: 67
Enter grade: 87
Enter grade: 98
Enter grade: 93
Enter grade: 85
Enter grade: 82
Enter grade: 100

Total of all 10 grades is 846
Class average is 84
```

**Fig. 3.1** | Solving the class-average problem using counter-controlled iteration.

##### Local Variables in Method `main`

Line 8 declares and initializes `Scanner` variable `input`, which is used to read values entered by the user. Lines 11, 12, 17 and 23 declare the local `int` variables `total`, `gradeCounter`, `grade` and `average`. Variable `grade` stores the user input.

These declarations appear in `main`’s body. Variables declared in a method body are **local variables**. They can be used only from the line of their declaration to the method’s closing right brace. A local variable’s declaration must appear before the variable is used in that method. A local variable cannot be accessed outside the method in which it’s declared. Variable `grade`, declared in the `while` loop’s body, can be used only in that block.

##### Initialization Phase: Initializing Variables `total` and `gradeCounter`

The assignments (in lines 11–12) initialize `total` to `0` and `gradeCounter` to `1`. These initializations occur before the variables are used in calculations.

All local variables must be initialized before their values are used in expressions; otherwise, compilation errors occur. Totals are generally initialized to 0\. Counters are generally initialized to 0 or 1, depending on how they’re used. Throughout the book, we’ll show examples of when to use 0 and when to use 1.

##### Processing Phase: Reading 10 Grades from the User

Line 15 indicates that the `while` statement should continue looping (also called **iterating**) as long as `gradeCounter`’s value is less than or equal to 10\. While this condition remains `true`, the `while` statement repeatedly executes the statements in lines 16–19:

*   Line 16 displays the prompt `"Enter grade: "`.

*   Line 17 reads the grade entered by the user and assigns it to variable `grade`.

*   Line 18 adds the new `grade` into the `total`, replacing its previous value.

*   Line 19 adds `1` to `gradeCounter` (replacing its previous value) to indicate that the program processed a grade and is ready to input the next grade from the user.

Incrementing `gradeCounter` eventually causes it to exceed 10\. Then, the loop terminates because its condition (line 15) becomes `false`.

##### Termination Phase: Calculating and Displaying the Class Average

When the loop terminates:

*   Line 23 calculates the average and assigns the result to the variable `average`.

*   Line 26 uses `System.out`’s `printf` method to display the text `"Total of all 10 grades is "` followed by `total`’s value.

*   Line 27 uses `printf` to display the text `"Class average is "` followed by the `average`’s value.

When execution reaches line 28, the program terminates.

#### 3.6.2 Integer Division and Truncation

Line 23’s averaging calculation produces an integer result. In the sample output, the sum of the grades is 846, which, when divided by 10, should yield 84.6\. This is a **floating-point number**—a number with a decimal point. In line 23, however, the result of `total / 10` is the integer 84 because `total` and `10` are both integers. Dividing two integers results in **integer division**—any fractional part of the calculation is **truncated** (i.e., lost). In the next section, we’ll see how to obtain a floating-point result from the averaging calculation. Assuming that integer division rounds (rather than truncates) can lead to incorrect results.

#### 3.6.3 Arithmetic Overflow

In [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01), line 18 adds each `grade` entered by the user to the `total`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0081-01)

```
total = total + grade; // add grade to total
```

Even this simple statement has a potential problem—adding the integers could result in a value too large to store in an `int` variable. This is known as **arithmetic overflow** and causes undefined behavior, which can lead to unintended results.^([4](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_4a)) [Figure 2.5](#ch02.xhtml_ch02fig05)’s `Addition` program had the same issue in line 17, which calculated the sum of two `int` values entered by the user:

[4](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_4). “Integer Overflow.” Wikipedia, last modified May 18, 2024\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_overflow#Security_ramifications`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_overflow#Security_ramifications). [Discusses potential problems associated with integer overflow.]

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0082-01)

```
int sum = number1 + number2; // add numbers, then store total in sum
```

The constants `Integer.MIN_VALUE` and `Integer.MAX_VALUE` represent the minimum and maximum values an `int` variable can store. There are similar constants for the other numeric primitive types. You can find the values of these constants in each class’s online documentation. `Integer`’s documentation is located at:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0082-02)

```
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   lang/Integer.html
```

#### 3.6.4 Input Validation

Whenever a program receives input from the user, various problems might occur. For example, line 17 of [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01)

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0082-03)

```
int grade = input.nextInt(); // input next grade
```

assumes the user will enter an integer grade in the range 0 to 100, but the user could enter:

*   an integer less than 0,

*   an integer greater than 100,

*   an integer outside the range of values that can be stored in an `int` variable,

*   a number containing a decimal point or

*   a value containing letters or special symbols that do not even represent a number.

Industrial-strength programs must test for all possible erroneous cases to ensure valid inputs. A program that inputs grades should validate them using **range checking** to ensure they are values from 0 to 100\. You can then ask the user to re-enter any out-of-range value. If a program requires inputs from a specific set of values (such as non-sequential product codes), you should ensure that each input matches a value in the set.

### 3.7 Sentinel-Controlled Iteration

Let’s generalize [Section 3.6](#ch03.xhtml_ch03lev1sec6)’s class-average problem. Consider the following problem:

Develop a class-averaging program that processes grades for an arbitrary number of students each time it is run.

In the previous class-average example, the number of grades (10) was known in advance. For this problem, we do not know how many grades the user will enter during the program’s execution. The program must process an arbitrary number of grades.

One way to solve this problem is to use a **sentinel value** (also called a **signal value** or a **flag value**) indicating the end of data entry. After entering all the legitimate grades, the user enters the sentinel value to indicate that no more grades will be entered.

You must choose a sentinel value that cannot be confused with an acceptable input value. Grades on a quiz are nonnegative integers, so –1 is an acceptable sentinel value for this problem. Thus, a run of the class-averaging program might process a stream of inputs such as 95, 96, 75, 74, 89 and –1\. The program would then compute and print the class average for the five grades, excluding –1, because it’s the sentinel value and should not enter into the averaging calculation.

#### 3.7.1 Implementing Sentinel-Controlled Iteration

[Figure 3.2](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig02) implements sentinel-controlled iteration. Much of [Fig. 3.2](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig02) is identical to [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01), so we concentrate on the new content here. Although each grade the user enters is an integer, the average calculation will likely produce a floating-point number like 84.6, which an `int` cannot represent. You store floating-point numbers using the types `float` and `double`:

*   Variables of the `float` primitive type represent **single-precision floating-point numbers.** They have up to seven significant digits to the right of the decimal point.

*   Variables of the `double` primitive type represent **double-precision floating-point numbers**. These require twice as much memory as `float` variables. They have up to 15 significant digits—about twice a `float` variable’s precision.

Most programmers use type `double` because all floating-point numbers in a program’s source code, such as 7.33 and 0.0975, are represented as type `double` by default. Such values are known as **floating-point literals**. For the precise ranges of Java’s floating-point types, visit the Java Language Specification [Section 4.2](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec2), “Primitive Types and Values.”^([5](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_5a))

[5](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_5). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. “4.2\. Primitive Types and Values.” Accessed May 21, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2).

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0084-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 3.2: ClassAverage.java
 2   // Solving the class-average problem using sentinel-controlled iteration.
 3   import java.util.Scanner; // program uses class Scanner
 4
 5   public class ClassAverage {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // create Scanner to obtain user input
 8         Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
 9
10         // initialization phase
11         int total = 0; // initialize grade total
12         int gradeCounter = 0; // initialize # of grades entered so far
13
14         // processing phase
15         // prompt for input and read grade from user
16         System.out.print("Enter grade or -1 to quit: ");
17         int grade = input.nextInt();
18
19         // loop until sentinel value read from user
20         while (grade != -1) {
21            total = total + grade; // add grade to total
22            gradeCounter = gradeCounter + 1; // increment counter
23
24            // prompt for input and read next grade from user
25            System.out.print("Enter grade or -1 to quit: ");
26            grade = input.nextInt();
27         }
28
29         // termination phase
30         // if user entered at least one grade...
31         if (gradeCounter != 0) {
32            // use a number with decimal point to calculate the average
33            double average = (double) total / gradeCounter;
34
35            // display total and average (with two digits of precision)
36            System.out.printf("%nTotal of the %d grades entered is %d%n",
37               gradeCounter, total);
38            System.out.printf("Class average is %.2f%n", average);
39         }
40         else { // no grades were entered, so output appropriate message
41            System.out.println("No grades were entered");
42         }
43      }
44   }
```

```
Enter grade or -1 to quit: 97
Enter grade or -1 to quit: 88
Enter grade or -1 to quit: 72
Enter grade or -1 to quit: -1

Total of the 3 grades entered is 257
Class average is 85.67
```

**Fig. 3.2** | Solving the class-average problem using sentinel-controlled iteration.

##### Program Logic for Sentinel-Controlled Iteration vs. Counter-Controlled Iteration

Line 12 initializes `gradeCounter` to `0` because no grades have been entered yet. Remember that we’re using sentinel-controlled iteration to input the grades, so we increment the variable `gradeCounter` only when the user enters a valid grade. Line 33 declares the `double` variable `average`, which stores the class average as a floating-point number.

Compare this program’s logic for sentinel-controlled iteration with [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01)’s counter-controlled iteration:

*   In counter-controlled iteration, each loop iteration (lines 15–20 of [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01)) reads a value from the user for the specified number of iterations.

*   In sentinel-controlled iteration, lines 16–17 of [Fig. 3.2](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig02) prompt for and input the first value before reaching the `while`. This value determines whether the flow of control should enter the `while`’s body. If the condition is `false`, the user entered the sentinel value—no grades were entered, so the `while`’s body does not execute. If the condition is `true`, the body adds the `grade` to the `total` and increments the `gradeCounter`. Then, lines 25–26 prompt for and input the next grade. At this point, program control reaches the loop’s closing right brace (line 27). Execution continues by testing the `while`’s condition (line 20), using the most recently entered `grade` to determine whether the loop body should execute again.

Notice that the next `grade` is always input from the user immediately before the program tests the `while` statement’s condition. This allows the program to determine whether the value just input is the sentinel value before processing it (i.e., adding it to the `total`). If `grade` contains the sentinel value, the loop terminates without adding –1 to the `total`. In a sentinel-controlled loop, prompts should remind the user of the sentinel.

After the loop terminates, the `if`…`else` statement in lines 31–42 executes. The condition (line 31) determines whether any grades were input. If none were input, the `else` part displays `"No grades were entered"`. After the `if`…`else` executes, the program terminates.

#### 3.7.2 Explicitly and Implicitly Converting Between Primitive Types

If at least one grade was entered, line 33 calculates the average of the grades. Recall from [Fig. 3.1](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig01) that integer division yields an integer result. Even though variable `average` is declared as a `double`, if we had written the averaging calculation as

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0085-01)

```
double average = total / gradeCounter;
```

it would lose the fractional part of the quotient before the result is assigned to `average`. This occurs because `total` and `gradeCounter` are both integers, and integer division yields an integer result.

Most averages are floating-point numbers. To perform a floating-point calculation with integer values, we must temporarily treat these values as floating-point numbers. The **unary cast operator** accomplishes this task. Line 33 of [Fig. 3.2](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig02) uses the **`(double)`** cast operator to create a temporary floating-point copy of its operand `total` (which appears to the operator’s right). Using a cast operator in this manner is called **explicit conversion** or **type casting**. The value stored in `total` is still an integer.

The calculation now consists of a floating-point value (the temporary `double` copy of `total`) divided by the integer `gradeCounter`. In mixed-type arithmetic expressions, Java performs an operation called **promotion** (or **implicit conversion**) on selected operands. In an arithmetic expression containing `int` and `double` values, copies of the `int` values are promoted to `double` values for use in the expression. In this example, `gradeCounter`’s value is promoted to type `double`, then floating-point division is performed, and the calculation’s result is assigned to `average`. Later in this chapter, we discuss all the primitive types. You’ll learn more about the promotion rules in [Section 5.11](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec11).

#### 3.7.3 Formatting Floating-Point Numbers

Lines 36–37 display `gradeCounter`’s and `total`’s values. Line 38 displays the `double` variable `average`’s value. Method `printf` uses the **`%f`** **format specifier** to format floating-point numbers. By default, `%f` formats `double`s with six digits of precision to the right of the decimal point, but you can specify a **custom precision** between the `%` and the `f`. The average of the three grades in the sample execution was 85.666666…, with the sequence of 6s repeating infinitely. In the format specifier `%.2f`, the `.2` is the custom precision. This rounds the average to the hundredths position, producing `85.67` with `2` digits to the right of the decimal point.

##### A Note Regarding Floating-Point Number Precision

Floating-point numbers are not always 100% precise, but they have numerous applications. For example, when we speak of a “normal” body temperature of 98.6 °F, we do not need to be precise to many digits. When we read the temperature on a thermometer as 98.6, it may actually be 98.5999473210643\. Calling this number simply 98.6 is fine for most applications involving body temperatures.

Floating-point numbers often arise from division, as in this example’s class-average calculation. In conventional arithmetic, when we divide 10 by 3, the result is 3.3333333…, with the 3s repeating infinitely. The computer allocates only a fixed amount of space to hold such a value, so the stored floating-point value can be only an approximation.

Due to the imprecise nature of floating-point numbers, type `double` is preferred to `float` because `double` variables can represent floating-point numbers more accurately. So, we primarily use type `double` throughout the book. Assuming floating-point numbers are represented precisely can lead to incorrect results. In some cases, the precision of `float` and `double` variables will be inadequate. For precise floating-point numbers (such as those required by monetary calculations), Java provides class `BigDecimal` (package `java.math`), which we’ll discuss in [Section 4.11](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec11)’s Objects-Natural Case Study.

### 3.8 Nested Control Statements

We’ve seen that control statements can be stacked on top of one another (in sequence). In this case study, we examine the only other structured way control statements can be connected—namely, by **nesting** one control statement within another.

#### 3.8.1 Problem Statement

Consider the following problem statement:

A college offers a course that prepares students for the state licensing exam for real-estate brokers. Last year, ten of the students who completed this course took the exam. The college wants to know how well its students did on the exam. You’ve been asked to write a program to summarize the results.

You’ve been given a list of these 10 students. Next to each name is written a 1 if the student passed the exam or a 2 if the student failed.

Your program should analyze the results of the exam as follows:

1.  Input each test result (i.e., a 1 or a 2). Display “Enter result” each time the program requests another test result.

2.  Count the number of test results of each type.

3.  Display a summary of the test results, indicating the number of students who passed and the number who failed.

4.  If more than eight students passed, print “Bonus to instructor!”

##### Problem Statement Observations

After reading the problem statement carefully, we make the following observations:

*   The program must process test results for 10 students. A counter-controlled loop can be used because the number of test results is known in advance.

*   Each test result is either a 1 or a 2\. As the program reads each result, it must determine whether it’s a 1 or a 2\. We test for a 1 in our algorithm. If the number is not a 1, we assume it’s a 2.

*   Two counters are used to keep track of the exam results—one to count the number of students who passed the exam and one to count the number who failed.

*   After the program has processed all the results, it must decide whether more than eight students passed the exam.

#### 3.8.2 Implementing the Program

[Figure 3.3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig03) implements the program with counter-controlled iteration and shows two sample executions. Lines 11–13 and 19 declare the variables we use to process the examination results. Initializing local variables when they’re declared helps you avoid compilation errors from attempts to use uninitialized variables. While Java does not require that local-variable initializations be incorporated into declarations, it does require that local variables have values before they’re used in an expression; otherwise, compilation errors occur.

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0088-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 3.3: Analysis.java
 2   // Analysis of examination results using nested control statements.
 3   import java.util.Scanner; // class uses class Scanner
 4
 5   public class Analysis {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // create Scanner to obtain user input
 8         Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
 9
10         // initializing variables in declarations
11         int passes = 0;
12         int failures = 0;
13         int studentCounter = 1;
14
15         // process 10 students using counter-controlled iteration
16         while (studentCounter <= 10) {
17            // prompt user for input and obtain value from user
18            System.out.print("Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): ");
19            int result = input.nextInt();
20
21            // if...else is nested in the while statement
22            if (result == 1) {
23               passes = passes + 1;
24            }
25            else {
26               failures = failures + 1;
27            }
28
29            // increment studentCounter so loop eventually terminates
30            studentCounter = studentCounter + 1;
31         }
32
33         // termination phase; prepare and display results
34         System.out.printf("Passed: %d%nFailed: %d%n", passes, failures);
35
36         // determine whether more than 8 students passed
37         if (passes > 8) {
38            System.out.println("Bonus to instructor!");
39         }
40      }
41   }
```

```
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 2
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Passed: 9
Failed: 1
Bonus to instructor!
```

```
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 2
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 2
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 2
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 2
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Enter result (1 = pass, 2 = fail): 1
Passed: 6

**Fig. 3.3** | Analysis of examination results using nested control statements.

The `while` statement (lines 16–31) loops 10 times. During each iteration, it inputs and processes one exam result. The `if`…`else` statement (lines 22–27) for processing each result is nested in the `while` statement. If the `result` is `1`, the `if`…`else` statement increments `passes`; otherwise, it assumes the `result` is `2` and increments `failures`. Line 30 increments `studentCounter` before the loop condition is tested again at line 16\. After 10 values have been input, the loop terminates, and line 34 displays the number of `passes` and `failures`. The `if` statement at lines 37–39 determines whether more than eight students passed the exam and, if so, outputs the message `"Bonus to instructor!"`.

[Figure 3.3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig03) shows the input and output from two sample executions of the program. During the first, the condition at line 37 is `true`—more than eight students passed the exam, so the program outputs a message to bonus the instructor.

### 3.9 Compound Assignment Operators

The **compound assignment operators** enable you to abbreviate assignment expressions. You can abbreviate the statement

```
c = c + 3; // adds 3 to c
```

with the **addition compound assignment operator**, **`+=`**, as

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0091-01)

```
c += 3; // adds 3 to c more concisely
```

The `+=` operator adds its right operand’s value to the left-side variable’s value then stores the result in the left-side variable. Thus, the assignment expression `c+=3` adds `3` to `c`. Compound assignment operators perform an implicit conversion on the right-hand expression’s value to match the type of the variable on the operator’s left side. So, if the left-side variable is an `int` and the right-side expression results in a `double`, the `double` value’s floating-point part will be truncated.^([6](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_6a)) The following table shows the arithmetic compound assignment operators, sample expressions and explanations of what the operators do:

| Operator | Sample expression | Explanation | Assigns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Assume:* `int c = 3, d = 5, e = 4, f = 6, g = 12;` |  |
| `+=` | `c += 7` | `c = c + 7` | `10` to `c` |
| `-=` | `d -= 4` | `d = d - 4` | `1` to `d` |
| `*=` | `e *= 5` | `e = e * 5` | `20` to `e` |
| `/=` | `f /= 3` | `f = f / 3` | `2` to `f` |
| `%=` | `g %= 9` | `g = g % 9` | `3` to `g` |

[6](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_6). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. Section 15.26.2, “Compound Assignment Operators.” Accessed August 28, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.26.2`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-15.html#jls-15.26.2).

### 3.10 Increment and Decrement Operators

The following table summarizes the unary operators for adding 1 to or subtracting 1 from the value of a numeric variable—these are the unary **increment operator**, **`++`**, and the unary **decrement operator**, **`--`**. Unlike binary operators, the unary increment and decrement operators, by convention, should be placed next to their operands with no intervening spaces:

| Operator | Operator name | Expression | Explanation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `++` | **prefix increment** | `++number` | Increment `number` by `1`, then use the new value of `number` in the expression in which `number` resides. |
| `++` | **postfix increment** | `number++` | Use the current value of `number` in the expression in which `number` resides, then increment `number` by `1`. |
| `--` | **prefix decrement** | `--number` | Decrement `number` by `1`, then use the new value of `number` in the expression in which `number` resides. |
| `--` | **postfix decrement** | `number--` | Use the current value of `number` in the expression in which `number` resides, then decrement `number` by `1`. |

##### Prefix Increment vs. Postfix Increment

[Figure 3.4](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig04) demonstrates the difference between the prefix increment and postfix increment versions of the `++` increment operator. The decrement operator (`--`) works similarly.

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0092-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 3.4: Increment.java
 2   // Prefix increment and postfix increment operators.
 3
 4   public class Increment {
 5         public static void main(String[] args) {
 6            // demonstrate postfix increment operator
 7            int c = 5;
 8            System.out.printf("c before postincrement: %d%n", c); // prints 5
 9            System.out.printf("    postincrementing c: %d%n", c++); // prints 5
10            System.out.printf(" c after postincrement: %d%n", c); // prints 6
11
12            System.out.println(); // skip a line
13
14            // demonstrate prefix increment operator
15            c = 5;
16            System.out.printf(" c before preincrement: %d%n", c); // prints 5
17            System.out.printf("     preincrementing c: %d%n", ++c); // prints 6
18            System.out.printf("  c after preincrement: %d%n", c); // prints 6
19      }
20   }
```

```
c before postincrement: 5
    postincrementing c: 5
 c after postincrement: 6

 c before preincrement: 5
     preincrementing c: 6
  c after preincrement: 6
```

**Fig. 3.4** | Prefix increment and postfix increment operators.

Line 7 initializes the variable `c` to `5`, and line 8 outputs `c`’s initial value. Line 9 outputs the value of the expression `c++`. This expression postincrements the variable `c`, so the statement outputs `c`’s original value (`5`) again, then `c`’s value is incremented (to 6). Line 10 outputs `c`’s new value (`6`) to prove that the variable’s value was indeed incremented in line 9.

Line 15 resets `c`’s value to `5`, and line 16 outputs `c`’s value. Line 17 outputs the value of the expression `++c`, which preincrements `c`, so the statement outputs `c`’s new value (`6`). Line 18 outputs `c`’s value again to show that the value of `c` is still `6` after line 17 executes.

##### Simplifying Increment Statements

The arithmetic compound assignment operators and the increment and decrement operators can be used to simplify program statements. For example, the three assignment statements in [Fig. 3.3](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig03) (lines 23, 26 and 30)

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0093-01)

```
passes = passes + 1;
failures = failures + 1;
studentCounter = studentCounter + 1;
```

can be written more concisely with compound assignment operators as

```
passes += 1;
failures += 1;
studentCounter += 1;
```

with prefix increment operators as

```
++passes;
++failures;
++studentCounter;
```

or with postfix increment operators as

```
passes++;
failures++;
studentCounter++;
```

When incrementing or decrementing a variable in a statement by itself, the prefix increment and postfix increment forms have the same effect, and the prefix decrement and postfix decrement forms have the same effect. It’s only when a variable appears in the context of a larger expression that preincrementing and postincrementing the variable have different effects (and similarly for predecrementing and postdecrementing).

### 3.11 Primitive Types

Java requires all variables to have a type.^([7](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_7a)) In C and C++, programmers frequently have to write separate versions of programs to support different computer platforms because the primitive types are not guaranteed to be identical among computers. For example, an `int` on one machine might be represented by 16 bits (2 bytes) of memory, on another machine by 32 bits (4 bytes), and on another by 64 bits (8 bytes). In Java, `int` values are always 32 bits (4 bytes). The eight primitive types in Java—`boolean`, `byte`, `char`, `double`, `float`, `int`, `long` and `short`—are portable across all computer platforms that support Java. For a summary of these types’ value ranges, visit the Java Language Specification [Section 4.2](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec2), Primitive Types and Values.^([8](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_8a)) Because the designers of Java want to ensure portability, they use internationally recognized standards for character formats (Unicode; [`https://unicode.org`](https://unicode.org)) and floating-point numbers (IEEE 754; [`https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/`](https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/)).

[7](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_7). We’ll see an exception to this with lambdas in [Chapter 14](#ch14.xhtml_ch14), [Functional Programming with Lambdas & Streams](#ch04.xhtml_ch04).

[8](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_8). The Java Language Specification, Java SE 22 Edition. [Section 4.2](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec2), “Primitive Types and Values.” Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se22/html/jls-4.html#jls-4.2).

### 3.12 Objects-Natural Case Study: Super-Sized Integers

The explosive growth of Internet communications and data storage on Internet-connected devices has dramatically increased the importance of privacy and security. Cryptography has been used for thousands of years to encode data, making it difficult (and hopefully impossible) for unauthorized users to read,^([9](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_9a),[10](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_10a)) which is critically important in today’s connected world. Most websites (including [`deitel.com`](http://deitel.com)) use HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) to encrypt and decrypt your Internet interactions.

[9](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_9). “Cryptography.” Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography#History`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography#History).

[10](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_10). Binance Academy, “History of Cryptography.” Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://www.binance.vision/security/history-of-cryptography`](https://www.binance.vision/security/history-of-cryptography).

##### Some Applications Need Integers Outside a `long` Integer’s Range

Java’s primitive type `long` can store values in the range –9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807—a maximum of 19 decimal digits, which can represent integers in the low quintillions. Many cryptography algorithms perform calculations with integers far larger than we can store in a `long`.

One of the most popular encryption/decryption schemes is **RSA Public-Key Cryptography**, commonly used to secure data transmitted over the Internet.^([11](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_11a),[12](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_12a),[13](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_13a)) Industrial-strength RSA implementations work with enormous prime numbers consisting of hundreds of digits, far more than primitive type `long` can hold.

[11](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_11). “RSA (Cryptosystem).” Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)).

[12](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_12). “RSA Algorithm.” Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm`](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm).

[13](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_13). K. Moriarty, B. Kaliski, J. Jonsson and A. Rusch, “PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2,” November 2016\. Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017`](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017).

A key reason RSA is so secure is the sheer amount of time required to factor the product of those primes, even for today’s most powerful supercomputers. Public-key cryptography is also used to secure the blockchain technology behind cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin.^([14](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_14a)) Later in the book, we’ll discuss public-key cryptography.

[14](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_14). Sarah Rothrie, “How Blockchain Cryptography Is Fighting the Rise of Quantum Machines,” December 28, 2018\. Accessed June 1, 2024\. [`https://coincentral.com/blockchain-cryptography-quantum-machines/`](https://coincentral.com/blockchain-cryptography-quantum-machines/).

##### Integers Outside `long`’s Range Require Custom Programming

So, how can we manipulate huge integers with arbitrary numbers of digits? Applications requiring integers outside `long`’s range require custom programming. We could use the Java class mechanism (mentioned in [Section 1.4](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev1sec4) and covered in detail in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)) to develop a custom class that handles huge-integer arithmetic—but that could take months of effort. The objects-natural approach encourages us to check first for classes in the Java API or in free, open-source class libraries to determine if such a “huge-integer” class already exists.

##### Huge Integers with the Java API’s `java.math.BigInteger` Class

There are preexisting classes for creating and manipulating huge integers. For this example, we’ll demonstrate the **`BigInteger`** **class** from the Java API’s `java.math` package:

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0095-01)

```
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/
   math/BigInteger.html
```

With the objects-natural approach in [Fig. 3.5](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig05), we’ll use objects of the `BigInteger` class without having to understand how that class is implemented.^([15](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_15a),[16](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_16a)) We `import` it (line 4), use it to create `BigInteger` objects (lines 12–15), then perform calculations with them and display the results (lines 23–30).

[15](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_15). If you drive a car, you use it effectively without having to understand how car engines, steering, brakes and transmission systems work internally. After you get deeper into Java, you might want to study `BigInteger`’s source code (approximately 5,000 lines, including extensive Javadoc comments) to learn how it’s implemented. In our object-oriented programming presentation later in this book, you’ll learn techniques you could use to create your own huge-integer class.

[16](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_16). You might say, “I insist on knowing how everything I use in Java is implemented.” Reflect for a moment on the fact that you’re using a Java compiler to translate your Java programs into the bytecodes that the Java Virtual Machine then translates into your computer’s machine language. Do you know how the compiler is implemented? Are you sure that it correctly translates each of your Java programs so they’ll run properly and produce correct results?

[Click here to view code image](#ch03_images.xhtml_f0096-01)

##### Largest Value of a `long`

Line 9 displays **`Long.MAX_VALUE`**—a constant representing the maximum value a `long` variable can store (9,223,372,036,854,775,807). As you’ll see, each `BigInteger` calculation in this example results in a value greater than `Long.MAX_VALUE`. Each primitive type (e.g., `long`) has a corresponding class (e.g., the **`Long`** **class**) in the `java.lang` package. These classes provide the constants `MIN_VALUE` and `MAX_VALUE`, representing the smallest and largest values the corresponding primitive types can store.

##### Initializing a `BigInteger` with a String

If a `BigInteger`’s initial value exceeds the maximum integer value Java supports, you can initialize a new `BigInteger` object with a string representing the integer value, as we did with the 30-digit integer in lines 12–13.

##### Initializing a `BigInteger` with an Integer

Lines 14–15 ask the `BigInteger` class to create new `BigInteger` objects and initialize them with primitive-type integer values. Classes provide methods to perform tasks. Each method we’ve used so far was called on an object. For example, to display text, [Fig. 3.5](#ch03.xhtml_ch03fig05) calls the `printf` and `println` methods on the `System.out` object. Some classes provide methods you call directly on the class rather than on an object of the class. These are called **`static`** methods. You call a `static` method by specifying the class name followed by a dot (`.`) separator and the method name, as in

```
ClassName.methodName(arguments)
```

Class **`BigDecimal`****’s** **`static valueOf`** **method** creates and returns a new `BigInteger` object initialized with `valueOf`’s primitive-type integer argument:

*   Line 14 initializes `value2` with a `BigInteger` containing a `long`’s maximum value. The **`L`** (“el”) suffix at the end of `9_223_372_036_854_775_807L` indicates that the value is a `long` integer. Without the `L`, the Java compiler treats whole numbers in code as `int` values—in this case, line 14 would cause a compilation error because this value is much larger than an `int`’s maximum positive value (2,147,483,647).^([17](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_17a))

    [17](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_17). We could have used `Long.MAX_VALUE` in line 14 rather than `9_223_372_036_854_775_807L`.

*   Line 15 initializes `value3` with a `BigInteger` containing the `int` value 17.

Lines 18–20 display the initial values of the `BigInteger`s `value1`, `value2` and `value3`.

##### How Does `printf`’s String Specifier `%s` Understand a `BigInteger` Object?

Every Java primitive-type value and object has a string representation. When you format any value or object using `printf` with the `%s` specifier, Java converts that value or object to a string. For an object, Java does this by calling the object’s `toString` method, which we’ll discuss in later chapters. The `toString` method is also called when you display an object with `System.out`’s `print` and `println` methods.

##### Performing `BigInteger` Arithmetic

Class `BigInteger` provides various methods for common arithmetic operations. Lines 23–30 demonstrate the `BigInteger` methods **`add`**, **`subtract`** and **`multiply`**. `BigInteger` correctly handles integers of any number of digits. Each result is a value with more digits than can be represented by Java’s integer primitive types. The multiplication in line 28, for example, produces a 48-digit integer. Though a `BigInteger` can represent any integer value, it does not use the primitive types understood by the Java virtual machine. So calculations with `BigInteger` run (possibly much) slower than those with primitive types.^([18](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_18a))

[18](#ch03.xhtml_fn3_18). For more details on `BigInteger` performance, refer to the API Note in `BigInteger`’s documentation. “Class `BigInteger`.” Accessed September 21, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/math/BigInteger.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/math/BigInteger.html).
