### 8.6 Case Study: Card Shuffling and Dealing Simulation

[Chapter 6](#ch06.xhtml_ch06)’s examples demonstrated arrays containing only primitive-type elements. An array’s elements can have primitive or reference types. This section uses random-number generation and an array of reference-type elements—namely objects representing playing cards—to develop a class that simulates card shuffling and dealing, which you can use to implement programs that play card games.

This example contains three classes. The `Card` class ([Fig. 8.7](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig07)) represents a playing card with a face (`"Ace"`, `"Deuce"`, `"Three"`, …, `"Jack"`, `"Queen"`, `"King"`) and a suit (`"Hearts"`, `"Diamonds"`, `"Clubs"`, `"Spades"`). The `DeckOfCards` class ([Fig. 8.8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig08)) creates a deck of 52 playing cards in which each element is a `Card` object. Finally, the `DeckOfCardsTest` class ([Fig. 8.9](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig09)) demonstrates class `DeckOfCards`’s card-shuffling-and-dealing capabilities.

##### Class `Card`

Class `Card` ([Fig. 8.7](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig07)) contains `String` instance variables `face` and `suit` that store references to a specific `Card`’s face and suit names. We declared these `final` because a real card’s face and suit cannot be modified.^([4](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_4a)) The `Card` constructor (lines 9–12) receives two `String`s to initialize `face` and `suit`. Method `toString` (lines 15–17) returns a `String` consisting of the `Card`’s `face`, `"of "` and the `Card`’s `suit` (e.g., `"Ace of Spades"`).^([5](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_5a)) Java calls `toString` implicitly when an object is used where a `String` is expected—for example, when `printf` outputs an object as a `String` using the `%s` format specifier or when you concatenate an object with a `String` using the `+` operator. For this behavior to occur, you must declare `toString` with the header shown in line 15.

[4](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_4). We’ll discuss `final` instance variables in more detail in [Section 8.18](#ch08.xhtml_ch08lev1sec18).

[5](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_5). You’ll learn in [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09) that when we provide a custom `toString` method, we are “overriding” a version “inherited” from class `Object`. As of [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), every method we explicitly override will be preceded by the annotation `@Override`, which prevents a common programming error.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0279-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.7: Card.java
 2   // Card class represents a playing card.
 3
 4   public class Card {
 5      private final String face; // face of card ("Ace", "Deuce", ...)
 6      private final String suit; // suit of card ("Hearts", "Diamonds", ...)
 7
 8      // two-argument constructor initializes card's face and suit
 9      public Card(String face, String suit) {
10         this.face = face; // initialize face of card
11         this.suit = suit; // initialize suit of card
12      }
13
14      // return String representation of Card
15      public String toString() {
16         return face + " of " + suit;
17      }
18   }
```

**Fig. 8.7** | `Card` class represents a playing card.

##### Class `DeckOfCards`

Class `DeckOfCards` ([Fig. 8.8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig08)) creates and manages an array of `Card` references. We split this class into parts for discussion purposes. `NUMBER_OF_CARDS` (line 9) specifies the number of `Card`s in a deck (52). Line 10 declares and initializes the instance variable `deck`, which refers to a new array of `Card`s with `NUMBER_OF_CARDS` (52) elements. The `deck` array’s elements are `null` by default. Recall that `null` represents a “reference to nothing,” so no `Card` objects exist yet. Class `DeckOfCards` also declares `int` instance variable `currentCardIndex` (line 11), representing the sequence number (0–51) of the next `Card` to deal from the `deck` array.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0279-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.8: DeckOfCards.java
 2   // DeckOfCards class represents a deck of playing cards.
 3   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 4
 5   public class DeckOfCards {
 6      // random number generator
 7      private static final RandomGenerator randomNumbers =
 8         RandomGenerator.getDefault();
 9      public static final int NUMBER_OF_CARDS = 52; // constant # of Cards
10      private Card[] deck = new Card[NUMBER_OF_CARDS]; // Card references
11      private int currentCardIndex = 0; // index of next Card to deal (0-51)
12
```

**Fig. 8.8** | `DeckOfCards` class represents a deck of playing cards.

##### `DeckOfCards` Constructor

The constructor uses a loop (lines 20–22) to fill the `deck` array with `Card` objects. The loop iterates from `0` while the `count` is less than `deck.length`, causing `count` to take on each value from 0 through 51 (the array’s indices). We initialize each `Card` with two `String`s—one from the `faces` array containing the `String`s `"Ace"` through `"King"` and one from the `suits` array containing the `String`s `"Hearts"`, `"Diamonds"`, `"Clubs"` and `"Spades"`. The calculation `count % 13` results in a value from 0 to 12 (the 13 indices of the `faces` array in lines 15–16), and the calculation `count / 13` results in a value from 0 to 3 (the four indices of the `suits` array in line 17). When the loop completes, the `deck` contains `Card`s with faces `"Ace"` through `"King"` of each suit—13 `"Hearts"`, then 13 `"Diamonds"`, then 13 `"Clubs"`, then 13 `"Spades"`. This example represents the faces and suits as arrays of `String`s. You could also represent the faces and suits as arrays of `enum` constants.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0280-01)

```
13      // constructor fills deck of Cards
14      public DeckOfCards() {
15         String[] faces = {"Ace", "Deuce", "Three", "Four", "Five", "Six",
16            "Seven", "Eight", "Nine", "Ten", "Jack", "Queen", "King"};
17         String[] suits = {"Hearts", "Diamonds", "Clubs", "Spades"};
18
19         // populate deck with Card objects
20         for (int count = 0; count < deck.length; ++count) {
21            deck[count] = new Card(faces[count % 13], suits[count / 13]);
22         }
23      }
24
```

##### `DeckOfCards` Method `shuffle`

Method `shuffle` (lines 26–40) shuffles the `Card`s. For each `Card`, line 33 chooses a random index 0–51 to select another `Card`. Then, lines 36–38 swap the current and randomly chosen `Card`s in the array. The extra variable `temp` (line 36) temporarily stores one of the two `Card` objects being swapped. The `for` loop shuffles the `Card` objects by performing 52 swaps in a single pass of the array.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0280-02)

```
25      // shuffle deck of Cards with one-pass algorithm
26      public void shuffle() {
27         // next call to method dealCard should start at deck[0] again
28         currentCardIndex = 0;
29
30         // for each Card, pick another random Card (0-51) and swap them
31         for (int first = 0; first < deck.length; ++first) {
32            // select a random number between 0 and 51
33            int second = randomNumbers.nextInt(NUMBER_OF_CARDS);
34
35            // swap current Card with randomly selected Card
36            Card temp = deck[first];
37            deck[first] = deck[second];
38            deck[second] = temp;
39         }
40      }
41
```

Method `shuffle`’s algorithm is considered biased because it sometimes swaps a `Card` with itself. You should use an unbiased algorithm for real games to ensure that all possible shuffled sequences are equally likely to occur. Refer to this section’s genAI exercises, where you’ll investigate how the Fisher-Yates unbiased shuffling algorithm works and ask the generative AIs to modify the `shuffle` method to use the unbiased algorithm.

##### Why Do We Need Variable `temp` to Perform the Swap?

You cannot perform the swap in lines 36–38 with only the two statements

```
deck[first] = deck[second];
deck[second] = deck[first];
```

If `deck[first]` is the `"Ace"` of `"Spades"` and `deck[second]` is the `"Queen"` of `"Hearts"`, after the first assignment, both array elements would contain the `"Queen"` of `"Hearts"` and the `"Ace"` of `"Spades"` would be lost.

##### `DeckOfCards` Method `dealCard`

Method `dealCard` (lines 43–51) deals one `Card`. Recall that `currentCardIndex` is the index of the next `Card` to deal—the `Card` at the deck’s top. Line 45 compares `currentCardIndex` to the `deck` array’s `length`. If the `deck` is not empty (`currentCardIndex` is less than 52), line 46 returns the top `Card` and postincrements `currentCardIndex` to prepare for the next `dealCard` call; otherwise, line 49 returns `null`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0281-01)

```
42      // deal one Card
43      public Card dealCard() {
44         // determine whether Cards remain to be dealt
45         if (currentCardIndex < deck.length) {
46            return deck[currentCardIndex++]; // return current Card in array
47         }
48         else {
49            return null; // return null to indicate that all Cards were dealt
50         }
51      }
52   } // end class DeckOfCards
```

##### Shuffling and Dealing Cards

The program of [Fig. 8.9](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig09) demonstrates the `DeckOfCards` class. Line 7 creates a `DeckOf-Cards` object named `myDeckOfCards`, calling its constructor to create the deck with the 52 `Card` objects in order by suit and face. Line 8 invokes `myDeckOfCards`’s `shuffle` method to rearrange the `Card` objects. Lines 11–18 deal all 52 `Card`s, printing them in four columns of 13 `Card`s each. Line 13 deals one `Card` object by invoking `myDeckOfCards`’s `deal-Card` method, then displays the `Card` left justified in a field of 19 characters. When a `Card` is output as a `String`, Java invokes its `toString` method ([Fig. 8.7](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig07)) implicitly. Lines 15–17 in [Fig. 8.9](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig09) start a new line after every four `Card`s.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0281-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.9: DeckOfCardsTest.java
 2   // Card shuffling and dealing.
 3
 4   public class DeckOfCardsTest {
 5      // execute program
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         var myDeckOfCards = new DeckOfCards();
 8         myDeckOfCards.shuffle(); // place Cards in random order
 9
10         // print all 52 Cards in the order in which they are dealt
11         for (int i = 1; i <= DeckOfCards.NUMBER_OF_CARDS; ++i) {
12            // deal and display a Card
13            System.out.printf("%-19s", myDeckOfCards.dealCard());
14
15            if (i % 4 == 0) { // output a newline after every fourth card
16               System.out.println();
17            }
18         }
19      }
20   }
```

```
Six of Spades      Eight of Spades    Six of Clubs       Nine of Hearts
Queen of Hearts    Seven of Clubs     Nine of Spades     King of Hearts
Three of Diamonds  Deuce of Clubs     Ace of Hearts      Ten of Spades
Four of Spades     Ace of Clubs       Seven of Diamonds  Four of Hearts
Three of Clubs     Deuce of Hearts    Five of Spades     Jack of Diamonds
King of Clubs      Ten of Hearts      Three of Hearts    Six of Diamonds
Queen of Clubs     Eight of Diamonds  Deuce of Diamonds  Ten of Diamonds
Three of Spades    King of Diamonds   Nine of Clubs      Six of Hearts
Ace of Spades      Four of Diamonds   Seven of Hearts    Eight of Clubs
Deuce of Spades    Eight of Hearts    Five of Hearts     Queen of Spades
Jack of Hearts     Seven of Spades    Four of Clubs      Nine of Diamonds
Ace of Diamonds    Queen of Diamonds  Five of Clubs      King of Spades
Five of Diamonds   Ten of Clubs       Jack of Spades     Jack of Clubs

**Fig. 8.9** | Card shuffling and dealing.

##### Preventing `NullPointerException`s

In [Fig. 8.8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig08), we created a `deck` array of 52 `Card` references—by default, each is initialized to `null`. A `NullPointerException` occurs when you try to call a method on a `null` reference. In industrial-strength code, ensuring references are not `null` before you use them to call methods prevents `NullPointerException`s.

### 8.7 Case Study: `Time` Class

Our next example consists of classes `Time1` ([Fig. 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig10)) and `Time1Test` ([Fig. 8.11](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig11)). Class `Time1` represents the time of day. Class `Time1Test`’s `main` method creates one `Time1` object and invokes its methods. The program’s output appears in [Fig. 8.11](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig11).

##### `Time1` Class Declaration

Class `Time1`’s `private int` instance variables `hour`, `minute` and `second` ([Fig. 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig10), lines 5–7) represent the time in universal-time format (24-hour clock format in which hours are in the range 0–23, and minutes and seconds are each in the range 0–59). `Time1` contains `public` methods `setTime` (lines 11–22), `toUniversalString` (lines 25–27) and `toString` (lines 30–34). These methods are the **`public`** **services** or the **`public`** **interface** the class provides to its clients.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0283-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.10: Time1.java
 2   // Time1 class declaration maintains the time in 24-hour format.
 3
 4   public class Time1 {
 5      private int hour; // 0 - 23
 6      private int minute; // 0 - 59
 7      private int second; // 0 - 59
 8
 9      // set a new time value using universal time; throw an
10      // exception if the hour, minute or second is invalid
11      public void setTime(int hour, int minute, int second) {
12         // validate hour, minute and second
13         if (hour < 0 || hour >= 24 || minute < 0 || minute >= 60 ||
14            second < 0 || second >= 60) {
15            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
16               "hour, minute and/or second was out of range");
17         }
18
19         this.hour = hour;
20         this.minute = minute;
21         this.second = second;
22      }
23
24      // convert to String in universal-time format (HH:MM:SS)
25      public String toUniversalString() {
26         return String.format("%02d:%02d:%02d", hour, minute, second);
27      }
28
29      // convert to String in standard-time format (H:MM:SS AM or PM)
30      public String toString() {
31         return String.format("%d:%02d:%02d %s",
32            ((hour == 0 || hour == 12) ? 12 : hour % 12),
33            minute, second, (hour < 12 ? "AM" : "PM"));
34      }
35   }
```

**Fig. 8.10** `| Time1` class declaration maintains the time in 24-hour format.

##### Default Constructor

Class `Time1` does not declare a constructor, so the compiler supplies a default constructor. Each instance variable implicitly receives the default `int` value (`0`).

##### Method `setTime` and Throwing Exceptions

Method `setTime` (lines 11–22) is a `public` method with three `int` parameters used to set the time. Lines 13–14 test each argument to determine whether the value is outside the proper range. The `hour` value must be greater than or equal to `0` and less than `24` because the universal-time format represents hours as integers from 0 to 23 (e.g., 1 PM is hour 13, 11 PM is hour 23, midnight is hour 0, and noon is hour 12). Similarly, both `minute` and `second` values must be greater than or equal to `0` and less than `60`. If the argument values are valid, lines 19–21 assign them to the `hour`, `minute` and `second` instance variables. You should modify an object’s instance variables only if a method’s arguments are all valid.

For invalid values, `setTime` throws an **`IllegalArgumentException`** (lines 15–16) to notify the client code of the problem. Line 15 creates a new `IllegalArgumentException` object and calls its constructor that receives a custom error message. Next, the **`throw`** **statement** immediately terminates `setTime` and returns the exception to the calling method. Then, the client code can handle the exception using `try`...`catch` ([Section 6.12](#ch06.xhtml_ch06lev1sec12)).

##### Method `toUniversalString`

Method `toUniversalString` (lines 25–27) takes no arguments and returns a `String` in universal-time format, consisting of two digits each for the hour, minute and second—recall that you can use the `0` flag in a `printf` format specification (e.g., `"%02d"`) to display leading zeros for a value that doesn’t use all the character positions in the specified field width. For example, if the time were 1:30:07 PM, the method would return `13:30:07`. Line 26 uses **`static String`** **method** **`format`** to return a `String` containing the formatted `hour`, `minute` and `second` values, each with two digits and possibly a leading `0` (specified with the `0` flag). The `format` method is similar to `printf`, but returns a formatted `String` rather than displaying it.

##### Method `toString`

Method `toString` (lines 30–34) takes no arguments and returns a `String` in 12-hour format, consisting of the `hour`, `minute` and `second` values separated by colons and followed by AM or PM (e.g., `11:30:17 AM` or `1:27:06 PM`). Like `toUniversalString`, `toString` uses `static String` method `format` to format the `minute` and `second` as two-digit values, with leading zeros if necessary. Line 32 uses a conditional operator (`?:`) to determine the `hour` value in the `String`. If the `hour` is `0` or `12` (AM or PM), it appears as 12; otherwise, it appears as a value from 1 to 11\. The conditional operator in line 33 determines whether AM or PM will be returned as part of the `String`.

##### Using Class `Time1`

Class `Time1Test` ([Fig. 8.11](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig11)) uses class `Time1`. Line 7 declares the `Time1` variable `time` and initializes it with a new `Time1` object. Operator `new` implicitly invokes class `Time1`’s default constructor because `Time1` does not declare any constructors. To confirm that the `Time1` object was initialized properly, line 10 calls the `private` method `displayTime` (lines 31–34), which, in turn, calls the `Time1` object’s `toUniversalString` and `toString` methods to output the time in universal-time format and standard-time format, respectively. Note that `toString` could have been called implicitly here rather than explicitly. Next, line 14 calls the `time` object’s `setTime` method to change the time. Then, line 15 outputs the time in both formats again to confirm the time was set correctly.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0285-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.11: Time1Test.java
 2   // Time1 object used in an app.
 3
 4   public class Time1Test {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         // create and initialize a Time1 object
 7         var time = new Time1(); // invokes Time1 constructor
 8
 9         // output string representations of the time
10         displayTime("After time object is created", time);
11         System.out.println();
12
13         // change time and output updated time
14         time.setTime(13, 27, 6);
15         displayTime("After calling setTime", time);
16         System.out.println();
17
18         // attempt to set time with invalid values
19         try {
20            time.setTime(99, 99, 99); // all values out of range
21         }
22         catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
23            System.out.printf("Exception: %s%n%n", e.getMessage());
24         }
25
26         // display time after attempt to set invalid values
27         displayTime("After calling setTime with invalid values", time);
28      }
29
30      // displays a Time1 object in 24-hour and 12-hour formats
31      private static void displayTime(String header, Time1 t) {
32         System.out.printf("%s%nUniversal time: %s%nStandard time: %s%n",
33            header, t.toUniversalString(), t.toString());
34      }
35   }
```

```
After time object is created
Universal time: 00:00:00
Standard time: 12:00:00 AM

After calling setTime
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM

Exception: hour, minute and/or second was out of range

After calling setTime with invalid values
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM
```

**Fig. 8.11** `| Time1` object used in an app.

Methods declared `private`, such as `displayTime`, can be called only by other methods of the same class. Such methods are **utility methods** or **helper methods** because that support the operation of the class’s other methods.

##### Calling `Time1` Method `setTime` with Invalid Values

To illustrate that method `setTime` validates its arguments, line 20 calls method `setTime` with invalid arguments of `99` for the `hour`, `minute` and `second`. This statement is placed in a `try` block (lines 19–21) in case `setTime` throws an `IllegalArgumentException`, which it will do since the arguments are all invalid. When this occurs, the exception is caught at lines 22–24, and line 23 displays the exception’s error message by calling its `getMessage` method. Line 27 outputs the time again in both formats to confirm that `setTime` did not change the time when invalid arguments were supplied.

##### Software Engineering of the `Time1` Class Declaration

Consider class `Time1`’s design. Instance variables `hour`, `minute` and `second` are `private`. The data representation used in the class is of no concern to the class’s clients. For example, it would be reasonable for `Time1` to represent the time internally as the number of seconds since midnight or the number of minutes and seconds since midnight. Clients could use the same `public` methods and get the same results without being aware of this change. You’ll ask generative AIs to make this change in Generative AI question 1.

Classes simplify programming because the client can use only a class’s `public` methods. Such methods are client-oriented rather than implementation-oriented. Clients are neither aware of nor involved in a class’s implementation. Clients generally care about what the class does, not how the class does it.

Interfaces change less frequently than implementations. When an implementation changes, implementation-dependent code must change accordingly. Hiding the implementation reduces the possibility that other program parts will become dependent on a class’s implementation details.

##### Java Date/Time API

This section’s example and several of this chapter’s later examples demonstrate various class-implementation concepts in classes that represent dates and times. In professional Java development, you should use the Java Date/Time API’s features, like those we introduced in [Section 5.12](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec12), rather than building your own date and time classes. We use some additional Date/Time API features in [Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18).

### 8.8 Controlling Access to Members

The access modifiers `public` and `private` control access to a class’s variables and methods. In [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), we’ll introduce the additional access modifier `protected`. The primary purpose of `public` methods is to present to the class’s clients a view of the class’s services—the class’s `public` interface.

[Figure 8.12](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig12) demonstrates that `private` class members are not accessible outside the class. Lines 7–9 attempt to access the `private` instance variables `hour`, `minute` and `second` of the `Time1` object `time`. This program assumes that the `Time1` class from [Fig. 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig10) is used. An attempt by a method that’s not a member of a class to access a `private` member of that class generates a compilation error.

### 8.9 Referring to the Current Object’s Members with the `this` Reference

Every object can access a reference to itself with keyword `this`. When an instance method is called for a particular object, the method’s body implicitly uses “`this.`” to refer to the object’s instance variables and other methods, enabling the class’s code to know which object to manipulate. As you’ll see in [Fig. 8.13](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig13), you can also use “`this.`” explicitly in an instance method’s body. [Section 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08lev1sec10) shows another interesting use of the `this` keyword. [Section 8.16](#ch08.xhtml_ch08lev1sec16) explains why “`this.`” cannot be used in a `static` method.

[Figure 8.13](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig13) demonstrates implicit and explicit use of the `this` reference. This example is the first in which we declare two classes in one file—class `ThisTest` is declared in lines 4–9, and class `SimpleTime` in lines 12–41\. When you compile a source-code (`.java`) file, the compiler produces a separate `.class` file for every class in that file. In this case, two files are produced—`SimpleTime.class` and `ThisTest.class`. The compiler places these files in the same folder. Note also in [Fig. 8.13](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig13) that only class `ThisTest` is declared `public`. A source-code (`.java`) file may contain only one `public` class—recall that every public class must be declared in a file that has the class’s name followed by the `.java` filename extension. Non-`public` classes can be used only by other classes in the same package, and classes compiled into the same folder are in the same package. So, `SimpleTime` can be used only in class `ThisTest`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0288-01)

```

 2   // this used implicitly and explicitly to refer to members of an object.
 3

 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         var time = new SimpleTime(15, 30, 19);
 7         System.out.println(time.buildString());
 8      }
 9   }
10

13      private int hour; // 0-23
14      private int minute; // 0-59
15      private int second; // 0-59
16

18      // instance variable names the "this" reference is
19      // required to distinguish between the names

21         this.hour = hour; // set "this" object's hour
22         this.minute = minute; // set "this" object's minute
23         this.second = second; // set "this" object's second
24      }
25
26      // use explicit and implicit "this" to call toUniversalString
27      public String buildString() {

29            "this.toUniversalString()", this.toUniversalString(),
30            "toUniversalString()", toUniversalString());
31      }
32

```
this.toUniversalString(): 15:30:19
     toUniversalString(): 15:30:19
```

**Fig. 8.13** | `this` used implicitly and explicitly to refer to members of an object.

Class `SimpleTime` (lines 12–41) declares three `private` instance variables—`hour`, `minute` and `second` (lines 13–15). The class’s constructor (lines 20–24) receives three `int` arguments to initialize a `SimpleTime` object. Once again, we used parameter names for the constructor that are identical to the class’s instance-variable names (lines 13–15), so we use “`this.`” to refer to the instance variables in lines 21–23\. Most IDEs will issue a warning if you say `x = x;` instead of `this.x = x;`. The statement `x = x;` is often called a no-op (no operation)—in this case, the statement would assign `x` to itself, which does not modify `x`.

Method `buildString` (lines 27–31) returns a `String` created by a statement that uses the `this` reference to call `toUniversalString` explicitly (line 29) and implicitly (line 30). Both lines perform the same operation. You typically will not use `this` explicitly to reference other methods within the current object. Also, line 39 in `toUniversalString` explicitly uses “`this.`” to access each instance variable, though this is not required because the method has no local variables that shadow the class’s instance variables.

There’s only one copy of each method per class—every object of the class shares the method’s code. On the other hand, each object has its own copy of the class’s instance variables. The class’s non-`static` methods implicitly use `this` to determine the specific object of the class to manipulate.

Class `ThisTest`’s `main` method (lines 5–8) demonstrates class `SimpleTime`. Line 6 creates a `SimpleTime` object and invokes its constructor. Line 7 invokes the object’s `build-String` method then displays the results.

### 8.10 Case Study: `Time` Class Overloaded Constructors

Next, we demonstrate a class with **overloaded constructors**, enabling objects of our class to be initialized various ways. Like overloaded methods ([Section 5.7](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec7)), you overload constructors by providing multiple constructor declarations with different signatures.

##### Class `Time2` with Overloaded Constructors

The `Time1` class’s default constructor in [Fig. 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig10) initialized `hour`, `minute` and `second` to their default `0` values (i.e., midnight in universal time). To initialize objects with non-default values, you must provide custom constructors. Class `Time2` ([Fig. 8.14](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig14)) contains five overloaded constructors that enable flexible initialization of `Time2` objects by passing different arguments. We broke this class into parts for discussion purposes. Lines 5–7 declare the class’s `hour`, `minute` and `second` instance variables.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0290-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.14: Time2.java
 2   // Time2 class declaration with overloaded constructors.
 3
 4   public class Time2 {
 5      private int hour; // 0 - 23
 6      private int minute; // 0 - 59
 7      private int second; // 0 - 59
 8
```

**Fig. 8.14** `| Time2` class declaration with overloaded constructors.

##### Class `Time2`’s Constructors—Calling One Constructor from Another via `this`

Each constructor accomplishes the same basic job—initialize a `Time2` object’s instance variables. Portions of that work are identical for each constructor, so we’ll share validation and initialization code by having four of them invoke a fifth that, in turn, ensures the `hour` is in the range 0–23, the `minute` and `second` are each in the range 0–59, then initializes them. As with overloaded functions, the compiler invokes the appropriate constructor by matching the number, types and order of a constructor call’s argument types with the number, types and order of the parameter types specified in each constructor declaration. Class `Time2` also provides *set* and *get* methods for each instance variable.

##### `Time2` Constructor with No Arguments

Lines 11–13 declare a **no-argument constructor**. Once you declare any constructors in a class, the compiler will not provide a default constructor. This no-argument constructor ensures that class `Time2`’s clients can create `Time2` objects with default values.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0290-02)

```
 9      // Time2 no-argument constructor:
10      // initializes each instance variable to zero
11      public Time2() {
12         this(0, 0, 0); // delegate to three-argument constructor
13      }
14
```

Line 12 uses `this` to invoke the `Time2` constructor that takes three parameters (lines 26–42) with 0 for the `hour`, `minute` and `second`. Using the `this` keyword as shown here must be the constructor’s first statement and is a common way to avoid duplicate initialization code. A constructor that entrusts its work to another constructor in the same class is a **delegating constructor**. We use this syntax in four of the five `Time2` constructors to make the class easier to maintain and modify—we’ll say more about this momentarily.

Lines 16–18 declare a `Time2` constructor with a single `int` parameter representing the `hour`. We pass this with 0 for the `minute` and `second` to the constructor at lines 26–42.

18      }
19

Lines 21–23 declare a `Time2` constructor that receives two `int` parameters representing the `hour` and `minute`. We pass these with 0 for the `second` to the constructor at lines 26–42.

##### `Time2` Constructor with a `Time2` Argument

Lines 45–48 declare a `Time2` constructor that receives a reference to another `Time2` object. This constructor copies the argument object’s `hour`, `minute` and `second` values by passing them to the three-argument constructor. (Some languages call this a copy constructor, but this is not a formal Java concept.) The `time.hour`, `time.minute` and `time.second` expressions directly access the argument object’s `hour`, `minute` and `second` instance variables—even though they’re `private`. This is allowed due to a special relationship between objects of the same class. When one object has a reference to another of the same class, the first object can access all the second object’s data and methods—even `private` ones.

##### Notes Regarding Class `Time2`’s *Set* and *Get* Methods and Constructors

Methods `toUniversalString` and `toString` call `Time2`’s *get* methods in line 111 and lines 117–118, respectively. These methods could have accessed `Time2`’s `private` data directly without calling the *get* methods but there’s a software-engineering benefit to calling them.

Our internal time representation uses three `int`s, requiring 12 bytes of memory. Consider changing this to the total seconds since midnight—a single `int` requiring only four bytes. If we make this change, only the methods that access `private` data directly need to change. In this case, we’d modify the three-argument constructor, the `setTime` method and the individual *set* and *get* methods for the `hour`, `minute` and `second`. There would be no need to modify `toUniversalString` and `toString` because they do not access the data directly. Designing the class in this manner reduces the likelihood of programming errors when altering the class’s implementation.

Similarly, each `Time2` delegating constructor could have included a copy of the appropriate statements from the three-argument constructor. This might be slightly more efficient because it would eliminate extra constructor calls. However, duplicating statements makes changing the class’s internal data representation more difficult.^([6](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_6a)) Having the `Time2` delegating constructors call the constructor with three arguments requires making changes only to the three-argument constructor’s implementation. Also, the compiler can optimize programs by removing calls to simple methods and replacing them with the expanded code of their declarations—a technique known as **inlining the code**, which improves program performance.

[6](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_6). In [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), we’ll explain why we chose to duplicate code between class `Time2`’s constructor and `setTime` methods.

### 8.11 Default and No-Argument Constructors

Every class must have at least one constructor. The compiler creates a default constructor with no arguments in a class that does not contain custom constructors. The default constructor initializes the instance variables to the initial values specified in the instance variables’ declarations; otherwise, it uses default values (zero for primitive numeric types, `false` for `boolean` values and `null` for references).

The compiler will not create a default constructor if your class declares constructors. In this case, you must declare a no-argument constructor if default initialization is required. Like a default constructor, a no-argument constructor is invoked with empty parentheses. The `Time2` no-argument constructor (lines 11–13 of [Fig. 8.14](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig14)) explicitly initializes a `Time2` object by passing to the three-argument constructor 0 for each parameter. Since 0 is the default value for `int` instance variables, the no-argument constructor in `Time2` could be declared with an empty body. In this case, each instance variable would receive its default value when the no-argument constructor is called. If we omit the no-argument constructor, clients of this class would not be able to create a `Time2` object with the expression `new Time2()`.

Ensure that you do not include a return type in a constructor definition. Java allows other methods of the class besides its constructors to have the same name as the class and specify return types. Such methods are not constructors and will not be called when an object of the class is instantiated.

### 8.12 Notes on *Set* and *Get* Methods

As you know, client code can manipulate a class’s `private` fields only through the class’s methods. *Set* methods are commonly called **mutator methods** because they change an object’s state—i.e., modify the values of instance variables.^([7](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_7a)) *Get* methods are commonly called **accessor methods** or **query methods**.

[7](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_7). Other methods besides *set* methods can also be mutator methods.

##### Set and Get Methods vs. `public` Data

It would seem that providing *set* and *get* capabilities is essentially the same as making a class’s instance variables `public`. This is one of the subtleties that makes Java desirable for software engineering.

A `public` non-`final` instance variable can be read or written by any method that has a reference to an object containing that variable. A `public` *get* method certainly allows client-code methods to access a `private` instance variable, but the *get* method can control how the client “sees” the data. For example, a *get* method might format the data it returns, shielding the client code from the actual data representation. A `public` *set* method can—and should—carefully scrutinize attempts to modify the variable’s value and throw an exception if necessary. For example, attempts to *set* the day of the month to 37 or a person’s weight to a negative value should be rejected. Thus, although *set* and *get* methods provide access to `private` data, the access can be carefully restricted by the method implementations, promoting good software engineering.

Classes should never have `public` non-constant data. Declaring data `public static final` enables lets you make constants available to your class’s clients. For example, class `Math` offers `public static final` constants `Math.PI` and `Math.E`.

##### Validity Checking in Set Methods

The benefits of data integrity do not follow automatically simply because instance variables are declared `private`—you must provide validity checking. A class’s *set* methods could prevent attempts to assign invalid data to objects of the class. Typically, *set* methods have the `void` return type and use exception handling to indicate attempts to assign invalid data. We discuss exception handling in detail in [Chapter 10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10).

When appropriate, provide `public` methods to access `private` instance variables. This architecture helps hide the implementation of a class from its clients, which improves program modifiability. Using *set* and *get* methods helps you create classes that are easier to debug and maintain. If only one method performs a particular operation, such as setting an instance variable in an object, it’s easier to debug and maintain the class. If the instance variable is not being set correctly, the code that actually modifies the instance variable is localized to one *set* method. Your debugging efforts can be focused on that one method.

##### Predicate Methods

Another common use for accessor methods is to test whether a condition is true or false—such methods are often called **predicate methods.** An example is class `ArrayList`’s `isEmpty` method, which returns `true` if the `ArrayList` is empty and `false` otherwise. A program might test `isEmpty` before attempting to read another item from an `ArrayList`. By convention, predicate method names begin with `is` rather than `get`.

### 8.13 Composition

A class can have references to objects of other classes as members. This is called **composition** and is sometimes referred to as a ***has-a*** **relationship**. For example, an `AlarmClock` object needs to know the current time and when it’s supposed to sound its alarm, so it’s reasonable to include two references to `Time` objects in an `AlarmClock` object. A car *has-a* steering wheel, a brake pedal, an accelerator pedal and more.

##### Class `Date`

This composition example contains classes `Date` ([Fig. 8.16](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig16)), `Employee` ([Fig. 8.17](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig17)) and `EmployeeTest` ([Fig. 8.18](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig18)). Class `Date` declares instance variables `month`, `day` and `year` (lines 5–7) to represent a date. The constructor receives three `int` parameters. Lines 15–18 validate the `month`—if it’s out-of-range, lines 16–17 throw an exception. Lines 21–25 validate the `day`. If the day is incorrect based on the number of days in the particular `month`—except February 29th which requires special leap-year testing—lines 23–24 throw an exception. Lines 28–29 perform the leap-year testing for February. If the month is February, the day is 29 and the `year` is not a leap year, lines 30–31 throw an exception. If no exceptions are thrown, then lines 34–36 initialize the `Date`’s instance variables and line 38 outputs the `this` reference as a `String`. Since `this` refers to the current `Date` object, the object’s `toString` method (lines 42–44) is called implicitly to get the object’s `String` representation. In this example, we assume that the `year` value is correct—an industrial-strength `Date` class should also validate the year.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0298-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.16: Date.java
 2   // Date class declaration.
 3
 4   public class Date {
 5      private int month; // 1-12
 6      private int day; // 1-31 based on month
 7      private int year; // any year
 8
 9      private static final int[] daysPerMonth =
10         {0, 31, 28, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31, 31, 30, 31, 30, 31};
11
12      // constructor: confirm proper value for month and day given the year
13      public Date(int month, int day, int year) {
14         // check if month in range
15         if (month <= 0 || month > 12) {
16            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
17               "month (" + month + ") must be 1-12");
18         }
19
20         // check if day in range for month
21         if (day <= 0 ||
22            (day > daysPerMonth[month] && !(month == 2 && day == 29))) {
23            throw new IllegalArgumentException("day (" + day +
24               ") out-of-range for the specified month and year");
25         }
26
27         // check for leap year if month is 2 and day is 29
28         if (month == 2 && day == 29 && !(year % 400 == 0 ||
29              (year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0))) {
30            throw new IllegalArgumentException("day (" + day +
31               ") out-of-range for the specified month and year");
32         }
33
34         this.month = month;
35         this.day = day;
36         this.year = year;
37
38         System.out.printf("Date object constructor for date %s%n", this);
39      }
40
41      // return a String of the form month/day/year
42      public String toString() {
43         return String.format("%d/%d/%d", month, day, year);
44      }
45   }
```

### 8.14 `enum` Types

In [Fig. 5.4](#ch05.xhtml_ch05fig04), we introduced the basic `enum` type, which defines a set of constants represented as unique identifiers. In that program, the `enum` constants represented the game’s status. In this section, we discuss the relationship between `enum` types and classes. Like classes, all `enum` types are reference types. An **`enum`** **declaration** creates an `enum` type containing a comma-separated list of `enum` constants. The declaration may optionally include other components of traditional classes, such as constructors, fields and methods (as you’ll see momentarily). Each `enum` declaration declares an `enum` class with the following restrictions:

1.  `enum` constants are implicitly `final` because constants cannot be modified.

2.  `enum` constants are implicitly `static`—since they can’t be modified, only one copy of the constant is needed.

Any attempt to create an object of an `enum` type with operator `new` results in a compilation error. The `enum` constants can be used anywhere constants can be used, such as in the `case` labels of `switch` statements and to control enhanced `for` statements.

##### Declaring Instance Variables, a Constructor and Methods in an `enum` Type

[Figure 8.19](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig19) demonstrates instance variables, a constructor and methods in an `enum` type. The `enum` declaration contains two parts—the `enum` constants and the other members of the `enum` type.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0301-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.19: Book.java
 2   // Declaring an enum type with a constructor and explicit instance fields
 3   // and accessors for these fields
 4
 5   public enum Book {
 6      // declare constants of enum type
 7      JHTP("Java How to Program", "2025"),
 8      CHTP("C How to Program", "2020"),
 9      CPP20FP("C++20 for Programmers", "2023"),
10      CPPHTP("C++ How to Program", "2024"),
11      PYCDS("Intro to Python for Computer Science and Data Science", "2020"),
12      PYFP("Python for Programmers", "2020");
13
14      // instance fields
15      private final String title; // book title
16      private final String copyrightYear; // copyright year
17
18      // enum constructor
19      Book(String title, String copyrightYear) {
20         this.title = title;
21         this.copyrightYear = copyrightYear;
22      }
23
24      // accessor for field title
25      public String getTitle() {
26         return title;
27      }
28
29      // accessor for field copyrightYear
30      public String getCopyrightYear() {
31         return copyrightYear;
32      }
33   }
```

**Fig. 8.19** | Declaring an `enum` type with a constructor and explicit instance fields and accessors for these fields.

Lines 7–12 declare six constants. Each is optionally followed by arguments that are passed to the **`enum Book`****’s constructor** (lines 19–22). Like the constructors in classes, an `enum` constructor can specify any number of parameters and can be overloaded. In this example, the `enum` constructor requires two `String` parameters, specifying the book’s title and copyright year. To properly initialize each `enum` constant, we follow it with parentheses containing two `String` arguments. In an `enum` declaration, the `enum` constants must be declared before the `enum`’s constructors, fields and methods.

The second part (lines 15–32) declares the `enum`’s other members—instance variables `title` and `copyrightYear` (lines 15–16), a constructor (lines 19–22) and two methods (lines 25–27 and 30–32) that return the book title and copyright year, respectively. Each constant in type `Book` is an object of type `Book` that has its own copy of instance variables.

##### Using `enum` type `Book`

[Figure 8.20](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig20) tests the `Book enum` and illustrates how to iterate through a range of its constants. For every `enum`, the compiler generates the **`static`** **method** **`values`** (called in line 10), which returns an array of the `enum`’s constants in their declaration order. Lines 10–13 display the constants. Line 12 invokes the `enum Book`’s `getTitle` and `getCopyrightYear` methods to get the title and copyright year associated with the constant. When an `enum` constant is implicitly converted to a `String` (e.g., `book` in line 11), the constant’s identifier is used as the `String` representation (e.g., `JHTP` for the first `enum` constant).

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0302-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.20: EnumTest.java
 2   // Testing enum type Book.
 3   import java.util.EnumSet;
 4
 5   public class EnumTest {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.println("All books:");
 8
 9         // print all books in enum Book
10         for (Book book : Book.values()) {
11            System.out.printf("%-10s%-57s%s%n", book,
12                book.getTitle(), book.getCopyrightYear());
13         }
14
15         System.out.printf("%nDisplay a range of enum constants:%n");
16
17         // print first four books
18         for (Book book : EnumSet.range(Book.JHTP, Book.CPPHTP)) {
19            System.out.printf("%-10s%-57s%s%n", book,
20                book.getTitle(), book.getCopyrightYear());
21         }
22      }
23   }
```

```
All books:
JHTP      Java How to Program                                       2025
CHTP      C How to Program                                          2020
CPP20FP   C++20 for Programmers                                     2023
CPPHTP    C++ How to Program                                        2024
PYCDS     Intro to Python for Computer Science and Data Science     2020
PYFP      Python for Programmers                                    2020

Display a range of enum constants:
JHTP      Java How to Program                                       2025
CHTP      C How to Program                                          2020
CPP20FP   C++20 for Programmers                                     2023
CPPHTP    C++ How to Program                                        2024

**Fig. 8.20** | Testing `enum` type `Book`.

Lines 18–21 use the **`static`** **method** **`range`** **of class** **`EnumSet`** (package `java.util`) to display a range of the `enum Book`’s constants. Method `range` takes two parameters—the first and the last `enum` constants in the range—and returns an `EnumSet` that contains all the constants between these two constants, inclusive. For example, the expression `EnumSet.range(Book.JHTP`, `Book.CPPHTP)` returns an `EnumSet` containing `Book.JHTP`, `Book.CHTP`, `Book.CPP20FP` and `Book.CPPHTP`. The enhanced `for` statement can be used with an `EnumSet` just as it can with an array. Lines 18–21 use it to display the title and copyright year of every book in the `EnumSet`. Class `EnumSet` provides several other `static` methods for creating sets of `enum` constants from the same `enum` type.

### 8.15 Garbage Collection

Every object uses system resources, such as memory. We need a disciplined way to give resources back to the system when they’re no longer needed; otherwise, “resource leaks” might occur that would prevent resources from being reused by your program or others. The JVM performs automatic **garbage collection** to reclaim the memory occupied by objects that are no longer used.

If there are no more references to an object, the object is eligible to be collected when the JVM executes its **garbage collector**. This might not occur right away. If a program terminates before garbage collection occurs, all of its memory is returned to the system. So, memory leaks common in other languages like C and C++ (because they do not automatically reclaim memory) are less likely in Java. However, some can still happen in subtle ways.

Resource leaks other than memory leaks can also occur. For example, a program may open a file on secondary storage to modify its contents. If the program does not close the file, it must terminate before another program can use the file.

Many Java API classes (e.g., class `Scanner` and classes that read from or write to files) provide `close` or `dispose` methods that can release resources when they’re no longer needed in a program.

### 8.16 `static` Class Members

Every object has its own copy of its class’s instance variables. Sometimes, one variable should be shared by all objects of a class. A **`static`** **field**—called a class variable—represents **classwide information**. All objects of the class share the class’s `static` fields.

##### Motivating `static`

Let’s motivate `static` data with an example. Suppose we have a video game with `Martian`s and other space creatures. Each `Martian` tends to be brave and willing to attack other space creatures when the `Martian` is aware that at least four other `Martian`s are present. If fewer than five `Martian`s are present, each becomes cowardly. Thus, each `Martian` needs to know the `martianCount`. We could endow class `Martian` with `martianCount` as an instance variable. Then, every `Martian` would have a separate copy of the instance variable, and every time we create a new `Martian` or destroy an existing one, we’d have to update the `martianCount` in every `Martian` object. This wastes space with the redundant copies, wastes time updating the separate copies and is error-prone. Instead, we declare `martianCount` to be `static`, making `martianCount` classwide data so every `Martian` can access it. This saves space. The `Martian` constructor would increment the `static martianCount` as each new `Martian` is created. Since there’s only one copy, we do not have to increment separate copies for each `Martian` object. Similarly, when a `Martian` is destroyed, a method of the class would be called to decrement the `martianCount`.

##### Class Scope

A class’s `static` variables have class scope—they can be used in all of the class’s methods. We can access a class’s `public static` members through a reference to any object of the class or by qualifying the member name with the class name and a dot (`.`), as in `Math.sqrt(2)`. A class’s `private static` class members can be accessed by client code only through the class’s methods. The `static` class members exist even when no objects of the class exist—they’re available as soon as the class is loaded into memory at execution time. To access a `public static` member when no objects of the class exist (and when they do), prefix the class name and a dot (`.`) to the `static` member, as in `Math.PI`. To access a `private static` member when no objects of the class exist, provide a `public static` method and call it by qualifying its name with the class name and a dot.

##### `static` Methods Cannot Directly Access Instance Variables and Instance Methods

A `static` method cannot directly access a class’s instance variables and instance methods because a `static` method can be called even when no objects of the class have been instantiated. So, “`this.`” cannot be used in a `static` method. Java creates the `this` reference only in instance methods because it must refer to a specific object of the class. When a `static` method is called, there might not be any objects of its class in memory.

##### Tracking the Number of Employee Objects That Have Been Created

Our next program declares two classes—`Employee` ([Fig. 8.21](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig21)) and `EmployeeTest` ([Fig. 8.22](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig22)). Class `Employee` declares `private static` variable `count` ([Fig. 8.21](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig21), line 6) and `public static` method `getCount` (lines 32–34). The `static` variable `count` maintains a count of the number of `Employee` objects created so far. This class variable is initialized to `0` in line 6\. If a `static` variable is not initialized, the compiler assigns it a default value—in this case, `0`, the default value for type `int`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0305-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.21: Employee.java
 2   // static variable used to maintain a count of the number of
 3   // Employee objects in memory.
 4
 5   public class Employee {
 6      private static int count = 0; // number of Employees created
 7      private String firstName;
 8      private String lastName;
 9
10      // initialize Employee, add 1 to static count and output
11      // a String indicating that the constructor was called
12      public Employee(String firstName, String lastName) {
13         this.firstName = firstName;
14         this.lastName = lastName;
15
16         ++count; // increment static count of employees
17         System.out.printf("Employee constructor: %s %s; count = %d%n",
18            firstName, lastName, count);
19      }
20
21      // get first name
22      public String getFirstName() {
23         return firstName;
24      }
25
26      // get last name
27      public String getLastName() {
28         return lastName;
29      }
30
31      // static method to get static count value
32      public static int getCount() {
33         return count;
34      }
35   }
```

**Fig. 8.21** `| static` variable used to maintain a count of the number of `Employee` objects in memory.

When `Employee` objects exist, the variable `count` can be used in any method of an `Employee` object. This example increments `count` in the constructor (line 16). The `public static` method `getCount` (lines 32–34) returns the number of `Employee` objects created so far. When no objects of class `Employee` exist, client code can access variable `count` by calling method `getCount` via the class name, as in `Employee.getCount()`. Invoke every `static` method using the class name and a dot (`.`) to emphasize that the method is `static`.

##### Class `EmployeeTest`

`EmployeeTest` method `main` ([Fig. 8.22](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig22)) instantiates two `Employee` objects (lines 11–12). When each `Employee` object’s constructor is invoked, it initializes the `Employee`’s instance variables `firstName` and `lastName`, then adds one to the `Employee static` variable `count`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0306-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.22: EmployeeTest.java
 2   // static member demonstration.
 3
 4   public class EmployeeTest {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         // show that count is 0 before creating Employees
 7         System.out.printf("Employees before instantiation: %d%n",
 8            Employee.getCount());
 9
10         // create two Employees; count should then be 2
11         var e1 = new Employee("Anna", "Gruber");
12         var e2 = new Employee("Teva", "Maihi");
13
14         // show that count is 2 after creating two Employees
15         System.out.printf("%nEmployees after instantiation:%n");
16         System.out.printf("via e1.getCount(): %d%n", e1.getCount());
17         System.out.printf("via e2.getCount(): %d%n", e2.getCount());
18         System.out.printf("via Employee.getCount(): %d%n",
19            Employee.getCount());
20
21         // get names of Employees
22         System.out.printf("%nEmployee 1: %s %s%nEmployee 2: %s %s%n",

```
Employees before instantiation: 0
Employee constructor: Anna Gruber; count = 1
Employee constructor: Teva Maihi; count = 2

Employees after instantiation:
via e1.getCount(): 2
via e2.getCount(): 2
via Employee.getCount(): 2

Employee 1: Anna Gruber
Employee 2: Teva Maihi

**Fig. 8.22** `| static` member demonstration.

When `main` terminates, local variables `e1` and `e2` are discarded—remember that a local variable exists only until the block in which it’s declared completes execution. Because `e1` and `e2` were the only references to the `Employee` objects created in lines 11–12 ([Fig. 8.22](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig22)), these objects become “eligible for garbage collection” as `main` terminates.

In a typical app, the garbage collector might eventually reclaim the memory for any objects that are eligible for collection. If any objects are not reclaimed before the program terminates, the operating system will reclaim the memory used by the program. The JVM does not guarantee when, or even if, the garbage collector will execute. When it does, it’s possible that no objects or a subset of the eligible objects will be collected.

### 8.17 `static` Import

In [Section 5.8](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec8), you learned about the `static` fields and methods of class `Math`—we access these by preceding each with the class name `Math` and a dot (`.`). A **`static`** **import declaration** enables you to import a class’s `static` members so you can access them via their unqualified names in your class—without the class name and a dot (`.`).

##### `static` Import Forms

A `static` import declaration has two forms that are listed in the Java Language Specification’s language grammar as ***SingleStaticImportDeclaration*** and ***StaticImportOnDemand-Declaration***:

*   A *SingleStaticImportDeclaration* imports a specific `static` member.

*   A *StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration* imports all `static` members of a class.

A *SingleStaticImportDeclaration* consists of a package name (e.g., `java.lang`), a class name and the name of a `static` method or field, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0307-01)

```
import static packageName.ClassName.staticMemberName;
```

A *StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration* consists of a package name (e.g., `java.lang`), a class name and an asterisk (`*`) indicating that *all* `static` members of the class should be available for use in the file, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0307-02)

```
import static packageName.ClassName.*;
```

Such declarations import only `static` class members. Regular `import` statements should be used to specify the classes used in a program.

##### Demonstrating `static` Import

[Figure 8.23](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig23) demonstrates a `static` import. Line 3 is a *StaticImportOnDemandDeclaration*, which imports all of class `Math`’s `static` fields and methods. Lines 7–10 access the `Math` class’s `static` methods `sqrt` (line 7) and `ceil` (line 8) and its `static` fields `E` (line 9) and `PI` (line 10) without qualifying their names with class name `Math` and a dot.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0307-03)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.23: StaticImportTest.java
 2   // Static import of Math class methods.
 3   import static java.lang.Math.*;
 4
 5   public class StaticImportTest {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         System.out.printf("sqrt(900.0) = %.1f%n", sqrt(900.0));
 8         System.out.printf("ceil(-9.8) = %.1f%n", ceil(-9.8));
 9         System.out.printf("E = %f%n", E);
10         System.out.printf("PI = %f%n", PI);
11      }
12   }
```

```
sqrt(900.0) = 30.0
ceil(-9.8) = -9.0
E = 2.718282
PI = 3.141593
```

**Fig. 8.23** | `static` import of `Math` class methods.

### 8.18 `final` Instance Variables

The principle of least privilege is fundamental to good software engineering. In the context of an app’s code, it states that code should be granted only the amount of privilege and access needed to accomplish its designated operation, but no more. This makes your programs more robust by preventing code from accidentally (or maliciously) modifying variable values and calling methods that should not be accessible.

Let’s see how this principle applies to instance variables. Some should be modifiable, and some should not. You can use the keyword `final` to specify that a variable is not modifiable (i.e., it’s a constant) and that any attempt to modify it is an error. For example,

```
private final int INCREMENT;
```

declares a `final` (constant) `int` instance variable `INCREMENT`. Such variables can be initialized when they’re declared. If they’re not, they must be initialized in every constructor and cannot be changed after the object is constructed. Initializing constants in constructors enables each object of the class to have a different value for the constant. A compilation error occurs if a `final` variable is not initialized in its declaration or in every constructor. By convention, identifiers for constants use all capital letters with words separated by underscores (`_`).

Attempting to modify a `final` instance variable after it’s initialized is a compilation error caught at compilation time rather than execution time. It’s always preferable to get bugs out at compilation time, if possible, rather than at execution time (where experience has shown that repair is often far more costly).

Declaring an instance variable as `final` helps enforce the principle of least privilege. If an instance variable should not be modified, declare it `final` to prevent modification. For example, in [Fig. 8.17](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig17), the instance variables `firstName`, `lastName`, `birthDate` and `hireDate` are never modified after initialization, so they should be declared `final`. Testing, debugging and maintaining programs is easier when every variable that can be `final` is, in fact, `final`. You’ll see additional benefits of `final` in [Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18), [Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads](#ch18.xhtml_ch18).

A `final` field should be `static` if it’s initialized in its declaration to a value that’s the same for all objects of the class. Making the field `static` enables all objects of the class to share the `final` field.

### 8.19 Package Access

If a method or field of a class is not declared with an access modifier, it has **package access** by default. In a program with one class, this has no effect. In a program with multiple classes in the same package, the classes can access each other’s package-access members directly through references to objects of those classes or through the class name for `static` members. Package access is rarely used.

[Figure 8.24](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig24) demonstrates package access. The program contains two classes in one source-code file—class `PackageDataTest` (lines 5–19) and class `PackageData` (lines 22–30). Classes in the same source file are part of the same package. So, `PackageDataTest` is allowed to modify the package-access data of `PackageData` objects. In the `PackageData` class declaration, lines 23–24 declare the instance variables `number` and `string` with no access modifiers—so, these are package-access instance variables. Class `PackageDataTest`’s `main` method creates a `PackageData` object (line 7) then modifies the `PackageData` instance variables directly (lines 13–14). When you compile this program, the compiler produces the files `PackageDataTest.class` and `PackageData.class` and places them in the same folder.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0309-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.24: PackageDataTest.java
 2   // Package-access members of a class are accessible by other classes
 3   // in the same package.
 4
 5   public class PackageDataTest {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         var packageData = new PackageData();
 8
 9         // output String representation of packageData
10         System.out.printf("After instantiation:%n%s%n", packageData);
11
12         // change package access data in packageData object
13         packageData.number = 77;
14         packageData.string = "Goodbye";
15
16         // output String representation of packageData
17         System.out.printf("%nAfter changing values:%n%s%n", packageData);
18      }
19   }
20
21   // class with package access instance variables
22   class PackageData {
23      int number = 0; // package-access instance variable
24      String string = "Hello"; // package-access instance variable
25
26      // return PackageData object String representation
27      public String toString() {
28         return String.format("number: %d; string: %s", number, string);
29      }
30   }
```

```
After instantiation:
number: 0; string: Hello

After changing values:
number: 77; string: Goodbye
```

**Fig. 8.24** | Package-access members of a class are accessible by other classes in the same package.

### 8.20 `record` Classes

Some programming languages provide a fixed-size, immutable data structure called a tuple that simply groups related data items. In those languages, you can pass tuple objects to methods, return them from methods and conveniently access their data items. They basically carry data from one portion of a program to another. Java’s **`record`** **classes**^([8](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_8a)) provide a compact syntax for declaring **data-carrier classes** that enable you to create objects and use them similarly to tuples.

[8](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_8). “JEP 395: Records.” Accessed July 12, 2024\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/395`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/395).

When declaring a `record` class, you specify its instance variable names and types, and the Java compiler conveniently autogenerates “boilerplate” code for you, including:

*   a `private final` instance variable for each of the related data items you specify—a `record`’s instance variables are immutable,^([9](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_9a))

    [9](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_9). In [Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18), [Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads](#ch18.xhtml_ch18), we’ll discuss various benefits of immutable objects in programs that perform operations concurrently.

*   a `public` constructor with arguments to initialize each instance variable—this constructor does not validate its arguments, but you can provide validation code,

*   *get* methods with the same names as the instance variables—each returns its corresponding instance variable’s value,

*   a `toString` method that returns a `record`’s `String` representation in the following form, where *variable1*, *variable2*, … are the instance variable names:

    [Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0310-01)

    ```
    TypeName[variable1=value1,  variable2=value2,  …]
    ```

*   an `equals` method that returns `true` or `false`, based on whether the contents of two `record` objects of the same type have the same contents, and

*   a `hashCode` method—we discuss this method and the data structures concept known as “hashing” in [Section 12.10](#ch12.xhtml_ch12lev1sec10).

##### Defining a `record` Class

[Figure 8.25](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig25) defines the `record` class `Employee` (lines 3–15), representing an employee’s first name (a `String`), last name (a `String`), salary (a `double` for simplicity in this example) and department (a `String`). We broke the program into pieces for discussion purposes. A `record` class begins with the **`record`** **keyword** and a type name followed by parentheses containing the class’s instance variables. After the parentheses, the `record` class’s body is delimited by braces (`{` and `}`). The body’s braces will be empty for `record` classes that require only the default compiler-generated code.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0311-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.25: Records.java
 2   // Demonstrating an Employee record class.
 3   record Employee(
 4      String first,
 5      String last,
 6      double salary,
 7      String department) {
 8
 9      // compact constructor for validation
10      Employee {
11         if (salary < 0.0) {
12            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salary must be >= 0.0");
13         }
14      }
15   }
16
```

**Fig. 8.25** | Demonstrating an `Employee record` class.

You can customize the compiler-generated constructor and methods. For the constructor, `record`s use a shorthand notation (lines 10–14) consisting of the `record` class’s name followed immediately by braces containing the constructor’s data validation code—this code is added to the autogenerated constructor. If the data validation does not throw an exception, the constructor automatically assigns each constructor argument to the corresponding instance variable.

##### `record` Notes

Java `record`s can also declare `static` data, `static` methods and instance methods, and can implement interfaces ([Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09)). Unlike regular Java classes, `record` classes may be declared in a method’s body for use only in that method. For example, a method that reads and processes data from a file might use a local `record` class to create objects for storing and processing the file’s records.
