#### 8.20.1 Pattern Matching for `switch` Expressions

Since `switch` expressions were introduced in Java 14, they’ve been enhanced with reference-type pattern-matching capabilities in Java 21.^([10](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_10a)) Each `case` can specify a reference type and a variable name to which the controlling-expression object is assigned if its type matches the type in a given `case`. That `case` can then manipulate the object via the variable. [Figure 8.26](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig26) defines `record` classes for a `Rectangle` (line 6) with instance variables `length` and `width`, and a `Circle` (line 7) with instance variable `radius`. We use these with the `getPerimeter` method (lines 20–26) to calculate a `Rectangle`’s and a `Circle`’s perimeters. Lines 10–11 in `main` create and initialize a `Rectangle` and a `Circle`. Lines 12–15 display each object’s `String` representation and perimeter.

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0313-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.26: RecordPatternMatchingDemo.java
 2   // Assigning result of a switch expression to a variable.
 3
 4   public class RecordPatternMatchingDemo {
 5      // record classes representing data for a Rectangle and a Circle
 6      record Rectangle(double length, double width) { }
 7      record Circle(double radius) { }
 8
 9      public static void main(String[] args) {
10         Rectangle r = new Rectangle(10, 5);
11         Circle c = new Circle(10);
12         System.out.printf("Rectangle r: %s%nperimeter: %.2f%n%n",
13            r, getPerimeter(r));
14         System.out.printf("Circle c : %s%nperimeter: %.2f%n",
15            c, getPerimeter(c));
16      }
17
18      // uses pattern-matching switch to calculate perimeter of a
19      // Rectangle or Circle; throws IllegalArgumentException for other types
20      public static double getPerimeter(Object shape) {
21         return switch (shape) {
22            case Rectangle r -> 2 * r.length() + 2 * r.width();
23            case Circle c -> 2 * Math.PI * c.radius() ;
24            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid type");
25         };
26      }
27   }
```

```
Rectangle r: Rectangle[length=10.0, width=5.0]
perimeter: 30.00

Circle c : Circle[radius=10.0]
perimeter: 62.83
```

**Fig. 8.26** | Assigning result of a `switch` expression to a variable.

[10](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_10). “JEP 441: Pattern Matching for `switch`.” Accessed July 18, 2024. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/441`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/441).

Method `getPerimeter` (lines 20–26) receives an `Object` and returns the calculation result as a `double`. The parameter type `Object` indicates that the method can receive any reference-type object as an argument. The **pattern-matching** **`switch`** (lines 21–25) determines the type of the object in its controlling expression:

*   If its type matches a `case`, the `switch` stores the object in that `case`’s variable.

*   Then, the expression to the right of the matching `case`’s `->` uses the variable to get the `record` object’s data and perform the appropriate perimeter calculation.

The `default` case executes for any type the `switch` does not recognize. This example `throw`s an `IllegalArgumentException` for anything that is not a `Rectangle` or a `Circle`.

#### 8.20.2 Decomposing `record`s in `switch` Expressions

In pattern-matching `switch` expressions, you can use a **`record`** **pattern**^([11](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_11a)) to automatically assign the values in a `record` object to variables used in the `case`. This is known as **decomposing** **`record`****s**, and it enables you to access the data items without having to call the `record`’s *get* methods. [Figure 8.27](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig27) modifies [Fig. 8.26](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig26), using `record` patterns (lines 23–24) to decompose the `Rectangle` and `Circle` objects. You define a `record` pattern as the `record` class name followed by parentheses containing the variables in which to place a matching object’s values. The pattern’s variable names need not match the `record`’s instance variable names. The `case` can then process the matching object’s data using the pattern’s variables. We used local-variable type inference (`var`) here to infer the pattern’s variable types from the `record` classes’ instance variables. [Figure 8.27](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig27) produces the same results as [Fig. 8.26](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig26).

[11](#ch08.xhtml_fn8_11). “JEP 440: Record Patterns.” Accessed March 24, 2024\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/440`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/440).

[Click here to view code image](#ch08_images.xhtml_f0315-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 8.27: RecordPatternMatchingDemo2.java
 2   // Using record patterns in a switch expression to assign
 3   // record members to variables for use in a given case.
 4
 5   public class RecordPatternMatchingDemo2 {
 6      // record classes representing data for a Rectangle and a Circle
 7      record Rectangle(double length, double width) { }
 8      record Circle(double radius) { }
 9
10      public static void main(String[] args) {
11         Rectangle r = new Rectangle(10, 5);
12         Circle c = new Circle(10);
13         System.out.printf("Rectangle r: %s%nperimeter: %.2f%n%n",
14            r, getPerimeter(r));
15         System.out.printf("Circle c : %s%nperimeter: %.2f%n",
16            c, getPerimeter(c));
17      }
18
19      // uses pattern-matching switch to calculate perimeter of a
20      // Rectangle or Circle; throws IllegalArgumentException for other types
21      public static double getPerimeter(Object shape) {
22         return switch (shape) {
23            case Rectangle(var length, var width) -> 2 * length + 2 * width;
24            case Circle(var radius) -> 2 * Math.PI * radius;
25            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid type");
26         };
27      }
28   }
```

```
Rectangle r: Rectangle[length=10.0, width=5.0]
perimeter: 30.00

Circle c : Circle[radius=10.0]
perimeter: 62.83
```

**Fig. 8.27** | Using `record` patterns in a `switch` expression to assign `record` members to variables for use in a given case.

### 8.21 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, you declared custom classes, created objects of those classes and called their methods to perform useful actions. You declared instance variables to maintain data for each object and methods to operate on that data. We discussed the difference between a method’s local variables and a class’s instance variables, and you saw that instance variables are initialized automatically to default values. You used constructors to specify initial values for an object’s instance variables.

We presented a card-shuffling-and-dealing simulation. The `Time` class case study showed a complete class declaration consisting of `private` data, overloaded `public` constructors for initialization flexibility, *set* and *get* methods for manipulating the class’s data, and methods that returned `String` representations of a `Time` object in standard time and universal time formats. You saw that a class’s `toString` method returns an object’s `String` representation and can be called explicitly or implicitly when an object is used where a `String` is expected. We showed how to `throw` an exception to indicate that a problem has occurred.

You learned that the `this` reference is used implicitly in a class’s instance methods to access the class’s instance variables and other instance methods. You also saw explicit uses of `this` to access the class’s members (including shadowed fields) and, from a constructor, to call another constructor of the same class.

We discussed the differences between default constructors provided by the compiler and no-argument constructors provided by the programmer. You saw that with composition, a class can have references to objects of other classes as members. We discussed more features of `enum` types. We mentioned Java’s garbage-collection capability and how it (unpredictably) reclaims the memory of objects that are no longer used. We motivated `static` fields, and demonstrated how to declare and use `static` fields and methods. You also saw how to declare and initialize `final` fields.

We discussed package access for fields and methods without an access modifier. You saw the relationship between classes in the same package that allows each class to access the package-access members of other classes in the package.

We introduced `record` classes and showed that the Java compiler autogenerates various common methods for them. We also showed how `record` objects can be used with `switch` expressions to perform different operations based on `record` class types. Finally, you used `record` patterns to decompose `record` objects into their individual data items.

We’ve now introduced the basic concepts of control statements, methods, arrays, collections, classes and objects. The next chapter discusses a core aspect of object-oriented programming in Java—inheritance. You’ll see that all classes in Java are related by inheritance, directly or indirectly, to the class called `Object`. You’ll explore how the relationships among classes enable you to build powerful applications.

## 9

## Real-World Modeling with Inheritance, Polymorphism & Interfaces

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this chapter, you’ll:

*   Use inheritance to develop new classes based on existing ones.

*   Understand the relationship between superclasses and subclasses.

*   Create a class that `extends` another class to inherit its attributes and behaviors.

*   Call a superclass method from a subclass override via `super`.

*   Learn how constructors are used in inheritance hierarchies.

*   Learn about class `Object`, the direct or indirect superclass of all classes.

*   Observe how polymorphism can make programming more convenient and systems more easily extensible.

*   Use overridden methods to effect polymorphism.

*   Distinguish between concrete and `abstract` classes.

*   Declare `abstract` methods and `abstract` classes.

*   Declare and implement interfaces and become familiar with `default`, `static` and `private` interface methods.

*   Learn how `protected` gives subclass methods direct access to superclass members.

*   Use `sealed` to control which classes can extend a class or implement an interface.

Outline

### 9.1 Introduction

In [Chapter 1](#ch01.xhtml_ch01), we introduced the basics of object-oriented programming (OOP) in the context of real-world things—automobiles. With the objects-natural approach, you've been creating objects from preexisting classes and conveniently getting them to perform powerful operations without having to know how they’re built on the inside. This is much like driving an automobile without knowing how to build one.

In [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08), you started building custom classes, which are software models of real-world things. Here in [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09), you'll study the key object-oriented technologies of inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces, which enable you to model the relationships and interactions among real-world objects.

##### Inheritance

With inheritance, you can base new classes on existing proven software—a new class is created by acquiring an existing class’s capabilities and possibly modifying them or adding new ones. As you’ll see, this is done without copying and pasting source code.

When creating a class, rather than declaring completely new members, you can specify that the new class should inherit the members of an existing one. The existing class is the **superclass**, and the new class is the **subclass.** A subclass can add its own fields and methods, making it more specialized than its superclass. The subclass exhibits the behaviors of its superclass. It can override them to operate appropriately for the subclass, so inheritance is sometimes called **specialization**. A subclass can become a superclass for future subclasses.

We distinguish between the inheritance ***is-a*** **relationship** and composition’s *has-*a relationship. In an *is-a* relationship, an object of a subclass can also be treated as an object of its superclass. For example, a car *is a* vehicle, and a square *is a* shape. In a *has-a* relation-ship, an object contains as members references to other objects. For example, a car *has a* steering wheel (and a car object *has a* reference to a steering-wheel object).

New classes can inherit from abundant classes in class libraries. Organizations develop their own class libraries and can use others (mostly open-source) available worldwide. This facilitates the rapid development of more powerful, proven and economical software.

##### Polymorphism

We demonstrate **polymorphism** with inheritance hierarchies, which enables you to conveniently “program in the general” rather than “program in the specific.” You can write programs with objects that share the same superclass, either directly or indirectly, as if they were all objects of that superclass—this can simplify programming. Polymorphism’s key concept is relying on each object to “do the right thing”—i.e., what’s appropriate for that type of object in response to the same method call. Thus, the same message sent to various types of objects can have many forms of results, hence the term polymorphism.

With polymorphism, we can design and implement systems that are easily extensible—new classes can be added with little or no modification to the general portions of the program. The new classes simply “plug right in.”

Occasionally, when performing polymorphic processing, we might want to “program in the specific.” We’ll see that a program can determine the type of an object at execution time and act on that object accordingly.

##### Interfaces

We introduce interfaces, which are particularly useful for assigning common functionality to possibly unrelated classes, enabling objects of these classes to be processed polymorphically. Objects of classes that **implement** the same interface can respond to all of that inter-face’s method calls.

Interfaces define and standardize how things, such as people and systems, can interact. For example, a radio’s controls serve as an interface between radio users and the radio’s internal components. The controls allow users to perform a common set of operations (e.g., turn the radio on or off, change the station, adjust the volume and choose between AM and FM). Radios may implement the controls differently (e.g., push buttons, dials and voice commands). The interface specifies *what* operations a radio must permit users to perform but does not specify *how* the operations are performed.^([1](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_1a))

[1](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_1). You’ll see later in this chapter that Java interfaces may define `default` methods that specify *how* operations are performed by default.

**1** Prompt genAIs for examples of how Java’s inheritance, polymorphism and interfaces help us model real-world things.

### 9.2 Superclasses and Subclasses

Often, an object of one class *is an* object of another class as well—e.g., a `CarLoan` *is a* `Loan`, as are `HomeImprovementLoan`s and `MortgageLoan`s. Thus, `CarLoan` can be said to inherit from `Loan`. In this context, `Loan` is a superclass, and `CarLoan` is a subclass. A `CarLoan` is a `Loan` type, but it’s incorrect to claim that every `Loan` is a `CarLoan`—it could be any loan type.

##### Examples of Superclasses and Subclasses

The following table lists several simple examples of superclasses and subclasses. Super-classes tend to be “more general” and subclasses “more specific:”

| Superclass | Subclasses |
| --- | --- |
| `Loan` | `CarLoan`, `HomeImprovementLoan`, `MortgageLoan` |
| `Student` | `GraduateStudent`, `UndergraduateStudent` |
| `Shape` | `Circle`, `Triangle`, `Rectangle`, `Sphere`, `Cube` |
| `Employee` | `Faculty`, `Staff` |
| `BankAccount` | `CheckingAccount`, `SavingsAccount` |
| `Vehicle` | `Car`, `Truck`, `Airplane`, `Boat` |

Because every subclass object *is an* object of its superclass, and one superclass can have many subclasses, the set of objects a superclass represents is often larger than the set of objects any of its subclasses represent. For example, the superclass `Vehicle` represents all vehicles, including `Car`s, `Truck`s, `Airplane`s, `Boat`s, etc. By contrast, subclass `Car` rep-resents a smaller, more specific subset of `Vehicle`s.

##### University Community Member Class Hierarchy

Inheritance relationships form treelike hierarchical structures—a superclass exists in a hierarchical relationship with its subclasses. Let’s consider a sample class hierarchy—also called an **inheritance hierarchy**. A university community can have thousands of members, including employees, students and alumni, as shown in the following UML class diagram. Every class hierarchy begins with class `Object` (in package `java.lang`), which every class directly or indirectly **extends** (or “inherits from”). For just this first diagram, we explicitly show class `Object` at the top of the hierarchy, as all Java classes inherit from it:

![Images](graphics/f0320-02.jpg)

`Employee`s are either `Faculty` or `Staff` members. `Faculty` are either `Administrator`s (e.g., deans and department chairpersons) or `Teacher`s. The hierarchy could contain many other classes. For example, `Student`s can be `Graduate` or `Undergraduate` students. `Undergraduate` students can be `Freshmen`, `Sophomore`s, `Junior`s or `Senior`s, and so on.

Each upward-pointing arrow in this class hierarchy represents an *is-a* relationship. As we follow the arrows, we can state, for example, that “an `Employee` is a `CommunityMember`” and “a `Teacher` is a `Faculty` member.” The **direct superclass** is the superclass from which the subclass explicitly inherits. `CommunityMember` is the direct superclass of the classes `Employee`, `Student` and `Alum`. An **indirect superclass** is any class above the direct superclass in the **class hierarchy**, which defines the inheritance relationships among classes. `CommunityMember` is the indirect superclass of all the classes below `Employee` in the diagram. Starting from the bottom, you can follow the arrows upward and apply the *is-a* relation-ship to the topmost superclass. For example, an `Administrator` *is a* `Faculty` member, *is an* `Employee`, *is a* `CommunityMember` and, of course, *is an* `Object`. [Section 9.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec4) discusses class `Object` in detail.

Java supports **single inheritance**, in which each class derives from one direct super-class. Java does not support multiple inheritance in which a class derives from more than one direct superclass. Later in the chapter, we explain how to use Java interfaces to realize the benefits of multiple inheritance while avoiding associated problems.

##### Shape Hierarchy

Now consider the following `Shape` inheritance hierarchy:

![Images](graphics/f0321-01.jpg)

The hierarchy begins with superclass `Shape`. `Shape`s are either `TwoDimensionalShape`s or `ThreeDimensionalShape`s—the **direct subclasses** of `Shape`. The hierarchy’s third level contains specific `TwoDimensionalShape` and `ThreeDimensionalShape` types. Again, we can follow the arrows from the bottom of the diagram upward to the topmost superclass in this class hierarchy to identify several *is-a* relationships. For example, a `Triangle` *is a* `TwoDimensionalShape` and *is a* `Shape`, while a `Sphere` *is a* `ThreeDimensionalShape` and is *a* `Shape`. This hierarchy could contain many other classes. For example, `Ellipse`s and `Trapezoid`s are also `TwoDimensionalShape`s and a `Cylinder` is a `ThreeDimensionalShape`.

Not every class relationship is an inheritance relationship. For example, [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08) discussed the *has-a* (composition) relationship, in which classes have instance variables that reference objects of other classes. Given `Employee`, `BirthDate` and `TelephoneNumber` classes, it’s improper to say that an `Employee` *is a* `BirthDate` or that an `Employee` *is a* `TelephoneNumber`. However, it is proper to say that an `Employee` *has a* `BirthDate`, and an `Employee` *has a* `TelephoneNumber`.

It’s possible to treat superclass and subclass objects similarly—their commonalities are expressed in the superclass’s members. Objects of all classes that extend (i.e., inherit from) a common superclass can be treated as objects of that superclass—such objects have an *isa* relationship with the superclass.

A subclass can customize the methods it inherits from its superclass. To do this, the subclass method **overrides** (redefines) the superclass method with an implementation appropriate for the subclass.

#### Generative AI

**1** Prompt genAIs to create a text-based `Shape` hierarchy diagram consisting of `TwoDimensionalShapes` and `ThreeDimensionalShapes`. Compare the results to our `Shape` hierarchy diagram.

### 9.3 Relationship Between Superclasses and Subclasses

We now use an inheritance hierarchy of employee types in a company’s payroll application to demonstrate the relationship between superclasses and subclasses:

*   The superclass `SalariedEmployee`s are paid a fixed weekly salary.

*   The subclass `SalariedCommissionEmployee`s receive a weekly salary plus a percentage of their sales.

We divide our discussion of the relationship between these classes into two examples. The first declares class `SalariedEmployee`, which directly inherits from class `Object` and contains the `private` instance variables `name` and `salary`. The second example declares class `SalariedCommissionEmployee`, which directly inherits from `SalariedEmployee` and adds `private` instance variables `grossSales` and `commissionRate` and corresponding methods. It also customizes (i.e., overrides) two inherited `SalariedEmployee` methods. The software reuse provided by inheritance lets us write less code when developing the new subclass than if we had to write it from scratch. Then, we show how a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object can use the inherited `SalariedEmployee public` methods to manipulate (in a controlled manner) the `private` instance variables inherited from `SalariedEmployee`.

#### 9.3.1 Creating and Using a `SalariedEmployee` Class

Let’s examine class `SalariedEmployee` ([Fig. 9.1](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig01)). Line 5 begins the class declaration and indicates that the class **`extends`** (i.e., inherits from) class **`Object`** (from package `java.lang`). This causes class `SalariedEmployee` to inherit `Object`’s methods—it does not have any fields. If you don’t specify which class a new class `extends`, it implicitly `extends Object`. For this reason, you typically will not include “`extends Object`” in your code—we do so in this one example for demonstration purposes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0322-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.1: SalariedEmployee.java
 2   // SalariedEmployee class represents an employee paid a fixed salary.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4
 5   public class SalariedEmployee extends Object {
 6      private final String name;
 7      private BigDecimal salary; // fixed weekly Salary
 8
 9      // two-argument constructor
10      public SalariedEmployee(String name, BigDecimal salary) {
11         // implicit call to Object's default constructor occurs here
12
13         // if salary is invalid throw exception
14         if (salary.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
15            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salary must be >= 0.0");
16         }
17
18         this.name = name;
19         this.salary = salary;
20      }
21
22      // return name
23      public String getName() {return name;}
24
25      // set salary amount
26      public void setSalary(BigDecimal salary) {
27         if (salary.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
28            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salary must be >= 0.0");
29         }
30
31         this.salary = salary;
32      }
33
34      // return salary amount
35      public BigDecimal getSalary() {return salary;}
36
37      // calculate earnings
38      public BigDecimal calculateEarnings() {return getSalary();}
39
40      // return String representation of SalariedEmployee object
41      @Override // indicates that this method overrides a superclass method
42      public String toString() {
43         return String.format("name: %s%nsalary: $%s",
44            getName(), getSalary());
45      }
46   }
```

**Fig. 9.1** | `SalariedEmployee` class represents an employee paid a fixed salary.

##### Overview of Class `SalariedEmployee`’s Methods and Instance Variables

The class declares its instance variables as `private` (lines 6–7), so objects of other classes cannot directly access these variables. Class `SalariedEmployee`’s `public` services include:

*   a constructor (lines 10–20),

*   a `public getName` method (line 23) to *get* the value of the `final` instance variable `name` (line 6),

*   `public` methods `setSalary` and `getSalary` (lines 26–35) to *set* and *get* the instance variable `salary` (line 7),

*   method `calculateEarnings` (line 38) to calculate a `SalariedEmployee`’s earnings, and

*   method `toString` (lines 41–45) to create a `SalariedEmployee`’s `String` representation.

The constructor and `setSalary` each validate their `salary` arguments to ensure they’re greater than or equal to 0 before modifying the instance variable `salary`.

##### Class `SalariedEmployee`’s Constructor

**A superclass’s constructors are not inherited, but can be called by subclasses. In fact, Java requires each subclass constructor to call its direct superclass’s constructor explicitly or implicitly to initialize the inherited superclass instance variables.** We discuss the syntax for calling a superclass constructor explicitly in [Section 9.3.2](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev2sec7).

In this example, `SalariedEmployee`’s constructor implicitly calls class `Object`’s constructor. **If the code does not include an explicit call to the superclass constructor, Java implicitly calls the superclass’s default or no-argument constructor.** The comment in line 11 indicates where Java implicitly calls the superclass `Object`’s default constructor. **Even if a class does not have constructors, the default constructor that the compiler implicitly declares for the class will call the superclass’s default or no-argument constructor.**

We did not validate the `name` argument before assigning it to the `name` instance variable (line 18). We could validate it—perhaps to ensure that the name has a reasonable length.

##### `SalariedEmployee` Member Function `calculateEarnings`

Method `calculateEarnings` (line 38) calls `getSalary` and returns the result. You may wonder why we bother to provide `calculateEarnings` given that we can call `getSalary` directly and get the same result. As you’ll see in [Section 9.3.2](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev2sec7), class `SalariedCommission-Employee` will override `calculateEarnings` to customize how to calculate the earnings for objects of that class. Then, in [Section 9.6](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec6), we’ll show that polymorphism requires methods in each class that have the same signature.

##### `SalariedEmployee` Member Function `toString`

Method `toString` (lines 41–45) returns a `String` containing a `SalariedEmployee` object’s information, which we obtain by calling the class’s *get* methods. Method `toString` is one of the methods that every class inherits directly or indirectly from class `Object` (summarized in [Section 9.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec4)). As you’ve seen, the JVM calls `toString` implicitly when an object must be converted to a `String` representation, such as when you output an object as a `String` with `printf` or format an object as a `String` with `String` method `format`. Class `Object`’s `toString` method returns a `String` that includes the object’s class name and the object’s hashcode (see [Section 9.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec4)). This `toString` is primarily a placeholder a subclass can override to specify an appropriate `String` representation for a subclass object’s data.

`SalariedEmployee`’s `toString` method (lines 41–45) overrides (redefines) the inherited `Object` version. To override a superclass method, a subclass must declare a method with the same signature (method name, number of parameters, parameter types and order of parameter types) as the superclass method. `Object`’s `toString` method takes no parameters, so `SalariedEmployee` declares `toString` with no parameters.

##### `@Override` Annotation

Line 41 uses the optional **`@Override`****annotation** to indicate that the following method declaration (i.e., `toString`) should override an existing superclass method. This annotation helps the compiler catch a few common errors. In this example, we intend to override superclass method `toString`, which is spelled with a lowercase “`t`” and an uppercase “`S`.” If you inadvertently use a lowercase “`s`,” the compiler will flag this as an error because the superclass does not contain a method named `tostring` with a lowercase “`s`.” If you didn’t use the `@Override` annotation, `tostring` would be an entirely different method that would not be called if a `SalariedEmployee` object were used where a `String` was needed.

Another common overriding error is declaring the wrong number or types of parameters in the subclass method’s parameter list. This creates an unintentional overload of the superclass method rather than overriding the existing method. If you then attempt to call the method (with the correct number and types of parameters) on a subclass object, the superclass’s version is invoked—potentially leading to subtle logic errors. When the compiler encounters a method declared with `@Override`, it compares the method’s signature with the superclass’s method signatures. If there isn’t an exact match, the compiler issues an error message, such as “method does not override or implement a method from a super-type.” You can then correct your method’s signature so that it matches one in the super-class.

Though `@Override` is optional, declare overridden methods with it so the compiler can ensure that you defined their signatures correctly. It’s always better to find errors at compile time rather than at runtime. For this reason, the `toString` methods in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)’s examples should have been declared with `@Override` as well.

##### You Cannot Reduce a Method’s Visibility in a Subclass

A `public` superclass method must be `public` in each of that class’s direct and indirect subclass. It’s a compilation error to override a method with a more restricted access modifier:

*   a `public` superclass method cannot be `protected`^([2](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_2a)) or `private` in a subclass and

*   a `protected` superclass method cannot be `private` in a subclass.

[2](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_2). We discuss `protected` in [Section 9.16](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec16).

Doing so would break the *is-a* relationship, which requires that all subclass objects be able to respond to method calls made to `public` methods declared in the superclass. If a `public` method could be overridden as a `private` method, the subclass objects would not be able to respond to the same method calls as superclass objects.

##### Class `SalariedEmployeeTest`

[Figure 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig02) tests class `SalariedEmployee`. Lines 9–10 instantiate a `SalariedEmployee` object. Lines 14–15 use `SalariedEmployee`’s *get* methods to retrieve the object’s instance-variable values for output. Line 17 invokes the object’s `setSalary` method to change the `salary`. Lines 20–23 output the updated `SalariedEmployee`’s `String` representation and earnings. Again, when you output an object using the `%s` format specifier, the JVM implicitly invokes the object’s `toString` method to obtain its `String` representation.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0326-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.2: SalariedEmployeeTest.java
 2   // SalariedEmployee class test program.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4   import java.math.RoundingMode;
 5
 6   public class SalariedEmployeeTest {
 7      public static void main(String[] args) {
 8         // instantiate SalariedEmployee object
 9         var employee = new SalariedEmployee(
10            "Sierra Dembo", new BigDecimal("1000.00"));
11
12         // get SalariedEmployee data
13         System.out.println("Employee information obtained by get methods:");
14         System.out.printf("name: %s%nsalary: $%s%n", employee.getName(),
15            employee.getSalary().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));
16
17         employee.setSalary(new BigDecimal("1200.00")); // change salary
18
19         // display updated information and calculate and display earnings
20         System.out.printf("%n%s:%n%s%n%nearnings: $%s%n",
21            "Updated employee information obtained by toString", employee,
22            employee.calculateEarnings().setScale(
23               2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));
24      }
25   }
```

```
Employee information obtained by get methods:
name: Sierra Dembo
salary: $1000.00

Updated employee information obtained by toString:
name: Sierra Dembo
salary: $1200.00

earnings: $1200.00
```

#### 9.3.2 Creating a `SalariedEmployee`/`SalariedCommissionEmployee` Inheritance Hierarchy

Now, let’s create a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` class ([Fig. 9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig03)) that inherits from class `SalariedEmployee` ([Fig. 9.1](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig01)). A `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object *is a* `SalariedEmployee`, as indicated by line 6’s `extends` clause. Inheritance passes on `SalariedEmployee`’s capabilities to the subclass. A `SalariedCommissionEmployee` also has `BigDecimal gross-Sales` and `commissionRate` instance variables ([Fig. 9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig03), lines 7–8), which we’ll multiply to calculate the commission earned.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0327-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.3: SalariedCommissionEmployee.java
 2   // SalariedCommissionEmployee class inherits from SalariedEmployee and
 3   // accesses the superclass’s private data via inherited public methods.
 4   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 5
 6   public class SalariedCommissionEmployee extends SalariedEmployee {
 7      private BigDecimal grossSales; // gross weekly sales
 8      private BigDecimal commissionRate; // commission percentage
 9
10      // four-argument constructor
11      public SalariedCommissionEmployee(String name, BigDecimal salary,
12         BigDecimal grossSales, BigDecimal commissionRate) {
13
14         super(name, salary); // call superclass constructor
15
16         // if grossSales is invalid throw exception
17         if (grossSales.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
18            throw new IllegalArgumentException("gross sales must be >= 0.0");
19         }
20
21         // if commissionRate is invalid throw exception
22         if (commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 ||
23             commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ONE) >= 0) {
24            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
25               "commission rate must be > 0.0 and < 1.0");
26         }
27
28         this.grossSales = grossSales;
29         this.commissionRate = commissionRate;
30      }
31
32      // set gross sales
33      public void setGrossSales(BigDecimal grossSales) {
34         if (grossSales.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
35            throw new IllegalArgumentException("gross sales must be >= 0.0");
36         }
37
38         this.grossSales = grossSales;
39      }
40
41      // return gross sales
42      public BigDecimal getGrossSales() {return grossSales;}
43
44      // set commission rate
45      public void setCommissionRate(BigDecimal commissionRate) {
46         if (commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 ||
47             commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ONE) >= 0) {
48            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
49               "commission rate must be > 0.0 and < 1.0");
50         }
51
52         this.commissionRate = commissionRate;
53      }
54
55      // return commission rate
56      public BigDecimal getCommissionRate() {return commissionRate;}
57
58      // calculate earnings
59      @Override
60      public BigDecimal calculateEarnings() {
61         return super.calculateEarnings().add(
62            getGrossSales().multiply(getCommissionRate()));
63      }
64
65      // return String representation of SalariedCommissionEmployee
66      @Override
67      public String toString() {
68         return String.format("%s%ngross sales: $%s%ncommission rate: %s",
69            super.toString(), getGrossSales(), getCommissionRate());
70      }
71   }
```

**Fig. 9.3** | `SalariedCommissionEmployee` class inherits from `SalariedEmployee` and accesses the superclass’s `private` data via inherited `public` methods.

##### Inheritance

`SalariedCommissionEmployee` inherits all of `SalariedEmployee`’s members, except its constructor, which is specific to the `SalariedEmployee` superclass. Only the superclass’s `public` and `protected`^([3](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_3a)) members are directly accessible in the subclass. In inheritance, `public` superclass members remain `public` in the subclass, and `protected` ones remain `protected`. There’s only one copy of the inherited members. This makes the code easier to maintain, modify and debug because the code related to a `SalariedEmployee` exists only in that class.

[3](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_3). We discuss `protected` in [Section 9.16](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec16). There are no `protected` members in this class.

##### `SalariedCommissionEmployee` Services Provided to Client Code

Class `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s `public` services ([Fig. 9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig03)) include:

*   its own constructor (lines 11–30),

*   the methods `setGrossSales`, `getGrossSales`, `setCommissionRate`, `getCommissionRate`, `calculateEarnings` and `toString` (lines 33–70), and

*   the `public` methods inherited from `SalariedEmployee`.

The `setGrossSales` (lines 33–39) and `setCommissionRate` (lines 45–53) methods validate their arguments before modifying the instance variables `grossSales` and `commissionRate`:

*   `setGrossSales` ensures that the `grossSales` value is greater than 0, and

*   `setCommissionRate` ensures that the `commissionRate` value is greater than 0 and less than 1.

Recall that `BigDecimal`’s `compareTo` method returns a negative value, zero or a positive value if the method’s caller is less than, equal to or greater than the method’s argument. We compare these return values to 0 to determine whether the `grossSales` are negative (lines 17 and 34) and whether the `commissionRate` is less than or equal to 0 or greater than or equal to 1 (lines 22–23 and 46–47).

Although `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s source code does not contain the inherited `SalariedEmployee` members, they’re nevertheless a part of the subclass. A `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object also contains `SalariedEmployee`’s `private` instance variables, but they’re not directly accessible within the subclass. You can access them only via the inherited `SalariedEmployee public` methods (or `protected` methods if there were any).

##### `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s Constructor

Each subclass constructor must call a constructor in its direct superclass to initialize the instance variables inherited from that superclass. So, instantiating a subclass object begins a chain of constructor calls. For each new object you create, class `Object`’s constructor is always the last constructor called in the chain.

The constructor (lines 11–30) does this explicitly via **superclass constructor call syntax** (line 14), which consists of keyword **`super`**, followed by a set of parentheses containing the superclass constructor arguments—this initializes the inherited superclass instance variables `name` and `salary`. The explicit superclass constructor call must be the first statement in the constructor’s body—this requirement will be relaxed in a future Java version.^([4](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_4a))

[4](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_4). Java 23’s “JEP 482: Flexible Constructor Bodies (Second Preview)” proposes changing this requirement so a subclass constructor can validate its arguments before calling the superclass constructor. This will enable you to prevent unnecessary work in the event that the subclass constructor throws an exception for an invalid argument. See the book’s webpage at [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5) for an example. Accessed September 19, 2024\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/482`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/482).

After calling the superclass constructor, the `SalariedCommissionEmployee` constructor validates the `grossSales` and `commissionRate` arguments and, if valid, assigns them to the corresponding instance variables. When a superclass contains a no-argument constructor, you can use `super()` to call that constructor explicitly, but this is rarely done.

We mentioned in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08) that you should not call a class’s instance methods from its constructor(s). If you follow this advice, you’ll avoid subtle problems caused by calling the class’s overridable methods either directly or indirectly, which can lead to runtime errors—see [Section 9.10](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec10) for additional details.

##### `SalariedCommissionEmployee` Method `calculateEarnings`

`SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s `calculateEarnings` method (lines 59–63) overrides `SalariedEmployee`’s version to calculate a `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s earnings. Line 61 uses the expression

```
super.calculateEarnings()
```

to calculate the portion of the earnings based on `salary`. The method then adds that value to the commission and returns the total earnings.

Note the syntax used to invoke an overridden superclass method from a subclass—you place the keyword `super` and a dot (`.`) separator before the superclass method name. This method invocation is a good software engineering practice—if a method performs all or some of the actions needed by another method, call that method rather than duplicate its code. This reduces code-maintenance problems.^([5](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_5a))

[5](#ch09.xhtml_fn9_5). A downside is that this creates tight coupling between superclass and subclasses that can make large-scale systems difficult to modify. We discuss this further in [Section 9.13](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec13).

When a subclass overrides a superclass method, the subclass version often calls the superclass version to do a portion of the work. Failure to prefix the superclass method name with the keyword `super` and the dot (`.`) separator when calling the superclass’s method causes the subclass method to call itself, potentially creating an error called **infinite recursion**, which would eventually cause the method-call stack to overflow—a fatal runtime error. Recursion, used correctly, is a powerful capability discussed in [Chapter 22](#ch22.xhtml_ch22), [Recursion and Big *O*](#ch22.xhtml_ch22).

##### `SalariedCommissionEmployee` Method `toString`

Similarly, `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s `toString` method ([Fig. 9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig03), lines 66–70) overrides `SalariedEmployee`’s `toString` method. The new version returns a `String` containing `SalariedEmployee`’s `String` representation obtained by the expression in line 69:

```
super.toString()
```

followed by the `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s `grossSales` and `commissionRate`.

[Figure 9.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig04) creates the `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object `employee` (lines 9–11). Lines 14–21 output the `employee`’s data by calling its *get* methods to retrieve the object’s instance variable values. Lines 24–25 use `setGrossSales` and `setCommissionRate` to change the `employee`’s `grossSales` and `commissionRate` values, respectively. Then, lines 28–31 display the `employee`’s updated information and earnings, calling `toString` (implicitly) to get the `employee`’s `String` representation and `calculateEarnings` to get the `employee`’s earnings.

##### Notes on Class `SalariedCommissionEmployee`

We could have copied code from class `SalariedEmployee` and pasted it into class `SalariedCommissionEmployee`, then modified class `SalariedCommissionEmployee` to include `grossSales` and `commissionRate` instance variables and methods to manipulate them. This “copy-and-paste” approach would be error-prone and time-consuming. Worse yet, it spreads copies of the same code throughout a system, creating code-maintenance problems—changes to the duplicated code would need to be made in multiple classes.

With inheritance, the instance variables and methods that are the same for all the classes in the hierarchy are declared in a superclass. Changes made to these common features in the superclass are inherited by the subclasses. Without inheritance, changes would need to be made to all the source-code files that contain a copy of the code in question. By using inheritance and by calling superclass methods that hide the superclass’s `private` data and ensure its consistency, we’ve efficiently and effectively constructed a well-engineered subclass. But can we do better?

##### Class Design

At the design stage in an object-oriented system, you’ll often find that classes share common characteristics. You can identify and “factor out” the common instance variables and methods and place them in a superclass. Then, you can use inheritance to create subclasses that extend these shared characteristics with additional specialized capabilities. Declaring a subclass does not affect its superclass’s source code. While inheritance is a powerful tool, experience has shown that it has weaknesses. [Section 9.13](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec13) discusses why you might prefer composition and interfaces to inheritance.

### 9.4 Class `Object`

All classes in Java inherit directly or indirectly from class `Object` (package `java.lang`), so they all inherit the `Object` methods summarized in the following table. We discuss several of these throughout this book (as indicated in the table).

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `equals` | This method compares two objects for equality and returns `true` if they’re equal and `false` otherwise. The method takes any `Object` as an argument. When objects of a particular class must be compared for equality, the class should override `equals` to compare the contents of the two objects. For the requirements of implementing this method (which include also overriding method `hashCode`), see [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html). The default `equals` implementation uses the `==` operator to determine whether two references refer to the same object in memory. |
| `hashCode` | Returns an object’s hashcode—an `int` value typically used for high-speed storage and retrieval of information in a hashtable data structure ([Section 12.10](#ch12.xhtml_ch12lev1sec10)). This method is also called as part of `Object`’s default `toString` method implementation. |
| `toString` | This method ([Section 9.3.1](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev2sec5)) returns an object’s `String` representation. The default implementation returns the package name and class name of the object’s class, followed by the object’s `hashCode` value. |
| `wait`, `notify`, `notifyAll` | Methods `notify`, `notifyAll` and the three overloaded versions of `wait` are related to multithreading. |
| `getClass` | Every object in Java knows its own type at execution time. Method `getClass` (used in [Section 9.8.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev2sec19)) returns an object of class `Class` (package `java.lang`) containing information about the object’s type, such as its class name (returned by `Class` method `getName`). |
| `clone` | This `protected` method, which takes no arguments and returns an `Object` reference, makes a copy of the object on which it’s called. The default implementation performs a **shallow copy**—instance-variable values in one object are copied into another object of the same type. Only the references are copied for reference types. A typical overridden `clone` method’s implementation would perform a **deep copy** that creates a new object for each reference-type instance variable. Implementing `clone` correctly is difficult. For this reason, its use is discouraged. |

### 9.5 Intro to Polymorphism: Polymorphic Video Game

Suppose we’re designing a video game containing `Martian`s, `Venusian`s, `Plutonian`s, `SpaceShip`s and `LaserBeam`s. Each inherits from a `SpaceObject` superclass with the method `draw` and implements this method appropriately for that subclass.

##### Screen Manager

A screen-manager program maintains an `ArrayList` of `SpaceObject` references to objects of the various classes. The screen manager periodically sends each object the same `draw` message to refresh the screen. Each object responds in its unique way. For example,

*   a `Martian` might draw itself in red with the appropriate number of antennae,

*   a `SpaceShip` might draw itself as a silver flying saucer and

*   a `LaserBeam` might draw itself as a bright red beam across the screen.

The same `draw` message has many forms of results—hence the term polymorphism.

##### Adding New Classes to the System

A polymorphic screen manager facilitates adding new classes to a system with minimal code modifications. Suppose we want to add `Mercurian` objects to our game. We build a class `Mercurian` that inherits from `SpaceObject` and defines method `draw`, then add the object’s reference to the `ArrayList` of `SpaceObject`s. The screen-manager code invokes `draw` the same way for every object the `ArrayList` refers to, regardless of the object’s type. So, the new `Mercurian` objects just “plug right in.”

Polymorphism enables you to deal in generalities and let the execution-time environment concern itself with the specifics. You can direct objects to behave appropriately without knowing their types as long as they belong to the same class hierarchy and are accessed via a superclass variable.

Polymorphism enhances extensibility by allowing software to operate independently of specific object types. New object types can be integrated into a system without altering its core functionality, as long as they can respond to existing messages. Only code that instantiates new objects must be modified to accommodate new types.

### 9.6 Demonstrating Polymorphic Behavior

[Section 9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec3) created a class hierarchy, in which `SalariedCommissionEmployee` inherited from `SalariedEmployee`. The examples in that section manipulated `SalariedEmployee` and `SalariedCommissionEmployee` objects by using references to them to invoke their methods. We aimed a superclass variable at a superclass object and a subclass variable at a subclass object. These assignments are natural and straightforward, as superclass variables are intended to refer to superclass objects, and subclass variables are intended to refer to subclass objects. Other assignments are possible.

In the next example, we aim a superclass reference at a subclass object. We then show how invoking a method on a subclass object via a superclass reference invokes the subclass functionality. **The referenced object’s type, not the variable’s type, determines which method is called.** This example demonstrates that **an object of a subclass can be treated as an object of its superclass**, enabling various interesting manipulations. For example, **a program can create an array of superclass variables that refer to objects of many subclass types**. This is allowed because each subclass object is an object of its superclass. We can assign the reference of a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object to a superclass `SalariedEmployee` variable because a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` *is a* `SalariedEmployee`.

The example in [Fig. 9.5](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig05) demonstrates three ways to use superclass and subclass variables to store references to superclass and subclass objects. The first two are straightforward—we assign a superclass reference to a superclass variable and a subclass reference to a subclass variable. Then, we demonstrate the relationship between subclasses and super-classes (i.e., the *is-a* relationship) by assigning a subclass reference to a superclass variable. This program uses classes `SalariedEmployee` and `SalariedCommissionEmployee` from [Figs. 9.1](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig01) and [9.3](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig03).

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0334-01)

**Fig. 9.5** | Assigning superclass and subclass references to superclass and subclass variables.

##### Creating Superclass and Subclass Objects

Lines 10–11 create a `SalariedEmployee` object and assign its reference to a variable of type `SalariedEmployee`. Lines 14–16 create a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` object and assign its reference to a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` variable. These assignments are natural—for example, a `SalariedEmployee` variable’s primary purpose is to hold a reference to a `SalariedEmployee` object.

##### Calling Superclass Methods Via a Superclass Variable

Lines 19–25 use the superclass variable `salariedEmployee` to invoke `SalariedEmployee` methods `toString` (line 23) and `calculateEarnings` (line 24). Because the variable refers to a `SalariedEmployee` superclass object, the superclass versions of both methods are called.

##### Calling Subclass Methods Via a Subclass Variable

Similarly, lines 28–34 use the subclass variable `salariedCommissionEmployee` to invoke `SalariedCommissionEmployee` methods `toString` (line 32) and `calculateEarnings` (line 33). Because `salariedCommissionEmployee` refers to a `SalariedCommissionEmployee` subclass object, the subclass versions of both methods are called.

##### Calling Subclass Methods Via a Superclass Variable

Line 37 assigns the `SalariedCommissionEmployee` subclass object referenced by `salaried-CommissionEmployee` to the superclass `SalariedEmployee` variable `salariedEmployee2`. Lines 38–44 use this superclass variable to invoke `SalariedCommissionEmployee` subclass methods `toString` (line 42) and `calculateEarnings` (line 43). **When a superclass variable refers to a subclass object and is used to call a method, the subclass version of the method is called.** Hence, lines 42–43 call class `SalariedCommissionEmployee`’s methods `toString` and `calculateEarnings`. The Java compiler allows assigning a subclass object to a superclass variable because **an object of a subclass *is an* object of its superclass** (but not vice versa).

When the compiler encounters a method call made through a variable, the compiler determines if the method can be called by checking the variable’s class type. The call is compiled if that class contains the proper method declaration (or inherits one). **At execution time, the type of the object to which the variable refers determines the actual method to use.** This process—called **dynamic binding**—enables polymorphic behavior.

### 9.7 `abstract` Classes and Methods

Sometimes, it’s useful to declare **abstract classes** for which you never intend to create objects. We refer to them as **abstract superclasses** because**t**hey’re used only as superclasses in inheritance hierarchies. As we’ll soon see, these classes cannot be used to instantiate objects because they’re incomplete. We demonstrate an abstract class in [Section 9.8](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec8)’s code example.

##### Purpose of `abstract` Classes

An `abstract` class provides a superclass from which other classes can inherit and thus share a common design. In [Section 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec2)’s `Shape` hierarchy, for example, subclasses inherit the notion of what it means to be a `Shape`—perhaps common attributes such as `location`, `fillPattern`, `color` and `borderThickness`, and behaviors such as `draw`, `move`, `resize`, `rotate` and `setColor`.

Classes used to instantiate objects are called **concrete classes**. Such classes implement every method they declare (some implementations might be inherited). For example, we could derive concrete classes `Circle`, `Square` and `Triangle` from the `abstract` superclass `TwoDimensionalShape`. Similarly, we could derive concrete classes `Sphere`, `Cube` and `Tetrahedron` from the `abstract` superclass `ThreeDimensionalShape`.

`abstract` superclasses are too general to instantiate real objects—they specify only commonality among subclasses. We need to be more specific before we can instantiate objects. For example, if you send the `draw` message to `abstract` class `TwoDimensionalShape`, the class knows that two-dimensional shapes should be drawable, but it does not know what specific shape to draw, so it cannot implement a real `draw` method. **Concrete classes provide the specifics that make it possible to instantiate objects.**

Not all hierarchies contain `abstract` classes. However, you’ll often write client code that uses only variables of `abstract` superclass types to reduce the client code’s dependencies on a range of subclass types. For example, **you can write a method that receives an** **abstract superclass type parameter. When called, such a method can receive an object of any concrete class that directly or indirectly** **`extends`** **that superclass.**

`abstract` classes sometimes constitute several levels of a hierarchy. For example, In [Section 9.2](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec2)’s `Shape` hierarchy, class `Shape` and its direct subclasses `TwoDimensionalShape` and `ThreeDimensionalShape` would each be `abstract` because they are not specific enough to determine the actual shape. The hierarchy’s third level declares concrete `TwoDimensionalShape`s(`Circle`, `Square` and `Triangle`) and `ThreeDimensionalShape`s (`Sphere`, `Cube` and `Tetrahedron`).

##### Declaring an `abstract` Class and `abstract` Methods

You declare a class `abstract` by placing the **`abstract`** **keyword** before the `class` keyword. An `abstract` class declares common attributes and behaviors (`abstract` and concrete) for the classes in a class hierarchy. An `abstract` class’s instance variables and concrete methods are subject to the standard rules of inheritance.

An `abstract` class normally contains one or more **`abstract`****methods**, but this is not required. An `abstract` method is an instance method declared `abstract`, as in

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0337-01)

```
public abstract void draw(); // abstract method
```

**`abstract`** **methods do not provide implementations.** A class containing any `abstract` methods must be explicitly declared `abstract`. Subclasses must declare the “missing piece(s),” if any, to become concrete classes from which you can instantiate objects. So, a concrete subclass of an `abstract` class must provide a concrete implementation for each `abstract` method. Otherwise, the subclass must be declared `abstract`.

##### Some Methods Cannot Be `abstract`

**Constructors and** **`static`** **methods cannot be** **`abstract`**. Constructors are not inherited, so an `abstract` constructor could never be implemented. Though non-`private static` methods are inherited, they cannot be overridden. An `abstract` method is meant to be overridden for polymorphic processing of objects. A `static` method is associated with a class, not specific objects, so declaring a `static` method `abstract` would not make sense.

##### Using `abstract` Classes to Declare Variables

Although we cannot instantiate objects of `abstract` superclasses, you’ll soon see that **we can use an** **`abstract`** **superclass to declare variables that can refer to objects of any concrete class derived from that superclass. We’ll use such variables to manipulate subclass objects polymorphically.** You can also use `abstract` superclass names to invoke `static` methods declared in those `abstract` superclasses.

##### Layered Software Systems

Polymorphism is particularly effective for implementing so-called layered software systems. In operating systems, for example, each physical device type could operate quite differently. Even so, commands to read or write data from and to devices may have a certain uniformity. For each device, the operating system uses software called a device driver to control all communication between the system and the device. The write message sent to a device-driver object needs to be interpreted specifically in the context of that driver and how it manipulates devices of a specific type. However, the write call to one device is no different from the write to any other device in the system—place some number of bytes from memory onto that device.

An object-oriented operating system might use an `abstract` superclass to provide a common “interface” appropriate for all device drivers. Then, subclasses that behave similarly are formed through inheritance from that `abstract` superclass. The device-driver methods are declared as `abstract` methods in the superclass. The implementations of these `abstract` methods are provided in the concrete subclasses that correspond to the specific types of device drivers. New devices are constantly being developed, often long after the operating system has been released. When you buy a new device, it comes with a device driver provided by the device vendor. The device is immediately operational after you install the driver and connect the device to your computer. The new devices and their drivers “plug right in.” This is another elegant example of how polymorphism makes systems extensible.

**1** Prompt genAIs, asking why we would want to declare a Java class `abstract` even if it has no `abstract` methods.

### 9.8 Case Study: Payroll System Using Polymorphism

Let’s use an `abstract` class and polymorphism to calculate payroll for two employee types. We create an `Employee` hierarchy to solve the following problem:

A company pays its employees weekly. The employees are of two types:

1.  Salaried employees receive a fixed salary regardless of their hours worked.

2.  Commission employees receive a percentage of their sales.

For the current pay period, the company has decided to reward salaried employees by raising their salaries by 10%. The company wants to implement a program that performs its payroll calculations polymorphically.

##### `Employee` Hierarchy

We use the `abstract` class `Employee` to represent the general concept of an employee and define the “interface” to the hierarchy—that is, the methods all `Employee` subclasses must have so a program can invoke those methods on all `Employee` objects. Classes `SalariedEmployee` and `CommissionEmployee` inherit directly from `Employee`. The following UML class diagram shows our polymorphic payroll application’s inheritance hierarchy. The `abstract` class name `Employee` is italicized, per UML convention.

![Images](graphics/f0338-01.jpg)

The `abstract` superclass `Employee` declares the “interface” to the hierarchy—that is, the methods that a program can invoke on all `Employee` objects throughout the hierarchy. We use the term “interface” here in a general sense to refer to the various ways programs can communicate with objects of any `Employee` subclass. Be careful not to confuse the general notion of an “interface” with the formal notion of a Java interface ([Section 9.11](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec11)). Each employee, regardless of how their earnings are calculated, has a name, so we’ll declare the `private` instance variable `name` in the `abstract` superclass `Employee`.

The following diagram shows each class in the hierarchy down the left side and methods `calculateEarnings` and `toString` across the top. For each class, the diagram shows the desired results of each method. We do not list superclass `Employee`’s `getName` method because it’s not overridden by any subclasses—it’s inherited and used “as is.”

![Images](graphics/f0339-01.jpg)

The following sections implement the `Employee` class hierarchy. The first declares `abstract` superclass `Employee`. Each of the next two sections implements one of the concrete subclasses. The last section implements a test program that builds objects of all these classes and processes them polymorphically.

#### 9.8.1 `abstract` Superclass `Employee`

Class `Employee` ([Fig. 9.6](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig06)) provides methods `getName`, `toString` and `calculateEarnings`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0339-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.6: Employee.java
 2   // Employee abstract superclass.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4
 5   public abstract class Employee {
 6      private final String name;
 7
 8      // constructor
 9      public Employee(String name) {this.name = name;}
10
11      // return name
12      public String getName() {return name;}
13
14      // return String representation of Employee object
15      @Override
16      public String toString() {return String.format("name: %s", getName());}
17
18      // abstract method must be overridden by concrete subclasses
19      public abstract BigDecimal calculateEarnings(); // no implementation
20   }
```

**Fig. 9.6** | `Employee abstract` superclass.

Class `Employee`’s declaration ([Fig. 9.6](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig06)) includes:

*   a constructor (line 9) that receives a `String` to initialize the `final` instance variable `name` (declared at line 6)—the constructor does not validate its parameters in this example,

*   a `getName` method to return the `name` (line 12),

*   a `toString` method (lines 15–16) to return the `String` representation of an `Employee`, and

*   an `abstract` method `calculateEarnings` (line 19)—this will be overridden by each concrete `Employee` subclass.

Each `Employee` subclass will override `toString` to create a `String` representation that contains all of the employee’s information.

##### `abstract` Method `calculateEarnings`

Why did we declare `calculateEarnings` as an `abstract` method? Calculating earnings certainly applies to all employees. However, we cannot calculate the earnings for the general notion of an `Employee`—we first must know the specific `Employee`. Declaring this method `abstract` indicates that each concrete subclass must override `calculateEarnings` with an appropriate implementation.

You cannot create `Employee` objects directly because `Employee` is an `abstract` class. However, due to inheritance, every object of any `Employee` subclass *is an* `Employee` and thus is guaranteed to provide method `calculateEarnings`. So, a program can invoke the method polymorphically on any object that *is an* `Employee` via a superclass `Employee` variable.

In [Section 9.8.4](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev2sec19), we’ll create an array of superclass `Employee` variables, each referencing a subclass object that *is an* `Employee`. The program will iterate through the array, polymorphically calling `calculateEarnings` on each object. The compiler allows calls to method `calculateEarnings` via `Employee` variables because it’s declared in class `Employee`—again, the variable’s type determines which methods a program can call using that variable.

#### 9.8.2 Concrete Subclass `SalariedEmployee`

Class `SalariedEmployee` ([Fig. 9.7](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig07)) extends class `Employee` (line 5) and overrides `abstract` method `calculateEarnings` (lines 33–34), which makes `SalariedEmployee` a concrete class. The class includes:

*   a constructor (lines 9–18) that receives a `name` and a `salary` and passes the name to superclass `Employee`’s constructor (line 10) to initialize `Employee`’s `private` instance variable;

*   a `setSalary` method to assign a new nonnegative value to the `salary` instance variable (lines 21–27),

*   a `getSalary` method to return `salary`’s value (line 30),

*   a `calculateEarnings` method (lines 33–34) that overrides the superclass version to calculate a `SalariedEmployee`’s earnings and

*   a `toString` method (lines 37–41) that overrides the superclass version to return a `String` including the information returned by superclass `Employee`’s `toString` and `SalariedEmployee`’s `getSalary` methods.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0341-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.7: SalariedEmployee.java
 2   // SalariedEmployee concrete class extends abstract class Employee.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4
 5   public class SalariedEmployee extends Employee {
 6      private BigDecimal salary; // fixed weekly Salary
 7
 8      // constructor
 9      public SalariedEmployee(String name, BigDecimal salary) {
10         super(name);
11
12         // if salary is invalid throw exception
13         if (salary.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
14            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salary must be >= 0.0");
15         }
16
17         this.salary = salary;
18      }
19
20      // set salary amount
21      public void setSalary(BigDecimal salary) {
22         if (salary.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
23            throw new IllegalArgumentException("salary must be >= 0.0");
24         }
25
26         this.salary = salary;
27      }
28
29      // return salary amount
30      public BigDecimal getSalary() {return salary;}
31
32      // calculate earnings
33      @Override
34      public BigDecimal calculateEarnings() {return getSalary();}
35
36      // return String representation of SalariedEmployee object
37      @Override // indicates that this method overrides a superclass method
38      public String toString() {
39         return String.format("%s%nsalary: $%s",
40            super.toString(), getSalary());
41      }
42   }
```

**Fig. 9.7** | `SalariedEmployee` concrete class extends `abstract` class `Employee`.

Method `calculateEarnings` overrides `Employee`’s `abstract` method to provide a concrete implementation that returns the `SalariedEmployee`’s `salary`. If we do not implement `calculateEarnings`, class `SalariedEmployee` must be declared `abstract`. Of course, we want class `SalariedEmployee` to be concrete in this example.

Method `toString` (lines 37–41) overrides `Employee`’s `toString`. If class `SalariedEmployee` did not override `toString`, it would inherit `Employee`’s version. In that case, class `SalariedEmployee`’s `toString` method would return only the `name`, which does not adequately represent a `SalariedEmployee`.

#### 9.8.3 Concrete Subclass `CommissionEmployee`

Class `CommissionEmployee` ([Fig. 9.8](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig08)) extends class `Employee` (line 5). The class includes:

*   a constructor (lines 10–28) that receives a name, a gross sales amount and a commission rate and passes the name to superclass `Employee`’s constructor (line 12) to initialize `Employee`’s `private` instance variable;

*   *set* methods (lines 31–37 and 43–51) to assign valid new values to instance variables `grossSales` and `commissionRate`;

*   *get* methods (lines 40 and 54) to return the values of `grossSales` and `commissionRate`;

*   a `calculateEarnings` method (lines 57–60) that overrides the superclass version to calculate a `CommissionEmployee`’s earnings; and

*   a `toString` method (lines 63–67) that overrides the superclass version to return a `String` including the information returned by superclass `Employee`’s `toString` and `CommissionEmployee`’s `getGrossSales` and `getCommissionRate` methods.

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0342-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.8: CommissionEmployee.java
 2   // CommissionEmployee class extends Employee.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4
 5   public class CommissionEmployee extends Employee {
 6      private BigDecimal grossSales; // gross weekly sales
 7      private BigDecimal commissionRate; // commission percentage
 8
 9      // constructor
10      public CommissionEmployee(String name,
11         BigDecimal grossSales, BigDecimal commissionRate) {
12         super(name);
13
14         // if grossSales is invalid throw exception
15         if (grossSales.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
16            throw new IllegalArgumentException("gross sales must be >= 0.0");
17         }
18
19         // if commissionRate is invalid throw exception
20         if (commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 ||
21             commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ONE) >= 0) {
22            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
23               "commission rate must be > 0.0 and < 1.0");
24         }
25
26         this.grossSales = grossSales;
27         this.commissionRate = commissionRate;
28      }
29
30      // set gross sales
31      public void setGrossSales(BigDecimal grossSales) {
32         if (grossSales.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) < 0) {
33            throw new IllegalArgumentException("gross sales must be >= 0.0");
34         }
35
36         this.grossSales = grossSales;
37      }
38
39      // return gross sales
40      public BigDecimal getGrossSales() {return grossSales;}
41
42      // set commission rate
43      public void setCommissionRate(BigDecimal commissionRate) {
44         if (commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 ||
45             commissionRate.compareTo(BigDecimal.ONE) >= 0) {
46            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
47               "commission rate must be > 0.0 and < 1.0");
48         }
49
50         this.commissionRate = commissionRate;
51      }
52
53      // return commission rate
54      public BigDecimal getCommissionRate() {return commissionRate;}
55
56      // calculate earnings
57      @Override
58      public BigDecimal calculateEarnings() {
59         return getGrossSales().multiply(getCommissionRate());
60      }
61
62      // return String representation of CommissionEmployee
63      @Override
64      public String toString() {
65         return String.format("%s%ngross sales: $%s%ncommission rate: %s",
66            super.toString(), getGrossSales(), getCommissionRate());
67      }
68   }
```

**Fig. 9.8** | `CommissionEmployee` class extends `Employee`.

#### 9.8.4 Polymorphic Processing, Operator `instanceof` and Downcasting

[Figure 9.9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09fig09) tests our `Employee` hierarchy. Lines 9–12 create a `SalariedEmployee` object and a `CommissionEmployee` object. The program manipulates these objects non-polymorphically, via variables of each object’s own type, then polymorphically, using an array of `Employee` variables. While processing the objects polymorphically, the program increases the salary of each `SalariedEmployee` by 10%—this requires determining the object’s type at execution time. Finally, the program polymorphically determines and outputs the type of each object in the `Employee` array. Lines 14–21 output each object’s `String` representation and earnings non-polymorphically, using the `salariedEmployee` variable to call the `SalariedEmployee` methods and the `commissionEmployee` variable to call the `Commission-Employee` methods. Each object’s `toString` method is called implicitly by `printf` when the object is output as a `String` with the `%s` format specifier (lines 16 and 19).

[Click here to view code image](#ch09_images.xhtml_f0344-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 9.9: PayrollSystemTest.java
 2   // Employee hierarchy test program.
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4   import java.math.RoundingMode;
 5
 6   public class PayrollSystemTest {
 7      public static void main(String[] args) {
 8         // create subclass objects
 9         var salariedEmployee = new SalariedEmployee("Sierra Dembo",
10            new BigDecimal("1000.00"));
11         var commissionEmployee = new CommissionEmployee("James Davis",
12            new BigDecimal("10000.00"), new BigDecimal("0.06"));
13
14         System.out.println("Employees processed individually:");
15
16         System.out.printf("%s%nearned: $%s%n%n", salariedEmployee,
17            salariedEmployee.calculateEarnings().setScale(
18               2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));

20            commissionEmployee.calculateEarnings().setScale(
21               2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));
22
23         // create and initialize Employee array
24         Employee[] employees = {salariedEmployee, commissionEmployee};
25
26         System.out.println("Employees processed polymorphically:");
27
28         // generically process each element in array employees
29         for (Employee currentEmployee : employees) {
30            System.out.println(currentEmployee); // invokes toString
31
32            // determine whether element is a SalariedEmployee
33            if (currentEmployee instanceof SalariedEmployee employee) {
34               employee.setSalary(
35                  employee.getSalary().multiply(new BigDecimal("1.10")));
36
37               System.out.printf(
38                  "new salary with 10%% increase is: $%s%n",
39                  employee.getSalary().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));
40            }
41
42            System.out.printf("earned: $%s%n%n",
43               currentEmployee.calculateEarnings().setScale(
44                  2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN));
45         }
46
47         // get type name of each object in employees array
48         for (int j = 0; j < employees.length; ++j) {
