If the `Path` represents a directory (line 31), lines 35–36 use the **`Files`** **class’s** **`static`** **method** **`newDirectoryStream`** to get a `DirectoryStream<Path>` containing `Path` objects for the directory’s contents. `DirectoryStream` is a generic type like `ArrayList`. Lines 38–40 display the `String` representation of each `Path` in the `DirectoryStream<Path>`.

Once you’ve confirmed that a `Path` exists, the methods [Fig. 11.1](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig01) demonstrates may still throw `IOException`s—we do not `catch` these checked exceptions in this program, so we added a `throws` clause to `main` (line 10). For example, the file or directory represented by the `Path` could be deleted from the system after the call to `Files` method `exists` and before the other statements in lines 20–41 execute. Industrial strength file- and directory-processing programs require extensive exception handling to deal with such possibilities.

##### Separator Characters

A **separator character** is used to separate directories and files in a path. On a Windows computer, the separator character is a backslash (`\`). On a Linux or macOS system, it’s a forward slash (`/`). Java processes both characters identically in a pathname.

When building `Path` objects, the `Path` method `of` can handle the separator characters for you. For example, the statement

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0412-01)

```
Path documentsPath =
   Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"), "Documents");
```

creates a `Path` object representing your user account’s `Documents` folder. The call

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0412-02)

```
System.getProperty("user.home")
```

uses the **`System`** **class’s** **`getProperty`** **method** to get your user account’s folder (represented by `"user.home"`). On a Windows system, this would represent the path

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0412-03)

```
c:\Users\YourAccount\Documents
```

and on macOS, this would represent the path

```
/Users/YourAccount/Documents
```

We’ll use this capability in subsequent examples.

### 11.4 Sequential Text Files

Next, we create and manipulate sequential files in which records^([3](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_3a)) are stored in order by the record-key field. We begin with text files, enabling the reader to quickly create and edit human-readable files. We discuss creating, writing data to, reading data from and updating sequential text files. We’ll use binary files to read and write images and audio files in **[Chapter 19](#ch19.xhtml_ch19), [Building API-Based Java Generative AI Applications](#ch19.xhtml_ch19)**.

[3](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_3). In this chapter, we use the term “record” to refer to records in a file. Many examples also use `record` classes. When we refer to a `record` class, we format the word “`record`” using a computer font.

#### 11.4.1 Creating a Sequential Text File

Java imposes no structure on a file—notions such as records do not exist as part of the Java language. Therefore, you must structure files to meet the requirements of your programs. The following example shows how to impose a keyed record structure on a file.

The program in this section creates a simple sequential file that might be used in an accounts receivable system to keep track of the amounts owed to a company by its credit clients. For each client, the program obtains from the user an account number and the client’s name and balance (i.e., the amount the client owes the company for goods and services received). Each client’s data constitutes a record for that client. This program uses the account number as the record key—we will write the file’s records in account-number order. In a comprehensive accounts-receivable system (based on sequential files) that includes data input, a sorting capability would be provided so users could enter the records in any order. The records would then be sorted and written to the file.

##### Class `CreateTextFile`

Class `CreateTextFile` ([Fig. 11.2](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig02)) uses a `Formatter` to output formatted `String`s, using the same formatting features as `System.out.printf`. We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes. Line 8 declares the `record` class `Account` to represent an `Account`’s `accountNumber`, `name` and `balance`—for this chapter’s examples, we use only last names.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0413-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.2: CreateTextFile.java
 2   // Writing data to a sequential text file with class Formatter.
 3   import java.util.Formatter;
 4   import java.nio.file.Path;
 5   import java.util.List;
 6
 7   // record class to represent an account
 8   record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
 9
```

**Fig. 11.2** | Writing data to a sequential text file with class `Formatter`.

##### `List<Account>` and `List static` Method `of`

[Section 6.20](#ch06.xhtml_ch06lev1sec20) introduced the generic class `ArrayList` for creating dynamically resizable array-like data structures. As you’ll see in [Chapter 12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12), [Generic Collections](#ch12.xhtml_ch12), the **generic** **`List`** **interface** (package `java.util`) specifies the common features for lists of objects, like `ArrayList`s.

Many of this chapter’s examples use the same five `Account` objects without changing their data. For such cases, the **`List static`** **method** **`of`** creates and returns an immutable (unmodifiable) object that implements the `List` interface and contains the method’s arguments. Immutable means you cannot add objects to or remove objects from the `List` after you create it. The `List`’s element type is determined from `of`’s arguments. Lines 13–19 create a `List<Account>` containing the five `Account` objects we’ll write to the text file in this example.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0414-01)

```
10   public class CreateTextFile {
11      public static void main(String[] args) {
12         // account data to write to a text file
13         List<Account> accounts = List.of(
14            new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
15            new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67),
16            new Account(300, "Huber", 0.00),
17            new Account(400, "Ito", -42.16),
18            new Account(500, "Lopez", 224.62)
19         );
20
```

##### `Path` to the `clients.txt` File

Lines 22–23 create a `Path` object representing the `clients.txt` file. This example writes the file into your user account’s `Documents` folder.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0414-02)

```
21         // Path to clients.txt in the user's Documents folder
22         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
23            "Documents", "clients.txt");
24
```

##### Using a `Formatter` to Write the `Account`s to a File

A `Formatter` object can output to various locations, such as a command window or a file, as we do in this example. Line 26 creates the `Formatter` in the `try`-with-resources statement (introduced in [Section 10.12](#ch10.xhtml_ch10lev1sec12)). Recall that `try`-with-resources closes its resource(s) when the `try` block terminates successfully or due to an exception. This ensures we close the file when we no longer need it so other programs can use it. The `Formatter` constructor we use here takes one argument—a `String` containing the file’s location and name. We call the `filePath` object’s `toString` method to get its `String` representation. If you were to specify only the file’s name, the JVM would assume the file is in the directory from which you execute the program. For text files, we use the `.txt` file extension. If the file does not exist, the `Formatter` constructor will create it. If no exception occurs, the file is open for writing, and the `Formatter` object can be used to write data to the file.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0415-01)

```
25         // open clients.txt, output data to the file then close clients.txt
26         try (var output = new Formatter(filePath.toString())) {
27            // output each Account to file
28            for (var account : accounts) {
29               output.format("%d %s %.2f%n", account.accountNumber(),
30                  account.name(), account.balance());
31            }
32
33            System.out.printf(
34               "Text file created at: %s%n", filePath.toAbsolutePath());
35         }
36         catch (Exception e) {
37            System.err.printf(
38               "Error writing text file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
39         }
40      }
41   }
```

```
Text file created at: C:\Users\pauldeitel\Documents\clients.txt
```

If no exception occurs while opening the file, lines 28–31 output each `Account`’s data using **`Formatter`****’s** **`format`** **method**, which works like `System.out.printf` but writes a formatted `String` to the `Formatter` object’s output destination (the file `clients.txt`). The format string `"%d %s %.2f%n"` indicates that the current record will be stored as an `int` (the account number) followed by a `String` (the name) and a `double` (the balance). We separate each piece of information from the next by a space and output the `double` value with two digits of precision.

When the `try` block terminates, the `try`-with-resources statement closes the `Formatter` and the underlying output file by calling **`Formatter`** **method** **`close`**. If a program does not explicitly call method `close`, the operating system will close the file when program execution terminates—an example of operating-system “termination housekeeping.” You should always explicitly close a file when it’s no longer needed.

##### Possible Exceptions

Line 36 catches any `Exception`s that occur in the `try` block. There are several:

*   A **`SecurityException`** occurs if the user does not have permission to write data to the file opened in line 26.

*   A **`FileNotFoundException`** occurs if the file does not exist and a new file cannot be created or if there’s an error opening the file in line 26.

*   A **`FormatterClosedException`** occurs if the `Formatter` object is closed when you attempt to use it in lines 29–30 to write into a file.

For these exceptions, we display that there was an error writing the file and show the exception’s message.

##### Caution: Check Whether a File Exists Before Opening It for Writing

In general, you should use the features in [Fig. 11.1](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig01) to check whether a file exists before you open it for output. Opening an existing file for output **truncates** its contents—all the data in the file is discarded.

##### Sample Output

This program’s output simply indicates that it wrote the `Account`s into `clients.txt`. It does not show how the data records actually appear in the file. In [Section 11.4.2](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev2sec8), we present a program that reads the file and prints its contents to verify that the file was created successfully. Because this is a text file, you can also verify the information simply by opening the file in a text editor.

#### 11.4.2 Reading Data from a Sequential Text File

We store data in files so we can retrieve it for processing when needed. In [Fig. 11.3](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig03), we read the data sequentially from the file `"clients.txt"` created by the program of [Fig. 11.2](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig02). Previously, we’ve used `Scanner`s to input data from the user. Here, we use one to input each record from the file and display its contents.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0416-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.3: ReadTextFile.java
 2   // Reading a text file using a Scanner.
 3   import java.nio.file.Path;
 4   import java.util.Scanner;
 5
 6   public class ReadTextFile {
 7      public static void main(String[] args) {
 8         // Path to clients.txt in user's Documents folder
 9         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
10            "Documents", "clients.txt");
11
12         // open clients.txt, read its contents and close the file
13         try (var input = new Scanner(filePath)) {
14            System.out.printf("%-10s%-12s%10s%n",
15               "Account", "Name", "Balance");
16
17            // read record from file
18            while (input.hasNext()) { // while there is more to read
19               // display record contents
20               System.out.printf("%-10d%-12s%10.2f%n",
21                  input.nextInt(), input.next(), input.nextDouble());
22            }
23         }
24         catch (Exception e) {
25            System.err.printf(
26               "Error reading file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
27         }
28      }
29   }
```

```
Account   Name     Balance
100       Devi       24.98
200       Taylor    345.67
300       Huber       0.00
400       Ito       -42.16
500       Lopez     224.62
```

**Fig. 11.3** | Reading a text file using a `Scanner`.

The `try`-with-resources statement (line 13) opens the file for reading by creating a `Scanner` object. We pass a `Path` object to the constructor, which specifies that the `Scanner` object will read from the file `"clients.txt"` in the user’s `Documents` folder.

Lines 14–15 display headers for the columns in the program’s output. Lines 18–22 read and display the file’s content until end-of-file is reached—in which case, the `hasNext` method will return `false` at line 18\. Lines 20–21 use `Scanner` methods `nextInt`, `next` and `nextDouble` to input an `int` (the account number), a `String` (the name) and a `double` (the balance). Each record is one line of text in the file.

The format string in line 20 left-aligns the account number and name and right-aligns the balance with two digits of precision. Each iteration of the loop inputs one line (record) from the text file. When the loop terminates and line 23 is reached, the `try`-with-resources statement implicitly calls the **`Scanner`****’s** **`close`** **method** to close the `Scanner` and the file.

##### Potential Exceptions

Several exceptions can occur in the `try` block:

*   If the `Scanner` cannot open the file in line 14, an `IOException` occurs.

*   If the information in the file is not correctly formatted (e.g., there’s a name where there should be a balance), a `InputMismatchException` occurs when the record is input.

*   If the `Scanner` is closed before the data is input, an **`IllegalStateException`** occurs.

These exceptions are handled by lines 25–28.

#### 11.4.3 Updating Sequential Files

The data in many sequential files cannot be modified without the risk of destroying other data in the file. For example, if you need to change the name “`Pappas`” to “`Papadopoulou`”, the old name cannot simply be overwritten, because the new name requires more space. The record for `Pappas` was written to the file as

```
300 Pappas 0.00
```

If you were to rewrite the record beginning at the same location in the file using the new name, the record would be

```
300 Papadopoulou 0.00
```

The new record is larger (has more characters) than the original record. “`Papadopoulou`” would overwrite the “`0.00`” in the current record, and the characters beyond the last “`u`” in “`Papadopoulou`” would overwrite the beginning of the next sequential record in the file.

The problem here is that fields in a text file—and hence records—can vary in size. For example, 7, 14, –117, 2074 and 27383 are all `int`s stored in the same number of bytes (4) internally, but they’re different-sized fields when written to a file as text. Therefore, you do not usually update records in a sequential file in place—instead, you rewrite the entire file. To make the preceding name change:

*   the records before `300 Pappas 0.00` would be copied to a new file,

*   the new record (which can be of a different size than the one it replaces) would be written and

*   the records after `300 Pappas 0.00` would be copied to the new file.

Rewriting the entire file is uneconomical to update just one record, but reasonable if a substantial number of records need to be updated.

### 11.5 Case Study: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Serialization

More and more computing today is done “in the cloud”—that is, distributed across the Internet. Many applications you use daily communicate over the Internet with **cloud-based services** that use massive clusters of computing resources (computers, processors, memory, storage, databases, etc.).

A service that provides access to itself over the Internet is known as a **web service**. Applications typically communicate with web services by sending and receiving **JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)** objects. JSON is a text-based, human- and computer-readable data-interchange format that represents objects as collections of name-value pairs. JSON has become the preferred data format for transmitting objects between platforms over the Internet. In this case study, we’ll explore using JSON in Java.

##### JSON Data Format

Each JSON object contains a comma-separated list of property names and values in curly braces. For example, the following name–value pairs might represent a client record:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0418-01)

```
{"accountNumber": 100, "name": "Devi", "balance": 24.98}
```

JSON also supports arrays as comma-separated values in square brackets. For example, the following represents a JSON array of numbers:

```
[100, 200, 300]
```

Values in JSON objects and arrays can be

*   strings in double quotes (like `"Devi"`),

*   numbers (like `100` or `24.98`),

*   JSON Boolean values (represented as `true` or `false`),

*   `null` (to represent no value),

*   arrays of any valid JSON value and

*   other JSON objects containing values and arrays of the types mentioned above.

JSON arrays may contain elements of the same or different types.

##### Serialization

Converting an object into a format suitable for storage or transmission over the Internet is known as **serialization**. Similarly, reconstructing an object from serialized data is known as **deserialization**. JSON is just one of several serialization formats. Another common one is XML (eXtensible Markup Language). JSON is generally preferred for its simplicity (it’s less verbose than XML), ease of use, efficiency and widespread adoption.^([4](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_4a),[5](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_5a),[6](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_6a),[7](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_7a))

[4](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_4). Hackr.io. “JSON vs XML in 2024: Comparing Features and Examples.” Accessed November 29, 2024\. [`https://hackr.io/blog/json-vs-xml`](https://hackr.io/blog/json-vs-xml).

[5](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_5). W3Schools. “JSON vs XML.” Accessed November 29, 2024\. [`https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_json_xml.asp`](https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_json_xml.asp).

[6](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_6). Imaginary Cloud. “JSON vs XML: Which One Is Faster and More Efficient?” Accessed November 29, 2024\. [`https://www.imaginarycloud.com/blog/json-vs-xml`](https://www.imaginarycloud.com/blog/json-vs-xml).

[7](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_7). Coursesity. “JSON vs XML Comparison: Which Is Better? [2024].” Accessed November 29, 2024\. [`https://coursesity.com/blog/json-vs-xml/`](https://coursesity.com/blog/json-vs-xml/).

##### Serialization Security

Some programming languages (including Java) have serialization mechanisms that use a language-native format. Deserializing objects using these native formats is a source security issues. According to the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP), these “can be repurposed for malicious effect when operating on untrusted data. Attacks against deserializers have been found to allow denial-of-service, access control, and remote code execution (RCE) attacks.” OWASP indicates that you can significantly reduce attack risk by avoiding language-native serialization formats in favor of “pure data” formats like JSON or XML.^([8](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_8a))

[8](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_8). “Deserialization Cheat Sheet.” OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. Accessed November 11, 2024\. [`https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html`](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Deserialization_Cheat_Sheet.html).

##### Jackson Open-Source Library

The **Jackson open-source library**^([9](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_9a)) is a popular Java library for converting objects to JSON and vice versa with minimal code. Jackson was initially developed as a JSON processing library but has since evolved into a multi-format data-processing library. Later in this chapter, we’ll also use it to process comma-separated value (CSV) files. You can access Jackson’s API documentation and download the library from the following links:

[9](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_9). “Jackson Project Home @github.” Accessed November 11, 2024\. [`https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson`](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson).

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0419-01)

```
https://javadoc.io/doc/com.fasterxml.jackson.core/jackson-core/latest

https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson
```

For basic JSON and CSV processing with the Jackson library, you typically need the following Jackson library components:

*   **`jackson-core`**: Provides the core capabilities for parsing and generating JSON.

*   **`jackson-databind`**: Provides capabilities for converting Java objects to and from JSON.

*   **`jackson-annotations`**: Provides Jackson-specific annotations used to customize serialization and deserialization.

*   **`jackson-dataformat-csv`**: Provides additional capabilities for reading and writing CSV files.

For your convenience, we’ve included these components in the subfolder `libs` with this chapter’s examples. After discussing [Fig. 11.4](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig04), we show the `javac` and `java` commands required to compile and run the Jackson-based examples.

#### 11.5.1 Serializing a `List<Account>`

[Figure 11.4](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig04) reimplements [Fig. 11.2](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig02) using JSON serialization. Jackson’s core functionality is provided by its **`ObjectMapper`** **class** (imported at line 3), which provides methods to serialize Java objects to JSON and deserialize JSON to Java objects.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0420-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.4: CreateJSONFile.java
 2   // Writing data to a JSON file using the Jackson open-source library.
 3   import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
 4   import java.io.IOException;
 5   import java.nio.file.Path;
 6   import java.util.List;
 7
 8   // record class to represent an account
 9   record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
10
11   public class CreateJSONFile {
12      public static void main(String[] args) {
13         // account data to write to JSON
14         List<Account> accounts = List.of(
15            new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
16            new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67),
17            new Account(300, "Huber", 0.00),
18            new Account(400, "Ito", -42.16),
19            new Account(500, "Lopez", 224.62)
20         );
21
22         // Path to clients.json in user's Documents folder
23         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
24            "Documents", "clients.json");
25
26         var mapper = new ObjectMapper(); // performs the serialization
27
28         try {
29            // Write accounts to a JSON file
30            mapper.writeValue(filePath.toFile(), accounts);
31            System.out.printf(
32               "JSON file created at: %s%n", filePath.toAbsolutePath());
33         }
34         catch (IOException e) {
35            System.err.printf(
36               "Error writing JSON file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
37         }
38      }
39   }
```

```
JSON file created at: C:\Users\pauldeitel\Documents\clients.json
```

**Fig. 11.4** | Writing data to a JSON file using the Jackson open-source library.

Line 26 creates an `ObjectMapper`. Line 30 uses **`ObjectMapper`****’s** **`writeValue`** **method** to serialize a Java object and write it directly to a file:

*   The first argument `filePath.toFile()` converts the `Path` object representing the file location into a `File` object in which `writeValue` writes the serialized data.

*   The second is the Java object to serialize—in this case, the `List<Account>` named `accounts`.

Jackson automatically converts the `List<Account>` into a JSON array in square brackets (`[` and `]`) in which each `Account` object is serialized as a JSON object in curly braces (`{` and `}`).

##### `clients.json` Contents

The resulting `clients.json` file contains the following JSON representation of the `List`. We reformatted the JSON for readability. Even though you may never have seen JSON-encoded data, you should find this to be well organized, readable and pretty understand-able—these are important reasons for JSON’s appeal.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0421-01)

```
 1   [
 2     {
 3        "accountNumber": 100,
 4        "name": "Devi",
 5        "balance": 24.98
 6     },
 7     {
 8        "accountNumber": 200,
 9        "name": "Taylor",
10        "balance": 345.67
11     },
12     {
13        "accountNumber": 300,
14        "name": "Huber",
15        "balance": 0.0
16     },
17     {
18        "accountNumber": 400,
19        "name": "Ito",
20        "balance": -42.16
21     },
22     {
23        "accountNumber": 500,
24        "name": "Lopez",
25        "balance": 224.62
26     }
27   ]
```

##### Requirements for Serializable Classes

By default, Jackson serializes all of a `record`’s instance variables. For classes, Jackson requires *get* methods for each instance variable to serialize. When deserializing JSON to a `record` object, Jackson uses the `record`’s constructor to reconstruct the object. For other classes, it requires a default constructor and *set* methods to store each instance variable in the new object.

##### Compiling and Running the Program

For your convenience, we included the Jackson library components that this chapter’s examples require in the subfolder `libs` with [Chapter 11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11)’s examples. To compile this example, use the following command on Windows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0422-01)

```
javac -cp ".;../libs/*" CreateJSONFile.java
```

For macOS, change the semicolon (`;`) to a colon (`:`). The **`-cp`** **option** specifies the **class-path**, which indicates where the classes this program needs to compile can be found. The dot (`.`) indicates the current folder. Depending on your operating system, the semicolon (`;`) or colon (`:`) separates one location from another. The relative path `../libs/*` specifies that the `libs` folder is up one level in the folder structure (i.e., in the `ch11` folder containing this chapter’s examples). Finally, the `*` indicates that all the files in that folder should be added to the classpath. To run this example, use the following command on Windows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0422-02)

```
java -cp ".;../libs/*" CreateJSONFile
```

For macOS, change the semicolon (`;`) to a colon (`:`).

#### 11.5.2 Deserializing a `List<Account>`

[Figure 11.5](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig05) reimplements [Fig. 11.3](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig03) using JSON deserialization to create a `List<Account>` representing the account data in the file. For Jackson to recreate objects of regular Java classes in memory, it must have access to each class’s default or no-argument constructor. It will use that to create an object then use that object’s *set* methods to place the data into the object. For a `record` class, Jackson uses the autogenerated constructor.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0423-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.5: ReadJSONFile.java
 2   // Reading data from a JSON file using the Jackson open-source library.
 3   import com.fasterxml.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
 4   import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
 5   import java.io.IOException;
 6   import java.nio.file.Path;
 7   import java.util.List;
 8
 9   // record class to represent an account
10   record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
11
12   public class ReadJSONFile {
13      public static void main(String[] args) {
14         // Path to clients.json in user's Documents folder
15         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
16            "Documents", "clients.json");
17
18         var mapper = new ObjectMapper(); // performs the deserialization
19
20         try {
21            // Read accounts from the JSON file
22            List<Account> accounts = mapper.readValue(
23               filePath.toFile(), new TypeReference<List<Account>>() {});
24
25            // display the accounts
26            System.out.printf(
27               "%-10s %-10s %7s%n", "Account", "Name", "Balance");
28
29            for (var account : accounts) {
30               System.out.printf("%-10d %-10s %7.2f%n",
31                  account.accountNumber(), account.name(),
32                  account.balance());
33            }
34         }
35         catch (IOException e) {
36            System.err.printf(
37               "Error reading JSON file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
38         }
39      }
40   }
```

```
Account    Name       Balance
100        Devi         24.98
200        Taylor      345.67
300        Huber         0.00
400        Ito         -42.16
500        Lopez       224.62
```

**Fig. 11.5** | Reading data from a JSON file using the Jackson open-source library.

Lines 22–23 use the **`ObjectMapper`****’s** **`readValue`** **method** to deserialize the JSON data from the file in its first argument into a `List<Account>`. Jackson needs to know the type of data you want to convert (in this case, a `List<Account>`), which is the purpose of method `readValue`’s second argument:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0424-01)

```
new TypeReference<List<Account>>() {}
```

This uses Jackson’s **`TypeReference`** **class** (imported at line 3) to provide Jackson with the type information the `ObjectMapper` needs to deserialize complex generic types (such as a `List<Account>`), mapping the JSON data to the correct Java object structure. This expression creates an object of an **anonymous inner class**—a class with no name that you create “on-the-fly” to extend another class or implement an interface. Such a class exists only in the place where it’s written. In the preceding expression, `TypeReference` is an `abstract` class from the Jackson library that helps it understand generic types like `List<Account>`. The expression creates a new unnamed class that extends

```
TypeReference<List<Account>>
```

and immediately creates one object of this new unnamed class. Jackson uses this object to help it deserialize your data into a `List<Account>`. The anonymous inner class is similar to the following class declaration:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0424-02)

```
class MyTypeReference extends TypeReference<List<Account>> {
   // empty class body
}
```

Once the data is deserialized, we display it using the same format as in [Fig. 11.3](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig03).

### 11.6 Case Study: Processing a JSON Response from a Web Service

[Section 1.8](#ch01.xhtml_ch01lev1sec8) introduced the Internet, the web, the cloud, web services and mashups. In this case-study, you’ll dive into the world of web services using Java’s built-in networking capabilities to invoke a web service and process the JSON results it returns. You’ll interact with an OpenWeatherMap free web service from

```
https://openweathermap.org/
```

to get the current weather report for a city of your choosing, which you’ll specify with the city name as a command-line argument to the application.

##### Web Services

The machine on which a web service resides is referred to as a **web-service host**. A **web-service client application** (in our case, a Java program) sends a **web-service request** over a network to the web-service host, which processes the request and returns a **web-service response** over the network to the client. This kind of distributed computing benefits systems in various ways. For example, an application without direct access to data on another system might be able to retrieve the data via a web service. Similarly, an application lacking the processing power to perform specific computations could use a web service to take advantage of another system’s superior resources.

##### Representational State Transfer (REST)

Most web services today use **Representational State Transfer (REST)** and are often called **RESTful web services**. In a RESTful web service, each function you can call is identified by a unique URL. **URLs (Uniform Resource Locators)** identify the locations of resources on the Internet, such as websites and web services. For example, [`https://deitel.com/`](https://deitel.com/) is the URL for the Deitel & Associates website. When a web server receives a request to a RESTful web service, it immediately knows what function to call on that server. RESTful web services can be called from programs, as you’ll do here, or directly from a web browser’s address bar by entering the appropriate URL.

##### OpenWeatherMap

OpenWeatherMap provides a free tier to several of its weather web services. Before using them, you must sign up for a free account at [`https://openweathermap.org/`](https://openweathermap.org/). They will send you an email to verify your account. Once you do, they’ll reply with an email that contains your free API key. You can also find this under the API Keys tab in your account when you log into the site.

You can view the variety of OpenWeatherMap APIs and their documentation at

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0425-01)

```
https://openweathermap.org/api
```

Some are free, and some are available only to subscribers. With a free API key, you can access:

*   the Current Weather Data for a specified location, which we use in this case study,

*   the One Call API, which returns a combination of current and future weather data for a specified location, and

*   the 5-Day/3-Hour Forecast for a specified location.

##### Storing the API Key in an Environment Variable

The program in this section assumes you store your API key in a system environment variable named `OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY`. On Windows, perform the following steps to store your API key in an environment variable:

1.  Enter `"environment"` in the taskbar’s Search field.

2.  In the search results, select Edit the system environment variables.

3.  In the System Properties dialog, select or press the Environment Variables button.

4.  Under User variables, click New….

5.  Enter the Variable name `OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY` then, for the Variable value, paste in the API key provided by OpenWeatherMap.org.

6.  Click OK to save the environment variable, then click OK in the System Properties dialog to close it.

On macOS, perform the following steps to store your API key in an environment variable:

1.  Open Terminal.

2.  Open `~/.zshrc` using a text editor (e.g., `nano ~/.zshrc`).

3.  Scroll to the end of the file and add the following line, replacing *YourAPIKey* with the API key provided by OpenWeatherMap.org:

    [Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0426-01)

    ```
    export OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY="YourAPIKey"
    ```

4.  Save and close the file.

5.  Run the following command in the Terminal:

    ```
    source ~/.zshrc
    ```

##### JSON and Web Services

Many cloud-based services like OpenWeatherMap communicate with your applications via JSON objects. ##### `record` Classes for Deserializing the JSON Response

The record classes `WeatherData` (lines 18–25), `Weather` (lines 27–32) and `Main` (lines 34–40) mimic the structure of the JSON data we’ll extract from the web service response. The entire response in [Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06) represents the weather data for a city. Class `WeatherData` contains instance variables named for each top-level JSON key ([Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06), lines 6, 15, 34, 42 and 44) we use in this example. We’ve used the compile-time annotation `@Override` in previous chapters. Many libraries use runtime annotations to inject code into your programs and perform tasks for you. Line 18 above class `WeatherData` uses the Jackson runtime annotation **`@JsonIgnoreProperties`** to tell Jackson to ignore the rest of the top-level JSON fields from [Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06) that we do not use in this example.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0428-01)

```
17   // record classes for JSON mapping
18   @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
19   record WeatherData(
20      Weather[] weather,
21      long dt, // date and time
22      Main main,
23      int timezone,
24      String name
25   ) {}
26
```

The JSON keys `dt`, `timezone` and `name` are each single values that map to the corresponding `WeatherData` instance variables. The JSON key `weather` ([Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06), line 6) has as its value a JSON array of JSON objects—in [Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06), the array contains one JSON object. Similarly, the JSON key `main` ([Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06), line 15) has as its value a JSON object containing many name-value pairs. So, our `WeatherData` class declares instance variable `weather` as an array of `Weather` objects (defined in lines 27–32 below) and instance variable `main` as an object of class `Main` (defined in lines 34–40 below). We named these two classes based on the JSON keys they represent. Again, we do not use all the JSON name-value pairs, so both classes use the Jackson annotation `@JsonIgnoreProperties` to ignore the name-value pairs that do not match these classes’ instance variables.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0428-02)

```
27   @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
28   record Weather(
29      String main,
30      String description,
31      String icon
32   ) {}
33
34   @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
35   record Main(
36      double temp,
37      double feels_like,
38      int pressure,
39      int humidity
40   ) {}
41
```

##### Getting the City from the Command-Line Argument

Lines 45–50 check if there is a command-line argument for the city and, if so, assign it to the `String city`.

47            System.exit(1);
48         }
49

51

##### Getting the API Key

Line 53 uses **`System`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`getenv`** to load the API key from the environment variable `OPENWEATHERMAP_API_KEY`. Lines 56–60 ensure the API key is not null or empty.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0429-02)

##### Creating the URL that Invokes the Web Service

Lines 63–70 construct a valid URL for requesting weather data from the OpenWeatherMap web service. **`URLEncoder`** **method** **`encode`** converts the `city` variable into a format safe for use in a URL—in case the command-line argument contains characters not allowed in URLs. Next, we insert the `encodedCity` into the URL, which specifies

*   the web service API endpoint ([`https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather`](https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather)),

*   the city name, which replaces `%s` in `q=%s`,

*   the temperature units (`units=metric`), and

*   the required API key, which replaces `%s` in `appid=%s`

The API endpoint is followed by `?` and the options, each separated from the next by `&`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0429-03)

```
62         // URL encode the city parameter
63         String encodedCity =
64            URLEncoder.encode(city, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
65
66         // create the API URL as a String
67         String apiUrl = String.format(
68             "https://api.openweathermap.org/" +
69             "data/2.5/weather?q=%s&units=metric&appid=%s",
70             encodedCity, apiKey);
71
```

##### Setting up the Web Service Request and Receiving the Response

To obtain the JSON response in [Fig. 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig06), our application uses the **`HttpClient`** **class** (package **`java.net.http`**)^([10](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_10a)) to make a request to the OpenWeatherMap web service.

[10](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_10). “JEP 321: HTTP Client (Standard).” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/321`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/321).

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0430-01)

```
72         // use Java's HttpClient to make the request
73         HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
74
75         // build the request that HttpClient will use to
76         // invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service
77         HttpRequest request =
78            HttpRequest.newBuilder()
79               .uri(URI.create(apiUrl))
80               .GET()
81               .build();
82
83         // send the HTTP request and get the response
84         HttpResponse<String> response =
85            client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
86
87         // check if the request was successful
88         if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
89            System.out.printf("Error: Received HTTP status %d\n",
90               response.statusCode());
91            System.exit(1);
92         }
93
```

Class `HttpClient` encapsulates the mechanisms to request information from web services and receive their responses. Line 73 calls the class’s **`HttpClient`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`newHttpClient`** to get an `HttpClient` object. Next, lines 77–81 use a chained method call to build an `HttpRequest`:

*   Line 78 calls **`static`** **method** **`newBuilder`** to get an **`HttpRequest.Builder`** object for configuring the request.

*   Line 79 calls the builder’s **`uri`** **method** to specify where the web service resides on the Internet using the `apiUrl` created in lines 67–70\. A **Uniform Resource Identifier (URI)** is a more general form of the Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) used to locate websites. **`URI`** **method** **`create`** converts the URL to a URI.

*   Line 80 uses the **`GET`** **method** to set the HTTP request method to GET, which indicates that the program will request data.

*   Line 81 calls the builder’s **`build`** **method** to create the `HttpRequest` object.

Next, lines 84–85 send the request using the `HttpClient` object’s `send` method:

*   The first argument is the `HttpRequest`.

*   The second argument uses the **`HttpResponse.BodyHandlers`** **class’s** **`ofString`** **method** to indicate that we expect the response to be a `String`.

The response is stored in an `HttpResponse<String>` object, which holds the status code that indicates whether the request was successful and, if so, the response content. Line 88 checks the status code—the status code 200 confirms the server processed the request successfully. Otherwise, the program prints an error message with the received status code and terminates. For more information on HTTP status codes, visit [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_HTTP_status_codes`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_HTTP_status_codes).

98
```

### 11.7 Case Study: Creating and Reading CSV Files

The **CSV (comma-separated values)** file format, which uses the **`.csv`** **file extension**, is popular for datasets used in big data, data analytics and data science, and in artificial intelligence applications like machine learning and deep learning. Here, we’ll demonstrate writing to and reading from a CSV file.

##### Datasets

There’s an enormous variety of free datasets available online. The OpenML machine learning resource site

```
https://openml.org
```

contains almost 6000 free datasets in CSV format. Other great sources of datasets include:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0433-01)

```
https://github.com/awesomedata/awesome-public-datasets
https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/articles/data.html
```

Also, many local and national governments publish free datasets. For example, as of December 2024, the U.S. government listed 25,515 CSV format datasets on `data.gov`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0433-02)

```
https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/?res_format=CSV
```

##### `account.csv`

For our two examples, we’ll create the file `clients.csv` with the following data

```
accountNumber,name,balance
100,Devi,24.98
200,Taylor,345.67
300,Huber,0.0
400,Ito,-42.16
500,Lopez,224.62
```

then we’ll read that file. The first row of a CSV file typically contains column names. Each subsequent row contains one data record representing the values for those columns. This dataset has three columns representing an `accountNumber`, `name` and `balance`.

#### 11.7.1 Creating a CSV File

[Figure 11.8](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig08) reimplements [Fig. 11.4](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig04) using CSV format.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0433-03)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.8: CreateCSVFile.java
 2   // Writing data to a CSV file using the Jackson open-source library.
 3   import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectWriter;
 4   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvMapper;
 5   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvSchema;
 6   import java.io.IOException;
 7   import java.nio.file.Path;
 8   import java.util.List;
 9
10   // record class to represent an account
11   record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
12
13   public class CreateCSVFile {
14      public static void main(String[] args) {
15         // account data to write to
16         List<Account> accounts = List.of(
17            new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
18            new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67),
19            new Account(300, "Huber", 0.00),
20            new Account(400, "Ito", -42.16),
21            new Account(500, "Lopez", 224.62)
22         );
23
24         // Path to clients.csv in user's Documents folder
25         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
26            "Documents", "clients.csv");
27
28         // create Jackson CsvMapper and Schema
29         var mapper = new CsvMapper();
30         CsvSchema schema =
31            mapper.schemaFor(Account.class) // determines CSV files's fields
32               .withHeader(); // first line in clients.csv is the field names
33
34         try {
35            // ObjectWriter writes data to CSV file using specified schema
36            ObjectWriter writer = mapper.writer(schema);
37            writer.writeValue(filePath.toFile(), accounts);
38            System.out.printf(
39               "CSV file created at: %s%n", filePath.toAbsolutePath());
40         }
41         catch (IOException e) {
42            System.err.printf(
43               "Error writing CSV file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
44         }
45      }
46   }
```

```
CSV file created at: C:\Users\pauldeitel\Documents\clients.csv
```

**Fig. 11.8** | Writing data to a CSV file using the Jackson open-source library.

Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program. The primary differences in this example are Jackson’s CSV handling in lines 29–32 and 36–37:

*   Line 29 creates a **`CsvMapper`** object. This is similar to the `ObjectMapper` used for JSON but converts Java objects into CSV format and vice versa.

*   Lines 30–32 use chained method calls to build a **`CsvSchema`** for class `Account`. This defines the CSV file’s structure based on `Account`’s instance variables. The **`CsvSchema`** **method** **`schemaFor`** determines the schema from `Account.class`—a shorthand for a Java object that represents the `Account` class’s definition. **Method** **`withHeader`** specifies that the CSV file’s first line should contain `Account`’s instance variable names as column headers for the CSV records’ fields. By default, a CSV record’s fields are separated by commas, but Jackson allows you to customize this to use other separators.

*   An **`ObjectWriter`** writes the header and data to the CSV file. Line 36 creates an `ObjectWriter` configured with the `CsvSchema` from lines 30–32.

*   Finally, line 37 uses the **`ObjectWriter`****’s** **`writeValue`** **method** to write the `List` of `Account`s to the file at the specified path. This method serializes the accounts list into CSV format, producing a file with rows corresponding to each `Account` object and columns matching the fields in the schema.

#### 11.7.2 Reading a CSV File

[Figure 11.9](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig09) reimplements [Fig. 11.5](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig05) to read the CSV data, then display it in the same format as [Fig. 11.5](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig05). Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0435-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.9: ReadCSVFile.java
 2   // Reading data from a CSV file using the Jackson open-source library.
 3   import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.MappingIterator;
 4   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvMapper;
 5   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvSchema;
 6
 7   import java.io.IOException;
 8   import java.nio.file.Path;
 9   import java.util.List;
10
11   // record class to represent an account
12   record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
13
14   public class ReadCSVFile {
15      public static void main(String[] args) {
16         // Path to clients.csv in user's Documents folder
17         Path filePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
18            "Documents", "clients.csv");
19
20         var mapper = new CsvMapper(); // reads CSV records
21
22         // specify that Jackson should map each CSV column to
23         // an instance variable in the record class Account
24         CsvSchema schema =
25            mapper.schemaFor(Account.class) // fields map to Account objects
26                  .withHeader(); // first line of text is the field names
27
28         // read the CSV file
29         try {
30            // MappingIterator provides access to records as Account objects
31            MappingIterator<Account> iterator =
32               mapper.readerFor(Account.class).with(schema).readValues(
33                  filePath.toFile());
34
35            List<Account> accounts = iterator.readAll();
36
37            // display the accounts
38            System.out.printf(
39               "%-10s %-10s %7s%n", "Account", "Name", "Balance");
40
41            for (var account : accounts) {
42               System.out.printf("%-10d %-10s %7.2f%n",
43                  account.accountNumber(), account.name(),
44                  account.balance());
45            }
46         }
47         catch (IOException e) {
48            System.err.printf(
49               "Error reading CSV file: %s%n", e.getMessage());
50         }
51      }
52   }
```

```
Account    Name       Balance
100        Devi         24.98
200        Taylor      345.67
300        Huber         0.00
400        Ito         -42.16
500        Lopez       224.62
```

**Fig. 11.9** | Reading data from a CSV file using the Jackson open-source library.

The primary differences in this example are Jackson’s CSV handling in lines 20, 24–26 and 31–35:

*   Line 20 creates a `CsvMapper` object that will convert CSV records into Java objects.

*   Lines 24–26 create a `CsvSchema` for the `Account` class. This schema defines how the columns in the CSV file correspond to the instance variables in an `Account`. As in [Fig. 11.8](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig08), we indicate that the CSV file’s first row contains column headers. Jackson uses these to map the columns to the corresponding fields in the `Account record` object.

*   To read the CSV file, we use a **`MappingIterator`**. Lines 31–33 create a `Mapping-Iterator<Account>` using a chained method call. An “iterator” is an object that enables a program to iterate over a collection’s elements one by one. For example, an enhanced `for` loop uses an iterator to access each element in a collection, such as an `ArrayList`. The `MappingIterator` enables this program to access each record in the CSV file. **`CsvMapper`****’s** **`readerFor`** **method** receives `Account.class` to indicate it will create `Account` objects. The **`with`** **method** provides the schema Jackson will use when deserializing the CSV records into `Account` objects. Finally, the **`readValues`** **method** indicates that the `MappingIterator` will read data from the file specified in its argument.

*   Line 35 calls the **`MappingIterator`****’s** **`readAll`** **method** to iterate through all the records in the CSV file, reading them into a `List<Account>`. This makes it easy to work with all the CSV file’s data in memory.

##### Caution: Commas in CSV Data Fields

Be careful when working with strings containing embedded commas, such as the name `"Flores, Silvio"`. If this name were accidentally stored as the two strings `"Flores"` and `"Silvio"`, that CSV record would have four fields, not three. Programs that read CSV files typically expect every record to have the same number of fields; otherwise, problems occur.

##### Caution: Missing Commas and Extra Commas in CSV Files

Be careful when preparing and processing CSV files. For example, suppose your file is composed of records, each with four comma-separated `int` values, such as

```
100,85,77,9
```

If you accidentally omit one of these commas, as in

```
100,8577,9
```

then the record has only three fields, one with the invalid value `8577`.

If you put two adjacent commas where only one is expected, as in

```
100,85,,77,9
```

then you have five fields rather than four, and one of the fields erroneously would be empty. Each of these comma-related errors could confuse programs trying to process the record.

### 11.8 Case Study: Reading and Analyzing a CSV File Containing the *Titanic* Disaster Dataset

The ***Titanic*** **disaster dataset**^([11](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_11a)) is one of the most commonly used datasets for data analytics beginners. It lists all the passengers and whether they survived when the ship *Titanic* struck an iceberg and sank during its first voyage of April 10–15, 1912\. In this case, study, we’ll load the dataset, view some of its data and perform some basic data analytics.

[11](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_11). “TitanicSurvival” dataset on [`https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets`](https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets). Dataset authors: Frank E. Harrell, Jr., and Thomas Cason.

The dataset is available from numerous dataset repositories. We used the version from the Rdatasets repository at

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0437-01)

```
https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/carData/
   TitanicSurvival.csv
```

We placed this file in the same folder as the example’s code.

##### Getting to Know Your Data

In data analytics, you’ll often begin by getting to know your data. One way is to simply look at the raw data. If you open the `TitanicSurvival.csv` file in a text editor or spreadsheet application, you’ll see that the dataset contains 1,309 rows, each with five columns—often called **features** in data analytics. We ignore the first column containing the passenger’s names and use only the last four columns in this case study:

*   `survived`: `"yes"` or `"no"`.

*   `sex`: `"female"` or `"male"`.

*   `age`: The passenger’s age. Most ages are integers, but some children under 1 year of age have floating-point values, so we’ll process this column as `double` values.

*   `passengerClass`: `"1st"`, `"2nd"` or `"3rd"` for first, second or third class, respectively.

To learn more about the dataset’s origins, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0438-01)

```
https://hbiostat.org/data/repo/titanic
```

##### Missing Data

Bad data values and missing values can significantly impact data analysis. The *Titanic* dataset is missing the `age`s for 263 passengers. These are represented as empty fields in the CSV file—that is, there is no data between the commas that delimit the age field in those records. In this example, when we produce descriptive statistics for the passengers’ ages, we’ll “clean” the data to filter out and ignore the missing values. In data science, preparing data for analysis is called **data munging** or **data wrangling**.

Some data scientists advise against any attempts to insert “reasonable values.” Instead, they advocate clearly marking missing data and leaving it up to a data analytics package to handle the issue. Others offer strong cautions.^([12](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_12a))

[12](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_12). This footnote was abstracted from a comment sent to us July 20, 2018, by one of our Python textbook’s academic reviewers, Dr. Alison Sanchez of the University of San Diego School of Business. She commented: “Be cautious when mentioning ‘substituting reasonable values’ for missing or bad values. A stern warning: ‘Substituting’ values that increase statistical significance or give more ‘reasonable’ or ‘better’ results is not permitted. ‘Substituting’ data should not turn into ‘fudging’ data. The first rule students should learn is not to eliminate or change values that contradict their hypotheses. ‘Substituting reasonable values‘ does not mean students should feel free to change values to get the results they want.”

##### Loading the Dataset

[Figure 11.10](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig10) loads the dataset and performs our analysis. We broke the program into parts for discussion purposes. Remember to add Jackson to the classpath when compiling and running this program.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0438-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 11.10: TitanicAnalysis.java
 2   // Reading the Titanic dataset from a CSV file, then analyzing it.
 3   import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonIgnoreProperties;
 4   import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.MappingIterator;
 5   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvMapper;
 6   import com.fasterxml.jackson.dataformat.csv.CsvSchema;
 7   import java.nio.file.Path;
 8   import java.util.ArrayList;
 9   import java.util.List;
10
```

**Fig. 11.10** | Reading the Titanic dataset from a CSV file, then analyzing it.

##### `record` Class `TitanicAnalysis` for Storing Each Dataset Record

Jackson can read CSV records and create objects of a type you specify so you can conveniently access the record’s fields. Lines 13–19 declare the `record` class `TitanicRecord`, which has instance variables representing the four dataset columns we use in this example. As discussed previously, line 13 tells Jackson to ignore JSON name-value pairs that do not have a matching instance variable in class `TitanicRecord`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0439-01)

```
11   public class TitanicAnalysis {
12      // record class representing the fields in each dataset row
13      @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)
14      public record TitanicRecord(
15         String survived,
16         String sex,
17         String age,
18         String passengerClass
19      ) {}
20
```

##### Loading the Dataset

Lines 22 and 26 create the `CsvMapper` and `CsvSchema` we’ll use to configure Jackson to read the CSV file and convert each record to a `TitanicRecord` object. In this example, we use **`CsvSchema`****’s** **`static emptySchema`** **method** to indicate that Jackson should automatically determine how to map the CSV records to `TitanicRecord`s. At the end of this section, you’ll prompt genAIs, asking for the benefits and disadvantages of this approach. Lines 30–32 configure the `MappingIterator` that converts each record to a `TitanicRecord` object, then line 35 uses it to read all the CSV file’s records into a `List<TitanicRecord>`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0439-02)

```
21      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
22         var mapper = new CsvMapper(); // reads CSV records
23
24         // specify that Jackson should map each CSV column
25         // to an object based on the column names
26         CsvSchema schema = CsvSchema.emptySchema().withHeader();
27
28         // create the MappingIterator that knows how to read
29         // the file's records into TitanicRecord objects
30         MappingIterator<TitanicRecord> iterator =
31            mapper.readerFor(TitanicRecord.class).with(schema).readValues(
32               Path.of("TitanicSurvival.csv").toFile());
33
34         // load dataset into a List of TitanicRecord objects
35         List<TitanicRecord> titanic = iterator.readAll();
36
```

##### Extracting the Column Data into `ArrayList`s

Lines 38–41 create `ArrayList`s for each column. The loop at lines 44–58 populates each `ArrayList` with the corresponding column’s data. As we add each age to the `age Array-List`, we check whether it’s empty. If not, we convert it to a `double` and add it to the `ArrayList`; otherwise, we add the value `Double.NaN` (not a number) to indicate the missing value. You’ll learn in [Chapter 12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12) that Java collections can store only objects and that `double`s and `int`s are converted to their `Double` object and `Integer` object equivalents (and vice versa) automatically. As we add each passenger class to the `pclass ArrayList`, we convert it from the `String "1st"`, `"2nd"` or `"3rd"` to the number `1`, `2` or `3`. We’ll use these as array indexes when summarizing the number of passengers in each class.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0440-01)

```
37         // create lists representing each column with the correct type
38         var survived = new ArrayList<String>();
39         var sex = new ArrayList<String>();
40         var age = new ArrayList<Double>();
41         var pclass = new ArrayList<Integer>();
42
43         // populate the column lists
44         for (TitanicRecord record : titanic) {
45            survived.add(record.survived());
46            sex.add(record.sex());
47            age.add(!record.age().isEmpty() ?
48               Double.parseDouble(record.age()) : Double.NaN);
49            pclass.add(
50               switch (record.passengerClass()) {
51                  case "1st" -> 1;
52                  case "2nd" -> 2;
53                  case "3rd" -> 3;
54                  default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(
55                     "Unknown class: " + record.passengerClass());
56               }
57            );
58         }
59
```

##### Data Munging: Cleaning the Age Column for Calculating Descriptive Statistics

As part of getting to know a dataset, data scientists often use statistics to describe and summarize data. We’ll calculate several **descriptive statistics** for the age column, including the number of passengers for which we have ages, and the average, minimum, maximum and median age values. Before performing these calculations, we must remove `NaN` values, because a calculation that includes the value `NaN` produces `NaN` as the result. So, lines 80–85 create the `ArrayList cleanAge` containing only the values from `age` that are not `NaN`. **`Double`** **method** **`isNaN`** returns `true` if the value is `NaN`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0441-02)

```
79         // clean the age column (remove NaN)
80         var cleanAge = new ArrayList<Double>();
81         for (Double value : age) {
82            if (!value.isNaN()) {
83               cleanAge.add(value);
84            }
85         }
86
```

##### Basic Descriptive Statistics for the Cleaned Age Column

Now, we can calculate the descriptive statistics. Line 88 sorts `cleanAge`, so we can determine the minimum, maximum and median values. When `sort`’s argument is `null` the `ArrayList`’s element type must implement the `Comparable` interface so `sort` can compare the elements to determine sort order—class `Double` implements `Comparable`. To count the number of people for which we have valid `age`s, we simply get `cleanAge`’s `size` (line 89). Lines 92–94 determine the median. If `cleanAge`’s `size` is even, the median is the average of the two middle elements (line 93); otherwise, it’s the middle element (line 94). Lines 97–103 calculate the average age.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0442-01)

```
87         // descriptive statistics for cleaned age column
88         cleanAge.sort(null); // helps determine min, max and median ages
89         int size = cleanAge.size();
90
91         // get median age
92         double medianAge = (size % 2 == 0) ?
93            (cleanAge.get(size / 2 - 1) + cleanAge.get(size / 2)) / 2.0 :
94            cleanAge.get(size / 2);
95
96         // calculate average of ages
97         double sum = 0.0;
98
99         for (double value : cleanAge) {
100           sum += value;
101        }
102
103        double averageAge = sum / size;
104
```

Lines 106–111 display the descriptive statistics. The `ArrayList` is sorted, so lines 109–110 call the **`ArrayList`****’s** **`getFirst`** and **`getLast`** **methods** to get first and last elements, which contain the minimum and maximum values, respectively. The average and median are **measures of central tendency**. Each produces a single value that represents a “central” value in a set of values—a value that is, in some sense, typical of the others. For the `1046` people with valid `age`s, the average `age` was `29.88` years old. The youngest passenger (i.e., the minimum) was just over two months old (`0.17 * 12` is `2.04`), and the oldest (i.e., the maximum) was 80\. The `median age` was `28`.

### 11.9 Objects-Natural Security Case Study: RSA Public-Key Cryptography

In [Section 7.9](#ch07.xhtml_ch07lev1sec9), you began learning about secret-key cryptography. The sender’s plaintext was encrypted with a secret key to form ciphertext. The receiver used the same secret key to decode the ciphertext, forming the original plaintext—this process is called symmetric encryption because the same key is used by both the sender and the recipient.

##### Public-Key Cryptography

A problem with secret-key cryptography is that the security of the ciphertext is only as good as the security of the secret key, and several copies of that key are “floating around.” In their paper “New Directions in Cryptography,”^([14](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_14a)) Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, introduced **public-key cryptography** to address the weakness of secret-key cryptography—the vulnerability of the secret key having to be known by both the sender and the recipient. They came up with the idea but not an implementation of the scheme.

[14](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_14). “New Directions in Cryptography.” November 6, 1976\. Accessed January 1, 2025. [`https://ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/publications/24.pdf`](https://ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/publications/24.pdf).

##### RSA Public-Key Cryptography

Rivest, Shamir and Adelman were the first to publish a working implementation of public-key cryptography. The scheme, called RSA, bears the initials of their last names.^([15](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_15a)) RSA is one of the world’s most widely implemented public-key cryptography schemes.^([16](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_16a)) Because RSA can be slow,^([17](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_17a)) many organizations prefer to stick to faster private-key encryption, using RSA only to securely send the secret key. Such encryption and decryption techniques are critical for securing data stored in files and transmitted over networks.

[15](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_15). R. Rivest; A. Shamir; L. Adleman (February 1978). “A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems” (PDF). Communications of the ACM. 21 (2): 120–126\. Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/Rsapaper.pdf`](https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/Rsapaper.pdf).

[16](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_16). Cobb, Michael. “RSA algorithm (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman).” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://searchsecurity.techtarget.com/definition/RSA`](https://searchsecurity.techtarget.com/definition/RSA).

[17](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_17). “RSA (cryptosystem).” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)).

##### Historical Note

Clifford Cocks in the U.K. created a workable public-key scheme several years before the RSA paper was published,^([18](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_18a)) but his work was classified, so it was not revealed until about 20 years after RSA appeared. The company RSA Security held a patent on the RSA algorithm. In 2000, that patent was coming due for renewal—instead of renewing, they placed the algorithm into the public domain.^([19](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_19a))

[18](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_18). “Clifford Cocks.” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Cocks`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Cocks).

[19](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_19). “RSA Security Releases RSA Encryption Algorithm into Public Domain.” September 6, 2000\. Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://web.archive.org/web/20071120112201/http://www.rsa.com/press_release.aspx?id=261`](https://web.archive.org/web/20071120112201/http://www.rsa.com/press_release.aspx?id=261).

##### Enhanced Cryptography Demo

In this case study, we enhance our AES private-key encryption example to demonstrate how to securely encrypt the secret key using **RSA public-key cryptography**.^([20](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_20a),[21](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_21a),[22](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_22a)) In particular, we focus on how to generate:

*   the **public key** any sender can use to encrypt an AES secret key for transmission to a specific recipient, and

*   the **private key** only the specific recipient can use to decrypt the AES secret key.

[20](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_20). “RSA (cryptosystem).” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem)).

[21](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_21). “RSA Algorithm.” Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm`](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_algorithm).

[22](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_22). “PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.2.” November 2016. Accessed January 1, 2025\. [`https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017`](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8017).

Public-key cryptography is also called asymmetric-key cryptography because different keys are used for encryption and decryption. This technique is often used to transmit the secret keys used in symmetric encryption. RSA is based on sophisticated mathematics using enormous prime numbers consisting of hundreds of digits, but the Java cryptography APIs encapsulate this complexity, hiding it from you. Much of [Fig. 11.11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11fig11)’s code is identical to the AES cryptography demo in [Fig. 7.23](#ch07.xhtml_ch07fig23), so we focus on the enhancements. We split the example into parts for discussion purposes.

##### Generating the RSA Public and Private Keys

Lines 38–45 generate an RSA key pair that we’ll use to simulate the secure transmission of an encrypted AES secret key:

*   Line 38 calls the **`KeyPairGenerator static`** **method** **`getInstance`** with the argument `"RSA"` to get a `KeyPairGenerator` object for RSA encryption.

*   Line 39 uses the **`KeyPairGenerator`** **method** **`initialize`** to set the key size to 2048 bits, as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends^([23](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_23a))—this defines the encryption strength.

    [23](#ch11.xhtml_fn11_23). National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Recommendation for Key Management: Part 3 — Application-Specific Key Management Guidance. Special Publication 800-57 Part 3 Revision 1\. Gaithersburg, MD: National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2015\. [`https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57Pt3r1.pdf`](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-57Pt3r1.pdf).

*   Line 40 generates the RSA **`KeyPair`** by calling the **`KeyPairGenerator`** **method** **`generateKeyPair`**.

*   Lines 44–45 get the `KeyPair`’s `PublicKey` and a `PrivateKey` via **`KeyPair`** **methods** **`getPublic`** and **`getPrivate`**.

You share your `PublicKey` with anyone sending you encrypted data. You keep the `Private-Key` secret and use it to decrypt data encrypted with your `PublicKey`, ensuring that only the intended recipient (you) can read the message.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0448-01)

```
37            // generate RSA key pair -- normally done by message receiver
38            var keyPairGenerator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
39            keyPairGenerator.initialize(2048); // set key size to 2048 bits
40            KeyPair rsaKeyPair = keyPairGenerator.generateKeyPair();
41
42            // get RSA public and private keys -- recipient sends the
43            // public key to anyone who needs to send them something securely
44            PublicKey publicKey = rsaKeyPair.getPublic();
45            PrivateKey privateKey = rsaKeyPair.getPrivate();
46
```

##### Encrypting the AES Secret Key

Lines 49–50 use RSA to encrypt the AES `SecretKey`. Method `encryptRSA` (lines 117–130) takes the `SecretKey`’s `byte` array representation (`secretKey.getEncoded()`) and the RSA `publicKey` and uses the `publicKey` to encrypt the AES `SecretKey`—this ensures only the intended recipient can later decrypt it using their corresponding RSA private key. Encrypting the AES secret key allows it to be transmitted securely. For demo purposes, we display the encrypted AES `SecretKey` so you can confirm later that it was decrypted properly—your output will differ as the RSA `publicKey` was generated randomly. In real-world cryptography, we’d send the `cipherText` (line 34) and the `encryptedAESKey` to the recipient.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0448-02)

```
47            // encrypt the AES secret key with the RSA public key;
48            // this would be sent to recipient with the encrypted message
49            String encryptedAESKey =
50               encryptRSA(secretKey.getEncoded(), publicKey);
51            System.out.printf(
52               "%nRSA Encrypted AES SecretKey:%n%s%n", encryptedAESKey);
53

##### Decrypting the AES Secret Key

To decrypt the `ciphertext`, the recipient must first decrypt the AES secret key that was used to produce the `ciphertext`. Lines 55–56 call method `decryptRSA` (lines 133–148) to decrypt the AES `SecretKey` using RSA decryption. The method `decryptRSA` receives the encrypted AES key and the RSA private key—the only key that can decrypt data encrypted by the corresponding public key, ensuring the AES secret key’s security. This process ensures that only the intended recipient, who possesses the private key, can obtain the original AES key and read the encrypted message. For demonstration purposes, we display the decrypted AES secret key, so you can compare it to the one output by lines 30–31 and see that it was decrypted properly.

[Click here to view code image](#ch11_images.xhtml_f0449-01)

56               decryptRSA(encryptedAESKey, privateKey);
57            System.out.printf("%nDecrypted AES SecretKey:%n%s%n",
58               Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(
59                  decryptedSecretKey.getEncoded()));

##### `generateKey`, `encrypt` and `decrypt` Methods

The methods in lines 76–113 perform the same tasks as in [Section 7.9](#ch07.xhtml_ch07lev1sec9) for generating an AES secret key, encrypting plain text using an AES secret key and decrypting ciphertext using the same AES secret key.
