To use this skeleton to create your controller class, click the Copy button, then paste the contents into a file named `TipCalculatorController.java` in the same folder as the `TipCalculator.fxml` file you created in this section.

#### 15.5.4 `TipCalculator` Class

A simple JavaFX FXML-based application has two Java source-code files. For the Tip Calculator application, these are:

*   `TipCalculator.java`—This file contains the `TipCalculator` class (discussed in this section), which declares the `main` method that loads the FXML file to create the GUI and attaches the GUI to a `Scene` displayed on the application’s `Stage`.

*   `TipCalculatorController.java`—This file contains the controller class (discussed in [Section 15.5.5](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec19)), where you’ll specify the `Slider` and `Button` controls’ event handlers.

[Figure 15.1](#ch15.xhtml_ch15fig01) presents class `TipCalculator`. As we discussed in [Section 15.5.2](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec16), the starting point for a JavaFX application is an `Application` subclass, so class `TipCalculator` extends `Application` (line 9). The `main` method calls class `Application`’s `static launch` method (line 23) to initialize the JavaFX runtime and to begin executing the application. This method causes the JavaFX runtime to create an object of the `TipCalculator` class and calls its `start` method (lines 10–19), passing the `Stage` object representing the window in which the application will be displayed. The JavaFX runtime creates the window.

[Click here to view code image](#ch15_images.xhtml_f0589-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 15.1: TipCalculator.java
 2   // Main application class that loads and displays the Tip Calculator's GUI
 3   import javafx.application.Application;
 4   import javafx.fxml.FXMLLoader;
 5   import javafx.scene.Parent;
 6   import javafx.scene.Scene;
 7   import javafx.stage.Stage;
 8
 9   public class TipCalculator extends Application {
10      @Override
11      public void start(Stage stage) throws Exception {
12         Parent root =
13            FXMLLoader.load(getClass().getResource("TipCalculator.fxml"));
14
15         var scene = new Scene(root); // attach scene graph to scene
16         stage.setTitle("Tip Calculator"); // displayed in window's title bar
17         stage.setScene(scene); // attach scene to stage
18         stage.show(); // display the stage
19      }
20
21      public static void main(String[] args) {
22         // create a TipCalculator object and call its start method
23         launch(args);
24      }
25   }
```

**Fig. 15.1** | Main application class that loads and displays the Tip Calculator’s GUI.

##### Overridden `Application` Method `start`

Method `start` (lines 10–19) creates the GUI, attaches it to a `Scene` and places it on the `Stage` that method `start` receives as an argument. Lines 12–13 use class `FXMLLoader`’s `static` method `load` to create the GUI’s scene graph. This method:

*   Returns a `Parent` (package `javafx.scene`) reference to the scene graph’s root node—this is a reference to the GUI’s `GridPane` in this application.

*   Creates an object of the `TipCalculatorController` class that we specified in the FXML file.

*   Initializes the controller’s instance variables for the components that are manipulated programmatically.

*   Registers the event handlers specified in the FXML with the appropriate controls, enabling them to call their event handlers in response to user interactions.

We discuss the initialization of the controller’s instance variables and the registration of the event handlers in [Section 15.5.5](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec19).

##### Creating the `Scene`

To display the GUI, you must attach it to a `Scene`, then attach the `Scene` to the `Stage` that method `start` receives as an argument. To attach the GUI to a `Scene`, line 15 creates a `Scene`, passing `root` (the scene graph’s root node) as an argument to the constructor. By default, the `Scene`’s size is determined by the size of the scene graph’s root node. Overloaded versions of the `Scene` constructor allow you to specify the `Scene`’s size and fill (a color, gradient or image), which appears in the `Scene`’s background. Line 16 uses `Stage` method `setTitle` to specify the text that appears in the `Stage` window’s title bar. Line 17 calls `Stage` method `setScene` to place the `Scene` onto the `Stage`. Finally, line 18 calls `Stage` method `show` to display the `Stage` window.

#### 15.5.5 `TipCalculatorController` Class; Implementing an Event Handler with a Lambda

[Figure 15.2](#ch15.xhtml_ch15fig02) presents the `TipCalculatorController` class that responds to user interactions with the application’s `Button` and `Slider`. We split the class into pieces for discussion purposes. Lines 3–10 show the class’s `import` statements:

[Click here to view code image](#ch15_images.xhtml_f0590-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 15.2: TipCalculatorController.java
 2   // Controller that handles calculateButton and tipPercentageSlider events
 3   import java.math.BigDecimal;
 4   import java.math.RoundingMode;
 5   import java.text.NumberFormat;
 6   import javafx.event.ActionEvent;
 7   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 8   import javafx.scene.control.Label;
 9   import javafx.scene.control.Slider;
10   import javafx.scene.control.TextField;
11
```

**Fig. 15.2** | `TipCalculatorController`’s `import` declarations.

The classes and interfaces used by class `TipCalculatorController` include:

*   Class `BigDecimal` (line 3; introduced in [Section 4.11](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec11)) is used to perform precise monetary calculations. The `RoundingMode enum` of package `java.math` (line 4) is used to specify how `BigDecimal` values are rounded during calculations or when formatting floating-point numbers as `String`s.

*   Class `NumberFormat` of package `java.text` (line 5) provides numeric formatting capabilities, such as locale-specific currency and percentage formats. For example, in the U.S. locale, the monetary value 34.95 is formatted as $34.95 and the percentage 15 is formatted as 15%. Class `NumberFormat` determines the locale of the system on which your application runs then formats currency amounts and percentages accordingly.

*   A `Button`’s event handler receives an `ActionEvent` object (line 6; package `javafx.event`) indicating which `Button` the user clicked. Many JavaFX controls support `ActionEvent`s.

*   The annotation `FXML` (line 7; package `javafx.fxml`) is used in a JavaFX controller class’s code (as `@FXML`) to mark instance variables that should refer to JavaFX components in the GUI’s FXML file and methods that can respond to the events of JavaFX components in the GUI’s FXML file.

*   Package `javafx.scene.control` (lines 8–10) contains many JavaFX control classes, including `Label`, `Slider` and `TextField`.

##### `TipCalculatorController`’s `static` Variables and Instance Variables

Lines 14–35 declare class `TipCalculatorController`’s `static` and instance variables. The `NumberFormat` objects (lines 14–17) are used to format currency values and percentages, respectively. **`NumberFormat`** **method** **`getCurrencyInstance`** returns a `NumberFormat` object that formats values as currency using the default locale for the system on which the application is running. Similarly, **`NumberFormat`** **method** **`getPercentInstance`** returns a `NumberFormat` object that formats values as percentages using the system’s default locale. The `BigDecimal` object `tipPercentage` (line 19) stores the current tip percentage and is used in the tip calculation when the user clicks the Calculate `Button`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch15_images.xhtml_f0591-01)

```
12   public class TipCalculatorController {
13      // formatters for currency and percentages
14      private static final NumberFormat currency =
15         NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance();
16      private static final NumberFormat percent =
17         NumberFormat.getPercentInstance();
18
19      private BigDecimal tipPercentage = new BigDecimal("0.15"); // 15%
20
21      // GUI controls defined in FXML and used by the controller's code
22      @FXML
23      private TextField amountTextField;
24
25      @FXML
26      private Label tipPercentageLabel;
27
28      @FXML
29      private Slider tipPercentageSlider;
30
31      @FXML
32      private TextField tipTextField;
33
34      @FXML
35      private TextField totalTextField;
36
```

##### `@FXML` Annotation

Recall from [Section 15.5.3](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec17) that each control that this application manipulates in its Java source code needs an fx:id. Lines 22–35 declare the controller class’s corresponding instance variables. The **`@FXML`** **annotation** that precedes each declaration (lines 22, 25, 28, 31 and 34) indicates that the variable name can be used in the FXML file that describes the application’s GUI. The variable names that you specify in the controller class must precisely match the fx:id values you specified when building the GUI; otherwise, the `FXMLLoader` will throw a `LoadException`. When the `FXMLLoader` loads `TipCalculator.fxml` to create the GUI, it also initializes each of the controller’s instance variables declared with `@FXML` to ensure that they refer to the corresponding GUI components.

##### `TipCalculatorController`’s `calculateButtonPressed` Event Handler

Lines 38–53 declare `TipCalculatorController`’s `calculateButtonPressed` method, which is called when the user clicks the Calculate `Button`. The `@FXML` annotation (line 38) preceding the method indicates that this method can be used to specify a control’s event handler in the FXML file that describes the application’s GUI. For a control that generates an `ActionEvent` (as many JavaFX controls do), the event-handling method must return `void` and receive one `ActionEvent` parameter (line 39).

[Click here to view code image](#ch15_images.xhtml_f0592-01)

```
37      // calculates and displays the tip and total amounts
38      @FXML
39      private void calculateButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
40         try {
41            BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(amountTextField.getText());
42            BigDecimal tip = amount.multiply(tipPercentage);
43            BigDecimal total = amount.add(tip);
44
45            tipTextField.setText(currency.format(tip));
46            totalTextField.setText(currency.format(total));
47         }
48         catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
49            amountTextField.setText("Enter amount");
50            amountTextField.selectAll();
51            amountTextField.requestFocus();
52         }
53      }
54
```

##### Registering the Calculate Button’s Event Handler

When the `FXMLLoader` loads `TipCalculator.fxml` to create the GUI, it creates and registers an event handler for the Calculate `Button`’s `ActionEvent`. The event handler for this event must implement interface **`EventHandler<ActionEvent>`** (**package** **`javafx.event`**)—`EventHandler` is a generic interface containing a **`handle`** **method** that returns `void` and receives an `ActionEvent` parameter. This method, in turn, calls `calculateButtonPressed` when the user clicks the Calculate `Button`. `FXMLLoader` performs similar tasks for every event listener you specify via the Scene Builder Inspector window’s Code section.

##### Calculating and Displaying the Tip and Total Amounts

Lines 41–46 calculate and display the tip and total. Line 41 calls the `amountTextField`’s **`getText`** **method** to get the bill amount entered by the user. This `String` is passed to `Big-Decimal`’s constructor, which throws a `NumberFormatException` if its argument is not a number. In that case, line 49 calls `amountTextField`’s **`setText`** **method** to display `"Enter amount"` in the `TextField`. Line 50 calls `amountTextField`’s **`selectAll`** **method** to select the `TextField`’s text. Line 51 calls `amountTextField`’s **`requestFocus`** **method** to give the `TextField` the focus. Now, the user can enter a new value in the `amountTextField` without having to first select the text. `TextField` inherits methods `getText`, `setText` and `selectAll` from class `TextInputControl` (package `javafx.scene.control`) and method `requestFocus` from class `Node` (package `javafx.scene`).

If line 41 does not throw an exception, line 42 calculates the `tip` by calling method `multiply` to multiply the `amount` by the `tipPercentage`, and line 43 calculates the `total` by `add`ing the `tip` to the bill `amount`. Next, lines 45 and 46 use the `currency` object’s **`format`** **method** to create currency-formatted `String`s representing the tip and total amounts, which we display in `tipTextField` and `totalTextField`, respectively.

##### `TipCalculatorController`’s `initialize` Method

Lines 56–69 declare `TipCalculatorController`’s `private initialize` method. When present and annotated with `@FXML`, JavaFX will call this method to configure the controller before the GUI is displayed. Line 59 calls the `currency` object’s `setRoundingMode` method to specify that currency values should be rounded using the `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN` (as discussed in [Section 4.11](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec11)).

[Click here to view code image](#ch15_images.xhtml_f0593-01)

```
55      // called by FXMLLoader to initialize the controller
56      @FXML
57      private void initialize() {
58         // 0-4 rounds down, 5-9 rounds up
59         currency.setRoundingMode(RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
60
61         // listener for changes to tipPercentageSlider's value
62         tipPercentageSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
63            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
64               tipPercentage =
65                  BigDecimal.valueOf(newValue.intValue() / 100.0);
66               tipPercentageLabel.setText(percent.format(tipPercentage));
67            }
68         );
69      }
70   }
```

##### Using a Lambda for Event Handling

Each JavaFX control has properties. Some—such as a `Slider`’s value—can generate events when they change. For such events, you must manually register as the event handler an object that implements the `ChangeListener` interface (package `javafx.beans.value`).

`ChangeListener` is a generic type that’s specialized with the property’s type. The call to `valueProperty` (line 62) returns a `DoubleProperty` (package `javax.beans.property`) that represents the `Slider`’s value. A `DoubleProperty` is an **`ObservableValue<Number>`** that can notify listeners when a value changes. Each class that implements interface `ObservableValue` provides **method** **`addListener`** (called in lines 62–68) to register an event-handler that implements interface `ChangeListener`. For a `Slider`’s value, `addListener`’s argument is an object that implements `ChangeListener<Number>` because the `Slider`’s value is a numeric value.

`ChangeListener` is a generic functional interface, so we can conveniently implement it using a lambda (lines 63–67; introduced in [Section 14.3](#ch14.xhtml_ch14lev1sec3)). **`ChangeListener`****’s** **`abstract changed`** **method** receives three arguments:

*   an `ObservableValue<T>`,

*   the old value of type `T`, and

*   the new value of type `T`.

Since the `Slider`’s `addListener` method expects a `ChangeListener<Number>` object, the compiler infers that `T` is `Number` for the lambda’s three parameters:

*   `ov`—the `ObservableValue<Number>` that changed,

*   `oldValue`—a `Number` containing the `Slider`’s old value before the event occurred and

*   `newValue`—a `Number` containing the `Slider`’s new value.

When the user moves the `Slider`’s thumb, lines 64–65 store the new tip percentage and line 66 updates the `tipPercentageLabel`.

### 15.6 Features Covered in the Other JavaFX Chapters

JavaFX is a robust GUI, graphics and multimedia technology. In [Chapters 16](#ch16.xhtml_ch16) and [17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17), you’ll:

*   Learn additional JavaFX layouts and controls.

*   Handle other event types (such as `MouseEvent`s).

*   Apply transformations (such as moving, rotating, scaling and skewing) and effects (such as drop shadows, blurs, reflection and lighting) to a scene graph’s nodes.

*   Use CSS to specify the look-and-feel of controls.

*   Use JavaFX properties and data binding to enable automatic updating of controls as corresponding data changes.

*   Access files and folders on disk using `FileChooser` and `DirectoryChooser` dialogs.

*   Use JavaFX graphics capabilities.

*   Perform JavaFX animations.

*   Use JavaFX multimedia capabilities to play audio and video.

### 15.7 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we introduced JavaFX for creating graphical user interfaces (GUIs). We briefly discussed JavaFX’s benefits over the older AWT and Swing GUI technologies. We explored a JavaFX application window’s structure, including its stage, scene and various controls. We explained key JavaFX concepts such as using Scene Builder to create the FXML that declaratively specifies a GUI’s layout and controls, the Model-View-Controller (MVC) design pattern, and how a controller class responds to the events generated by users interacting with GUI controls.

We used two examples to introduce key JavaFX concepts. In the simple Welcome application, we used drag-and-drop visual programming techniques in Scene Builder to design a GUI consisting of a `VBox` layout container, a `Label` and an `ImageView` without writing any Java code.

In the Tip Calculator application, we used Scene Builder to create a more elaborate GUI consisting of `Label`s, `TextField`s, a `Slider` and a `Button` arranged in a `GridPane` layout container with multiple rows and columns. We used class `FXMLLoader` to read the FXML created in Scene Builder, create the corresponding GUI, create an instance of the controller class and attach the GUI controls to the controller class’s `@FXML` annotated fields and methods.

The Tip Calculator’s controller class responded to user interactions with the application’s `Button` and `Slider` controls and updated the GUI accordingly. We showed that some event handlers (such as the `Button`’s On Action handler) can be specified directly in Scene Builder as part of the FXML, but event handlers for changes to a control’s property values (such as the `Slider`’s value) must be implemented directly in the controller’s code. We used a lambda to implement the event handler that responded to the `Slider`’s value changes. Throughout the examples, we emphasized JavaFX best practices, such as proper spacing and alignment of GUI elements.

In the next chapter, you’ll learn more details of laying out nodes in a scene graph with various JavaFX layout panels so you can build more intricate GUIs. We’ll demonstrate additional JavaFX controls and event types. We’ll use CSS to style GUIs. We’ll customize a control’s display. You’ll also learn more about JavaFX properties and how to use data binding to automatically update elements in a GUI with new data.

### 16.2 Laying Out Nodes in a Scene Graph

A layout determines the size and positioning of nodes in the scene graph.

##### Node Size

In general, a node’s size should not be defined explicitly. Doing so often creates a design that looks pleasing when it loads but deteriorates as the application is resized or the content updates. In addition to `width` and `height`, most JavaFX nodes have additional properties that specify a node’s range of acceptable sizes as it’s laid out within its parent node:

*   The **`minWidth`** and **`minHeight`** **properties** specify a node’s minimum size in pixels.

*   The **`maxWidth`** and **`maxHeight`** **properties** specify a node’s maximum size in pixels.

*   The **`prefWidth`** and **`prefHeight`** **properties** specify a node’s preferred size that should be used by the layout in most cases.

##### Node Position and Layout Panes

A node’s position should be defined relative to its parent node and the other nodes in its parent. JavaFX **layout panes** are container nodes that arrange their child nodes in a scene graph relative to one another based on their sizes and positions. Child nodes are controls, other layout panes, shapes and more.

Most JavaFX layout panes use relative positioning—if a layout-pane node is resized, it adjusts its children’s sizes and positions accordingly, based on their preferred, minimum and maximum sizes. The following table describes each of the JavaFX layouts, including those presented in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15)—these are defined in the packages `javafx.scene.layout` and `javafx.scene.controls`. In this chapter, we’ll use `Pane`, `BorderPane`, `GridPane` and `VBox` from the `javafx.scene.layout` package:

| Layout | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Accordion` | Displays multiple panes but allows only one to be expanded at a time. |
| `AnchorPane` | Enables you to set the position of child nodes relative to the pane’s edges. Resizing the pane does not alter the layout of the nodes. |
| `BorderPane` | Includes top, bottom, left, center and right area where you can place nodes. The top and bottom fill the `BorderPane`’s width and are vertically sized to their children’s preferred heights. The left and right fill the height (between the top and bottom) and are horizontally sized to their children’s preferred widths. The center area occupies all remaining space between the top, bottom, left and right. You might use the different areas for toolbars, navigation, a primary content area, etc. |
| `ButtonBar` | Arranges `Button`s and other controls, typically for use in dialog boxes. |
| `DialogPane` | Arranges a dialog box’s content area, including its header, content and buttons. |
| `FlowPane` | Lays out nodes consecutively—either horizontally or vertically. When the boundary for the pane is reached, the nodes wrap to a new line in a horizontal `FlowPane` or a new column in a vertical `FlowPane`. |
| `GridPane` | Creates a flexible grid for laying out nodes in rows and columns. |
| `HBox` | Arranges nodes horizontally in one row. |
| `Pane` | The base class for layout panes. Positions nodes at exact coordinates—known as absolute positioning. |
| `ScrollPane` | Provides scroll bars for its content, enabling users to scroll through content that cannot fit in the viewing area. |
| `SplitPane` | Divides a layout into user-resizable areas. |
| `StackPane` | Places nodes in a stack. Each new node is stacked atop the previous node. For example, you might use this to place text on top of images. |
| `Tab` | A single tab in a `TabPane` layout. |
| `TabPane` | A layout that manages multiple `Tab`s, similar to the tabs representing individual websites in a web browser window. |
| `TextFlow` | Displays and wraps text dynamically, similar to word-processing apps like Google Docs or Microsoft Word. |
| `TilePane` | A horizontal or vertical grid of equally sized tiles. Nodes that are tiled horizontally wrap at the `TilePane`’s width. Nodes that are tiled vertically wrap at the `TilePane`’s height. |
| `TitledPane` | Collapsible layout with a title and content. The content can be expanded or collapsed by clicking the title. |
| `ToolBar` | Horizontal or vertical bar containing a group of controls. Typically used to arrange `Button`s and other controls at the edges of a GUI. |
| `VBox` | Arranges nodes vertically in one column. |

### 16.3 Painter Application: RadioButtons, Mouse Events and Shapes

In this section, you’ll create the following simple Painter application that allows you to drag the mouse to draw—you can compile and run each of this chapter’s applications using `javac` and `java` commands similar to those you saw in [Section 15.5.1](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec15):

![Images](graphics/f0600-01.jpg)

First, we’ll overview the technologies you’ll use, then we’ll discuss creating the application’s project and building its GUI. Finally, we’ll present the source code for its `Painter` and `PainterController` classes.

#### 16.3.1 Technologies Overview

This section introduces the JavaFX features you’ll use in the Painter application.

##### `RadioButton`s and `ToggleGroup`s

**`RadioButton`****s** function as mutually exclusive options. You add multiple `RadioButton`s to a **`ToggleGroup`** to ensure that only one `RadioButton` in a given group is selected at a time. You’ll use JavaFX Scene Builder to specify each `RadioButton`’s `ToggleGroup` in FXML; however, you can also create a `ToggleGroup` programmatically, then use a **`RadioButton`****’s** **`setToggleGroup`** **method** to specify its `ToggleGroup`. In fact, some programmers create entire JavaFX GUI’s programmatically without using FXML.

##### `BorderPane` Layout Container

A **`BorderPane`** **layout container** arranges controls into one or more of the five regions shown in the following diagram:

![Images](graphics/f0601-01.jpg)

The top and bottom areas have the same width as the `BorderPane`. The left, center and right areas fill the vertical space between the top and bottom. Each area may contain only one control or one layout container—any layout container, in turn, may contain other controls, layouts and nodes. All the areas in a `BorderPane` are optional:

*   If the top or bottom area is empty, the left, center and right areas expand vertically to fill that area.

*   If the left or right area is empty, the center expands horizontally to fill that area.

##### `TitledPane` Layout Container

A **`TitledPane`** **layout container** displays a title at its top and is a collapsible panel containing a layout for other nodes. You’ll use `TitledPane`s to organize the application’s `RadioButton`s and to help the user understand the purpose of each `RadioButton` group.

##### JavaFX Shapes

The **`javafx.scene.shape`** **package** contains various classes for 2D and 3D shape nodes that can be displayed in a scene graph. In this application, you’ll programmatically create **`Circle`** objects as the user drags the mouse, then attach them to the application’s drawing area to display them in the scene graph.

##### `Pane` Layout Container

The drawing area will be a **`Pane`** **layout**. Each `Circle` object will be placed at an *x-y* coordinate measured from the `Pane`’s upper-left corner.

##### Mouse Event Handling

When you drag the mouse, the application’s controller responds by displaying a `Circle` in the currently selected color and pen size at the current mouse position in the `Pane`. JavaFX nodes support various mouse events, which are summarized in the following table:

| Mouse events | When the event occurs for a given node |
| --- | --- |
| **`onMouseClicked`** | The user clicks a mouse button—that is, presses and releases a mouse button without moving the mouse—with the mouse cursor within that node. |
| **`onMouseDragEntered`** | The mouse cursor enters a node’s bounds during a mouse drag—that is, the user is moving the mouse with a mouse button pressed. |
| **`onMouseDragExited`** | The mouse cursor exits the node’s bounds during a mouse drag. |
| **`onMouseDragged`** | The user begins a mouse drag with the mouse cursor within that node and continues moving the mouse with a mouse button pressed. |
| **`onMouseDragOver`** | A drag operation starts in a different node and continues with the mouse cursor over the given node. |
| **`onMouseDragReleased`** | The user completes a drag operation that began in that node. |
| **`onMouseEntered`** | The mouse cursor enters that node’s bounds. |
| **`onMouseExited`** | The mouse cursor exits that node’s bounds. |
| **`onMouseMoved`** | The mouse cursor moves within that node’s bounds. |
| **`onMousePressed`** | The user presses a mouse button with the mouse cursor within that node’s bounds. |
| **`onMouseReleased`** | The user releases a mouse button with the mouse cursor within that node’s bounds. |

For this application, you’ll configure the `Pane`’s **`onMouseDragged`** **event handler**. JavaFX also supports other types of input events. For example, for touchscreen devices, there are touch-oriented events, and for keyboards, there are key events. For a complete list of JavaFX node events, see the `Node` class’s properties that begin with the word “on” at:

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0602-02)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/Node.html
```

##### Setting a Control’s User Data

Each JavaFX control has a **`setUserData`** **method** that receives an `Object`. You can use this to store any object you’d like to associate with that control. With each drawing-color `RadioButton`, we store the specific `Color` that the `RadioButton` represents. With each pen size `RadioButton`, we store an `enum` constant for the corresponding pen size. We use these objects when handling the `RadioButton` events.

#### 16.3.2 Creating the `Painter.fxml` File

Create a folder on your system for this example’s files, then open Scene Builder and save the new FXML file as `Painter.fxml`. If you already have an FXML file open, you can also choose File > New to create a new FXML file, then save it.

#### 16.3.3 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Painter application’s GUI. Rather than providing the exact steps as we did in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15), we’ll provide general instructions for building the GUI and focus on specific details for new concepts. As you build the GUI, keep in mind that it’s often easier to manipulate layouts and controls via Scene Builder’s Hierarchy section than directly in the stage design area.

##### fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

The following diagram shows the fx:id properties of the Painter application’s programmatically manipulated controls. As you build the GUI, you should set the corresponding fx:id properties in the FXML document, as we discussed in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15):

![Images](graphics/f0603-01.jpg)

##### Step 1: Adding a `BorderPane` as the Root Layout Node

Drag a `BorderPane` from the Scene Builder Library window’s Containers section onto the content panel.

##### Step 2: Configuring the `BorderPane`

Set the `BorderPane`’s Pref Width and Pref Height properties to `640` and `480`. Recall that the stage’s size is determined based on the size of the root node in the FXML document. For the `BorderPane`, set the Padding property’s four values to `8` to inset it from the stage’s edges.

##### Step 3: Adding the `Pane` and `VBox`

Drag a `Pane` into the center area and a `VBox` into the `BorderPane`’s left area. As you drag over the `BorderPane`, Scene Builder shows the layout’s five regions and highlights the one where the item you’re dragging will appear when you release the mouse. Set the `Pane`’s fx:id to `drawingAreaPane`.

For the `VBox`, set its Spacing property (in the Inspector’s Layout section) to `8` to add some vertical space between the controls that you’ll place in this container. Set its right Margin property to `8` to add some horizontal spacing between the `VBox` and the `Pane`. Also, set its Max Height property to `MAX_VALUE`. This will enable the `VBox` to be as wide as it needs to be to accommodate its child nodes and occupy the full column height.

Reset the `Pane`’s Pref Width and Pref Height to their default `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` values, and set its Max Width and Max Height to `MAX_VALUE` so that it occupies the entire width and height of the `BorderPane`’s center area. In the `Pane`’s JavaFX CSS category of the Inspector window’s Properties section, click the field below Style (initially empty) and select

```
-fx-background-color
```

so you can specify the `Pane`’s background color. In the field to its right, specify `white`.

##### Step 4: Adding the `TitledPane`s to the `VBox`

From the Library window’s Containers section, drag two TitledPane (empty) objects onto the `VBox`. For the first `TitledPane`, set its Text property to `Drawing Color`. For the second, set its Text property to `Pen Size`.

##### Step 5: Customizing the `TitledPane`s

Each `TitledPane` in the completed GUI contains multiple `RadioButton`s. We’ll use a `VBox` in each `TitledPane` to help arrange those controls. Drag a `VBox` onto each `TitledPane`. Set each `VBox`’s Spacing property to `8` and Pref Width and Pref Height to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` so the `VBox`es will be sized based on their contents.

##### Step 6: Adding the `RadioButton`s to the `VBox`

From the Library window’s Controls section, drag four `RadioButton`s onto the `VBox` for the Drawing Color `TitledPane` and three `RadioButton`s onto the `VBox` for the Pen Size `Titled-Pane`. Configure their Text properties and fx:ids as shown previously. Next, select the `blackRadioButton` and ensure its Selected property is checked, then do the same for the `mediumRadioButton`.

##### Step 7: Specifying the `ToggleGroup`s for the `RadioButton`s

Select all four `RadioButton`s in the first `TitledPane`’s `VBox`. In the Inspector’s Properties section, set the Toggle Group property to `colorToggleGroup`. When the application loads the FXML file at execution time, the `FXMLLoader` will create a `ToggleGroup` object by that name and associate these four `RadioButton`s with it to ensure that only one is selected at a time. Repeat this step for the three `RadioButton`s in the second `TitledPane`’s `VBox`, but set the Toggle Group property to `sizeToggleGroup`.

##### Step 8: Changing the `TitledPane`s’ Preferred Width and Height

For each `TitledPane`, set its Pref Width and Pref Height to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` so the `TitledPane`s will be sized based on their contents.

##### Step 9: Adding the `Button`s

Add two `Button`s below the `TitledPane`s, then configure their Text properties and fx:ids as shown previously. Set each `Button`’s Max Width property to `MAX_VALUE` so that they fill the `VBox`’s width.

##### Step 10: Setting the `VBox`’s Width

We want the `VBox` to be only as wide as required for the controls in that column. Select the `VBox` in the Document window’s Hierarchy section. Set its Min Width and Pref Width properties to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE`, then set the Max Width to `USE_PREF_SIZE` to indicate that the maximum width should be the preferred width. Also, reset the Max Height to its default `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` value. The GUI should now appear as shown at the beginning of this section.

##### Step 11: Specifying the Controller Class’s Name

As we mentioned in [Section 15.5.2](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev2sec16), in a JavaFX FXML application, the application’s controller class typically defines instance variables for interacting with controls programmatically, as well as event-handling methods. To ensure that an object of the controller class is created when the application loads the FXML file at runtime, specify the controller class’s name in the FXML file:

1.  Expand Scene Builder’s Controller window (located below the Hierarchy window).

2.  In the Controller Class field, type `PainterController`.

##### Step 12: Specifying the Event-Handler Method Names

Next, specify in the Inspector window’s Code section the names of the methods that will be called to handle specific events:

*   For the `drawingAreaPane`, go to the Code section’s Mouse heading and specify `drawingAreaMouseDragged` as the On Mouse Dragged event handler. This method will draw a circle in the specified color and size for each mouse-dragged event.

*   For the four Drawing Color `RadioButton`s, specify `colorRadioButtonSelected` as each `RadioButton`’s On Action event handler. This method will set the current drawing color based on the user’s selection.

*   For the three Pen Size `RadioButton`s, specify `sizeRadioButtonSelected` as each `RadioButton`’s On Action event handler. This method will set the current pen size based on the user’s selection.

*   For the Undo `Button`, specify `undoButtonPressed` as the On Action event handler. This method will remove the last circle the user drew on the screen.

*   For the Clear `Button`, specify `clearButtonPressed` as the On Action event handler. This method will clear the entire drawing.

##### Step 13: Generating a Sample Controller Class

As you saw in [Section 15.5](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev1sec5), Scene Builder generates the initial controller-class skeleton when you select View > Show Sample Controller Skeleton. You can copy this code into a `PainterController.java` file and store the file in the same folder as `Painter.fxml`. We show the completed `PainterController` class in [Section 16.3.5](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev2sec7).

##### `PenSize enum`

Lines 15–25 define the nested `enum` type `PenSize`, which specifies three pen sizes—`SMALL`, `MEDIUM` and `LARGE`. Each contains a radius that will be used when creating a `Circle` object to display in response to a mouse-drag event. Java allows you to declare `class`es, `record`s, `interface`s and `enum`s as **nested types** inside other classes. Most previously presented types were top-level, not nested in other types. The `PenSize enum` is declared as a `private` nested type because it’s used only by the `PainterController`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0607-01)

23
24         public int getRadius() {return radius;}
25      };
26

Two of the `@FXML` instance variables are `ToggleGroup`s— the `RadioButton` event handlers use these to determine which `RadioButton` was selected. ##### Method `initialize`

Recall that when the `FXMLLoader` creates a controller-class object, it determines whether the controller class contains an `initialize` method declared with `@FXML` and no parameters and, if so, calls that method to initialize the controller. Lines 44–54 define method `initialize` to specify each `RadioButton`’s corresponding user data object—a `Color` or a `PenSize`. We use these objects in the `RadioButton`s’ event handlers.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0608-01)

##### `drawingAreaMouseDragged` Event Handler

Lines 57–62 define `drawingAreaMouseDragged`, which responds to drag events in the `drawingAreaPane`. Each mouse event handler receives a **`MouseEvent`** parameter (package **`javafx.scene.input`**). When the event occurs, this parameter contains information about the event, such as its location, whether any mouse buttons were pressed, which node the user interacted with and more. You specified `drawingAreaMouseDragged` in Scene Builder as the `drawingAreaPane`’s On Mouse Dragged event handler.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0608-02)

```
56      // handles drawingArea's onMouseDragged MouseEvent
57      @FXML
58      private void drawingAreaMouseDragged(MouseEvent e) {
59         var newCircle = new Circle(e.getX(), e.getY(),
60            radius.getRadius(), brushColor);
61         drawingAreaPane.getChildren().add(newCircle);
62      }
63
```

Lines 59–60 create a new `Circle` object using its constructor that receives its center’s *x*-*y* coordinates, its radius and its `Color`. Next, line 61 attaches the new `Circle` to the `drawingAreaPane`. A layout’s **`getChildren`** **method** returns an **`ObservableList<Node>`** collection containing its child nodes. An `ObservableList` has methods for adding and removing elements. Line 61 uses the `ObservableList`’s `add` method to add a new `Node` to the `drawingAreaPane`—all JavaFX shapes inherit indirectly from class `Node` in the `javafx.scene` package. You’ll learn more about `ObservableList` later in this chapter.

##### `colorRadioButtonSelected` Event Handler

Method `colorRadioButtonSelected` (lines 65–70) responds to the `ActionEvent`s of the Drawing Color `RadioButton`s, which occur when a new color `RadioButton` is selected. You specified this method in Scene Builder as the On Action event handler for all four Drawing Color `RadioButton`s. Lines 68–69 set the current drawing `Color`. `ColorToggleGroup`’s **`getSelectedToggle`** **method** returns the selected `Toggle`. `RadioButton` is one of several controls (others are `RadioButtonMenuItem` and `ToggleButton`) that implement interface **`Toggle`**. The **`Toggle`****’s** **`getUserData`** **method** returns the user data `Object` we associated with the selected `RadioButton` in method `initialize`—for `ColorToggleGroup`’s `RadioButton`s, the `Object` is always a `Color`, so we cast the `Object` to a `Color` and assign it to `brushColor`.

### 16.4 Color Chooser Application: Property Bindings and Property Listeners

This section demonstrates property bindings and property listeners by building a Color Chooser application. The following diagram shows the result of using the Red and Green `Slider`s to create an opaque orange color:

![Images](graphics/f0610-02.jpg)

The following diagram shows the result of using the Red, Green and Alpha `Slider`s to create a semitransparent orange color—notice that the semitransparent orange mixes with the color of the circle behind the colored square:

![Images](graphics/f0610-03.jpg)

#### 16.4.1 Technologies Overview

Let’s introduce the technologies you’ll use to build the Color Chooser.

##### RGBA Colors

The application uses the **RGBA color model** to display a rectangle of color based on the values of four `Slider`s. RGBA represents every color by its red, green and blue color values, each ranging from 0 to 255—0 denotes no color and 255 full color. For example, a color with a red value of 0 would contain no red component. The alpha value (A) ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and represents a color’s opacity—0.0 is transparent, and 1.0 is opaque. The two colors in the previous sample outputs have the same RGB values, but the color displayed in Part (b) is semitransparent. You’ll create an RGBA `Color` object then use it to fill a `Rectangle` with that `Color`.

##### Properties of a Class

JavaFX uses properties extensively. A **property** is an instance of a class that implements JavaFX’s **`Property`** **interface** (**package** **`javafx.beans.property`**) and is accessed via *set* and *get* methods. In general, the pair of methods that define a read/write property have the form:

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0611-01)

```
public final void setPropertyName(Type propertyName)
public final Type getPropertyName()
```

Typically, such methods manipulate a corresponding `private` instance variable with the same name as the property, but this is not required. For example, in a `Time` class, methods `setHour` and `getHour` together represent an `hour` property—they’d typically manipulate a private `hour` instance variable. If the property represents a `boolean` value, its *get* method name would begin with “`is`” rather than “`get`”—for example, `ArrayList` method `isEmpty`. Methods that define properties should be declared `final` to prevent subclasses from overriding the methods, which could lead to unexpected results in client code.

##### Property Bindings

JavaFX properties are implemented in a manner that makes them observable—when a property’s value changes, other objects can respond accordingly. This is similar to event handling. One way to respond to a property change is via a **property binding**, which enables a property of one object to be updated when a property of another object changes. You’ll use property bindings to update a `TextField` with the corresponding `Slider`’s current value when the user moves that `Slider`’s thumb. Property bindings are not limited to JavaFX controls. Package **`javafx.beans.property`** contains many classes that you can use to define bindable properties in your own classes.

##### Property Listeners

Property listeners are similar to property bindings. A **property listener** is an event handler that’s invoked when a property’s value changes. In the event handler, you can respond to the property change in a manner appropriate for your application. In this application, when a `Slider`’s value changes, a property listener will store the value in a corresponding instance variable, create a new `Color` based on the values of all four `Slider`s and set that `Color` as the fill color of a `Rectangle` object that displays the current color. For more information on properties, property bindings and property listeners, visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0611-02)

```
https://deitel.com/JavaFXPropertyBindingTutorial
```

#### 16.4.2 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Color Chooser application’s GUI. Rather than providing the exact steps as we did in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15), we’ll provide general instructions for building the GUI and focus on specific details for new concepts. As you build the GUI, recall that it’s often easier to manipulate layouts and controls via the Scene Builder Document window’s Hierarchy section than directly in the stage design area. Before proceeding, open Scene Builder and create an FXML file named `ColorChooser.fxml`.

##### fx:id Property Values for This Application’s Controls

The following diagram shows the fx:id properties for the Color Chooser application’s pro-grammatically manipulated controls. You should set these controls’ fx:id properties in the FXML document, as you learned in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15).

![Images](graphics/f0612-01.jpg)

##### Step 1: Adding a `GridPane`

Drag a `GridPane` from the Library window’s Containers section onto Scene Builder’s content panel.

##### Step 2: Configuring the `GridPane`

This application’s `GridPane` requires four rows and four columns. Use the techniques you’ve learned previously to add two columns and one row to the `GridPane`. Set the `Grid-Pane`’s Hgap and Padding properties to `8` to inset the `GridPane` from the stage’s edges and provide space between its columns.

##### Step 3: Adding the Controls

Using the previous diagram as a guide, add the `Label`s, `Slider`s, `TextField`s, a `Circle` and a `Rectangle` to the `GridPane`—`Circle` and `Rectangle` are located in the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section. When adding the `Circle` and `Rectangle`, place both in the rightmost column’s first row, adding the `Circle` before the `Rectangle` so it will be behind the rectangle in the layout. Set the text of the `Label`s and `TextField`s as shown and set all the appropriate fx:id properties as you add each control.

##### Step 4: Configuring the `Slider`s

For the red, green and blue `Slider`s, set the Max properties to `255` (the maximum amount of a given color in the RGBA color scheme). For the alpha `Slider`, set its Max property to ^(`1.0`) (the maximum opacity in the RGBA color scheme).

##### Step 5: Configuring the `TextField`s

Set all of the `TextField`’s Pref Width properties to `50`.

##### Step 6: Configuring the `Rectangle`

Set the `Rectangle`’s Width and Height properties to `100`, then set its Row Span property to `Remaining` so it spans all four rows in that column.

##### Step 7: Configuring the `Circle`

Set the `Circle`’s Radius property to `40`, then set its Row Span property to `Remainder` so it spans all four rows in that column.

##### Step 8: Configuring the Rows

Set all four rows’ Pref Height properties to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` so the rows are only as tall as their content.

##### Step 9: Configuring the Columns

Set all four columns’ Pref Width properties to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` so the columns are only as wide as their content. For the leftmost column, set the Halignment property to `RIGHT`. For the rightmost column, set the Halignment property to `CENTER`.

##### Step 10: Configuring the `GridPane`

Set the `GridPane`’s Pref Width and Pref Height properties to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE` so it sizes itself based on its contents. Your GUI is now complete.

##### Step 11: Specifying the Controller Class’s Name

To ensure that an object of the controller class is created when the application loads the FXML file at runtime, specify `ColorChooserController` as the controller class’s name in the FXML file.

##### Step 12: Generating a Sample Controller Class

Select View > Show Sample Controller Skeleton, then copy this code into a `ColorChooserController.java` file and store the file in the same folder as `ColorChooser.fxml`. We show the completed `ColorChooserController` class in [Section 16.4.4](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev2sec12).

##### Instance Variables

Lines 13–27 declare the controller’s instance variables. The variables `red`, `green`, `blue` and `alpha` store the `redSlider`, `greenSlider`, `blueSlider` and `alphaSlider` current values. We use these to update the `colorRectangle`’s fill color when the user adjusts a `Slider`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0614-02)

```
12      // instance variables for interacting with GUI components
13      @FXML private Slider redSlider;
14      @FXML private Slider greenSlider;
15      @FXML private Slider blueSlider;
16      @FXML private Slider alphaSlider;
17      @FXML private TextField redTextField;
18      @FXML private TextField greenTextField;
19      @FXML private TextField blueTextField;
20      @FXML private TextField alphaTextField;
21      @FXML private Rectangle colorRectangle;
22
23      // instance variables for managing
24      private int red = 0;
25      private int green = 0;
26      private int blue = 0;
27      private double alpha = 1.0;
28
```

##### Method `initialize`

Lines 29–66 define method `initialize` to complete the controller’s initialization after the `FXMLLoader` creates the GUI. In this application, `initialize` configures the property bindings and property listeners.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0615-01)

```
29      @FXML
30      private void initialize() {
31         // bind TextField values to corresponding Slider values
32         redTextField.textProperty().bind(
33            redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
34         greenTextField.textProperty().bind(
35            greenSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
36         blueTextField.textProperty().bind(
37            blueSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
38         alphaTextField.textProperty().bind(
39            alphaSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.2f"));
40
41         // listeners that set Rectangle's fill based on Slider changes
42         redSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
43            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
44               red = newValue.intValue();
45               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
46            }
47         );
48         greenSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
49            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
50               green = newValue.intValue();
51               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
52            }
53         );
54         blueSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
55            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
56               blue = newValue.intValue();
57               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
58            }
59         );
60         alphaSlider.valueProperty().addListener(
61            (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
62               alpha = newValue.doubleValue();
63               colorRectangle.setFill(Color.rgb(red, green, blue, alpha));
64            }
65         );
66      }
67   }
```

##### Property-to-Property Bindings

Lines 32–39 set up property bindings between each `Slider`’s value and the corresponding `TextField`’s text so `Slider` changes update the corresponding `TextField`. Consider lines 32–33, which bind the `redSlider`’s `valueProperty` to the `redTextField`’s `textProperty`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0616-01)

```
redTextField.textProperty().bind(
   redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f"));
```

A `TextField`’s **`textProperty`** **method** returns its `text` property as a **`StringProperty`** (package `javafx.beans.property`). **`StringProperty`** **method** **`bind`** receives an **`ObservableValue`** as an argument. When its `ObservableValue` changes, the bound property updates. In this case, the `ObservableValue` is returned by

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0616-02)

```
redSlider.valueProperty().asString("%.0f")
```

The `Slider`’s `valueProperty` method returns its `value` property as a **`DoubleProperty`**, which is an observable `double` value. However, the `TextField`’s `text` property must be bound to an observable `String`. So, we call the **`DoubleProperty`** **method** **`asString`** to get a **`StringBinding`** object—an `ObservableValue` that provides a `String` representation of the `DoubleProperty`. This version of `asString` receives a format-control `String` specifying the `DoubleProperty`’s `String` format.

Once you bind a `TextField`’s `textProperty` to a property of another control, the user may not edit the `TextField`, even though we did not disable its editable property in Scene Builder. In an end-of-chapter genAI exercise, you’ll investigate bidirectional property bindings, which would allow the `TextField` to remain editable by the user.

##### Property Listeners

You can register a property listener if you need to perform an arbitrary task when a property’s value changes. Lines 42–65 register property listeners for the `Slider`s’ `value` properties. Consider lines 42–47, which register the `ChangeListener` that handles changes to the `redSlider`’s value. As in [Section 15.5](#ch15.xhtml_ch15lev1sec5), we implement the `ChangeListener` interface with a lambda. Each `ChangeListener` stores the `newValue` parameter’s `int` value in the corresponding `ColorChooserController` instance variable, then calls the `colorRectangle`’s `setFill` method to change its color, using `Color` method `rgb` to create the new `Color` object.

### 16.5 Cover Viewer Application: Data-Driven GUIs with JavaFX Collections

Often, an application needs to edit and display data. JavaFX provides a comprehensive model for allowing GUIs to interact with data. In this section, you’ll build the Cover Viewer application (shown in the following diagram), which binds a list of `Book` objects to a `ListView`. When the user selects an item in the `ListView`, the corresponding `Book`’s cover image is displayed in an `ImageView`.

![Images](graphics/f0617-01.jpg)

#### 16.5.1 Technologies Overview

This application uses a `ListView` control to display a list of book titles. Though you can individually add items to a `ListView`, this application binds an **`ObservableList`** object to the `ListView`. If you change an `ObservableList`’s elements, its observer (the `ListView`) will automatically be notified. Package **`javafx.collections`** defines `ObservableList` (which, similar to an `ArrayList`, implements the `List` interface) and other observable collection interfaces. The package also contains class **`FXCollections`**, which provides `static` methods for creating and manipulating observable collections. You’ll use a property listener to display the correct image when the user selects an item from the `ListView`. For this control, the property that changes is the selected item.

Before building the application, copy the `images` folder (which contains the `large` and `small` subfolders) from this chapter’s examples folder into the folder where you’ll save this application’s FXML file and the `CoverViewer.java` and `CoverViewerController.java` source-code files. Though you’ll use only the `large` images in this example, you’ll copy this application’s folder to create [Section 16.6](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev1sec6)’s example, which uses both sets of images.

#### 16.5.2 Building the GUI

In this section, we’ll discuss the Cover Viewer application’s GUI. Use Scene Builder to create a new FXML file and save it as `CoverViewer.fxml`.

For the `ImageView`, set the Fit Width and Fit Height properties to `370` and `480`. To size the `BorderPane` based on its contents, set its Pref Width and Pref Height to `USE_COMPUTED_SIZE`. Also, set its Padding property to `8` to inset the `BorderPane` from the stage.

25         books.add(new Book("C++ How to Program",
26            "/images/small/cpphtp.jpg", "/images/large/cpphtp.jpg"));
27         books.add(new Book("Intro to Python",
28            "/images/small/python.jpg", "/images/large/python.jpg"));
29         books.add(new Book("Internet and World Wide Web How to Program",
30            "/images/small/iw3htp.jpg", "/images/large/iw3htp.jpg"));
31         books.add(new Book("Java How to Program",
32            "/images/small/jhtp.jpg", "/images/large/jhtp.jpg"));
33         books.add(new Book("Python for Programmers",
34            "/images/small/pythonfp.jpg", "/images/large/pythonfp.jpg"));
35         books.add(new Book("Visual Basic How to Program",
36            "/images/small/vbhtp.jpg", "/images/large/vbhtp.jpg"));
37         books.add(new Book("Visual C# How to Program",
38            "/images/small/vcshtp.jpg", "/images/large/vcshtp.jpg"));
39         booksListView.setItems(books); // bind booksListView to books
40
41         // when ListView selection changes, show large cover in ImageView
42         booksListView.getSelectionModel().selectedItemProperty().
43            addListener(
44               (ov, oldValue, newValue) -> {
45                  coverImageView.setImage(
46                     new Image(newValue.largeImage()));
47               }
48            );
49      }
50   }
```

##### Listening for `ListView` Selection Changes

To synchronize the displayed book cover with the currently selected book, we listen for changes to the `ListView`’s selected item. By default, a `ListView` supports single selection—one item at a time may be selected. `ListView`s also support multiple selection. The `ListView`’s **`MultipleSelectionModel`** (a subclass of **`SelectionModel`** from package `javafx.scene.control`) manages the selection type. This object contains observable properties and various methods for manipulating the corresponding `ListView`’s items.

To respond to selection changes, you register a listener for the `MultipleSelection-Model`’s `selectedItem` property (lines 42–48). **`ListView`** **method** **`getSelectionModel`** returns a `MultipleSelectionModel` object. In this example, **`MultipleSelectionModel`****’s** **`selectedItemProperty`** **method** returns a **`ReadOnlyObjectProperty<Book>`**, and the corresponding `ChangeListener` receives as its `oldValue` and `newValue` parameters the previously selected and newly selected `Book` objects, respectively.

Lines 45–46 use `newValue`’s large image path to initialize a new **`Image`** (package `javafx.scene.image`)—this loads the image from that path. We then pass the new `Image` to the `coverImageView`’s **`setImage`** **method** to display the `Image`.

### 16.6 Cover Viewer Application: Customizing `ListView` Cells

In the preceding example, the `ListView` displayed a `Book`’s `String` representation (its title). In this example, you’ll create a custom `ListView` cell factory to create cells that display each book as its thumbnail image and title using a `VBox`, an `ImageView` and a `Label`, as shown at the left side of the following screen capture:

![Images](graphics/f0622-01.jpg)

#### 16.6.1 Technologies Overview

##### `ListCell` Generic Class for Custom `ListView` Cell Formats

You saw in [Section 16.5](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev1sec5) that `ListView` cells display `ListView` items’ `String` representations by default. To create a custom cell format, you first define a subclass of the **`ListCell`** **generic class** (package `javafx.scene.control`) that specifies how to create a `ListView` cell. As the `ListView` displays items, it gets `ListCell`s from its cell factory. You’ll use **`ListView`****’s** **`setCellFactory`** **method** to replace the default cell factory with one that returns objects of your `ListCell` subclass. You’ll override this class’s **`updateItem`** **method** to specify the cells’ custom layout and contents.

##### Programmatically Creating Layouts and Controls

So far, you’ve created GUIs visually using JavaFX Scene Builder. In this application, you’ll also create a portion of the GUI programmatically. In fact, everything we’ve shown you in Scene Builder can also be accomplished directly in Java code. For this application, you’ll create and configure a custom `ListView` cell format using a `VBox` layout containing an `ImageView` and a `Label`.

#### 16.6.2 Copying the `CoverViewer` Application

This application’s FXML layout and classes `Book` and `CoverViewer` are identical to those in [Section 16.5](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev1sec5), and the `CoverViewerController` class has only one new statement. For this example, we’ll show a new class that implements the custom `ListView` cell factory and `CoverViewerController`’s new statement. Rather than creating a new application from scratch, copy the `CoverViewer` application from the previous example into a new folder named `CoverViewerCustomListView`.

#### 16.6.3 `ImageTextCell` Custom `ListView` Cell Layout

Class `ImageTextCell` ([Fig. 16.7](#ch16.xhtml_ch16fig07)) defines the custom `ListView` cell layout for this version of the Cover Viewer application. We broke the class into parts for discussion purposes. The `ImageTextCell` class extends `ListCell<Book>` because it defines a customized presentation of a `Book` in a `ListView` cell. For the best `ListView` performance, it’s considered best practice to define the custom presentation’s controls as instance variables in the `ListCell` subclass and configure them in the subclass’s constructor. This minimizes the amount of work required in each call to method `updateItem`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0623-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 16.7: ImageTextCell.java
 2   // Custom ListView cell factory that displays an Image and text
 3   import javafx.geometry.Pos;
 4   import javafx.scene.control.Label;
 5   import javafx.scene.control.ListCell;
 6   import javafx.scene.image.Image;
 7   import javafx.scene.image.ImageView;
 8   import javafx.scene.layout.VBox;
 9   import javafx.scene.text.TextAlignment;
10
11   public class ImageTextCell extends ListCell<Book> {
12      private VBox vbox = new VBox(8.0); // 8 pixels of gap between controls
13      private ImageView thumbImageView = new ImageView(); // initially empty
14      private Label label = new Label();
15
```

**Fig. 16.7** | Custom `ListView` cell factory that displays an image and text.

##### Constructor

The constructor (lines 17–29) configures the instance variables we use to build the custom presentation. Line 18 indicates that the `VBox`’s children should be centered. Lines 20–22 configure the `ImageView` and attach it to the `VBox`’s collection of children. Line 20 indicates that the `ImageView` should preserve the image’s aspect ratio, and line 21 indicates that the `ImageView` should be 100 pixels tall. Line 22 attaches the `ImageView` to the `VBox`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0623-02)

```
16      // constructor configures VBox, ImageView and Label
17      public ImageTextCell() {
18         vbox.setAlignment(Pos.CENTER); // center VBox contents horizontally
19
20         thumbImageView.setPreserveRatio(true);
21         thumbImageView.setFitHeight(100.0); // thumbnail 100 pixels tall
22         vbox.getChildren().add(thumbImageView); // attach to Vbox
23
24         label.setWrapText(true); // wrap if text too wide to fit in label
25         label.setTextAlignment(TextAlignment.CENTER); // center text
26         vbox.getChildren().add(label); // attach to VBox
27
28         setPrefWidth(USE_PREF_SIZE); // use preferred size for cell width
29      }
30
```

Lines 24–26 configure the `Label` and attach it to the `VBox`’s collection of children. Line 24 indicates that the `Label` should wrap its text if it’s too wide to fit in the `Label`’s width, and line 25 indicates that the text should be centered in the `Label`. Line 26 attaches the `Label` to the `VBox`. Finally, line 28 indicates that the cell should use its preferred width, which is determined from the width of its parent `ListView`.

##### Method `updateItem`

Method `updateItem` (lines 32–46) configures the `Label`’s text and the `ImageView`’s `Image`, then displays the custom presentation in the `ListView`. The `ListView`’s cell factory calls this method when a `ListView` cell is required—when the `ListView` is first displayed and when `ListView` cells are about to scroll onto the screen. The method receives the `Book` to display and a `boolean` indicating whether the cell about to be created is empty. You must call the superclass’s `updateItem` method (line 35) to ensure the custom cells display correctly.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0624-01)

```
31      // called to configure each custom ListView cell
32      @Override
33      protected void updateItem(Book item, boolean empty) {
34         // required to ensure that cell displays properly
35         super.updateItem(item, empty)
36
37         if (empty || item == null) {
38            setGraphic(null); // don't display anything
39         }
40         else {
41            // set ImageView's thumbnail image
42            thumbImageView.setImage(new Image(item.thumbImage()));
43            label.setText(item.title()); // configure Label's text
44            setGraphic(vbox); // attach custom layout to ListView cell
45         }
46      }
47   }
```

If the cell is empty or the item parameter is `null`, then there is no `Book` to display and line 38 calls the `ImageTextCell`’s inherited **`setGraphic`** **method** with `null`. This method receives the `Node` that should be displayed in the cell. Any JavaFX `Node` can be provided, giving you tremendous flexibility for customizing a cell’s appearance.

If there is a `Book` to display, lines 40–45 configure the `ImageTextCell`’s `Label` and `ImageView`. Line 42 creates the `Book`’s `Image` object and sets it to display in the `ImageView`. Line 43 sets the `Label`’s text to the `Book`’s title. Finally, line 44 uses method `setGraphic` to set the `ImageTextCell`’s `VBox` as the custom cell’s presentation.

#### 16.6.4 `CoverViewerController` Class

Once you’ve defined the custom cell layout, updating the `CoverViewerController` to use it requires setting the `ListView`’s cell factory. Insert the following code as the last statement in the `CoverViewerController`’s `initialize` method:

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0624-02)

```
// set custom ListView cell factory
booksListView.setCellFactory(
   listView -> new ImageTextCell();
);
```

The argument to `ListView` method `setCellFactory` is an implementation of the **functional interface** **`CallBack`** (package **`javafx.util`**). This generic interface provides a `call` method that receives one argument and returns a value. In this case, we implement interface `Callback` with a lambda. Though we don’t use it here, the compiler will infer that the lambda’s parameter is a `ListView<Book>`. The parameter represents the `ListView` in which the custom cells will appear. The compiler also infers that the lambda’s return type is a `ListCell<Book>` object—an `ImageTextCell` *is a* `ListCell<Book>`. The lambda returns a new `ImageTextCell` object. Each time the `ListView` requires a new cell, the lambda is invoked to get a new `ImageTextCell`. Then the `ImageTextCell`’s `updateItem` method is called to create the custom cell presentation.

### 16.7 `FileChooser` and `DirectoryChooser` Dialogs

JavaFX’s **`FileChooser`** and **`DirectoryChooser`** **classes** (package `javafx.stage`) are predefined dialogs that applications can display so users can select local system files and directories. To demonstrate these, we’ll enhance the file-and-directory processing example from [Section 11.3](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev1sec3). Sample screen captures are shown in the code discussion.

##### Creating the JavaFX GUI

The GUI (`FileChooserTest.fxml`) consists of a 600-by-400 `BorderPane` with the fx:id `borderPane`:

![Images](graphics/f0625-01.jpg)

The `BorderPane`’s top contains a **`ToolBar`** **layout** (from the Scene Builder Library’s Containers section), which arranges its controls horizontally (by default) or vertically. Typically, you place `ToolBar`s at your GUI’s edges, such as in a `BorderPane`’s top, right, bottom or left areas.

The `BorderPane`’s center contains a **`TextArea`** **control** with the fx:id `textArea`. We set the control’s Text property to `"Select file or directory"` and enabled its Wrap Text property to ensure that long lines of text wrap to the next line. If there are more lines of text to display than vertical lines in the `TextArea`, the control will show a vertical scrollbar. When Wrap Text is not enabled, the `TextArea` also shows a horizontal scrollbar if the text is too wide to display.

By default, the `ToolBar` you drag onto your layout has one `Button`. You can drag other controls onto the `ToolBar` and, if necessary, remove the default `Button`. We added a second `Button`. For the first `Button`, we set:

*   the Text property to `"Select File"`,

*   the fx:id property to `selectFileButton` and

*   the On Action event handler to `selectFileButtonPressed`.

For the second `Button`, we set:

*   the Text property to `"Select Directory"`,

*   the fx:id property to `selectDirectoryButton` and

*   the On Action event handler to `selectDirectoryButtonPressed`.

Finally, we specified `FileChooserTestController` as the FXML’s controller.

##### Class That Launches the Application

[Figure 16.8](#ch16.xhtml_ch16fig08) shows the `FileChooserTest` subclass of `Application`, which operates the same as the previous examples’ `Application` subclasses. The figure also shows the application’s initial GUI.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0626-01)

##### Controller Class

Class `FileChooserTestController` ([Fig. 16.9](#ch16.xhtml_ch16fig09)) responds to the `Button`s’ events. We broke the class into parts for discussion purposes. Lines 18–21 declare the variables for the controls with fx:ids in the FXML file.

**Fig. 16.9** | Displays information about a selected file or folder.

##### Method `selectFileButtonPressed`

When the user presses the Select File button, method `selectFileButtonPressed` (lines 24–44) creates, configures and displays a `FileChooser` (shown in the first screen capture below the code). Line 28 sets the text displayed in the `FileChooser`’s title bar. Line 31 specifies the initial directory that should be opened when the `FileChooser` is displayed. Method `setInitialDirectory` receives a `File` object representing the directory’s location—`"."` represents the current folder from which the application was launched.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0628-01)

```
23   // handles selectFileButton's event
24   @FXML
25   private void selectFileButtonPressed(ActionEvent e) {
26      // configure dialog allowing selection of a file
27      var fileChooser = new FileChooser();
28      fileChooser.setTitle("Select File");
29
30      // display files in folder from which the application was launched
31      fileChooser.setInitialDirectory(new File("."));
32
33      // display the FileChooser
34      File file = fileChooser.showOpenDialog(
35         borderPane.getScene().getWindow());
36
37      // process selected Path or display a message
38      if (file != null) {
39         analyzePath(file.toPath());
40      }
41      else {
42         textArea.setText("Select file or directory");
43      }
44   }
45
```

Lines 34–35 display the `FileChooser` by calling its **`showOpenDialog`** **method** to display a dialog with an Open button for opening a file. This method receives as its argument a reference to the application’s `Window`. A non-`null` argument makes the `FileChooser` a modal dialog that prevents the user from interacting with the rest of the application until the dialog is dismissed—when the user selects a file or clicks Cancel. To obtain the application’s `Window`, we use the `borderPane`’s `getScene` method to get a reference to its parent `Scene`, then use the `Scene`’s `getWindow` method to get a reference to the `Window` containing the `Scene`.

Method `showOpenDialog` returns a `File` representing the selected file’s location, or `null` if the user clicks the Cancel button. If the `File` is not `null`, line 39 calls `analyzePath` to display the selected file’s information—**`File`** **method** **`toPath`** returns a `Path` object representing the location. Otherwise, line 42 displays a message in the `TextArea` telling the user to select a file or directory. The screen captures following method `selectFileButtonPressed` show the `FileChooser` dialog with the `FileChooserTest.java` file selected and the file’s information displayed in the application after the user presses the dialog’s Open button. `FileChooser` also has a **`showSaveDialog`** **method** that displays a dialog with a Save button for saving a file.

When the user presses the Select Directory button, method `selectDirectoryButton-Pressed` (lines 47–67) creates, configures and displays a `DirectoryChooser`.

##### Method `analyzePath`

Both event handlers call method `analyzePath` (lines 70–110) to determine whether a `Path` is a file or directory, display information about it and, if it’s a directory, list its contents.

[Click here to view code image](#ch16_images.xhtml_f0630-01)

```
69      // display information about file or directory user specifies
70      public void analyzePath(Path path) {
71         try {
72            // if the file or directory exists, display its info
73            if (path != null && Files.exists(path)) {
74               // gather file (or directory) information
75               var builder = new StringBuilder();
76               builder.append(String.format("%s:%n", path.getFileName()));
77               builder.append(String.format("%s a directory%n",
78                  Files.isDirectory(path) ? "Is" : "Is not"));
79               builder.append(String.format("%s an absolute path%n",
80                  path.isAbsolute() ? "Is" : "Is not"));
81               builder.append(String.format("Last modified: %s%n",
82                  Files.getLastModifiedTime(path)));
83               builder.append(String.format("Size: %s%n", Files.size(path)));
84               builder.append(String.format("Path: %s%n", path));
85               builder.append(String.format("Absolute path: %s%n",
86                  path.toAbsolutePath()));
87
88               if (Files.isDirectory(path)) { // output directory listing
89                  builder.append(String.format("%nDirectory contents:%n"));
90
91                  // object for iterating through a directory's contents
92                  DirectoryStream<Path> directoryStream =
93                     Files.newDirectoryStream(path);
94
95                  for (Path p : directoryStream) {
96                     builder.append(String.format("%s%n", p));
97                  }
98               }
99
100              // display file or directory info
101              textArea.setText(builder.toString());
102           }
103           else { // Path does not exist
104              textArea.setText("Path does not exist");
105           }
106        }
107        catch (IOException ioException) {
108           textArea.setText(ioException.toString());
109        }
110     }
111  }
```

### 16.8 Other JavaFX Capabilities and JavaFX Accessibility

This section overviews various additional JavaFX capabilities.

##### `TableView` and `TreeTableView` Controls

[Section 16.5](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev1sec5) demonstrated how to bind data to a `ListView` control. You often load such data from a database ([Chapter 20](#ch20.xhtml_ch20), [Accessing Databases with JDBC and SQLite](#ch20.xhtml_ch20)). JavaFX’s `TableView` control (package `javafx.scene.control`) displays tabular data in rows and columns, and supports user interactions with that data. A `TreeTableView` control adds capabilities for hierarchical data with rows that can have child rows, such as a category and the items within that category.

##### Accessibility

JavaFX has accessibility features to help people with visual impairments use their devices. For example, the screen readers in various operating systems can speak screen text or text that you provide to help users with visual impairments understand the purpose of a control. Visually impaired users must enable their operating systems’ screen-reading capabilities. JavaFX controls also support:

*   GUI navigation via the keyboard—for example, the user can press the *Tab* key to jump from one control to the next. If a screen reader is enabled, as the user moves the focus from control to control, the screen reader will speak appropriate information about each control (discussed below).

*   A high-contrast mode to make controls more readable—as with screen readers, visually impaired users must enable this feature in their operating systems.

See your operating system’s documentation for information on enabling its screen reader and high-contrast mode.

Every JavaFX `Node` subclass also has the following accessibility-related properties:

*   `accessibleTextProperty`—A `String` that a screen reader speaks for a control. For example, a screen reader usually speaks the text displayed on a `Button`, but setting this property for a `Button` causes the screen reader to speak this property’s text instead. You can also set this property to provide accessibility text for controls that do not have text, such as `ImageView`s.

*   `accessibleHelpProperty`—A more detailed control description `String` than that provided by the `accessibleTextProperty`. This property’s text should help the user understand the purpose of the control in the context of your application.

*   `accessibleRoleProperty`—A value from the `enum AccessibleRole` (package `javafx.scene`). A screen reader uses this property value to determine the attributes and actions supported for a given control.

*   `accessibleRoleDescriptionProperty`—A `String` text description of a control that a screen reader typically speaks followed by the control’s contents (such as the text on a `Button`) or the value of the `accessibleTextProperty`.

In addition, you can add `Label`s to a GUI that describe other controls. In such cases, you should set each `Label`’s `labelFor` property to the specific control the `Label` describes. For example, a `TextField` in which the user can enter a phone number might be preceded by a `Label` containing the text `"Phone Number"`. If the `Label`’s `labelFor` property references the `TextField`, then a screen reader will read the `Label`’s text as well when describing the `TextField` to the user.

##### Creating Custom JavaFX Controls

You can create custom controls by extending existing JavaFX control classes to customize them or by extending JavaFX’s `Control` class directly.
