### 16.9 JavaFX Updates

This section overviews various JavaFX changes and enhancements.

##### Modularization

In [Chapter 21](#ch21.xhtml_ch21), [Java Platform Module System](#ch21.xhtml_ch21), we discuss Java’s module system in detail. JavaFX 9 and higher are modularized, enabling developers to bundle only the JavaFX modules their apps require. The key JavaFX modules are:

*   `javafx.base`—Contains the packages required by all JavaFX apps. All the other JavaFX modules depend on this one.

*   `javafx.controls`—Contains the packages for controls, layouts and charts, including the various controls shown in this chapter and [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15).

*   `javafx.fxml`—Contains the packages for working with FXML, including the FXML features we demonstrated in this chapter and [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15).

*   `javafx.graphics`—Contains the packages for working with graphics, animation, CSS (for styling nodes), text and more ([Chapter 17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17), [JavaFX Graphics and Multimedia](#ch17.xhtml_ch17)).

*   `javafx.media`—Contains the packages for incorporating audio and video ([Chapter 17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17), [JavaFX Graphics and Multimedia](#ch17.xhtml_ch17)).

*   `javafx.swing`—Contains the packages for integrating older Swing GUI components into JavaFX apps.

*   `javafx.web`—Contains the package for integrating web content.

##### Skinning APIs

[Chapter 17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17) demonstrates formatting JavaFX `Node`s using Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)— originally for styling web page elements. CSS specifies presentation (e.g., fonts, spacing, sizes, colors, positioning) separately from the GUI’s structure and content (layout containers, shapes, text, GUI components, etc.). If a JavaFX GUI’s presentation is determined entirely by a style sheet, you can swap in a new style sheet—sometimes called a skin—to change the GUI’s appearance. Each JavaFX control also has a skin class that determines its default appearance (located in **package** **`javafx.scene.control.skin`**). You can extend the appropriate skin class to customize the look-and-feel for a given type of control. You then create an object of your custom skin class and set it via a control’s `setSkin` method.

##### Subscription API

JavaFX 21 added the new `Subscription` API for adding and removing event listeners pro-grammatically. See [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5) for a demonstration.

##### High-DPI Screen Support

JavaFX supports high DPI (dots-per-inch) screens on Windows, macOS and Linux, as well as capabilities to programmatically manipulate the scale at which JavaFX apps are rendered.

##### Updated GStreamer

JavaFX implements its audio and video multimedia capabilities using the open-source GStreamer framework ([`https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org`](https://gstreamer.freedesktop.org)). JavaFX 23 incorporates a more recent version of GStreamer with bug fixes and performance enhancements.

##### Updated WebKit

JavaFX’s `WebView` control enables you to embed web content in your JavaFX apps. It’s based on the open-source WebKit framework ([`https://www.webkit.org`](https://www.webkit.org))—a web browser engine that supports loading and rendering web pages. JavaFX incorporates WebKit updates several times per year.

##### CSS Transitions

JavaFX 23 added support for CSS transitions, which allow smoother animations when CSS properties change. We’ll introduce CSS transitions in [Section 17.7](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec7).

### 16.11 Wrap-Up

In this chapter, we continued our presentation of JavaFX. We discussed JavaFX layout panes in more detail and used `BorderPane`, `TitledPane` and `Pane` to arrange controls.

We discussed the many mouse events supported by JavaFX nodes and used the `onMouseDragged` event in a simple Painter application that displayed `Circle`s as the user dragged the mouse across a `Pane`. We used `ToggleGroup`s and `RadioButton`s to manage mutually exclusive options and set the user data `Object` for a control. When you selected a `RadioButton`, the Painter application obtained the selected `RadioButton` from the corresponding `ToggleGroup`, then accessed the `RadioButton`’s user data `Object` for convenient access to the Painter application’s selected color or pen size.

We discussed property binding and property listeners then used them to implement a Color Chooser application. You bound a `TextField`’s text to a `Slider`’s value to automatically update the `TextField` when the user moved the `Slider`’s thumb. You also used a property listener to allow the application’s controller to update a `Rectangle`’s color when a `Slider`’s value changed.

In the Cover Viewer application, we showed how to bind a JavaFX `ObservableList` collection to a `ListView` control to populate it with the collection’s elements. By default, each object in the collection was displayed as a `String` in the `ListView`. You configured a property listener to display an image in an `ImageView` when the user selected an item in the `ListView`. We then modified the Cover Viewer application to use a custom `ListView` cell factory that specified a custom layout for the `ListView` cells’ contents. We displayed `FileChooser` and `DirectoryChooser` dialogs so the user could select a file or directory.

Finally, we introduced several other JavaFX capabilities and recent changes, and discussed several JavaFX online resources. In the next chapter, we’ll demonstrate additional JavaFX features, including graphics, multimedia and customizing a GUI’s look-and-feel with JavaFX’s CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) capabilities.

## JavaFX Graphics and Multimedia

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this chapter, you’ll:

*   Use JavaFX graphics and multimedia capabilities to make your apps “come alive” with graphics, animations, audio and video.

*   Use external Cascading Style Sheets to customize the look of `Nodes` while maintaining their functionality.

*   Customize font attributes like font family, size and style.

*   Display two-dimensional `Arc`, `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Line`, `Path`, `Polyline`, `Polygon` and `Rectangle` shape nodes.

*   Customize a shape’s stroke and fill using solid colors, images and gradients.

*   Use `Transform`s to reposition and reorient nodes.

*   Enable video playback with `Media`, `MediaPlayer` and `MediaView`.

*   Animate `Node` properties with `Transition`s and `Timelines`.

*   Use an `AnimationTimer` to create frame-based animations.

*   Apply JavaFX CSS transitions to CSS properties.

*   Draw graphics on a `Canvas`.

*   Display 3D shapes.

*   Be briefly introduced to FXGL for JavaFX game development.

Outline

### 17.1 Introduction

In this chapter, we continue our discussion of JavaFX from [Chapters 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15) and [16](#ch16.xhtml_ch16). Here, we present various JavaFX graphics and multimedia capabilities. You’ll:

*   Use Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) to customize the appearance of JavaFX nodes.

*   Customize fonts and font attributes used to display text.

*   Display two-dimensional shapes, including lines, rectangles, circles, ellipses, arcs, polylines, polygons and custom paths.

*   Apply transforms to `Node`s, such as rotating a `Node` around a particular point, scaling, translating (moving) and more.

*   Display video and control its playback (e.g., play and pause).

*   Dynamically modify JavaFX `Node`s with `Transition` and `Timeline` animations that change `Node` property values over time. As you’ll learn, built-in `Transition` animations change specific JavaFX `Node` properties (such as a `Node`’s stroke and fill colors), but `Timeline` animations can change any modifiable `Node` property.

*   Create frame-by-frame animations with an `AnimationTimer`.

*   Apply CSS transitions to a `Node`’s CSS properties.

*   Draw two-dimensional graphics on a `Canvas Node`.

*   Display three-dimensional shapes, including boxes, cylinders and spheres.

*   Get a brief introduction to FXGL for JavaFX game development.

This chapter does not include each example’s `Application` subclass because it performs the same tasks we discussed and demonstrated in [Chapters 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15) and [16](#ch16.xhtml_ch16). Some examples do not have controller classes because they display JavaFX controls or graphics only to demonstrate Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) capabilities.

### 17.2 Controlling Fonts with Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)

In [Chapters 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15)–[16](#ch16.xhtml_ch16), you built JavaFX GUIs using Scene Builder. You specified a particular JavaFX object’s appearance by selecting the object in Scene Builder then setting its property values in the Properties inspector. With this approach, if you want to change the GUI’s appearance, you must edit each object. This can be time-consuming and error-prone for more complex GUIs in which you want to make the same changes to multiple objects.

In this chapter, we format JavaFX objects using **Cascading Style Sheets (CSS)**—a technology typically used to style web page elements. A CSS style sheet specifies appearance details (fonts, spacing, sizes, colors, positioning, etc.) separately from the GUI’s structure and content (layout containers, shapes, text, GUI components, etc.) If a JavaFX GUI’s presentation is determined entirely by CSS rules, you update its appearance by swapping in a new style sheet.

In this section, you’ll use CSS to specify several `Label`s’ font properties and the `VBox` layout’s spacing and padding properties. You’ll place **CSS rules** that specify the font properties, spacing and padding in a separate file that ends with the **`.css`** **filename extension**, then reference that file from the FXML. You’ll observe that

*   before referencing the CSS file from the FXML, Scene Builder displays the GUI without styling and

*   after referencing the CSS file from the FXML, Scene Builder renders the GUI with the CSS rules applied to the appropriate objects.

For a complete reference containing

*   all the JavaFX CSS properties,

*   the JavaFX `Node` types to which the attributes can be applied, and

*   the allowed values for each attribute

visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0641-01)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html
```

#### 17.2.1 CSS That Styles the GUI

[Figure 17.1](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig01) presents this app’s CSS rules specifying the `VBox`’s and `Label`s’ styles. We split the file into parts for discussion purposes. We use the shorthand “app” for “application” throughout this chapter.

##### `.vbox` CSS Rule—Style Class Selectors

Lines 4–7 define the `.vbox` CSS rule that will be applied to this app’s `VBox` object (lines 8–18 of [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02)).

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0642-01)

```
 1   /* Fig. 17.1: FontsCSS.css */
 2   /* CSS rules that style the VBox and Labels */
 3
 4   .vbox {
 5      -fx-spacing: 10;
 6      -fx-padding: 10;
 7   }
 8
```

**Fig. 17.1** | CSS rules that style the `VBox` and `Label`s.

Each CSS rule begins with a **CSS selector** which specifies the JavaFX objects that will be styled according to the rule. In this rule, `.vbox` is a **style class selector**. The CSS properties in this rule are applied to any JavaFX object that has a `styleClass` property with the value `"vbox"`. In CSS, a style class selector begins with a dot (`.`) and is followed by its **class name** (not to be confused with a Java class). By convention, selector names typically have all lowercase letters, and multi-word names separate each word from the next with a dash (`-`).

Each CSS rule’s body is delimited by required braces (`{}`) containing the CSS properties applied to objects matching the CSS selector. JavaFX CSS property names begin with `-fx-` followed by the JavaFX object’s property name in all lowercase letters.^([1](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_1a)) So,

[1](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_1). According to [`https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html`](https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html), JavaFX CSS properties are considered extensions to CSS, so JavaFX’s CSS property names begin with “`-fx-`” to ensure they have distinct names from their HTML CSS counterparts.

*   **`-fx-spacing`** (line 5) defines the value for a JavaFX object’s `spacing` property and

*   **`-fx-padding`** (line 6) defines the value for a JavaFX object’s `padding` property.

Each property value is specified to the right of a required colon (`:`). In this case, we set

*   `-fx-spacing` to `10` for 10 pixels of vertical space between objects in the `VBox` and

*   `-fx-padding` to `10` to separate the `VBox`’s contents from the `VBox`’s edges by 10 pixels at the top, right, bottom and left edges.

You also can specify the `-fx-padding` with four values separated by spaces. For example,

```
-fx-padding: 10 5 10 5
```

specifies 10 pixels for the top padding, 5 for the right, 10 for the bottom and 5 for the left. In [Section 17.2.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev2sec2), you’ll apply the `.vbox` CSS rule to the `VBox` object.

##### `#label1` CSS Rule—ID Selectors

Lines 9–11 of [Fig. 17.1](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig01) define the `#label1` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Label` with the `fx:id label1`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0642-02)

```
 9   #label1 {
10      -fx-font: bold 14pt Arial;
11   }
12
```

Selectors that begin with `#` are **ID selectors**—they’re applied to objects with the specified ID. In this case, the `#label1` selector matches an object with the `fx:id label1`—that is, the `Label` object in line 12 of [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02). The `#label1` CSS rule

```
-fx-font: bold 14pt Arial;
```

sets an object’s `font` property so that a corresponding object displays its text in a bold, 14-point Arial font. The `-fx-font` property can specify all aspects of a font, including its style, weight, size and font family. The size and font family are required. There are also properties for each aspect of a font: **`-fx-font-style`**, **`-fx-font-weight`**, **`-fx-font-size`** and **`-fx-font-family`**. These are applied to a JavaFX object’s similarly named properties. For more information on CSS font attributes, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-01)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typefont
```

For a complete list of CSS selector types and how you can combine them, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-02)

```
https://www.w3.org/TR/selectors-3/
```

##### `#label2` CSS Rule

Lines 13–15 of [Fig. 17.1](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig01) define the `#label2` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Label` with the `fx:id label2`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-03)

```
13   #label2 {
14      -fx-font: 16pt "Times New Roman";
15   }
16
```

The CSS property

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-04)

```
-fx-font: 16pt "Times New Roman";
```

specifies only the required font size (`16pt`) and font family (`"Times New Roman"`) components—font family names with multiple words must be enclosed in quotes (`""`).

##### `#label3` CSS Rule

Lines 17–19 define the `#label3` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Label` with the `fx:id label3`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-05)

```
17   #label3 {
18      -fx-font: bold italic 16pt "Courier New";
19   }
20
```

The CSS property

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0643-06)

```
-fx-font: bold italic 16pt "Courier New";
```

specifies all the font components—weight (`bold`), style (`italic`), size (`16pt`) and font family (`"Courier New"`).

##### `#label4` CSS Rule

Lines 21–24 define the `#label4` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Label` with the `fx:id label4`.

```
21   #label4 {
22      -fx-font-size: 14pt;
23      -fx-underline: true;
24   }
25
```

The CSS property

```
-fx-font-size: 14pt;
```

specifies the font size `14pt`—all other aspects of this `Label`’s font are inherited from the `Label`’s parent container. The CSS property

```
-fx-underline: true;
```

indicates that the text in the `Label` should be underlined—this property’s default value is `false`.

##### `#label5` CSS Rule

Lines 26–28 define the `#label5` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Label` with the `fx:id label5` and set its font size to `14pt`.

```
26   #label5 {
27      -fx-font-size: 14pt;
28   }
29
```

##### `#label5 .text` CSS Rule

Lines 30–32 define the `#label5 .text` CSS rule that will be applied to the `Text` object within the `Label` that has the `fx:id` value `"label5"`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0644-01)

```
30   #label5 .text {
31      -fx-strikethrough: true;
32   }
```

This selector combines an ID selector and a style class selector. Each `Label` contains a `Text` object with the CSS class `.text`. When applying this CSS rule, JavaFX first locates the object with the ID `label5`, then within that object, looks for a nested object that specifies the class `text`.

The CSS property

```
-fx-strikethrough: true;
```

indicates that the text in the `Label` should be displayed with a line through it—this property’s default value is `false`.

#### 17.2.2 FXML That Defines the GUI—Introduction to XML Markup

[Figure 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02) presents `FontCSS.fxml`. The `FontCSS` app’s FXML GUI consists of a `VBox` layout element (lines 8–18) containing five `Label`s (lines 12–16). To create this in Scene Builder, drag five `Label`s onto the `VBox`. Configure their text as in [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02)(a) and set their fx:ids from top to bottom as `label1`, `label2`, `label3`, `label4` and `label5`. All the `Label`s initially have the same appearance, and there’s no spacing between or around them.^([2](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_2a))

[2](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_2). In many of this chapter’s examples, after creating a GUI in Scene Builder, we used a text editor to format the FXML, remove unnecessary properties that were inserted by Scene Builder and properties that we specified via CSS rules. The text editors in various popular IDEs also can be used to edit FXML. For this reason, when you build these examples from scratch, your FXML may differ from what’s presented in this chapter. You also can set a property to its default value in Scene Builder to remove it from the FXML.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0645-01)

```
 1   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
 2   <!-- Fig. 17.2: FontCSS.fxml -->
 3   <!-- FontCSS GUI that is styled via external CSS -->
 4
 5   <?import javafx.scene.control.Label?>
 6   <?import javafx.scene.layout.VBox?>
 7
 8   <VBox styleClass="vbox" stylesheets="@FontCSS.css"
 9      xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
10      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1">
11      <children>
12         <Label fx:id="label1" text="Arial 14pt bold" />
13         <Label fx:id="label2" text="Times New Roman 16pt plain" />
14         <Label fx:id="label3" text="Courier New 16pt bold and italic" />
15         <Label fx:id="label4" text="Default font 14pt with underline" />
16         <Label fx:id="label5" text="Default font 14pt with strikethrough" />
17      </children>
18   </VBox>
```

**Fig. 17.2** | `FontCSS` GUI that is styled via external CSS.

##### XML Declaration

Each FXML document begins with an **XML declaration** (line 1), which must be the first line in the file and indicates that the document contains XML markup. For FXML documents, line 1 must appear as in [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02). The XML declaration’s **`version`** **attribute** specifies the document’s XML syntax version (`1.0`). The **`encoding`** **attribute** specifies the document’s character format—XML documents typically contain Unicode characters in `UTF-8` format.^([3](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_3a)) Scene Builder automatically inserts the XML declaration.

[3](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_3). “UTF-8.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed September 26, 2024\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTF-8).

##### Attributes

Each XML attribute has the format

```
name="value"
```

The *name* and *value* are separated by `=`, and the *value* is placed in quotes (`""`). Multiple *name*=*value* pairs are separated by whitespace.

##### Comments

Lines 2–3 are XML comments. These are delimited by `<!--` and `-->` and can be placed almost anywhere in an XML document. XML comments can span multiple lines. We added these XML comments to state the FXML document’s figure number, filename and purpose, as we typically do in our Java code.

##### FXML `import` Declarations

Lines 5–6 are **FXML** **`import`** **declarations**—delimited by `<?import` and `?>`—specifying the fully qualified names of the JavaFX types used in the document. Scene Builder automatically inserts FXML `import` declarations based on the various JavaFX node types you add to the GUI.

##### Elements

XML documents contain **elements** specifying the document’s structure. Most elements are delimited by a **start tag** and an **end tag**:

*   A start tag consists of **angle brackets** (`<` and `>`) containing the element’s name followed by zero or more attributes. For example, the `VBox` element’s start tag (lines 8–10) has four attributes.

*   An end tag consists of the element name preceded by a **forward slash** (**`/`**) in angle brackets—for example, `</VBox>` in line 18.

An element’s start and end tags enclose the element’s contents. In this case, lines 11–17 declare other elements that describe the `VBox`’s contents. Every XML document must have exactly one **root element** containing the other elements. In [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02), `VBox` is the root.

A layout element always contains a **`children`** element (lines 11–17) that, in turn, contains the child `Node`s arranged by that layout. For a `VBox`, the `children` element’s child `Node`s are listed in their display order from top to bottom. The elements in lines 12–16 represent the `VBox`’s five `Label`s. These are **empty elements** that use the shorthand start-tag-only notation:

```
<ElementName attributes />
```

in which the empty element’s start tag ends with `/>` rather than `>`. The empty element:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0647-01)

```
<Label fx:id="label1" text="Arial 14pt bold"/>
```

is equivalent to

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0647-02)

```
<Label fx:id="label1" text="Arial 14pt bold">
</Label>
```

which does not have content between the start and end tags. Empty elements often have attributes (such as `fx:id` and `text` for each `Label` element).

##### XML Namespaces

In lines 9–10, the `VBox` attributes

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0647-03)

```
xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
```

specify the XML namespaces used in FXML markup. An XML **namespace** specifies a collection of element and attribute names you can use in the document. The attribute

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0647-04)

```
xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
```

specifies the default namespace. FXML `import` declarations (like those in lines 5–6) add names to this namespace for use in the document. The attribute

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0647-05)

```
xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
```

specifies JavaFX’s `fx` namespace. Elements and attributes from this namespace (such as the `fx:id` attribute) are used internally by the `FXMLLoader` class. For example, for each FXML element that specifies an `fx:id`, the `FXMLLoader` initializes a corresponding variable in the controller class. The `fx:` in `fx:id` is a **namespace prefix** that specifies the namespace (`fx`) that defines the attribute (`id`). Every element or attribute name in [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02) that does not begin with `fx:` is part of the default namespace.

#### 17.2.3 Referencing the CSS File from FXML

For the `Label`s to appear with the customized fonts, we must reference the `FontCSS.css` file from the FXML. This enables Scene Builder to apply the CSS rules to the GUI. To reference the CSS file:

1.  Select the `VBox` in the Scene Builder.

2.  In the Properties inspector, click the + button under the Stylesheets heading.

3.  In the dialog that appears, select the `FontCSS.css` file and click Open.

This adds the `stylesheets` attribute (line 8)

```
stylesheets="@FontCSS.css"
```

to the `VBox`’s opening tag (lines 8–10). The `@` symbol—called the local resolution operator in FXML—indicates that `FontCSS.css` is located relative to the FXML file on disk. The CSS and FXML files must be in the same folder if no path information is specified.

#### 17.2.4 Specifying the `VBox`’s Style Class

The preceding steps apply the font styles to the `Label`s based on their ID selectors but do not apply the spacing and padding to the `VBox`. For the `VBox`, we defined a CSS rule using a style class selector named `.vbox`. To apply this CSS rule to the `VBox`:

1.  Select the `VBox` in the Scene Builder.

2.  In the Properties inspector, under the Style Class heading, click the empty box and select `vbox` from the list of available selectors.

This adds the `styleClass` attribute

```
styleClass="vbox"
```

to the `VBox`’s opening tag (line 8). At this point, the GUI appears as in [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02)(b). You can now run the app to produce the output in [Fig. 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig02)(c).

#### 17.2.5 Programmatically Loading CSS

In the `FontCSS` app, the FXML referenced the CSS style sheet directly (line 8). It’s also possible to load CSS files dynamically and add them to a `Scene`’s collection of style sheets. You might do this, for example, in an app that enables users to choose their preferred look-and-feel, such as a light background with dark text vs. a dark background with light text.

To load a stylesheet dynamically, add the following statement to the `Application` subclass’s `start` method:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0648-01)

```
scene.getStylesheets().add(
   FontCSS.class.getResource("FontCSS.css").toExternalForm());
```

In the preceding statement:

*   The notation `FontCSS.class` creates a `Class` object representing the `FontCSS` subclass of `Application`. This is equivalent to calling the method `getClass()`, which all classes inherit.

*   `Class` method `getResource` returns a `URL` representing the location of the file `FontCSS.css`. Method `getResource` looks for the file in the same location from which class `FontCSS` was loaded by the JVM.

*   `URL` method `toExternalForm` returns the `URL`’s `String` representation. This is passed to the `add` method of the `Scene`’s collection of style sheets to add the style sheet to the scene.

Method `getStyleSheets` returns an `ObservableList` object, which supports standard `List` methods, so you may also `remove` a stylesheet and `clear` all the stylesheets programmatically.

### 17.3 Displaying Two-Dimensional Shapes

JavaFX has two ways to draw shapes:

*   You can define **`Shape`** and **`Shape3D`** (package `javafx.scene.shape`) subclass objects, add them to a container in the JavaFX stage and manipulate them like other JavaFX `Node`s.

*   You can add a **`Canvas`** object (package **`javafx.scene.canvas`**) to a container in the JavaFX stage, then draw on it using various `GraphicsContext` methods.

This section’s `BasicShapes` example displays **`Line`**, **`Rectangle`**, **`Circle`**, **`Ellipse`** and **`Arc`** `Shape`s. Like other `Node` types, you can drag these from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes category onto the design area, then configure them via the Inspector’s Properties, Layout and Code sections. You can also create objects of any JavaFX `Node` type programmatically.

#### 17.3.1 Defining Two-Dimensional Shapes with FXML

[Figure 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig03) contains the completed FXML for the `BasicShapes` app, which references the `BasicShapes.css` file (line 13) that we present in [Section 17.3.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev2sec8). For this app, we used Scene Builder to drag two `Line`s, a `Rectangle`, a `Circle`, an `Ellipse` and an `Arc` onto a `Pane` layout, then configured their dimensions and positions.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0649-01)

```
 1   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
 2   <!-- Fig. 17.3: BasicShapes.fxml -->
 3   <!-- Defining Shape objects and styling via CSS -->
 4
 5   <?import javafx.scene.layout.Pane?>
 6   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Arc?>
 7   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Circle?>
 8   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Ellipse?>
 9   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Line?>
10   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle?>
11
12   <Pane id="Pane" prefHeight="110.0" prefWidth="630.0"
13      stylesheets="@BasicShapes.css" xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
14      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1">
15      <children>
16         <Line fx:id="line1" endX="100.0" endY="100.0"
17            startX="10.0" startY="10.0" />
18         <Line fx:id="line2" endX="10.0" endY="100.0"
19            startX="100.0" startY="10.0" />
20         <Rectangle fx:id="rectangle" height="90.0" layoutX="120.0"
21            layoutY="10.0" width="90.0" />
22         <Circle fx:id="circle" centerX="270.0" centerY="55.0"
23            radius="45.0" />
24         <Ellipse fx:id="ellipse" centerX="430.0" centerY="55.0"
25            radiusX="100.0" radiusY="45.0" />
26         <Arc fx:id="arc" centerX="590.0" centerY="55.0" length="270.0"
27            radiusX="45.0" radiusY="45.0" startAngle="45.0" type="ROUND" />
28      </children>
29   </Pane>
```

**Fig. 17.3** | Defining `Shape` objects and styling via CSS.

Each property you can set in Scene Builder has a corresponding attribute in FXML. For example, the `Pane` object’s Pref Height property in Scene Builder corresponds to the `prefHeight` attribute (line 12) in FXML. When you build this GUI in Scene Builder, use the FXML attribute values in [Fig. 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig03). As you drag each shape onto your design, Scene Builder automatically configures certain properties, such as the Fill and Stroke colors for the `Rectangle`, `Circle`, `Ellipse` and `Arc`. For each property that does not have a corresponding attribute in [Fig. 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig03), you can remove the attribute by setting it to its default value in Scene Builder or by manually editing the FXML.

Lines 6–10 import the shape classes used in the FXML. We also specified `fx:id` values (lines 16 and 18) for the two `Line`s—we use these values in CSS rules with ID selectors to define separate styles for each `Line`. We removed the shapes’ `fill`, `stroke` and `stroke-Type` properties that Scene Builder autogenerated. The default `fill` for a shape is black. The default stroke is a one-pixel black line. The default `strokeType` is centered—based on the stroke’s thickness, half the thickness appears inside the shape’s bounds and half outside. You also may display a shape’s stroke entirely inside or outside the shape’s bounds. We specify the strokes and fills with the styles in [Section 17.3.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev2sec8).

##### `Line` Objects

Lines 16–17 and 18–19 define two `Line`s. Each connects two endpoints specified by the properties **`startX`**, **`startY`**, **`endX`** and **`endY`**. The *x*- and *y*-coordinates are measured from the top-left corner of the `Pane`, with *x*-coordinates increasing from left to right and *y*-coordinates increasing from top to bottom. If you specify a `Line`’s **`layoutX`** and **`layoutY`** properties, the `startX`, `startY`, `endX` and `endY` properties are measured from that point.

##### `Rectangle` Object

Lines 20–21 define a `Rectangle` object. A `Rectangle` is displayed based on its `layoutX`, `layoutY`, **`width`** and **`height`** properties:

*   A `Rectangle`’s upper-left corner is positioned at the coordinates specified by the `layoutX` and `layoutY` properties, which are inherited from class `Node`.

*   A `Rectangle`’s dimensions are specified by the `width` and `height` properties—in this case, they have the same value, so the `Rectangle` defines a square.

##### `Circle` Object

Lines 22–23 define a `Circle` object with its center at the point specified by the **`centerX`** and **`centerY`** properties. The **`radius`** property determines the `Circle`’s size (two times the `radius`) around its center point.

##### `Ellipse` Object

Lines 24–25 define an `Ellipse` object. Like a `Circle`, an `Ellipse`’s center is specified by the **`centerX`** and **`centerY`** properties. You also specify **`radiusX`** and **`radiusY`** properties that help determine the `Ellipse`’s width (left and right of the center point) and height (above and below the center point).

##### `Arc` Object

Lines 26–27 define an `Arc` object. Like an `Ellipse`, an `Arc`’s center is specified by the **`centerX`** and **`centerY`** properties, and the **`radiusX`** and **`radiusY`** properties determine the `Arc`’s width and height. For an `Arc`, you also specify:

*   **`length`**—The arc’s length in degrees (0–360). Positive values sweep counterclockwise.

*   **`startAngle`**—The angle in degrees at which the arc should begin.

*   **`type`**—How the arc should be closed. `ROUND` indicates that the starting and ending points of the arc should be connected to the center point by straight lines. You also may choose `OPEN`, which does not connect the start and end points, or `CHORD`, which connects the start and end points with a straight line.

#### 17.3.2 CSS That Styles the Two-Dimensional Shapes

[Figure 17.4](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig04) contains the CSS for the `BasicShapes` app. In this CSS file, we define two CSS rules with ID selectors (`#line1` and `#line2`) to style the app’s two `Line` objects. The remaining rules use **type selectors**, which apply to all objects of a given type. You specify a type selector by using the JavaFX class name. We split the file into parts for discussion purposes.

##### Specifying Common Attributes for Various Objects

The CSS rule in lines 4–6 defines the **`-fx-stroke-width`** CSS property for all the shapes in the app—this property specifies the thickness of the `Line`s and the border thickness of all the other shapes:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0652-01)

```
 1   /* Fig. 17.4: BasicShapes.css */
 2   /* CSS that styles various two-dimensional shapes */
 3
 4   Line, Rectangle, Circle, Ellipse, Arc {
 5       -fx-stroke-width: 10;
 6   }
 7
```

**Fig. 17.4** | CSS that styles various two-dimensional shapes.

We use CSS type selectors in a comma-separated list to apply this rule to multiple shapes. Line 4 indicates this should be applied to all objects of types `Line`, `Rectangle`, `Circle`, `Ellipse` and `Arc`.

##### Styling the First `Line`

The CSS rule in lines 8–10 sets the **`-fx-stroke`** to the solid color `red` for the `Line` with the `fx:id "line1"`:

```
 8   #line1 {
 9       -fx-stroke: red;
10   }
11
```

This rule is in addition to the one at lines 4–6, which sets the stroke width for all the shapes in this app. When JavaFX renders an object, it combines all the CSS rules that apply to the object to determine its appearance. Colors may be specified as

*   named colors (such as `"red"`, `"green"` and `"blue"`),

*   colors defined by their red, green, blue and alpha (transparency) components,

*   colors defined by their hue, saturation, brightness and alpha components,

and more. For details on all the ways to specify color in CSS, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0652-03)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typecolor
```

##### Styling the Second `Line`

The CSS rule in lines 12–15 applies to the `Line` with the `fx:id "line2"`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0652-02)

```
12   #line2 {
13       -fx-stroke: rgba(0%, 50%, 0%, 0.5);
14       -fx-stroke-line-cap: round;
15   }
16
```

For this rule, we specified the `-fx-stroke` property’s color using the CSS function **`rgba`**, which defines a color based on its red, green, blue and alpha (transparency) components. We used the version of `rgba` that receives percentages from 0% to 100%, specifying the amount of red, green and blue in the color and a value from 0.0 (transparent) to 1.0 (opaque) for the alpha component. Line 13 produces a semitransparent green line. Notice the interaction between the two `Line`s’ colors at the intersection point in [Fig. 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig03)’s output windows. The **`-fx-stroke-line-cap`** CSS property (line 14) indicates that the ends of the `Line` should be rounded—the rounding effect is more noticeable with thicker strokes.

##### Styling the `Rectangle`

For `Rectangle`s, `Circle`s, `Ellipse`s and `Arc`s, you can specify both the `-fx-stroke` for the shapes’ borders and the **`-fx-fill`** for the color or pattern that appears inside the shape. The rule in lines 17–22 uses a CSS type selector to indicate that all `Rectangle`s should have `red` borders (line 18) and `yellow` fill (line 21).

```
17   Rectangle {
18      -fx-stroke: red;
19      -fx-arc-width: 50;
20      -fx-arc-height: 50;
21      -fx-fill: yellow;
22   }
23
```

Lines 19–20 define the `Rectangle`’s **`-fx-arc-width`** and **`-fx-arc-height`** properties. These specify the width and height of an ellipse that’s divided in half horizontally and vertically, then used to round the `Rectangle`’s corners. Because these properties have the same value (`50`) in this app, the four corners are each a quarter of a circle with a diameter of 50.

##### Styling the `Circle`

The CSS rule in lines 24–27 applies to all `Circle` objects.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0653-01)

```
24   Circle {
25      -fx-stroke: blue;
26      -fx-fill: radial-gradient(center 50% 50%, radius 60%, white, red);
27   }
28
```

Line 25 sets the `Circle`’s stroke to `blue`. Line 26 sets the `Circle`’s fill with a **gradient**—colors that transition gradually from one color to the next. You can transition between as many colors as you like and specify the points at which to change colors—such points are called **color stops**. You can use gradients for any property that specifies a color. In this case, we use the CSS function **`radial-gradient`** to create a gradient in which the color changes gradually from a center point outward. The fill

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0653-02)

```
-fx-fill: radial-gradient(center 50% 50%, radius 60%, white, red);
```

indicates the gradient should begin from a `center` point at `50% 50%`—the shape’s horizontal and vertical middle. The `radius` specifies the distance from the center at which an even mixture of the two colors appears. This radial gradient begins with `white` in the center and ends with `red` at the outer edge of the `Circle`’s fill. We’ll discuss a linear gradient momentarily.

##### Styling the `Ellipse`

The CSS rule in lines 29–32 applies to all `Ellipse` objects.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0654-01)

```
29   Ellipse {
30      -fx-stroke: green;
31      -fx-fill: image-pattern("yellowflowers.png");
32   }
33
```

Line 30 specifies that an `Ellipse` should have a `green` stroke. Line 31 specifies that the `Ellipse`’s fill should be the image in `yellowflowers.png` (located in this app’s folder). If you’re building this app from scratch, copy the image from the `images` folder with the chapter’s examples into the app’s folder. To specify an image as fill, you use the CSS function **`image-pattern`**.^([4](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_4a))

[4](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_4). At the time of this writing, Scene Builder does not display a shape’s fill correctly if it’s specified with a CSS image-pattern. You must run the example to display the fill ([Fig. 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig03)(b)). We’ll post updates on the book’s web site: [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5).

##### Styling the `Arc`

The CSS rule in lines 34–37 applies to all `Arc` objects.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0654-02)

```
34   Arc {
35      -fx-stroke: purple;
36      -fx-fill: linear-gradient(to right, cyan, white);
37   }
```

Line 35 specifies that an `Arc` should have a `purple` stroke. In this case, line 36

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0654-03)

```
-fx-fill: linear-gradient(to right, cyan, white);
```

specifies that the `Arc` should be filled with a **linear gradient**—such gradients gradually transition from one color to the next horizontally, vertically or diagonally. You can transition between as many colors as you like and specify the points at which to change colors. To create a linear gradient, you use the CSS function **`linear-gradient`**. In this case,

```
to right
```

indicates that the gradient should start from the shape’s left edge and transition through colors to the shape’s right edge. We specified only two colors here—`cyan` at the left edge of the gradient and `white` at the right edge—but two or more colors can be specified in the comma-separated list. For more information on all the options for configuring radial gradients, linear gradients and image patterns, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0654-04)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typepaint
```

### 17.4 `Polyline`s, `Polygon`s and `Path`s

Several JavaFX classes enable you to create custom shapes:

*   **`Polyline`**—draws a series of connected lines defined by a collection of points.

*   **`Polygon`**—draws a series of connected lines defined by a set of points and connects the last point to the first point.

*   **`Path`**—draws a series of connected **`PathElement`****s** by moving to a given point, then drawing lines, arcs and curves.

In the `PolyShapes` app, you select the shape to display by clicking a `RadioButton` in the left column. You specify a shape’s points by clicking throughout the `AnchoredPane` in which the shapes are displayed.

#### 17.4.1 GUI and CSS

The following screen captures contain the `PolyShapes` app’s GUI. It’s similar to the `Painter` app in [Section 16.3](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev1sec3), so we show only the key GUI elements’ `fx:id` property values rather than the complete FXML. Each `fx:id` property value ends with the GUI element’s type.

![Images](graphics/f0655-01.jpg)

In this GUI:

*   The three `RadioButton`s are in a `ToggleGroup` with the `fx:id "toggleGroup"`. The Polyline `RadioButton` is Selected by default. We also set each `RadioButton`’s On Action event handler to `shapeRadioButtonSelected`.

*   We dragged a `Polyline`, a `Polygon` and a `Path` from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section onto the `Pane` that displays the shapes, and we set their `fx:id`s to `polyline`, `polygon` and `path`, respectively. We set each shape’s `visible` property to `false` by selecting the shape in Scene Builder then unchecking the Visible checkbox in the Properties inspector. We display only the shape with the selected `RadioButton` at runtime.

*   We set the `Pane`’s On Mouse Clicked event handler to `drawingAreaMouseClicked`.

*   We set the Clear `Button`’s On Action event handler to `clearButtonPressed`.

*   We set the controller class to `PolyShapesController`.

*   Finally, we edited the FXML to remove the `Path` object’s `<elements>` and the `Polyline` and `Polygon` objects’ `<points>`, as we’ll set these programmatically in response to the user’s mouse-click events.

The `PolyShapes.css` file defines the properties `-fx-stroke`, `-fx-stroke-width` and `-fx-fill` that are applied to all three shapes in this example. Each shape has a black, five-pixel outline and with red fill color:

```
Polyline, Polygon, Path {
   -fx-stroke: black;
   -fx-stroke-width: 5;
   -fx-fill: red;
}
```

#### 17.4.2 `PolyShapesController` Class

Class `PolyShapesController` ([Fig. 17.5](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig05)) responds to this app’s user interactions. We split the code into parts for discussion purposes. The `enum ShapeType` (line 17) defines constants we use to determine which shape to display.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0657-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.5: PolyShapesController.java
 2   // Drawing Polylines, Polygons and Paths.
 3   import javafx.event.ActionEvent;
 4   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 5   import javafx.scene.control.RadioButton;
 6   import javafx.scene.control.ToggleGroup;
 7   import javafx.scene.input.MouseEvent;
 8   import javafx.scene.shape.ArcTo;
 9   import javafx.scene.shape.ClosePath;
10   import javafx.scene.shape.MoveTo;
11   import javafx.scene.shape.Path;
12   import javafx.scene.shape.Polygon;
13   import javafx.scene.shape.Polyline;
14
15   public class PolyShapesController {
16      // enum representing shape types
17      private enum ShapeType {POLYLINE, POLYGON, PATH};
18
```

**Fig. 17.5** | Drawing `Polyline`s, `Polygon`s and `Path`s.

Lines 20–26 declare the variables corresponding to the GUI components and shapes with `fx:id`s in the FXML. The `shapeType` variable (line 29) stores whichever shape type is currently selected in the GUI’s `RadioButton`s. By default, the `Polyline` will be displayed. The `sweepFlag` variable will determine whether to draw an arc with a negative or positive sweep angle.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0657-02)

```
19      // instance variables that refer to GUI components
20      @FXML private RadioButton polylineRadioButton;
21      @FXML private RadioButton polygonRadioButton;
22      @FXML private RadioButton pathRadioButton;
23      @FXML private ToggleGroup toggleGroup;
24      @FXML private Polyline polyline;
25      @FXML private Polygon polygon;
26      @FXML private Path path;
27
28      // instance variables for managing state
29      private ShapeType shapeType = ShapeType.POLYLINE;
30      private boolean sweepFlag = true; // used with arcs in a Path
31
```

##### Method `initialize`

Recall from [Section 16.3.1](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev2sec3) that you can associate any `Object` with each JavaFX control via its `setUserData` method. For the shape `RadioButton`s in this app, method `initialize` (lines 33–41) stores the `ShapeType` that each `RadioButton` represents (lines 36–38). When handling the `RadioButton` events, we use these to set the `shapeType` instance variable. Line 40 calls method `displayShape` to display the currently selected shape (the `Polyline` by default). Initially, the shape is not visible because it has no points.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0658-01)

```
32      // set user data for the RadioButtons and display polyline object
33      @FXML
34      private void initialize() {
35         // user data on a control can be any Object
36         polylineRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.POLYLINE);
37         polygonRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.POLYGON);
38         pathRadioButton.setUserData(ShapeType.PATH);
39
40         displayShape(); // sets polyline's visibility to true when app loads
41      }
42
```

##### Method `drawingAreaMouseClicked`

When the user clicks the app’s `Pane`, method `drawingAreaMouseClicked` (lines 44–65) modifies all three shapes to incorporate the new point at which the user clicked.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0658-02)

```
43      // handles drawingArea's onMouseClicked event
44      @FXML
45      private void drawingAreaMouseClicked(MouseEvent e) {
46         polyline.getPoints().addAll(e.getX(), e.getY());
47         polygon.getPoints().addAll(e.getX(), e.getY());
48
49         // if path is empty, move to first click position and close path
50         if (path.getElements().isEmpty()) {
51            path.getElements().add(new MoveTo(e.getX(), e.getY()));
52            path.getElements().add(new ClosePath());
53         }
54         else { // insert a new path segment before the ClosePath element
55            // create an arc segment and insert it in the path
56            ArcTo arcTo = new ArcTo();
57            arcTo.setX(e.getX());
58            arcTo.setY(e.getY());
59            arcTo.setRadiusX(100.0);
60            arcTo.setRadiusY(100.0);
61            arcTo.setSweepFlag(sweepFlag);
62            sweepFlag = !sweepFlag;
63            path.getElements().add(path.getElements().size() - 1, arcTo);
64         }
65      }
66
```

`Polyline`s and `Polygon`s store their points as a collection of `Double`s—the first two values represent the first point’s location, the next two represent the second point’s location, etc. Line 46 adds the new click point to the `polyline` object’s points collection by calling `addAll` with the `MouseEvent`’s *x*- and *y*-coordinate values. This adds the new point’s information to the end of the collection. Line 47 performs the same task for the `polygon` object.

Lines 50–64 manipulate the `path` object. A `Path` is represented by a collection of `PathElement`s. The subclasses of `PathElement` used in this example are:

*   **`MoveTo`**—Moves to a specific position without drawing anything.

*   **`ArcTo`**—Draws an arc from the previous `PathElement`’s endpoint to the specified location. We’ll discuss this in more detail momentarily.

*   **`ClosePath`**—Closes the path by drawing a straight line from the last `PathElement`’s endpoint to the first `PathElement` start point.

Other `PathElement`s not covered here include `LineTo`, `HLineTo`, `VLineTo`, `CubicCurveTo` and `QuadCurveTo`.

When the user clicks the `Pane`, line 50 checks whether the `Path` contains elements. If not, line 51 moves the `path`’s starting point to the mouse-click location by adding a `MoveTo` element to the `path`’s `PathElement`s collection. Then, line 52 adds a new `Close-Path` element to complete the path. For each subsequent mouse-click event, lines 56–61 create an `ArcTo` element, and line 63 inserts it before the `ClosePath` element by calling the `PathElement`s collection’s `add` method that receives an index as its first argument.

Lines 57–58 set the `ArcTo` element’s endpoint to the `MouseEvent`’s coordinates. The arc is drawn as a piece of an ellipse for which you specify the horizontal radius and vertical radius (lines 59–60). Line 61 sets the `ArcTo`’s `sweepFlag`, which determines whether the arc sweeps in the positive angle direction (`true`; counter-clockwise) or the negative angle direction (`false`; clockwise). By default, an `ArcTo` element is drawn as the shortest arc between the last `PathElement`’s endpoint and the point specified by the `ArcTo` element. To sweep the arc the long way around the ellipse, set the `ArcTo`’s `largeArcFlag` to `true`. For each mouse click, line 62 reverses the value of our controller class’s `sweepFlag` instance variable so that the `ArcTo` elements toggle between positive and negative angles for variety.

##### Method `shapeRadioButtonSelected`

When the user clicks a shape `RadioButton`, lines 71–72 set the controller’s `shapeType` instance variable, then line 73 calls method `displayShape` to display the selected shape. Try creating a `Polyline` of several points, then changing to the `Polygon` and `Path` to observe how the points are used in each shape.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0659-01)

```

### 17.5 Transforms

A **transform** can be applied to any UI element to reposition or reorient the element. The built-in JavaFX transforms are subclasses of **`Transform`**. Some of these subclasses include:

*   **`Translate`**—moves an object to a new location.

*   **`Rotate`**—rotates an object around a point and by a specified rotation angle.

*   **`Scale`**—scales an object’s size by the specified amounts.

The next example draws stars using the `Polygon` control and uses `Rotate` transforms to create a circle of randomly colored stars. This app’s FXML consists of an empty 300-by-300 `Pane` layout with the `fx:id "pane"`. We also set the controller class to `DrawStarsController`. [Figure 17.6](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig06) contains the app’s controller and a sample output.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0660-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.6: DrawStarsController.java
 2   // Create a circle of stars using Polygons and Rotate transforms
 3   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 4   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 5   import javafx.scene.layout.Pane;
 6   import javafx.scene.paint.Color;
 7   import javafx.scene.shape.Polygon;
 8   import javafx.scene.transform.Transform;
 9
10   public class DrawStarsController {
11      private static final RandomGenerator random =
12         RandomGenerator.getDefault();
13      @FXML private Pane pane;
14
15      @FXML
16      private void initialize() {
17         // points that define a five-pointed star shape
18         Double[] points = {205.0,150.0, 217.0,186.0, 259.0,186.0,
19            223.0,204.0, 233.0,246.0, 205.0,222.0, 177.0,246.0, 187.0,204.0,
20            151.0,186.0, 193.0,186.0};
21
22         // create 18 stars
23         for (int count = 0; count < 18; ++count) {
24            // create a new Polygon and copy existing points into it
25            var newStar = new Polygon();
26            newStar.getPoints().addAll(points);
27
28            // create random Color and set as newStar's fill
29            newStar.setStroke(Color.GREY);
30            newStar.setFill(Color.rgb(random.nextInt(256),
31               random.nextInt(256), random.nextInt(256),
32               random.nextDouble()));
33
34            // apply a rotation to the shape
35            newStar.getTransforms().add(
36               Transform.rotate(count * 20, 150, 150));
37            pane.getChildren().add(newStar);
38         }
39      }
40   }
```

**Fig. 17.6** | Create a circle of stars using `Polygon`s and `Rotate` transforms.

Method `initialize` (lines 15–39) defines the stars, applies the transforms and attaches the stars to the app’s `pane`. Lines 18–20 define the ten *x-y* coordinates that form a star as a `Double` array. A `Polygon`’s collection of points is a generic collection, so you must use type `Double` rather than `double`—recall that primitive types cannot be used in Java generic collections. Each pair of values in the array represents a point’s *x*-*y* coordinates.

During each iteration of the loop, lines 25–36 create a `Polygon` using the points in the `points` array and apply a `Rotate` transform, resulting in a circle of `Polygon`s. To generate each star’s random colors, we use a `RandomGenerator` to create three random values from 0–255 for the red, green and blue components of the color and one random value from 0.0–1.0 for the color’s alpha transparency value. We pass those values to class `Color`’s `static rgb` method to create a `Color`.

To apply a rotation to the new `Polygon`, we add a `Rotate` transform to its collection of `Transform`s (lines 35–36). **`Transform`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`rotate`** (line 36) returns a `Rotate` object. The method’s first argument is the rotation angle. Each iteration of the loop assigns a new rotation-angle value by using the control variable multiplied by 20 as the `rotate` method’s first argument. The method’s next two arguments are the *x*-*y* coordinates of the point of rotation around which the `Polygon` rotates. The center of the circle of stars is the point *(150, 150)*—we rotated all 18 stars around that point. Adding each `Polygon` as a new child element of the `pane` object (line 37) allows the `Polygon` to be rendered on screen.

### 17.6 Playing Video with `Media`, `MediaPlayer` and `MediaView`

Many of today’s most popular apps are multimedia intensive. JavaFX provides audio and video multimedia capabilities via the **`javafx.scene.media`** package:

*   For simple audio playback, use class **`AudioClip`**.

*   For audio playback with more playback controls and for video playback, use classes **`Media`**, **`MediaPlayer`** and **`MediaView`**.

In this section, you’ll build a basic video player.^([5](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_5a)) We’ll explain `Media`, `MediaPlayer` and `MediaView` as we encounter them in this example’s controller class ([Section 17.6.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev2sec16)). #### 17.6.2 `VideoPlayerController` Class

Class `VideoPlayerController` ([Fig. 17.8](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig08)) configures video playback, responds to the `MediaPlayer`’s state changes and responds to the `playPauseButton`’s events. The controller uses classes `Media`, `MediaPlayer` and `MediaView` as follows:

*   A `Media` object specifies the location of the media to play and provides access to various information about the media, such as its duration, video dimensions and more.

*   A `MediaPlayer` object loads a `Media` object and controls its playback, transitioning through various states (ready, playing, paused, etc.) during loading and playback. You’ll use lambdas to define `Runnable`s that respond to these state transitions.

*   A `MediaView` object is a `Node` in the scene graph that displays the `Media` being played by a given `MediaPlayer` object.

We split the code into parts for discussion purposes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0665-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.8: VideoPlayerController.java
 2   // Using Media, MediaPlayer and MediaView to play a video.
 3   import java.net.URL;
 4   import javafx.beans.binding.Bindings;
 5   import javafx.beans.property.DoubleProperty;
 6   import javafx.event.ActionEvent;
 7   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 8   import javafx.scene.control.Button;
 9   import javafx.scene.media.Media;
10   import javafx.scene.media.MediaPlayer;
11   import javafx.scene.media.MediaPlayer.Status;
12   import javafx.scene.media.MediaView;
13   import javafx.util.Duration;
14   import org.controlsfx.dialog.ExceptionDialog;
15
16   public class VideoPlayerController {
```

**Fig. 17.8** | Using `Media`, `MediaPlayer` and `MediaView` to play a video.

##### Instance Variables

Lines 17–19 declare the controller’s instance variables. When the app loads, `mediaView` (line 17) is assigned a reference to the `MediaView` object declared in the app’s FXML. The `mediaPlayer` variable (line 19) is configured in method `initialize` to load the video specified by a `Media` object and used by method `playPauseButtonPressed` (lines 67–77) to play and pause the video.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0666-01)

```
17   @FXML private MediaView mediaView;
18   @FXML private Button playPauseButton;
19   private MediaPlayer mediaPlayer;
20
```

##### Creating a `Media` Object Representing the Video to Play

Method `initialize` (lines 21–64) configures media playback, registers event handlers for `MediaPlayer` events and sets up a data binding to change the Button’s text to Play or Pause based on the `MediaPlayer`’s state. Lines 24–25 get a `URL` representing the location of the video file. The notation

```
VideoPlayerController.class
```

is a `Class` object representing the `VideoPlayerController` class. This is equivalent to calling the inherited method `getClass()`. Next, line 28 creates a `Media` object representing the video. The argument to the `Media` constructor is a `String` representing the video’s location, which we obtain with `URL` method `toExternalForm`. The URL `String` can represent a local file on your computer or can be a location on the web. The `Media` constructor throws various exceptions, including `MediaException`s if the media cannot be found or is not of a supported media format.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0666-02)

```
21      @FXML
22      private void initialize() {
23         // get URL of the video file
24         URL url = VideoPlayerController.class.getResource(
25            "A1Launch~medium.mp4");
26
27         // create a Media object for the specified URL
28         var media = new Media(url.toExternalForm());
29
30         // create a MediaPlayer to control Media playback
31         mediaPlayer = new MediaPlayer(media);
32
33         // specify which MediaPlayer to display in the MediaView
34         mediaView.setMediaPlayer(mediaPlayer);
35
36         // set handler to be called when the video completes playing
37         mediaPlayer.setOnEndOfMedia(() -> {
38            mediaPlayer.seek(Duration.ZERO);
39            mediaPlayer.pause();
40         });
41
42         // set handler that displays an ExceptionDialog if an error occurs
43         mediaPlayer.setOnError(() -> {
44            var dialog = new ExceptionDialog(mediaPlayer.getError());
45            dialog.showAndWait();
46         });
47
48         // set handler to resize mediaView to window size once ready to play
49         mediaPlayer.setOnReady(() -> {
50            DoubleProperty width = mediaView.fitWidthProperty();
51            DoubleProperty height = mediaView.fitHeightProperty();
52            width.bind(Bindings.selectDouble(
53               mediaView.sceneProperty(), "width"));
54            height.bind(Bindings.selectDouble(
55               mediaView.sceneProperty(), "height"));
56         });
57
58         // bind playPauseButton's text to the MediaPlayer's status
59         playPauseButton.textProperty().bind(Bindings.when(
60            mediaPlayer.statusProperty().isEqualTo(Status.PLAYING))
61                       .then("Pause")
62                       .otherwise("Play")
63         );
64      }
65
```

##### Creating a `MediaPlayer` Object to Load the Video and Control Playback

To load the video and prepare it for playback, you must associate it with a `MediaPlayer` object (line 31). Playing multiple videos requires a separate `MediaPlayer` for each `Media` object. However, a given `Media` object can be associated with multiple `MediaPlayer`s. The `MediaPlayer` constructor throws

*   a `NullPointerException` if the `Media` is `null` or

*   a `MediaException` if a problem occurs while constructing the `MediaPlayer`.

##### Attaching the `MediaPlayer` Object to the `MediaView` to Display the Video

To display video, you must associate a `MediaPlayer` with a `MediaView`. When the `MediaView` already exists—e.g., when it’s created in FXML—you call the **`MediaView`****’s** **`setMediaPlayer`** **method** (line 34) to perform this task. When creating a `MediaView` object programmatically, you can pass the `MediaPlayer` to the `MediaView`’s constructor. A `MediaView` is like any other `Node` in the scene graph, so you can apply CSS styles, transforms and animations ([Sections 17.7](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec7)–[17.9](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec9)) to it as well.

##### Configuring Event Handlers for `MediaPlayer` Events

A `MediaPlayer` transitions through various states. Common states include ready, playing and paused. For these and other states, you can execute a task as the `MediaPlayer` enters the corresponding state. In addition, you can specify tasks that execute when the end of media playback is reached or when an error occurs during playback. To perform a task for a given state, you specify an object that implements the **`Runnable`** **interface** (package `java.lang`). This interface contains a no-parameter `run` method that returns `void`.

`Runnable` is a functional interface that can be implemented using a lambda. For example, lines 37–40 call the **`MediaPlayer`****’s** **`setOnEndOfMedia`** **method**, passing a lambda that executes when video playback completes. Line 38 calls **`MediaPlayer`** **method** **`seek`** to move to the beginning of the video, and line 39 pauses the video.

Lines 43–46 call the **`MediaPlayer`****’s** **`setOnError`** **method** to specify a task to perform if the `MediaPlayer` enters the error state, indicating that an error occurred during playback. In this case, we display a ControlsFX `ExceptionDialog` containing the error message. Calling the `ExceptionDialog`’s `showAndWait` method indicates that the app must wait for the user to dismiss the dialog before continuing.

##### Binding the `MediaView`’s Size to the Scene’s Size

Lines 49–56 call the **`MediaPlayer`****’s** **`setOnReady`** **method** to specify a task to perform if the `MediaPlayer` enters the ready state. We use property bindings to bind the `MediaView`’s `width` and `height` to the scene’s `width` and `height` so it resizes when the app’s window resizes. A `Node`’s `sceneProperty` returns an object of type **`ReadOnlyObjectProperty<Scene>`** you can use to access the `Scene` in which the `Node` is displayed. This object has many properties. To bind to its specific properties, you can use the methods of **class** **`Bindings`** (package `javafx.beans.binding`) to select the corresponding properties. The `Scene`’s `width` and `height` are each `DoubleProperty` objects. **`Bindings`** **method** **`selectDouble`** gets a reference to a `DoubleProperty`. The method’s first argument is the object that contains the property, and the second argument is the name of the property to which you’d like to bind.

##### Binding the `Button`’s Text to the `MediaPlayer`’s Status

Lines 59–63 bind the `Button`’s text to the `MediaPlayer`’s `Status`, so the text updates based on the current playback status. `Button` method `textProperty` returns the button’s text property, which we `bind` to the result of a condition configured using the **`Bindings`** **method** **`when`**. This method’s argument (line 60) gets the `MediaPlayer`’s status property and calls its `isEqualTo` method to compare the current status to `Status.PLAYING`. The `when` call returns a `When` object that specifies what to do based on the condition. If the condition is `true`, the `Button`’s text is set to `"Pause"` via the chained call `.then("Pause")`; otherwise, the `Button`’s text is set to `"Play"` via the chained call `.otherwise("Play")`.

##### Method `playPauseButtonPressed`

The event handler `playPauseButtonPressed` (lines 67–77) toggles video playback. We get the `MediaPlayer`’s `Status` (line 69), then when the status is either `Status.READY` (ready to play) or `Status.PAUSED` (currently paused), line 72 calls the **`MediaPlayer`****’s** **`play`** **method**; otherwise, line 75 sets calls the **`MediaPlayer`****’s** **`pause`** **method**.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0668-01)

```
66      // toggle media playback and the text on the playPauseButton
67      @FXML
68      private void playPauseButtonPressed(ActionEvent e) {
69         Status status = mediaPlayer.getStatus();
70
71         if (status == Status.READY || status == Status.PAUSED) {
72            mediaPlayer.play();
73         }
74         else {
75            mediaPlayer.pause();
76         }
77      }
78   }
```

### 17.7 `Transition` Animations

Animations in JavaFX apps transition a `Node`’s property values from one value to another in a specified amount of time. Most properties of a `Node` can be animated. This section focuses on several of JavaFX’s predefined **`Transition`** animations from the **`javafx.animations`** **package**. By default, the subclasses that define `Transition` animations change the values of specific `Node` properties. For example, a `FadeTransition` changes the value of a `Node`’s `opacity` property (which specifies whether the `Node` is opaque or transparent) over time, whereas a `PathTransition` changes a `Node`’s location by moving it along a `Path` over time. Though we include sample screen captures for all the animation examples, the best way to experience each is to run the examples yourself.

#### 17.7.1 `TransitionAnimations.fxml`

[Figure 17.9](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig09) contains this app’s GUI and sample screen captures of it running. When you click the `Button` (lines 17–18), its `startButtonPressed` event handler in the app’s controller creates a sequence of `Transition` animations for the `Rectangle` (lines 15–16) and plays them. The `Rectangle` is styled with the following CSS from the file `TransitionAnimations.css`:

```
Rectangle {
   -fx-stroke-width: 10;
   -fx-stroke: red;
   -fx-arc-width: 50;
   -fx-arc-height: 50;
   -fx-fill: yellow;
}
```

which produces a rounded rectangle with a 10-pixel red border and yellow fill.

#### 17.7.2 `TransitionAnimationsController` Class

Class `TransitionAnimationsController` ([Fig. 17.10](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig10)) defines the `startButton`’s event handler (lines 25–81). This event handler defines several animations that are played in sequence. We split the code—including the method `startButtonPressed`—into parts for discussion purposes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0671-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.10: TransitionAnimationsController.java
 2   // Applying Transition animations to a Rectangle.
 3   import javafx.animation.FadeTransition;
 4   import javafx.animation.FillTransition;
 5   import javafx.animation.Interpolator;
 6   import javafx.animation.ParallelTransition;
 7   import javafx.animation.PathTransition;
 8   import javafx.animation.RotateTransition;
 9   import javafx.animation.ScaleTransition;
10   import javafx.animation.SequentialTransition;
11   import javafx.animation.StrokeTransition;
12   import javafx.event.ActionEvent;
13   import javafx.fxml.FXML;

##### `FillTransition`

Lines 28–33 configure a one-second **`FillTransition`** that changes a shape’s fill color.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0672-01)

```
24      // configure and start transition animations
25      @FXML
26      private void startButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
27         // transition that changes a shape's fill
28         var fillTransition = new FillTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
29         fillTransition.setToValue(Color.CYAN);
30         fillTransition.setCycleCount(2);
31
32         // each even cycle plays transition in reverse to restore original
33         fillTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
34
```

Line 29 specifies the color (`CYAN`) to which the fill will transition. Line 30 sets the animation’s cycle count to 2—this determines the transition’s number of iterations to perform over the specified duration. Line 33 specifies that the animation should automatically play itself in reverse once the initial transition is complete. For this animation, during the first cycle, the fill color changes from the original fill color to `CYAN`, and during the second cycle, the animation transitions back to the original fill color.

##### `StrokeTransition`

Lines 36–39 configure a one-second **`StrokeTransition`** that changes a shape’s stroke color.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0672-02)

```
35         // transition that changes a shape's stroke over time
36         var strokeTransition = new StrokeTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
37         strokeTransition.setToValue(Color.BLUE);
38         strokeTransition.setCycleCount(2);
39         strokeTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
40
```

Line 37 specifies the color (`BLUE`) to which the stroke will transition. Line 38 sets the animation’s cycle count to 2, and line 39 specifies that the animation should automatically play itself in reverse once the initial transition is complete. For this animation, the stroke color changes from the original stroke color to `BLUE` during the first cycle and transitions back to the original stroke color during the second cycle.

##### `ParallelTransition`

Lines 42–43 configure a **`ParallelTransition`** that performs multiple transitions at the same time (that is, in parallel).

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0673-01)

```
41         // parallelizes multiple transitions
42         var parallelTransition =
43            new ParallelTransition(fillTransition, strokeTransition);
44
```

The `ParallelTransition` constructor receives a variable number of `Transition`s as a comma-separated list. In this case, the `FillTransition` and `StrokeTransition` will be performed in parallel on the app’s `Rectangle`.

##### `FadeTransition`

Lines 46–50 configure a one-second **`FadeTransition`** that changes a `Node`’s opacity.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0673-02)

```
45         // transition that changes a node's opacity over time
46         var fadeTransition = new FadeTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
47         fadeTransition.setFromValue(1.0); // opaque
48         fadeTransition.setToValue(0.0); // transparent
49         fadeTransition.setCycleCount(2);
50         fadeTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
51
```

Line 47 specifies the initial opacity—1.0 is fully opaque. Line 48 specifies the final opacity—0.0 is fully transparent. Once again, we set the cycle count to 2 and specified that the animation should auto-reverse itself.

##### `RotateTransition`

Lines 53–57 configure a one-second **`RotateTransition`** that rotates a `Node`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0673-03)

```
52         // transition that rotates a node
53         var rotateTransition = new RotateTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
54         rotateTransition.setByAngle(360.0);
55         rotateTransition.setCycleCount(2);
56         rotateTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_BOTH);
57         rotateTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
58
```

You can rotate a `Node` by a specified number of degrees (line 54), or you can use other methods of class `RotateTransition` to specify a start angle and end angle. Each `Transition` animation uses an **`Interpolator`** to calculate new property values throughout the animation’s duration. The default is a **`LINEAR`** `Interpolator`, which evenly divides the property value changes over the animation’s duration. For the `RotateTransition`, line 56 uses the `Interpolator` **`EASE_BOTH`**, which changes the rotation slowly at first (known as “easing in”), speeds up the rotation in the middle of the animation, then slows the rotation again to complete the animation (known as “easing out”). For a list of `Interpolator`s, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0673-04)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/animation/
   Interpolator.html
```

##### `PathTransition`

Lines 60–66 configure a two-second **`PathTransition`** that moves a node along a `Path`. The `Path` (lines 60–61) is specified as the second argument to the `PathTransition` constructor (lines 62–63). A **`LineTo`** object draws a straight line from the previous `PathElement`’s endpoint to the specified location. Line 65 specifies that this animation should use the `Interpolator` **`EASE_IN`**, which changes the position slowly at first before performing the animation at full speed.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0674-01)

```
59         // transition that moves a node along a Path
60         var path = new Path(new MoveTo(45, 45), new LineTo(45, 0),
61            new LineTo(90, 0), new LineTo(90, 90), new LineTo(0, 90));
62         var translateTransition =
63            new PathTransition(Duration.seconds(2), path);
64         translateTransition.setCycleCount(2);
65         translateTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_IN);
66         translateTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
67
```

##### `ScaleTransition`

Lines 69–74 configure a one-second **`ScaleTransition`** that changes a `Node`’s size. Lines 70–71 specify that the object will be scaled 75% larger along the *x*-axis (i.e., horizontally) and *y*-axis (i.e., vertically), respectively. Line 73 specifies that this animation should use the `Interpolator` **`EASE_OUT`**, which begins scaling the shape at full speed then slows down as the animation completes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0674-02)

```
68         // transition that scales a shape to make it larger or smaller
69         var scaleTransition = new ScaleTransition(Duration.seconds(1));
70         scaleTransition.setByX(0.75);
71         scaleTransition.setByY(0.75);
72         scaleTransition.setCycleCount(2);
73         scaleTransition.setInterpolator(Interpolator.EASE_OUT);
74         scaleTransition.setAutoReverse(true);
75
```

##### `SequentialTransition`

Lines 77–79 configure a **`SequentialTransition`** that performs a sequence of transitions—as each completes, the next one begins executing. The `SequentialTransition` constructor receives the `Node` to which the sequence of animations will be applied, followed by a comma-separated list of `Transition`s to perform. In fact, every transition animation class has a constructor that enables you to specify a `Node`. For this example, we did not specify `Node`s when creating the other transitions because they’re all applied to the `Rectangle` by the `SequentialTransition`. Every `Transition` has a **`play`** method (line 80) that begins the animation. Calling `play` on the `SequentialTransition` automatically calls `play` on each animation in the sequence.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0674-03)

```
76         // transition that applies a sequence of transitions to a node
77         var sequentialTransition = new SequentialTransition(
78            rectangle, parallelTransition, fadeTransition,
79            rotateTransition, translateTransition, scaleTransition);
80         sequentialTransition.play(); // play the transition
81      }
82   }
```
