### 17.8 `Timeline` Animations

Next, we’ll use a **`Timeline`** animation to bounce a `Circle` object around the app’s `Pane` over time. A `Timeline` animation can change any modifiable `Node` property. You specify how to change property values with one or more **`KeyFrame`** objects that the `Timeline` animation performs in sequence. For this app, we’ll specify a single `KeyFrame` that modifies a `Circle`’s location, then we’ll play that `KeyFrame` indefinitely.

##### `TimelineAnimation.fxml`

This app’s FXML ([Fig. 17.11](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig11)) defines a `Circle` object (lines 13–15) with the `fx:id "c"`, a five-pixel black border and the fill color `DODGERBLUE`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0675-01)

```
 1   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
 2   <!-- Fig. 17.11: TimelineAnimation.fxml -->
 3   <!-- FXML for a Circle that will be animated by the controller -->
 4
 5   <?import javafx.scene.layout.Pane?>
 6   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Circle?>
 7
 8   <Pane id="Pane" fx:id="pane" prefHeight="400.0"
 9      prefWidth="600.0" xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
10      xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
11      fx:controller="TimelineAnimationController">
12      <children>
13         <Circle fx:id="c" fill="DODGERBLUE" layoutX="142.0" layoutY="143.0"
14            radius="40.0" stroke="BLACK" strokeType="INSIDE"
15            strokeWidth="5.0" />
16      </children>
17   </Pane>
```

**Fig. 17.11** | FXML for a `Circle` that will be animated by the controller.

##### `TimelineAnimationController.java`

Class `TimelineAnimationController`’s ([Fig. 17.12](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig12)) `initialize` method (lines 20–43) configures then plays the `Timeline` animation. Lines 23–42 define the animation, line 41 specifies that the animation should cycle indefinitely (until the animation’s `stop` method is called), and line 42 plays the animation.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0676-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.12: TimelineAnimationController.java
 2   // Bounce a circle around a window using a Timeline animation
 3   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 4   import javafx.animation.KeyFrame;
 5   import javafx.animation.Timeline;
 6   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 7   import javafx.geometry.Bounds;
 8   import javafx.scene.layout.Pane;
 9   import javafx.scene.shape.Circle;
10   import javafx.util.Duration;
11
12   public class TimelineAnimationController {
13      private final static RandomGenerator random =
14         RandomGenerator.getDefault();
15      private int dx = random.nextInt(1, 6);
16      private int dy = random.nextInt(1, 6);
17      @FXML private Circle c;
18      @FXML private Pane pane;
19
20      @FXML
21      private void initialize() {
22         // define a timeline animation
23         var timelineAnimation = new Timeline(
24            new KeyFrame(Duration.millis(10), e -> {
25               // move the circle by the dx and dy amounts
26               c.setLayoutX(c.getLayoutX() + dx);
27               c.setLayoutY(c.getLayoutY() + dy);
28               Bounds bounds = pane.getBoundsInLocal();
29
30               if (hitRightOrLeftEdge(bounds)) {
31                  dx *= -1;
32               }
33
34               if (hitTopOrBottom(bounds)) {
35                  dy *= -1;
36               }
37            }) // end call to KeyFrame constructor
38         );
39
40         // indicate that the timeline animation should run indefinitely
41         timelineAnimation.setCycleCount(Timeline.INDEFINITE);
42         timelineAnimation.play();
43      }
44
45      // determines whether the circle hit the left or right of the window
46      private boolean hitRightOrLeftEdge(Bounds bounds) {
47         return (c.getLayoutX() <= (bounds.getMinX() + c.getRadius())) ||
48            (c.getLayoutX() >= (bounds.getMaxX() - c.getRadius()));
49         }
50
51      // determines whether the circle hit the top or bottom of the window
52      private boolean hitTopOrBottom(Bounds bounds) {
53         return (c.getLayoutY() <= (bounds.getMinY() + c.getRadius())) ||
54            (c.getLayoutY() >= (bounds.getMaxY() - c.getRadius()));
55      }
56   }
```

**Fig. 17.12** | Bounce a circle around a window using a `Timeline` animation.

##### Creating the `Timeline`

The `Timeline` constructor used in lines 23–38 can receive a comma-separated list of `Key-Frame`s as arguments—in this case, we pass one. Each `KeyFrame` issues an `ActionEvent` at a particular time in the animation. The app can respond to the event by changing a `Node`’s property values. The `KeyFrame` constructor used here specifies that, after ten milliseconds, the `ActionEvent` will occur. We set the `Timeline`’s cycle count to `Timeline.INDEFINITE`, so the `Timeline` will perform this `KeyFrame` every ten milliseconds. Lines 24–37 use a lambda to define the `EventHandler` for the `KeyFrame`’s `ActionEvent`. The lambda’s parameter (`e`) receives the `ActionEvent`.

##### `KeyFrame`’s `EventHandler`

The lambda uses class `TimelineAnimationController`’s instance variables `dx` and `dy` (declared and initialized at lines 15–16) to change the `Circle`’s *x*- and *y*-coordinates each time the `KeyFrame` plays. Lines 26–27 add these values to the `Circle`’s *x*- and *y*-coordinates. Next, lines 30–36 determine whether the `Circle` has collided with any of the `Pane`’s edges. If the `Circle` hits the left or right edge, line 31 multiplies `dx`’s value by `-1` to reverse the `Circle`’s horizontal direction. If the `Circle` hits the top or bottom edge, line 35 multiplies `dy`’s value by `-1` to reverse the `Circle`’s horizontal direction.

### 17.9 Frame-by-Frame Animation with `AnimationTimer`

A third way to implement JavaFX animations is via the `javafx.animation` package’s **class** **`AnimationTimer`**, which enables you to define frame-by-frame animations. You specify how your objects should move in a given frame. JavaFX aggregates all of the drawing operations and displays the frame. This can be used with objects in the scene graph or to draw shapes in a `Canvas`. JavaFX calls the **`handle`** method of every `AnimationTimer` before it draws an animation frame.

JavaFX tries to display animation frames at 60 frames per second for smooth animation. This frame rate varies based on the animation’s complexity, the processor speed and how busy the processor is at a given time. For this reason, method `handle` receives a time stamp in nanoseconds (billionths of a second) that you can use to determine the elapsed time since the last animation frame, then you can scale the movements of your objects accordingly. This enables you to define animations that operate at the same overall speed, regardless of the frame rate on a given device. We’ll discuss JavaFX performance issues in more detail in [Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18).

[Figure 17.13](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig13) reimplements the animation in [Fig. 17.12](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig12) using an `AnimationTimer`. The FXML is identical (other than the filename and controller class name). Much of the code is identical to [Fig. 17.12](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig12), so we focus on the new features.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0678-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.13: BallAnimationTimerController.java
 2   // Bounce a circle around a window using an AnimationTimer subclass.
 3   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 4   import javafx.animation.AnimationTimer;
 5   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 6   import javafx.geometry.Bounds;
 7   import javafx.scene.layout.Pane;
 8   import javafx.scene.shape.Circle;
 9
10   public class BallAnimationTimerController {
11      private final static RandomGenerator random =
12         RandomGenerator.getDefault();
13      private int dx = random.nextInt(1, 6);
14      private int dy = random.nextInt(1, 6);
15      @FXML private Circle c;
16      @FXML private Pane pane;
17
18      @FXML
19      private void initialize() {
20         // define an AnimationTimer
21         AnimationTimer timer = new AnimationTimer() {
22            int velocity = 60; // used to scale distance changes
23            long previousTime = System.nanoTime(); // time since app launch
24
25            // specify how to move Circle for current animation frame
26            @Override
27            public void handle(long now) {
28               double elapsedTime = (now - previousTime) / 1000000000.0;
29               previousTime = now;
30               double scale = elapsedTime * velocity;
31
32               Bounds bounds = pane.getBoundsInLocal();
33               c.setLayoutX(c.getLayoutX() + dx * scale);
34               c.setLayoutY(c.getLayoutY() + dy * scale);
35
36               if (hitRightOrLeftEdge(bounds)) {
37                  dx *= -1;
38               }
39
40               if (hitTopOrBottom(bounds)) {
41                  dy *= -1;
42               }
43            }
44         };
45
46         timer.start();
47      }
48
49      // determines whether the circle hit left/right of the window
50      private boolean hitRightOrLeftEdge(Bounds bounds) {
51         return (c.getLayoutX() <= (bounds.getMinX() + c.getRadius())) ||
52            (c.getLayoutX() >= (bounds.getMaxX() - c.getRadius()));
53      }
54
55      // determines whether the circle hit top/bottom of the window
56      private boolean hitTopOrBottom(Bounds bounds) {
57         return (c.getLayoutY() <= (bounds.getMinY() + c.getRadius())) ||
58            (c.getLayoutY() >= (bounds.getMaxY() - c.getRadius()));
59      }
60   }
```

**Fig. 17.13** | Bounce a circle around a window using an `AnimationTimer` subclass.

##### Extending `abstract` Class `AnimationTimer` Using an Anonymous Inner Class

Class `AnimationTimer` is an `abstract` class, so you must create a subclass. In this example, rather than defining an `AnimationTimer` subclass in a separate file, lines 21–44 create an **anonymous inner class**. Such a class does not have a name and is typically declared in a method. Lines 21–44 are one statement that

*   declares the `AnimationTimer` subclass,

*   immediately creates an object of that class and

*   assigns the new object’s reference to the `AnimationTimer` variable `timer` (line 21).

Since an anonymous inner class has no name, you must create an object of the class at the point where it’s declared, thus the keyword `new` in line 21\. The parentheses in

```
new AnimationTimer()
```

call the anonymous class’s constructor. After the parentheses are the braces that delimit the anonymous class’s body (lines 21 and 44), which may contain field and method declarations like other classes. Lines 22–23 define the anonymous inner class’s instance variables:

*   Variable `velocity` is used as a multiplier to determine the distance moved in each animation frame. We discuss this momentarily.

*   Variable `previousTime` represents the time stamp (in nanoseconds) of the previous animation frame—this will be used to determine the elapsed time between frames. We initialized `previousTime` to `System.nanoTime()`, which returns the number of nanoseconds since the JVM launched the app. `AnimationTimer`’s `handle` method also receives as its argument the number of nanoseconds since the JVM launched the app.

##### Overriding `AnimationTimer`’s `handle` Method

Lines 26–43 override class `AnimationTimer`’s `handle` method, which specifies what to do during each animation frame:

*   Line 28 calculates the `elapsedTime` in seconds since the last animation frame. If method `handle` is called 60 times per second, the elapsed time between frames will be approximately 0.0167 seconds—that is, 1/60 of a second.

*   Line 29 stores the time stamp in `previousTime` for use in the next animation frame.

*   When we change the `Circle`’s `layoutX` and `layoutY` (lines 33–34), we multiply `dx` and `dy` by the `scale` (line 30). In [Fig. 17.12](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig12), the `Circle`’s speed was determined by moving between one and five pixels along the *x-* and *y-*axes every 10 milliseconds—the larger the values, the faster the `Circle` moved. If we were to scale `dx` or `dy` by just `elapsedTime`, we’d move the `Circle` only small fractions of `dx` and `dy` during each frame—approximately 0.0167 seconds (1/60 of a second) to 0.083 seconds (5/60 of a second), based on their randomly chosen values. For this reason, we multiply the `elapsedTime` by the `velocity` (60) to scale the movement in each frame. This results in values that are approximately one to five pixels, as in [Fig. 17.12](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig12).

After creating the `AnimationTimer` object, the controller class’s `initialize` method calls the `AnimationTimer` object’s `start` method (line 46) to begin animating the ball.

##### Anonymous Inner Class Notes

An anonymous inner class can access its top-level class’s instance variables, `static` variables and methods. In this example, the anonymous inner class uses the controller class’s instance variables `dx` and `dy`. An anonymous inner class has limited access to the local variables of the method in which it’s declared. It can access only the `final` or effectively `final` local variables declared in the enclosing method’s body.

### 17.10 CSS Transitions

[Sections 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec2)–[17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3) introduced JavaFX CSS for styling JavaFX GUIs. JavaFX’s CSS support traditionally has focused on static `Node` styling. If you wanted to animate a `Node` property, you’d use the programmatically applied JavaFX transitions shown in [Section 17.7](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec7). In web development, **CSS transitions** are widely used to create smooth animation effects. These are often applied in response to the user **hovering** the mouse cursor over a webpage element—that is, moving the mouse cursor into a webpage element’s bounds. When the user moves the mouse cursor outside the element’s bounds, the element typically returns to its original appearance. Some CSS hover transitions include:^([7](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_7a),[8](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_8a),[9](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_9a))

[7](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_7). “[CSS Transitions](#ch16.xhtml_ch16lev3sec80).” Accessed October 3, 2024\. [`https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/`](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/).

[8](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_8). “Using CSS Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024\. [`https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions).

[9](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_9). “Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024\. [`https://web.dev/learn/css/transitions`](https://web.dev/learn/css/transitions).

*   changing an element’s appearance to indicate it’s clickable,

*   scaling an element’s size (zooming) to draw attention to it,

*   changing an image (such as an icon) temporarily to show that an element is interactive,

*   highlighting menu items as the user moves the mouse cursor over them,

*   moving elements to grab a user’s attention,

*   changing an element’s rotation angle,

*   adding shadows to make an element appear as if it’s raised off the screen, and

*   fading an element in so it’s visible or out so it’s not visible.

Other events that can trigger transitions include when a control receives the focus or is pressed.

##### CSS Transitions in JavaFX 23

JavaFX 23 adds support for webpage-style CSS transitions,^([10](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_10a)) which you can apply to any `Node` property styled with JavaFX CSS properties. The CSS transitions execute automatically in response to events, like hovering the mouse cursor over a `Node`. For precise animation control, you can use the other animation techniques shown in [Sections 17.7](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec7)–[17.9](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec9).

[10](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_10). “JavaFX CSS Reference Guide—Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024\. [`https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions`](https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions).

##### `CSSTransition.fxml`

To demonstrate CSS transitions, we’ll use an FXML GUI consisting of a `Pane` layout containing a rounded `Rectangle` ([Fig. 17.14](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig14)). Line 9 references the CSS stylesheet containing the `Rectangle`’s properties and the CSS transitions (presented in [Fig. 17.15](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig15)).

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0681-01)

 2   <!-- Fig. 17.14: CSSTransition.fxml -->
 3   <!-- FXML for a Pane and a Rectangle -->
 4
 5   <?import javafx.scene.layout.Pane?>
 6   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Rectangle?>
 7
 8   <Pane prefHeight="150.0" prefWidth="150.0"
 9      stylesheets="@CSSTransition.css"
10      xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
11      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1">

##### `TransitionAnimations.fxml`

Using CSS transitions, we’ll modify the `Rectangle`’s fill, stroke color, stroke width and rotation angle. The following screen captures show the transition progressions—they begin when the user hovers the mouse cursor over the `Rectangle` and transition back to the original state when the user moves the mouse outside the `Rectangle`’s bounds:

![Images](graphics/f0682-01.jpg)

##### `CSSTransition.css`

[Figure 17.15](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig15) contains this example’s CSS stylesheet. In the `Rectangle` CSS rule:

*   lines 4–9 specify the `Rectangle`’s initial styling, and

*   lines 10–12 specify the CSS transition settings (discussed momentarily).

The **`-fx-rotate`** **property** specifies the `Rectangle`’s rotation angle in degrees. The CSS rule in lines 15–20 specifies the values of the four CSS properties JavaFX will apply when the user hovers the mouse cursor over the `Rectangle`. The notation **`:hover`** is a **CSS pseudo-class**—JavaFX applies this rule only when the mouse cursor hovers over the `Node` that matches the rule.^([11](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_11a)) The CSS properties return to their original values in lines 4, 5, 8 and 9 when the user moves the mouse out of the `Rectangle`.

[11](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_11). Visit the “Pseudo-classes” section of the JavaFX CSS reference at [`https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html`](https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html) for other pseudo-classes that can trigger transitions.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0682-02)

```
 1   /* Fig. 17.15: CSSTransition.css */
 2   /* CSS rules to apply styling and CSS transitions to a Rectangle. */
 3   Rectangle {
 4      -fx-stroke-width: 5;
 5      -fx-stroke: black;
 6      -fx-arc-width: 50;
 7      -fx-arc-height: 50;
 8      -fx-fill: red;
 9      -fx-rotate: 0;
10      transition-property: -fx-fill, -fx-stroke,
11         -fx-stroke-width, -fx-rotate;
12      transition-duration: 3.0s;
13   }
14
15   Rectangle:hover {
16      -fx-stroke-width: 15;
17      -fx-stroke: red;
18      -fx-fill: black;
19      -fx-rotate: 180;
20   }
```

**Fig. 17.15** | CSS rules to apply styling and CSS transitions to a `Rectangle`.

##### Specifying the Transition Settings

The **CSS** **`transition-property`** (lines 10–11) specifies the `Rectangle` rule’s CSS properties that will participate in the CSS transition animation—in this case:

*   `-fx-fill` (the `Rectangle`’s fill color),

*   `-fx-stroke` (the `Rectangle`’s border color),

*   `-fx-stroke-width` (the `Rectangle`’s border thickness) and

*   `-fx-rotate` (the `Node`’s rotation angle in degrees).

The **CSS** **`transition-duration`** (line 12) specifies the transition animation’s duration (`3s` indicates three seconds).

When the user hovers the mouse over the `Rectangle`, JavaFX automatically applies a smooth animation for the properties listed in the `transition-property`. As with the `Transition` animations shown in [Section 17.7](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec7), CSS animations interpolate between the properties’ original values (lines 4, 5, 8 and 9) and their new values (lines 16–19). All the CSS transitions for the properties listed in the `transition-property` (lines 10–11) are applied to the `Rectangle` in parallel. When the user moves the mouse cursor out of `Rectangle`’s bounds, JavaFX automatically applies smooth transition animations that return each property to its original value (lines 4, 5, 8 and 9).

##### Other JavaFX CSS Transition Properties

Each CSS transition has an associated **`transition-timing-function`**. By default, CSS transitions use the **`ease`** **timing function**, which begins the transition slowly (“easing in”), speeds up the transition in the middle then slows the transition at the end (“easing out”)— like `Interpolator.EASE_BOTH` in [Fig. 17.10](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig10). You can customize the `transition-timing-function` by adding the property

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0683-01)

```
transition-timing-function: value;
```

to the CSS rule that specifies the `transition-property`. For the list of timing functions, visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0683-02)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-
   files/cssref.html#typeeasingfunction
```

You may also delay the transition animation’s start by a specified time interval using the **`transition-delay`** **property**.

You can combine all the CSS transition properties into a single shorthand **`transition`** **property** of the form:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0684-03)

```
transition:
   property duration timing-function delay,
   …
   property duration timing-function delay;
```

in which you specify the *property*, *duration*, *timing-function* and *delay* for each CSS property that participates in the CSS transition. For example, we could write this example’s `transition` property as:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0684-01)

```
transition:
   -fx-fill 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-stroke 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-stroke-width 3.0s ease 0s,
   -fx-rotate 3.0s ease 0s;
```

The *timing-function* and *delay* shown here are the defaults, so we can exclude them, as in:

```
transition:
   -fx-fill 3.0s,
   -fx-stroke 3.0s,
   -fx-stroke-width 3.0s,
   -fx-rotate 3.0s;
```

##### JavaFX CSS Transition Notes

There are several cases in which JavaFX CSS transitions are ignored or canceled:^([12](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_12a))

[12](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_12). “JavaFX CSS Reference Guide—Transitions.” Accessed October 3, 2024\. [`https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions`](https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/doc-files/cssref.html#introtransitions).

*   your program sets the corresponding `Node` property programmatically,

*   the property is used in a data binding,

*   the corresponding node is not visible on the screen or

*   the node has been removed from the scene.

##### CSS Transition Resources

At the time of this writing, JavaFX CSS transitions are new, and there is little online documentation about them. However, they’re based directly on the CSS transitions used in web development. By studying discussions of the transitions used in web development, you can get ideas for how JavaFX CSS properties can be animated. In particular, the **CSS Transition Generator** at

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0684-02)

```
https://dev.to/smpnjn/css-transition-generator-5de0
```

enables you to experiment with various transition settings and view the corresponding CSS. You can copy the settings into your JavaFX CSS stylesheets to apply the settings to JavaFX `Node`s with similar CSS properties. For additional CSS transition information, visit:

*   [`https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/`](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/)

*   [`https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_transitions/Using_CSS_transitions)

*   [`https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_transitions.asp`](https://www.w3schools.com/css/css3_transitions.asp)

**2** Prompt genAIs, asking the recommended duration for CSS hover animations.

### 17.11 Drawing on a `Canvas`

So far, you’ve displayed and manipulated JavaFX two-dimensional shape objects in the JavaFX scene graph. This section demonstrates similar drawing capabilities using the `javafx.scene.canvas` package, which contains two classes:

*   Class `Canvas` is a subclass of `Node` in which you can draw graphics.

*   **Class** **`GraphicsContext`** performs drawing operations on a `Canvas`.

A `GraphicsContext` object supports the same drawing characteristics you’ve previously used with `Shape`s, but you set these characteristics, then draw the shapes programmatically. [Figure 17.16](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig16) re-implements [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3)’s `BasicShapes` example to demonstrate `Canvas` capabilities, producing the following output:

![Images](graphics/f0685-01.jpg)

You’ll use various JavaFX classes and `enum`s from packages `javafx.scene.image`, `javafx.scene.paint` and `javafx.scene.shape`. JavaFX’s CSS capabilities use these behind the scenes to style `Shape`s. A `Canvas` is typically preferred for performance-oriented graphics, such as games with moving elements. We split the code (and specifically method `initialize`) into parts for discussion purposes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0685-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.16: CanvasShapesController.java
 2   // Drawing on a Canvas.
 3   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 4   import javafx.scene.canvas.Canvas;
 5   import javafx.scene.canvas.GraphicsContext;
 6   import javafx.scene.image.Image;
 7   import javafx.scene.paint.Color;
 8   import javafx.scene.paint.CycleMethod;
 9   import javafx.scene.paint.ImagePattern;
10   import javafx.scene.paint.LinearGradient;
11   import javafx.scene.paint.RadialGradient;
12   import javafx.scene.paint.Stop;
13   import javafx.scene.shape.ArcType;
14   import javafx.scene.shape.StrokeLineCap;
15
16   public class CanvasShapesController {
17      // instance variables that refer to GUI components
18      @FXML private Canvas drawingCanvas;
19
```

**Fig. 17.16** | Drawing on a `Canvas`.

##### Obtaining the `GraphicsContext` and Setting the Line Width for All Shapes

To draw on a `Canvas`, you first obtain its `GraphicsContext` by calling `Canvas` method **`getGraphicsContext2D`** (line 23).

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0686-01)

```
20      // draw on the Canvas
21      @FXML
22      private void initialize() {
23         GraphicsContext gc = drawingCanvas.getGraphicsContext2D();
24         gc.setLineWidth(10); // set all stroke widths
25
```

When you set a `GraphicsContext`’s drawing characteristics, they’re applied (as appropriate) to all subsequent shapes you draw. For example, line 24 calls the **`GraphicsContext`** **method** **`setLineWidth`** to specify the line thickness (`10`). All subsequent `GraphicsContext` method calls that draw lines or shape borders will use this line-width setting. This is similar to the `-fx-stroke-width` CSS attribute we specified for all shapes in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3).

##### Drawing Lines

Lines 27–34 draw the red and green lines:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0686-02)

```
26         // draw red line
27         gc.setStroke(Color.RED);
28         gc.strokeLine(10, 10, 100, 100);
29
30         // draw green line
31         gc.setGlobalAlpha(0.5); // half transparent
32         gc.setLineCap(StrokeLineCap.ROUND);
33         gc.setStroke(Color.GREEN);
34         gc.strokeLine(100, 10, 10, 100);
35
36         gc.setGlobalAlpha(1.0); // reset alpha transparency
37
```

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`setStroke`** **method** (lines 27 and 33) specifies the **`Paint`** object (package `javafx.scene.paint`) used to draw the line. This can be any of the `Paint` subclasses **`Color`**, **`ImagePattern`**, **`LinearGradient`** or **`RadialGradient`** (all from package `javafx.scene.paint`).

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`strokeLine`** **method** (lines 28 and 34) draws a line using the current `Paint` object we set as the stroke. The four arguments are the *x-y* coordinates of the start and end points.

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`setGlobalAlpha`** **method** (line 31) sets the alpha transparency of all subsequent shapes you draw. For the green line, we used `0.5`, which is 50% transparent. After drawing the green line, we reset this to the default `1.0` (line 35) so subsequent shapes are fully opaque.

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`setLineCap`** **method** (line 32) sets the line cap, like the CSS property `-fx-stroke-line-cap` in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3). This method’s argument is a constant from the **`enum StrokeLineCap`** (package `javafx.scene.shape`). Here, we round the line ends.

##### Drawing a Rounded Rectangle

Lines 39–42 draw a rounded rectangle with a red border and yellow fill:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0687-01)

```
38         // draw rounded rect with red border and yellow fill
39         gc.setStroke(Color.RED);
40         gc.setFill(Color.YELLOW);
41         gc.fillRoundRect(120, 10, 90, 90, 50, 50);
42         gc.strokeRoundRect(120, 10, 90, 90, 50, 50);
43
```

*   Line 38 sets the border color to `Color.RED`.

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`setFill`** **method** (lines 40, 50, 56 and 66) specifies the `Paint` object that fills a shape. Here we fill the rectangle with `Color.YELLOW`.

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`fillRoundRect`** **method** (line 41) draws a filled rectangle with rounded corners using the current `Paint` object as the fill. The first four arguments represent the rectangle’s upper-left *x*-coordinate, upper-left *y*-coordinate, width and height. The last two arguments specify the arc width and arc height for rounding the corners. These work identically to the CSS properties `-fx-arc-width` and `-fx-arc-height` properties in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3). `GraphicsContext` also provides a **`fillRect`** **method** that draws a rectangle without rounded corners.

*   **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`strokeRoundRect`** **method** (line 42) has the same arguments as method `fillRoundRect` but draws a hollow rectangle with rounded corners. `GraphicsContext` also provides a **`strokeRect`** **method** that draws a rectangle without rounded corners.

##### Drawing a Circle with a `RadialGradient` Fill

Lines 45–52 draw a circle with a blue border and a red-white, radial-gradient fill:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0687-02)

```
44         // draw circle with blue border and red/white radial gradient fill
45         gc.setStroke(Color.BLUE);
46         Stop[] stopsRadial =
47            {new Stop(0, Color.RED), new Stop(1, Color.WHITE)};
48         var radialGradient = new RadialGradient(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5,
49            0.6, true, CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, stopsRadial);
50         gc.setFill(radialGradient);
51         gc.fillOval(230, 10, 90, 90);
52         gc.strokeOval(230, 10, 90, 90);
53
```

Line 45 sets the border color to `Color.BLUE`. Lines 46–49 configure the `RadialGradient`—these lines perform the same tasks as the CSS function `radial-gradient` in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3). Lines 46–47 create an array of **`Stop`** objects (package `javafx.scene.paint`) representing the color stops. Each has an offset from 0.0 to 1.0 (a percentage from the gradient’s start point) and a `Color`. Here, the `Stop`s indicate that the radial gradient will transition from red at the gradient’s start point to white at its endpoint.

The `RadialGradient` constructor call in lines 48–49 creates a red-white radial gradient that starts with solid red at the shape’s center and transitions to white at 60% of the radial gradient’s radius. The constructor’s arguments are:

*   the focus angle, which specifies the direction of the radial gradient’s focal point from the gradient’s center,

*   the distance of the focal point as a percentage (0.0–1.0)—using 0 for both the focus angle and focal point indicates the gradient should begin from the oval’s center,

*   the center point’s *x* and *y* location as percentages (0.0–1.0) of the width and height for the shape being filled,

*   a `boolean` indicating whether the gradient should scale to fill its shape,

*   a constant from the **`CycleMethod enum`** (package `javafx.scene.paint`) indicating how the color stops are applied and

*   an array of `Stop` objects—this can also be a comma-separated list of `Stop`s or a `List<Stop>` object.

Line 50 sets the fill to the new `radialGradient`, then lines 51–52 call **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`fillOval`** and **`strokeOval`** **methods** to draw a filled oval and a hollow oval, respectively. Each method receives as arguments the upper-left *x*-coordinate, upper-left *y*-coordinate, width and height of the rectangular area in which the oval should be drawn—known as a bounding box. Because the width and height are the same, these calls draw circles.

##### Drawing an Oval with an `ImagePattern` Fill

Lines 55–58 draw an oval with a green border and containing an image:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0688-01)

```
54         // draw ellipse with green border and image fill
55         gc.setStroke(Color.GREEN);
56         gc.setFill(new ImagePattern(new Image("yellowflowers.png")));
57         gc.fillOval(340, 10, 200, 90);
58         gc.strokeOval(340, 10, 200, 90);
59
```

*   Line 55 sets the border color to `Color.GREEN`.

*   Line 56 sets the fill to an `ImagePattern`—a subclass of `Paint` that loads an `Image` from the local system or from a URL specified as a `String`. `ImagePattern` is the class used by the CSS function `image-pattern` in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3).

*   Lines 57–58 draw a filled and a hollow oval.

##### Drawing an Arc with a `LinearGradient` Fill

Lines 61–68 draw an arc with a purple border and filled with a cyan-white linear gradient:

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0689-01)

```
60         // draw arc with purple border and cyan/white linear gradient fill
61         gc.setStroke(Color.PURPLE);
62         Stop[] stopsLinear =
63            {new Stop(0, Color.CYAN), new Stop(1, Color.WHITE)};
64         var linearGradient = new LinearGradient(0, 0, 1, 0,
65            true, CycleMethod.NO_CYCLE, stopsLinear);
66         gc.setFill(linearGradient);
67         gc.fillArc(560, 10, 90, 90, 45, 270, ArcType.ROUND);
68         gc.strokeArc(560, 10, 90, 90, 45, 270, ArcType.ROUND);
69      }
70   }
```

*   Line 61 sets the border color to `Color.PURPLE`.

*   Lines 62–65 configure the `LinearGradient`—the class used by the CSS function `linear-gradient` in [Section 17.3](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec3). The constructor’s first four arguments are the endpoint coordinates that represent the direction and angle of the gradient. If the *x*-coordinates are the same, the gradient is vertical. If the *y*-coordinates are the same, the gradient is horizontal. All other linear gradients follow a diagonal line. When these values are specified in the range 0.0 to 1.0, and the constructor’s fifth argument is `true`, the gradient is scaled to fill the shape. The next argument is the `CycleMethod`. The last argument is an array of `Stop` objects—again, this can be a comma-separated list of `Stop`s or a `List<Stop>` object.

Lines 67–68 call **`GraphicsContext`****’s** **`fillArc`** and **`strokeArc`** **methods** to draw a filled arc and a hollow arc, respectively. Each method receives as arguments:

*   the upper-left *x*-coordinate, upper-left *y*-coordinate, width and height of the rectangular area (that is, the bounding box) in which the oval should be drawn,

*   the start angle and sweep of the arc in degrees, and

*   a constant from the **`ArcType enum`** (package `javafx.scene.shape`)

##### Additional `GraphicsContext` Features

There are many additional `GraphicsContext` features, which you can explore at

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0689-02)

```
https://openjfx.io/javadoc/23/javafx.graphics/javafx/scene/canvas/
   GraphicsContext.html
```

Some of the capabilities that we did not discuss here include:

*   Drawing and filling text—similar to the font features in [Section 17.2](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec2).

*   Drawing and filling polylines, polygons and paths—similar to the corresponding `Shape` subclasses in [Section 17.4](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec4).

*   Applying effects and transforms—similar to the transforms in [Section 17.5](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec5).

*   Drawing images.

*   Manipulating the individual pixels of a drawing in a `Canvas` via a `PixelWriter`.

*   Saving and restoring graphics characteristics via the `save` and `restore` methods.

### 17.12 Three-Dimensional Shapes

We’ve demonstrated many two-dimensional graphics capabilities. JavaFX provides several three-dimensional shapes and corresponding capabilities. The three-dimensional shapes are subclasses of `Shape3D` from the package `javafx.scene.shape`. In this section, you’ll use Scene Builder to create a **`Box`**, a **`Cylinder`** and a **`Sphere`** and specify several of their properties. Then, in the app’s controller, you’ll create materials that apply color and images to the 3D shapes.^([13](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_13a))

[13](#ch17.xhtml_fn17_13). At the time of this writing, 3D shapes are not rendering correctly on M-processor (ARM) Macs in Scene Builder or in the running app, and 3D shapes are not rendering at all on Windows 11 ARM. We’ll post updates to the book’s web page: [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5).

##### FXML for the `Box`, `Cylinder` and `Sphere`

[Figure 17.17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig17) presents the completed FXML that we created with Scene Builder:

*   Lines 16–21 define the `Box` object.

*   Lines 22–27 define the `Cylinder` object.

*   Lines 28–29 define the `Sphere` object.

We dragged objects of these `Shape3D` subclasses from the Scene Builder Library’s Shapes section onto the design area and gave them the fx:id values `box`, `cylinder` and `sphere`, respectively. We also set the controller to `ThreeDimensionalShapesController`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0690-01)

```
 1   <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
 2   <!-- Fig. 17.17: ThreeDimensionalShapes.fxml -->
 3   <!-- FXML that displays a Box, Cylinder and Sphere -->
 4
 5   <?import javafx.geometry.Point3D?>
 6   <?import javafx.scene.layout.Pane?>
 7   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Box?>
 8   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Cylinder?>
 9   <?import javafx.scene.shape.Sphere?>
10
11   <Pane prefHeight="200.0" prefWidth="510.0"
12      xmlns="http://javafx.com/javafx/23"
13      xmlns:fx="http://javafx.com/fxml/1"
14      fx:controller="ThreeDimensionalShapesController">
15      <children>
16         <Box fx:id="box" depth="100.0" height="100.0" layoutX="100.0"
17            layoutY="100.0" rotate="30.0" width="100.0">
18            <rotationAxis>
19               <Point3D x="1.0" y="1.0" z="1.0" />
20            </rotationAxis>
21         </Box>
22         <Cylinder fx:id="cylinder" height="100.0" layoutX="265.0"
23            layoutY="100.0" radius="50.0" rotate="-45.0">
24            <rotationAxis>
25               <Point3D x="1.0" y="1.0" z="1.0" />
26            </rotationAxis>
27         </Cylinder>
28         <Sphere fx:id="sphere" layoutX="430.0" layoutY="100.0"
29            radius="60.0" />
30      </children>
31   </Pane>
```

**Fig. 17.17** | FXML that displays a `Box`, `Cylinder` and `Sphere`.

All three shapes are initially gray. The shading in Scene Builder comes from the scene’s default lighting. Though we do not use them here, package `javafx.scene`’s classes `AmbientLight`, `PointLight`, `SpotLight` and `DirectionalLight` can be used to add lighting effects. You can also use camera objects to view the scene from different angles and distances. The `AmbientLight`, `PointLight` and camera capabilities are located in the Scene Builder Library’s 3D section.

##### `Box` Properties

Configure the `Box`’s properties in the Scene Builder Inspector’s Layout section as follows:

*   Set Width, Height and Depth to `100`, making a cube. The depth is measured along the *z*-axis, which runs perpendicular to your screen. When you move objects along the *z*-axis, they get bigger as they’re brought toward you and smaller as they’re moved away from you.

*   Set Layout X and Layout Y to `100` to specify the cube’s location.

*   Set Rotate to `30` to specify the rotation angle in degrees. Positive values rotate counter-clockwise.

*   For Rotation Axis, set the X, Y and Z values to `1` to indicate that the Rotate angle should be used to rotate the cube 30 degrees around each axis.

To observe how the Rotate angle and Rotation Axis values affect the `Box`’s rotation, set two of the three Rotation Axis values to `0`, then change the Rotate angle.

##### `Cylinder` Properties

Configure the `Cylinder`’s properties in Scene Builder as follows:

*   Set Height to `100.0` and Radius to `50`.

*   Set Layout X and Layout Y to `265` and `100`, respectively.

*   Set Rotate to `-45` to specify the rotation angle in degrees. Negative values rotate clockwise.

*   For Rotation Axis, set the X, Y and Z values to `1` to indicate that the Rotate angle should be applied to all three axes.

##### `Sphere` Properties

Configure the `Sphere`’s properties in Scene Builder as follows:

*   Set Radius to `60`.

*   Set Layout X and Layout Y to `430` and `100`, respectively.

##### `ThreeDimensionalShapesController` Class

[Figure 17.18](#ch17.xhtml_ch17fig18) presents this app’s controller and final output. The final shapes’ colors and images are created by applying so-called materials to the shapes. A **`PhongMaterial`** (package `javafx.scene.paint`) defines materials for 3D shapes. The name “Phong” is a 3D graphics term. Phong shading is a technique for applying color and shading to 3D surfaces. For more details on this technique, visit

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0692-01)

```
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phong_shading
```

[Click here to view code image](#ch17_images.xhtml_f0692-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 17.18: ThreeDimensionalShapesController.java
 2   // Setting the material displayed on 3D shapes.
 3   import javafx.fxml.FXML;
 4   import javafx.scene.paint.Color;
 5   import javafx.scene.paint.PhongMaterial;
 6   import javafx.scene.image.Image;
 7   import javafx.scene.shape.Box;
 8   import javafx.scene.shape.Cylinder;
 9   import javafx.scene.shape.Sphere;
10
11   public class ThreeDimensionalShapesController {
12      // instance variables that refer to 3D shapes
13      @FXML private Box box;
14      @FXML private Cylinder cylinder;
15      @FXML private Sphere sphere;
16
17      // set the material for each 3D shape
18      @FXML
19      private void initialize() {
20         // define material for the Box object
21         var boxMaterial = new PhongMaterial();
22         boxMaterial.setDiffuseColor(Color.CYAN);
23         box.setMaterial(boxMaterial);
24
25         // define material for the Cylinder object
26         var cylinderMaterial = new PhongMaterial();
27         cylinderMaterial.setDiffuseMap(new Image("yellowflowers.png"));
28         cylinder.setMaterial(cylinderMaterial);
29
30         // define material for the Sphere object
31         var sphereMaterial = new PhongMaterial();
32         sphereMaterial.setDiffuseColor(Color.RED);
33         sphereMaterial.setSpecularColor(Color.WHITE);
34         sphereMaterial.setSpecularPower(32);
35         sphere.setMaterial(sphereMaterial);
36      }
37   }
```

**Fig. 17.18** | Setting the material displayed on 3D shapes.

##### `PhongMaterial` for the `Box`

Lines 21–23 configure and set the `Box` object’s `PhongMaterial`. The **`setDiffuseColor`** **method** sets the color that’s applied to the `Box`’s surfaces (that is, sides). The scene’s lighting effects determine the shades of the color applied to each visible surface. These shades change based on the angle from which the light shines on the objects.

##### `PhongMaterial` for the `Cylinder`

Lines 26–28 configure and set the `Cylinder` object’s `PhongMaterial`. The **`setDiffuseMap`** **method** sets the `Image` applied to the `Cylinder`’s surfaces. Again, the scene’s lighting affects how the image is shaded on the surfaces. In the output, notice that the image is darker at the left and right edges (where less light reaches) and barely visible at the bottom (where almost no light reaches).

##### `PhongMaterial` for the `Sphere`

Lines 31–35 configure and set the `Sphere` object’s `PhongMaterial`. We set the diffuse color to red. ## 18

## Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this chapter, you’ll:

*   Understand concurrency, parallelism and multithreading.

*   Compare the performance of `Arrays` methods `sort` and `parallelSort`.

*   Use parallel streams for better multi-core performance.

*   Use `ExecutorService` to launch concurrent threads that execute `Runnable`s.

*   Be introduced to Project Loom for massively concurrent, high-throughput applications.

*   Launch tasks with lightweight virtual threads.

*   Group tasks and subtasks via structured concurrency.

*   Use structured concurrency and scoped values to share immutable data among tasks.

*   Understand producer/consumer relationships.

*   Coordinate access to shared mutable data via classes of `java.util.concurrent`.

*   Update JavaFX’s GUIs in a thread-safe manner.

*   Return intermediate results from a long-running task to a JavaFX GUI.

Outline

### 18.1 Introduction

It would be nice if we could focus on performing only one task at a time and doing it well. That’s usually difficult to do in a complex world with so much happening simultaneously. This chapter presents Java’s capabilities for creating and managing multiple tasks. As we’ll demonstrate, this can significantly improve program performance and responsiveness.

##### Concurrency

When we say that two tasks operate **concurrently**, we mean they’re both making progress. Until the early 2000s, most computers had only a single processor. Operating systems on such computers executed tasks concurrently by rapidly switching between them, doing a small portion of each before moving on to the next, so all tasks keep progressing. For example, it’s common for personal computers to concurrently accept keyboard input, compile a program, send a file to a printer, receive electronic mail messages over a network and more. Since its inception, Java has supported concurrency.

##### Parallelism

When we say that two tasks operate **in parallel**, we mean they’re executing simultaneously. In this sense, parallelism is a subset of concurrency. The human body performs a great variety of operations in parallel. Respiration, blood circulation, digestion, thinking and walking, for example, can occur in parallel, as can all the senses—sight, hearing, touch, smell and taste. It’s believed that this parallelism is possible because the human brain is thought to contain billions of “processors.” Today’s multi-core CPUs have multiple processors that can perform tasks in parallel. A key difference between concurrency and parallelism is that code can execute concurrently by sharing a single core, whereas executing code in parallel requires multiple cores.

##### Java Concurrency

Java makes concurrency available to you through the language and APIs—we use only API concurrency features in this chapter. Java programs can have multiple **threads of execution**, each with its own method-call stack, allowing it to execute concurrently with other threads while sharing system resources such as processors, memory and file handles. This is called **multithreading**. The JVM creates threads to run programs and perform housekeeping tasks such as garbage collection.

A problem with single-threaded programs that can lead to poor responsiveness is that lengthy activities must complete before others can begin. In a multithreaded program, threads can be distributed across multiple cores (if available) so multiple tasks execute in parallel. This enables programs to operate more efficiently and optimize system resource use. Multithreading can also increase performance on single-processor systems—when one thread cannot proceed (because, for example, it’s waiting for the result of an I/O operation), another can use the processor.

##### Concurrent Programming Uses

We’ll discuss many applications of **concurrent programming**. For example, when streaming an audio or video over the Internet, the user may not want to wait until the entire audio or video downloads before starting the playback. To solve this problem, multiple threads can be used:

*   one to download the audio or video (later in the chapter, we’ll refer to this as a producer) and

*   another to play it (later in the chapter, we’ll refer to this as a consumer).

These threads proceed concurrently. To avoid choppy playback, an audio/video player **synchronizes** the threads’ actions (that is, coordinates them) so the player thread doesn’t begin playing until there’s enough audio or video in memory to keep the player thread busy. Producer and consumer threads share memory—we’ll demonstrate one of Java’s concurrent collections that automatically coordinates such threads to ensure correct execution.

##### Concurrent Programming Is Difficult

Writing multithreaded programs can be error-prone. Although the human mind can perform functions concurrently, jumping between parallel trains of conscious thought can be difficult.

To understand why multithreaded programs can be challenging to write and comprehend, try the following experiment: Open three books to page 1 and try reading the books concurrently. Read a few words from the first book, then a few from the second, then a few from the third, then loop back and read the next few words from the first book, and so on. After this experiment, you’ll appreciate many of the challenges of multithreading— switching between the books, reading briefly, remembering your place in each book, moving the book you’re reading closer so you can read it and pushing the books you’re not reading aside—and, amid all this chaos, trying to comprehend the content of the books!

The reading-multiple-books analogy is similar to **context switching** in multithreaded applications. To switch between threads, your system must pause one thread, save its state, load another thread’s state and resume that thread’s execution. This context switching affects performance due to the time spent managing threads instead of running code. Frequent context switching makes it harder to process information efficiently.

##### Use the Prebuilt Classes of the Concurrency APIs Whenever Possible

In programs requiring thread synchronization, most programmers should use the Java Concurrency APIs from **package** **`java.util.concurrent`** that manage synchronization for you, like `ArrayBlockingQueue` ([Section 18.10](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec10)). The concurrency API classes are

*   written by experts,

*   designed to be correct and operate efficiently,

*   have been thoroughly tested and debugged, and

*   help you avoid common traps and pitfalls.

[Section 18.10.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec35) briefly overviews the Java Concurrency API’s other prebuilt concurrent collections.

##### Project Loom: Virtual Threads, Structured Concurrency and Scoped Values

In addition to several traditional concurrency and multithreading topics, this chapter focuses on Project Loom’s enhancements to Java’s threading model that provide simpler, lightweight virtual threads (finalized in Java 21). These require significantly less memory than Java’s traditional threads (known as platform threads), enabling applications to launch enormous numbers of concurrent virtual threads to meet the demands of today’s massively parallel applications. Project Loom also reduces the complexity of writing concurrent programs, making concurrency easier to use and get right.

We also introduce two emerging Project Loom technologies—structured concurrency and scoped values.^([1](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_1a)) Structured concurrency enables programmers to treat multiple threads as a single unit of work (a scope), making it easier to manage those threads, handle errors and reclaim resources no longer needed. Scoped values simplify data sharing among virtual threads in the same scope, reducing the need for complex thread-synchronization techniques. Scoped values become implicit arguments to every method called in a given structured concurrency scope.

[1](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_1). At the time of this writing, structured concurrency and scoped values were preview features. Once they are finalized, we’ll post the updated examples on our blog at [`https://deitel.com/blog`](https://deitel.com/blog).

##### Creating and Filling the Arrays

Line 16 creates a 100,000,000-element array of `int`s. Lines 17–18 fill the array with random `int` values using **`Arrays static`** **method** **`parallelSetAll`**, which splits the work of filling the array with values across multiple threads that can operate in parallel on your computer’s CPU cores. This makes filling the array faster for large arrays. The method receives as arguments the array to fill and a **generator function** that produces a value used to fill an array element. We’re filling an `int` array, so generator must be an `IntUnaryOperator` that receives an `int` and returns an `int`. Depending on which `parallelSetAll` overload you use, the generator function must implement one of the following `java.util.function` interfaces

*   `IntUnaryOperator` for `int` arrays,

*   `IntToLongFunction` for `long` arrays,

*   `IntToDoubleFunction` for `double` arrays or

*   `IntFunction<T>` for arrays of any non-primitive type.

In this example, we implemented `IntUnaryOperator` (introduced in [Section 14.9](#ch14.xhtml_ch14lev1sec9)) as a lambda expression (line 18) that calls

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0701-02)

ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt()

to choose a random `int` value for each array element.^([2](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_2a)) At the end of this section, we’ll explain why we used `ThreadLocalRandom` rather than `RandomGenerator`. Line 19 calls `array1`’s `clone` method to make a copy so the calls to `sort` and `parallelSort` sort the same values.

[2](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_2). The lambda’s parameter, `i`, is not used in this program. For such cases, you can replace the variable name with an underscore (`_`).

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0702-01)

18            i -> ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt());
19         var array2 = array1.clone();
20

##### `ThreadLocalRandom` vs. `RandomGenerator`

Java’s regular random-number generators, like the one returned by

```
RandomGenerator.getDefault()
```

are not designed to be shared among multiple threads. They are not “**thread-safe**”—when multiple threads share a random-number generator, they can interfere with one another, making the generated values less random. Each thread that calls **`ThreadLocalRandom`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`current`** receives its own `RandomGenerator` object. This prevents conflicts when `parallelSetAll` generates random numbers for multiple portions of an array in parallel.

Lines 51–58 demonstrate the performance improvement from calling `summaryStatistics` on a parallel stream that automatically takes advantage of multi-core processors. Calling `summaryStatistics` on a parallel stream took 10.4% of the time it took on the sequential stream and just 8.9% of the time it took to perform the individual operations sequentially.

### 18.4 Creating and Executing Platform Threads with the `Executor` Framework

In [Sections 18.2](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec2)–[18.3](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec3), we used parallel methods of the `Arrays` class and parallel streams that automatically “figure out” how to take advantage of your system’s CPU cores to improve performance. You can also create your own custom concurrent tasks.

##### Creating Concurrent Tasks with the `Runnable` Interface

You implement the **`Runnable`** **interface** (of package `java.lang`) to specify a task that can execute concurrently with other tasks. You specify the code that performs your task by overriding the **`Runnable`** **interface’s** **`run`** **method**.

##### Executing `Runnable` Objects with an `Executor`

You execute a `Runnable` to perform its task, typically using an object that implements the **`Executor`** **interface**. This interface’s **`execute`** **method** receives a `Runnable` and executes it at some point in the future. When an `Executor` begins executing a `Runnable`, it assigns the `Runnable` to a `Thread` and calls the `Runnable`’s `run` method to perform the specified task. Any method called from a `Runnable`’s `run` method executes as part of that task’s `Thread`.

You obtain an `Executor` object by calling a `static` method of the **`Executors`** **class** (package `java.util.concurrent`). This class’s methods return objects that implement the **`ExecutorService`** **interface** (package `java.util.concurrent`), which extends `Executor` and declares additional methods for managing an `Executor`’s life cycle. `ExecutorService` objects are `AutoCloseable`, so you can use them with the `try`-with-resources statement.

Though it’s possible to create `Thread`s explicitly, `Executor`s have many advantages. For example, some `Executor`s manage a group of platform threads called a **thread pool** and can reuse existing platform threads to eliminate the overhead of creating new ones for each task. Such `Executor`s can improve performance for CPU-intensive tasks by optimizing the number of threads to ensure that the CPU’s cores stay busy.

##### Implementing the `Runnable` Interface

Let’s use a mechanical example to demonstrate creating and executing `Runnable` tasks. Class `PrintTask` ([Fig. 18.3](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig03)) implements `Runnable` (line 5)—each `PrintTask` can execute concurrently with other tasks. Variable `sleepTime` (line 8) stores a random integer value from 0 to 5000 milliseconds (line 15)—we did not use `ThreadLocalRandom` here, as the PrintTask constructor is always called from the `main` thread. Each thread running a `Print-Task` sleeps for the amount of time specified by `sleepTime`, then outputs its task’s name and a message indicating that it’s done sleeping.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0707-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.3: PrintTask.java
 2   // PrintTask class sleeps for a random time from 0 to 5 seconds
 3   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 4
 5   public class PrintTask implements Runnable {
 6      private static final RandomGenerator generator =
 7         RandomGenerator.getDefault();
 8      private final int sleepTime; // random sleep time for thread
 9      private final String taskName;
1011      // constructor gives the PrintTask a name and
12      // picks random sleep time between 0 and 5 seconds
13      public PrintTask(String taskName) {
14         this.taskName = taskName;
15         sleepTime = generator.nextInt(5001); // milliseconds
16      }
17
18      // method run contains the code that a thread will execute
19      @Override
20      public void run() {
21         try { // put thread to sleep for sleepTime amount of time
22            System.out.printf("%s going to sleep for %d milliseconds.%n",
23               taskName, sleepTime);
24            Thread.sleep(sleepTime); // put thread to sleep
25         }
26         catch (InterruptedException exception) {
27            exception.printStackTrace();
28            Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // re-interrupt the thread
29         }
30
31         // print task name
32         System.out.printf("%s done sleeping%n", taskName);
33      }
34   }
```

**Fig. 18.3** | `PrintTask` class sleeps for a random time from 0 to 5 seconds.

A `PrintTask` executes when a thread calls its `run` method (lines 19–33). Lines 22–23 output a message indicating the task’s name and that it’s going to sleep for `sleepTime` milliseconds. Line 24 invokes **`Thread static`** **method** **`sleep`** to pause the thread for the specified amount of time. At this point, the thread loses the processor, and the operating system can allow another thread to execute. When the thread awakens, and the operating system eventually assigns it to a processor to continue executing, line 32 outputs a message indicating that the task is done sleeping, then method `run` terminates.

##### A `Runnable`’s `run` Method Must Catch `InterruptedException`s

The `catch` handler at lines 26–29 is required because method `sleep` might throw a checked **`InterruptedException`** if a sleeping thread’s **`interrupt`** **method** is called. Recall from [Chapter 10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10) that when you override a method, the `throws` clause may contain only the same exception types or a subset of those declared in the original method’s `throws` clause. In the `Runnable` interface’s definition, method `run` does not have a `throws` clause, so we cannot add one in line 20\. For this reason, you must catch `InterruptedException`s (and any other checked exceptions) in a `Runnable`’s `run` method.

When a thread is interrupted, it’s typically because another part of the program needs it to terminate—perhaps due to an error or another thread having already finished the required task. Every thread has a `boolean` interrupted status. A thread can periodically check this status by calling **`Thread static`** **method** **`isInterrupted`**. If this method returns `true`, the thread knows it has been interrupted and can decide how to terminate gracefully. When you catch an `InterruptedException`, the thread’s interrupted status is set to `false`, which could prevent the thread from terminating. For this reason, it’s considered good practice to set the thread’s interrupt status back to `true` in the `catch` handler to ensure that subsequent calls to `isInterrupted` return `true`. Line 28 obtains a reference to the currently executing `Thread` by calling **`Thread static`** **method** **`currentThread`**, then uses that `Thread`’s `interrupt` method to set the thread’s interrupted status to `true`.^([4](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_4a))

[4](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_4). For detailed information on handling thread interruptions, read [Chapter 7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07) of *Java Concurrency in Practice* by Brian Goetz, et al., Addison-Wesley Professional, 2006.

##### Executing `PrintTask`s Concurrently

[Figure 18.4](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig04) uses an `ExecutorService` object to execute `PrintTasks`. Lines 8–10 create three `PrintTask`s to execute. Line 18 in the `try`-with-resources statement calls **`Executors static`** **method** **`newCachedThreadPool`** to obtain an `ExecutorService` that manages a cached thread pool. Such a thread pool executes each task by

*   using an existing platform `Thread` if one is available in the pool or

*   creating a new platform `Thread` if no existing ones are available to reuse.

When a task completes, the cached thread pool `ExecutorService` keeps the platform `Thread` for 60 seconds. If the program submits another task to the `ExecutorService` within that time, it reuses the cached `Thread` to execute that task, eliminating the overhead of creating a new platform thread (we say more about this overhead in [Section 18.7](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec7)). Otherwise, the `ExecutorService` terminates the `Thread` and removes it from the cache. Cached thread pools are typically used in programs that execute many short tasks.^([5](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_5a))

[5](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_5). “Class `Executors`.” Accessed February 7, 2025\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newCachedThreadPool()`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html#newCachedThreadPool()).

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0709-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.4: TaskExecutor.java
 2   // Using an ExecutorService to execute Runnables.
 3   import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
 4
 5   public class TaskExecutor {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // create and name each runnable
 8         var task1 = new PrintTask("task1");
 9         var task2 = new PrintTask("task2");
10         var task3 = new PrintTask("task3");
11
12         System.out.println("Starting Executor\n");
13
14         // create ExecutorService for executing tasks; when the
15         // try-with-resources statement completes, the ExecutorService's
16         // close method shuts it down, preventing it from accepting new
17         // tasks and waiting for existing ones to complete execution
18         try (var executorService = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()) {
19            // start the three PrintTasks
20            executorService.execute(task1); // start task1
21            executorService.execute(task2); // start task2
22            executorService.execute(task3); // start task3
23         }
24
25         System.out.println("\nMain ends.");
26      }
27   }
```

```
Starting Executor

task1 going to sleep for 4610 milliseconds.
task3 going to sleep for 4833 milliseconds.
task2 going to sleep for 992 milliseconds.
task2 done sleeping
task1 done sleeping
task3 done sleeping

Main ends.
```

```
Starting Executor

task3 going to sleep for 357 milliseconds.
task1 going to sleep for 4670 milliseconds.
task2 going to sleep for 3360 milliseconds.
task3 done sleeping
task2 done sleeping
task1 done sleeping

Main ends.
```

**Fig. 18.4** | Using an `ExecutorService` to execute `Runnable`s.

Java maps each `Thread` in a cached thread pool to an operating system thread—the Java documentation refers to these as **platform threads**. Multi-core systems can schedule multiple platform threads (and the other programs running on your computer) on separate cores, enabling them to execute in parallel. Lines 20–22 use the cached thread pool to execute `Runnable`s—in this case, `PrintTask`s—at some time in the future. Method `execute` returns immediately from each invocation—the program does not wait for each `PrintTask` to finish.

##### Waiting for Tasks to Complete Execution

After scheduling tasks to execute, you’ll typically want to wait for them to complete—for example, so you can use the tasks’ results, as we’ll do in later examples. When the `try-`with-resources statement completes execution (line 23), it calls the **`ExecutorService`****’s** **`close`** **method**, which

*   calls **`ExecutorService`** **method** **`shutdown`** to prevent the `ExecutorService` from accepting new tasks then

*   calls **`ExecutorService`** **method** **`awaitTermination`** to wait for all the previously scheduled tasks to complete.

##### Main Thread

The code in `main` executes in the **`main`** **thread**, which is created by the JVM. The code in `PrintTask`’s `run` method (lines 19–33 of [Fig. 18.3](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig03)) executes sometime after each task is passed to the `ExecutorService`’s `execute` method ([Fig. 18.4](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig04), lines 20–22).

##### Sample Outputs

Each task displays its name and sleep time then puts its thread to sleep. In most cases, the thread running the task with the shortest sleep time awakens first (though this is not guaranteed), then indicates it’s done sleeping and terminates. In sample outputs, note that the tasks did not go to sleep in the same order they were launched. This illustrates that **we cannot predict the order in which the tasks will start executing, even if we know the order in which they were created and started.** Similarly, **we cannot predict when a thread that awakens from a sleep will be assigned to a processor to continue executing.**

### 18.5 Project Loom Overview

[Section 18.4](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec4) executed `PrintTask`s using resource-intensive platform threads. Each platform thread has its own default method-call stack size—typically one to two megabytes (depending on the hardware)^([6](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_6a)) to keep track of methods called by the task in that thread. The number of platform threads is limited not only by the amount of available memory but also by^([7](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_7a))

[6](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_6). “The `java` Command.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/java.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/java.html).

[7](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_7). Summary of responses from *ChatGPT*, *Claude*, *Gemini* and *Perplexity* to the prompt “What are the operating system limits for threads in an application?” [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com), [`https://claude.ai`](https://claude.ai), [`https://gemini.google.com/app`](https://gemini.google.com/app) and [`https://perplexity.ai`](https://perplexity.ai).

*   operating system limits on threads per process (i.e., per application) and

*   the overheads of scheduling and executing large numbers of concurrent tasks and sharing resources among those tasks.

These limitations make it difficult for developers to build scalable applications requiring thousands or even millions of concurrent tasks—like those that handle the enormous number of interactions between users and popular social media apps, such as YouTube, Face-book, WhatsApp, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, Reddit and X. In Java, such applications have typically required complex programming techniques and frameworks to reduce overhead and share limited resources.

**Project Loom** enhances Java with three new concurrency capabilities that simplify massively parallel application development:

*   virtual threads ([Sections 18.6](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec6)–[18.7](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec7)),^([8](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_8a))

*   structured concurrency ([Section 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec8))^([9](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_9a)) and

*   scoped values ([Section 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec8)).^([10](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_10a))

[8](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_8). “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/444`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444).

[9](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_9). “JEP 499: Structured Concurrency (Fourth Preview).” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/499`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/499).

[10](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_10). “JEP 487: Scoped Values (Fourth Preview).” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/487`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/487).

As we’ll discuss in [Section 18.6.1](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec11), **virtual threads do not replace platform threads—they have different use-cases.**

Virtual threads were finalized in Java 21\. Structured concurrency and scoped values were preview features at the time of this writing. If our code examples require changes when the final structured concurrency and scoped values versions are released, we’ll post updates on our blog at [`https://deitel.com/blog`](https://deitel.com/blog).

##### Virtual Threads Have Significantly Less Overhead than Platform Threads

**Virtual threads** are lightweight and managed by the JVM, not the operating system. Rather than pre-allocating a large method-call stack, the JVM allocates a few-hundred-byte **stack chunk** for each virtual thread. This stack chunk grows and shrinks dynamically based on the virtual thread’s required number of method-call stack frames—possibly as few as one if the task performs all its work in one method’s body.^([11](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_11a),[12](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_12a)) Due to the low virtual-thread memory requirements, an application can create thousands or even millions of virtual threads without overwhelming system resources. Creating millions of platform threads would quickly exhaust system resources, possibly causing the program to crash with an `OutOfMemoryError`.

[11](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_11). “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/444`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444).

[12](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_12). Goetz, Brian. “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022\. Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/`](https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/).

### 18.6 Creating and Executing Virtual Threads with the `Executor` Framework

Java provides several ways to execute tasks with virtual threads. [Section 18.6.1](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec11) modifies [Section 18.4](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec4)’s `PrintTask` example to demonstrate an `ExecutorService` that creates a separate virtual thread for each task. [Section 18.6.2](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec13) shows how to create `Thread` objects for virtual threads.

#### 18.6.1 Launching Virtual Threads with a Thread-Per-Task Executor

A primary virtual threads use-case is for server software that handles massive numbers of concurrent requests where each spends most of its time blocked from continuing to execute until I/O requests complete, such as

*   web servers that respond to user requests by returning web pages to their web browsers or

*   application servers that return the results of database queries to applications.

Platform threads are more appropriate for CPU-intensive tasks, such as sorting and long-running calculations. `Arrays` method `parallelSort` uses platform threads to execute the subtasks that sort portions of an array.

As an example of massive numbers of concurrent requests, consider the social media site [X.com](http://X.com). In December 2024, X had 4.6 billion visits, and each visitor viewed 12.35 pages on average.^([13](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_13a)) If we assume each page view requires one server request,^([14](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_14a)) there were approximately 56.81 billion requests (4.6 billion times 12.35) handled by [`X.com`](http://X.com)’s servers—about 21,200 requests per second. Lightweight virtual threads enable Java servers to handle huge numbers of concurrent requests like this with **thread-per-request code**—that is, creating a new virtual thread for each request.

[13](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_13). Similarweb, “[X.com](http://X.com) Traffic Analytics & Market Share.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://www.similarweb.com/website/x.com/#overview`](https://www.similarweb.com/website/x.com/#overview).

[14](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_14). A request for web-based content often requires many sub-requests for items like images, videos and advertisements that a web browser renders in a web page.

##### Launching Virtual Threads with an `ExecutorService`

[Figure 18.5](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig05) reuses [Fig. 18.3](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig03)’s `PrintTask` class and launches virtual threads. Line 18 of [Fig. 18.5](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig05) calls the **`Executors`** **class’s** **`static newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor`** **method** to get an `ExecutorService` that launches a new virtual thread for each task you submit. Lines 20–22 call the `ExecutorService`’s `execute` method to launch each `PrintTask`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0713-01)

```

 2   // Using virtual threads to execute Runnables.
 3   import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
 4
 5   public class VirtualThreadDemo {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // PrintTask constructor assigns random sleep time to each
 8         PrintTask task1 = new PrintTask("task1");
 9         PrintTask task2 = new PrintTask("task2");
10         PrintTask task3 = new PrintTask("task3");
11
12         System.out.println("Starting Virtual-Thread-Per-Task Executor\n");
13
14         // The ExecutorService returned by newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor
15         // runs each task in a virtual thread. The try-with-resources block
16         // calls ExecutorService's close method when the block terminates.
17         // The program then waits for the virtual threads to complete.
18         try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
19            // start the three PrintTasks
20            executor.execute(task1); // start task1
21            executor.execute(task2); // start task2
22            executor.execute(task3); // start task3
23         }
24
25         System.out.println("\nMain ends.");
26      }
27   }

##### Carriers, Mounting and Unmounting

A virtual thread’s **carrier** is the platform thread that runs the virtual thread. When the JVM schedules a virtual thread for execution, it **mounts** the virtual thread on a carrier. Then, the operating system is responsible for scheduling the carrier’s execution. The JVM **unmounts** a virtual thread from its carrier when it blocks for I/O, sleeps or completes its task. The runtime can then mount a different virtual thread on that carrier to efficiently use the system’s platform-thread resources.

##### Non-Daemon vs. Daemon Threads^([15](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_15a))

[15](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_15). “Class `Thread`.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html).

Platform threads may be **non-daemon** or **daemon threads**. A Java app runs while its non-daemon threads are still executing their tasks. Examples of non-daemon threads include:

*   the thread where the `main` method executes and

*   a JavaFX app’s event-handling thread.

A daemon thread typically performs background tasks that support a program’s execution. Examples of daemon threads include:

*   Java’s background garbage collector thread that reclaims unused objects from memory and

*   an “auto-save” background thread that watches for changes you make to a document and automatically saves them—a common feature in many apps that process files like documents, spreadsheets and more.

A Java app terminates if the only remaining threads are daemon threads.

##### Thread Defaults

By default, a platform thread is a non-daemon thread unless you

*   launch it from a daemon thread or

*   call `setDaemon(true)` on it to make it a daemon thread.

**Every virtual thread is always a daemon thread**.

##### Awaiting Virtual Thread Completion

**If you want your program to remain running until its virtual threads’ tasks complete, you must prevent** **`main`** **from terminating.** The `try`-with-resources statement and `ExecutorService` manage this for you. When the `try`-with-resources statement terminates, it automatically calls the `ExecutorService`’s `close` method, which, in turn, calls

*   the `ExecutorService`’s `shutdown` method to prevent the `ExecutorService` from accepting new tasks and

*   the `ExecutorService`’s `awaitTermination` method to wait for the `ExecutorSer-vice`’s previously launched tasks to complete execution.
