#### 18.6.2 Other Ways to Launch Virtual Threads

##### `Thread` Method `startVirtualThread`

Platform threads and virtual threads are each instances of the `java.lang` package’s `Thread` class, but a virtual thread is managed entirely by the JVM. If you need

*   more control over a virtual thread via class `Thread`’s methods or

*   a convenient way to launch a virtual thread without using an `ExecutorService`,

you can use **class** **`Thread`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`startVirtualThread`**. This method receives a `Runnable`, launches a virtual thread to execute it and returns a reference to the virtual thread’s `Thread` object. For example, the following statement creates a virtual thread for the `PrintTask` object `task1`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0716-01)

```
var virtualThread = Thread.startVirtualThread(task1);
```

In this case, if your program needs the task’s result, you must somehow wait for it to complete—typically by calling the `Thread`’s `join` method before `main` terminates, as in:

```
virtualThread.join();
```

Otherwise, `main` might terminate before the virtual thread executes its task.

##### Thread Method `ofVirtual`

When you need to specify virtual threads’ configuration options, you can use **class** **`Thread`****’s** **`static`** **method** **`ofVirtual`**, which returns a **`Thread.Builder.OfVirtual`** **object**.^([16](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_16a),[17](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_17a)) This object uses the **builder design pattern**—a common technique for constructing complex objects step-by-step via chained method calls.^([18](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_18a),[19](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_19a)) The builder design pattern is handy for flexible object configuration—you call only the builder’s methods that add the options you need. Without this pattern, a Java class might require many overloaded constructors for each possible combination of options.

[16](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_16). “Interface `Thread.Builder.OfVirtual`.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.Builder.OfVirtual.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.Builder.OfVirtual.html).

[17](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_17). `Thread`’s `static` method `ofPlatform` returns a `Thread.Builder.OfPlatform` object for similar creation and configuration of platform threads.

[18](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_18). Bloch, Joshua. *Effective Java*. 3rd ed. Upper Saddle River, NJ: Addison-Wesley, 2018.

[19](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_19). Kiwy, Frank. “Exploring Joshua Bloch’s Builder design pattern in Java.” May 28, 2021\. Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://blogs.oracle.com/javamagazine/post/exploring-joshua-blochs-builder-design-pattern-in-java`](https://blogs.oracle.com/javamagazine/post/exploring-joshua-blochs-builder-design-pattern-in-java).

A `Thread.Builder.OfVirtual` object enables you to specify several virtual thread options, including:

*   the virtual thread’s name,

*   a virtual thread’s name concatenated with a specified counter value—useful when launching multiple virtual threads to give each a unique name and

*   a method to call when an uncaught exception occurs in a virtual thread.

In the builder design pattern, you call a `static` method to get a builder object. Each subsequent method you call on the builder object adds a configuration option and returns a reference to the builder object so you can add more options. In the case of `Thread.Builder.OfVirtual` object, the last call in the chain is one of the following:

*   **`start`** creates a virtual thread to execute its `Runnable` argument, schedules the thread for execution and returns a reference to the corresponding `Thread` object.

*   **`factory`** returns a reference to a `ThreadFactory` that can create virtual threads with the settings specified in the previous calls to the builder object’s methods.

*   **`unstarted`** creates a virtual thread to execute its `Runnable` argument and returns a reference to the `Thread` object but does not start it. In this case, you must subsequently call the `Thread`’s `start` method to execute the virtual thread.

For example, assuming the variable `id` contains `1` and `task` is a `Runnable` object, the following chained method call would create a new virtual thread named `"Task1"`, schedule the `Runnable` for execution and return a reference to the corresponding `Thread` object:

```
Thread thread =
   Thread.ofVirtual()
         .name("Task", id)
         .start(task);
```

Again, you must call `thread.join()` if you want to ensure the thread executes before the program terminates.

### 18.7 Profiling Platform vs. Virtual Threads^([20](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_20a))

[20](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_20). This section’s example was inspired by Brian Goetz’s intro to virtual threads in the article “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022\. Accessed January 31, 2025\. [`https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/`](https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/).

In real-world applications—such as social media web servers handling millions to billions of requests per month—efficiently performing large numbers of concurrent tasks is crucial. As we mentioned, platform threads have large memory overhead and map one-to-one to operating system threads, making applications that use them more complicated to scale for massive numbers of concurrent tasks. Virtual threads address this limitation by enabling millions of lightweight threads to run concurrently with minimal overhead. To demonstrate this, we’ll build an example that executes large numbers of tasks using platform and virtual threads.

#### 18.7.1 `Future` and `Callable` Interfaces

Each task in the next example returns a result. Interface `Runnable`’s `run` method returns `void`, so it cannot return a value. **Interface** **`Callable`** (package `java.util.concurrent`) fixes this limitation—its **`call`** **method** returns a value representing a task’s result. `Callable`s typically run concurrently with other `Runnable`s and `Callable`s. **`ExecutorService`** **method** **`submit`** executes its `Callable` argument and returns an object that implements the **`Future`** **interface** (package `java.util.concurrent`)—this represents the `Callable`’s result, which will be available at some point in the future. The **`Future`** **interface’s** **`get`** **method** returns the task’s result, possibly blocking the calling thread to wait until that result is available. The interface also provides methods that enable you to

*   cancel a `Callable`’s execution,

*   determine whether the `Callable` was canceled and

*   determine whether the `Callable` completed its task.

#### 18.7.2 Threading Approaches We’ll Use

[Figure 18.6](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig06) demonstrates virtual threads vs. platform threads handling large numbers of concurrent tasks that simulate blocking operations. The example submits tasks to three `ExecutorService` objects that manage the tasks with the following threading approaches:

*   a fixed thread pool of 1000 pre-allocated platform threads that are shared among all the submitted tasks,

*   a cached thread pool of platform threads that dynamically adjusts its number of threads based on demand and

*   a separate virtual thread per task—because virtual threads use minimal resources and are easy to create in large numbers, you should not pool them.^([21](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_21a))

[21](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_21). “JEP 444: Virtual Threads.” Accessed February 9, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/444`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444).

We split the example into pieces for discussion purposes. Lines 3–9 import the classes and interfaces used in this example.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0718-01)

```

 2   // Timing large numbers of platform vs. virtual threads.
 3   import java.time.Duration;
 4   import java.time.InstantSource;
 5   import java.util.ArrayList;
 6   import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
 7   import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
 8   import java.util.concurrent.Future;
 9   import java.util.stream.LongStream;
10
11   public class PlatformAndVirtualThreads {
```

**Fig. 18.6** | Timing large numbers of platform vs. virtual threads.

#### 18.7.3 Launching and Timing Large Numbers of Concurrent Tasks

Method `executeAndTimeThreads` (lines 13–48) manages the process of launching and timing the execution of large numbers of concurrent tasks. For demo purposes, each task in this example sleeps for one second to simulate blocking, then calculates and returns the square of a `long` value. We sum these squared values and display them in the sample outputs. Method `executeAndTimeThreads` requires three arguments:

*   `tasks`—the number of concurrent tasks the method should execute,

*   `threadType`—a `String` description of the threading approach used and

*   `executor`—an `ExecutorService` implementation that creates the threads.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0718-02)

```
12      // execute and time threads; sum squares of 1 to number of tasks
13      private static void executeAndTimeThreads(int tasks,
14         String threadType, ExecutorService executor) throws Exception {
15         var clock = InstantSource.system(); // system clock for timing
16
17         // stores Futures for all the launched tasks
18         var futures = new ArrayList<Future<Long>>(tasks);
19
20         System.out.printf(
21            "Executing %d tasks on %s...%n", tasks, threadType);
22         var start = clock.instant();
23
24         // auto-closes the ExecutorService at the end of the try block;
25         // automatically waits for all tasks to complete
26         try (executor) {
27            // launch the number of tasks specified by tasks parameter
28            LongStream.rangeClosed(1, tasks).forEach(value ->
29               futures.add(executor.submit(() -> {
30                  Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // simulate blocking
31                  return value * value;
32               }))
33            );
34         }
35
36         // sum the results from the Futures
37         long sum = 0;
38         for (var future : futures) {
39            sum += future.get();
40         }
41
42         var end = clock.instant();
43
44         // display results
45         System.out.printf("Execution time: %.2f seconds%n",
46            Duration.between(start, end).toMillis() / 1000.0);
47         System.out.printf("Sum of squares 1-%d: %d%n%n", tasks, sum);
48      }
49
```

The method operates as follows:

*   Line 15 gets the system clock for the timing operations.

*   Line 18 creates an `ArrayList` to store `Future` objects for accessing each task’s results.

*   Lines 20–21 display the number of tasks being performed and the threading approach used in this call to `executeAndTimeThreads`.

*   Line 22 records the system time before launching any tasks.

*   Lines 26–34 are the `try`-with-resources statement in which we submit the tasks. We use a `LongStream` to count from `1` to `tasks`. For each `value`, we use the `executor` to `submit` a task—in this case, a lambda expression that implements the `Callable` interface, telling the thread to sleep for one second (to simulate a blocking), then returns the squared `value`. We store the `Future<Long>` returned by each call to `submit` in an `ArrayList`—we’ll use this to get all the tasks’ results later. When the stream finishes launching the tasks, control reaches the `try`-with-resources statement’s closing brace, automatically closing the `executor` and waiting for the launched tasks to complete execution.

*   When all the tasks complete, lines 37–40 total all the tasks’ results to determine the sum of the squares of the values from `1` through `tasks`.

*   Line 42 records the system time after the tasks and final calculation complete execution.

*   Lines 45–47 calculate and display the total execution time and final `sum`.

#### 18.7.4 Testing the Threading Approaches

In the `main` method (lines 50–73):

*   Lines 52–55 ensure the program was launched with one command-line argument. This value represents the number of threads to create, so we convert it to an `int` (line 58).

*   Lines 61–63 invoke `executeAndTimeThreads`, passing the number of tasks to launch, a description of the kind of threading that will be used to execute tasks and an `ExecutorService` to launch the tasks. In this case, we use an `ExecutorService` that manages a fixed-size pool of 1000 platform threads. This thread pool can execute only 1000 tasks concurrently. Additional tasks must wait for executing tasks to complete before they can be assigned to threads in the pool.

*   Lines 66–68 invoke `executeAndTimeThreads` with an `ExecutorService` that manages a cached thread pool, which dynamically adjusts its number of threads based on demand.

*   Lines 71–72 invoke `executeAndTimeThreads` with an `ExecutorService` that creates a virtual thread per task.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0720-01)

```
50      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
51         // check for proper command-line arguments
52         if (args.length != 1) {
53            System.out.println("Usage: PlatformAndVirtualThreads <count>");
54            System.exit(1);
55         }
56
57         // get number of threads to launch
58         final int TASKS = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);
59
60         // execute and time platform threads with fixed thread pool
61         executeAndTimeThreads(TASKS,
62            "Platform Threads (fixed pool of 1000 threads)",
63            Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1000));
64
65         // execute and time platform threads with cached thread pool
66         executeAndTimeThreads(TASKS,
67            "Platform Threads (cached thread pool)",
68            Executors.newCachedThreadPool());
69
70         // execute and time virtual threads
71         executeAndTimeThreads(TASKS,
72            "Virtual Threads", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
73      }
74   }
```

#### 18.7.5 Performance Analysis

The following sample executions for 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 50,000 tasks were performed on a MacBook Pro with an M2 MAX processor with 96GB of RAM. Depending on your system configuration, you may not be able to execute as many tasks (possibly running out of memory for large numbers of tasks), or you may be able to execute even more than we demonstrate here. You can run the example with the following command

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0721-01)

```
java PlatformAndVirtualThreads numberOfTasks
```

where *numberOfTasks* should be an integer representing the number of tasks to launch. The sample executions reveal interesting performance comparisons.

##### 1,000 Tasks

There’s little difference in execution times for the three threading approaches for 1,000 tasks—virtual threads had a slight advantage. In this case, the throughput using a fixed pool of platform threads is about 962 tasks-per-second (1000 / 1.04), using a cached pool of platform threads is about 971 (1000 / 1.03) and using virtual threads is about 980 tasks-per-second (1000 / 1.02):

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0721-02)

```
Executing 1000 tasks on Platform Threads (fixed pool of 1000 threads)...
Execution time: 1.04 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500

Executing 1000 tasks on Platform Threads (cached thread pool)...
Execution time: 1.03 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500

Executing 1000 tasks on Virtual Threads...
Execution time: 1.02 seconds
Sum of squares 1-1000: 333833500
```

##### 5,000 Tasks

In the sample execution for 5,000 tasks, the fixed-thread pool’s throughput (986 tasks-per-second) is similar to that of 1,000—the number of tasks-per-second this pool can handle is limited by the fixed number of threads in the pool. There are not enough platform threads to handle all the tasks, so many tasks must wait until threads become available. The cached pool throughput increased to 3,759 tasks-per-second and the virtual threads throughput increased to 4,762 tasks-per-second. The cached pool of platform threads and the virtual threads scale better than the fixed pool of platform threads, with virtual threads again performing best.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0721-03)

```
Executing 5000 tasks on Platform Threads (fixed pool of 1000 threads)...
Execution time: 5.07 seconds
Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500

Executing 5000 tasks on Platform Threads (cached thread pool)...
Execution time: 1.33 seconds
Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500

Executing 5000 tasks on Virtual Threads...
Execution time: 1.05 seconds
Sum of squares 1-5000: 41679167500
```

##### 10,000 Tasks

The Oracle virtual threads documentation indicates that “if your application never has 10,000 virtual threads or more, it is unlikely to benefit from virtual threads.”^([22](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_22a)) In the sample execution for 10,000 tasks, the benefits of virtual threads for large numbers of blocking tasks become more apparent. The fixed pool’s throughput is 992 tasks-per-second—similar in scale to the throughput for 1,000 tasks and 5,000 tasks. The cached pool throughput increased to 7,518 tasks-per-second and the virtual threads throughput to 9,523 tasks-per-second. Again, the cached pool of platform threads and the virtual threads scale better, but the spread between the tasks-per-second of virtual threads and the cached pool of platform threads increased.

##### 50,000 Tasks

In the sample execution for 50,000 tasks, the benefits of virtual threads for large numbers of blocking tasks become crystal clear. The fixed pool’s throughput (994 tasks-per-second) is similar to prior sample executions. The cached pool’s throughput actually decreased in this execution to 5,507 tasks-per-second, but **the virtual threads’ throughput increased to 34,468 tasks-per-second**.

The sample outputs indicate that virtual threads consistently outperform platform threads for highly concurrent tasks that spend most of their time blocked, especially as the number of threads increases. This enables applications with large numbers of blocking tasks to scale without the limitations of traditional platform threads.

### 18.8 Structured Concurrency and Scoped Values

This section introduces Project Loom’s two other key features—structured concurrency and scoped values:

*   **Structured concurrency** simplifies task management by enabling developers to treat groups of virtual threads performing related tasks as a single unit and program with them in a simple statement-by-statement sequential programming style. This makes the code more readable and easier to maintain, modify and debug. It also avoids more complex asynchronous programming techniques, such as reactive programming.^([23](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_23a)) Structured concurrency also simplifies resource management and error handling because those sequential statements can be placed in familiar `try` and `try`-with-resources statements.

*   **Scoped values** enable a task and its subtasks to share immutable data in a structured concurrency scope. They fix problems associated with `ThreadLocal` variables, introduced in Java almost three decades ago.^([24](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_24a)) Scoped values become implicit arguments to every method called from that structured concurrency scope.

[23](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_23). The details of reactive programming are beyond this book’s scope. For some details on how virtual threads are better than reactive techniques, read: Goetz, Brian. “Virtual Threads: New Foundations for High-Scale Java Applications.” InfoQ, November 2, 2022\. Accessed February 9, 2025. [`https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/`](https://www.infoq.com/articles/java-virtual-threads/).

[24](#ch18.xhtml_fn18_24). The details of `ThreadLocal` variables are beyond this book’s scope. For more information on how scoped values are better than `ThreadLocal` variables, visit [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/487`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/487) and see Generative AI Exercise 18.2.

##### Example Overview

To demonstrate structured concurrency and scoped values, let’s modify [Section 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev1sec6)’s OpenWeatherMap web-services example that returns the current weather for a specified city. Recall that virtual threads are primarily used for large numbers of concurrent tasks that spend most of their time blocking—a web-service request blocks until its results are available or the request fails. Let’s assume we’d like to build an application in which each user can submit a request that specifies a city for which the user would like the current weather and the forecast for the next few days—these are separate OpenWeatherMap web-service requests. As in [Section 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev1sec6), we’ll use the Jackson library to parse the JSON responses for convenient access to the weather data.

For demo purposes, we’ll build this as a command-line app that simulates “requests” (the individual cities) as command-line arguments. We’ll use **thread-per-request handling**, launching a virtual thread for each request. That thread, in turn, will launch two subtasks in separate virtual threads so they may proceed concurrently:

*   one to invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service that returns the city’s current weather and

*   one to invoke the OpenWeatherMap web service that returns the city’s five-day forecast in three-hour increments.

If a subtask fails, we’ll consider that an error for which we’d like the overall request and its subtasks to terminate immediately—structured concurrency can do this automatically. In addition, the request and its subtasks require a shared piece of data—the city for which to get the weather. This information does not change for a particular request’s duration, so we’ll use a scoped value to share that immutable data between the virtual thread handling the request and its subtask virtual threads.

##### `main` Method

The `main` method (lines 53–83) simulates a server that implements thread-per-request handling. The `try`-with-resources statement gets an `ExecutorService` for launching virtual threads (line 61). After launching a virtual thread for each request (i.e., city), this statement closes the `ExecutorService` and waits for all the launched virtual threads to complete. The loop in lines 62–81 uses the `executor` to launch a virtual thread for each city. The lambda expression in lines 66–79 defines a `Runnable` task:

*   Line 66 first calls the **`ScopedValue`****’s** **`where`** **method** to set the `ScopedValue`’s value to the current request’s city for which to get the weather. This returns an object of **class** **`ScopedValue.Carrier`** containing the unique scoped value for the task we’re about to launch.

*   Next, line 66 calls the **`ScopedValue.Carrier`** **object’s** **`run`** **method** to execute the `Runnable` task defined by the lambda expression in lines 68–78\. The `run` method provides the scoped value to that task. We’ll use structured concurrency in the `getWeather` method (called at line 71) to manage the task and its subtasks.

*   Lines 70–71 display the `String` returned by `getWeather`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0727-01)

```
53      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
54         // check for proper command-line arguments
55         if (args.length == 0) {
56            System.out.println("Usage: WeatherApp <city1> <city2> ...");
57            System.exit(1);
58         }
59
60         // simulate a server doing thread-per-request handling
61         try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
62            for (String city : args) {
63               executor.submit(
64                  // set the ScopedValue's value then run a task; the task
65                  // and its subtasks will have access to the ScopedValue
66                  () -> ScopedValue.where(CITY, city).run(
67                     // task: get and print the weather info for the city
68                     () -> {
69                        try {
70                           System.out.printf("%n%nWeather for %s:\n%s\n",
71                              city, getWeather());
72                        }
73                        catch (Exception ex) {
74                           System.err.printf(
75                              "Error fetching weather for %s: %s\n",
76                              city, ex.getMessage());
77                        }
78                     } // end nested lambda expression
79                  ) // end call to ScopedValue's run method
80               ); // end call to the executor object's submit method
81            } // end for loop
82         } // end try-with-resources statement
83      }
84
```

##### `getWeather` Method

The `getWeather` method (lines 86–116) uses the `CITY` **`ScopedValue`****’s** **`get`** **method** (line 89) to get the city to use in the task and subtasks launched from `getWeather`. The `get` method automatically accesses the scoped value in the `ScopedValue.Carrier` object associated with the current task. Lines 92–97 form the URLs for the two `OpenWeatherMap` web-service requests we’ll perform. Next, the `try`-with-resources statement (lines 100–115) creates a new **`StructuredTaskScope`** (line 100). For this example, we consider the task in method `getWeather` successful only if both web-service requests complete successfully. The expression in line 100

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0727-02)

```
new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()
```

creates a `StructuredTaskScope` that shuts down on failure. If a subtask launched in this scope fails, the other subtasks will be interrupted so they can shut down. Lines 101–104 call **`StructuredTaskScope`****’s** **`fork`** **method** to launch virtual threads that execute `Callable` tasks—implemented by the lambdas in lines 102 and 104\. Each lambda calls our generic `requestData` method (discussed momentarily), passing the URL for the web-service request and the `Class` object (`WeatherData.class` or `ForecastResponse.class`) the Jackson library will use when extracting the data items we need from the JSON responses.

Method `requestData` returns an object of the appropriate `record` class (`WeatherData` or `ForecastResponse`) for each request. Each `fork` call returns an object that implements the **`StructuredTaskScope.Subtask`** **interface**, which we’ll use to access the subtasks’ results when they become available.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0728-01)

```
85      // use structured concurrency to request current weather and forecast
86      public static String getWeather() throws Exception {
87         // URL encode the city parameter
88         String encodedCity =
89            URLEncoder.encode(CITY.get(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
90
91         // construct API URLs
92         String currentWeatherUrl = String.format(
93            "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/weather?q=%s" +
94            "&units=metric&appid=%s", encodedCity, API_KEY);
95         String forecastUrl = String.format(
96            "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/forecast?q=%s" +
97            "&units=metric&appid=%s", encodedCity, API_KEY);
98
99         // use StructuredTaskScope to manage concurrent tasks
100        try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
101           var currentWeatherTask = scope.fork(
102              () -> requestData(currentWeatherUrl, WeatherData.class));
103           var forecastTask = scope.fork(
104              () -> requestData(forecastUrl, ForecastResponse.class));
105
106           scope.join(); // waits for responses
107           scope.throwIfFailed(); // throws an exception if a task fails
108
109           // tasks completed successfully, retrieve results
110           WeatherData weatherData = currentWeatherTask.get();
111           ForecastResponse forecastResponse = forecastTask.get();
112
113           // format and return output
114           return formatWeatherOutput(weatherData, forecastResponse);
115        }
116     }
117
```

Line 106 calls **`StructuredTaskScope`****’s** **`join`** **method** to wait for the two web-service requests to complete. If either fails, line 107 calls **`StructuredTaskScope`****’s** **`throwIfFailed`** **method** to ensure the task’s exception can be handled. In this example, we handle it in `main` rather than in a `catch` handler following the `try`-with-resources statement. If both tasks complete successfully, lines 110–111 get the `WeatherData` or `ForecastResponse` objects by calling **`StructuredTaskScope.Subtask`** **method** **`get`**. Finally, line 114 calls method `formatWeatherOutput` to produce the weather report and returns the resulting `String` to `main` for display at lines 70–71.

##### `requestData` Method

The `requestData` method (lines 119–138) uses the techniques presented in [Section 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev1sec6) to

*   build an `HttpRequest` (lines 121–122),

*   submit the request via an `HttpClient` and wait for the response (lines 125–126),

*   check whether the response was successful (lines 123–133), and

*   deserialize the JSON data into a `record` object (line 137).

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0729-01)

```
118     // generic method to retrieve JSON data from OpenWeatherMap API
119     private static <T> T requestData(String url, Class<T> type)
120        throws Exception {
121        // build the request to the OpenWeatherMap web service
122        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
123           .uri(URI.create(url)).GET().build();
124
125        // send the HTTP request and get the response
126        HttpResponse<String> response = HTTP_CLIENT.send(request,
127           HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
128
129        // check if the request was successful; otherwise, throw Exception
130        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
131           throw new Exception(String.format(
132              "Error: HTTP status %d\n", response.statusCode()));
133        }
134
135        // use Jackson library to deserialize the JSON response
136        // into the format specified by type
137        return new ObjectMapper().readValue(response.body(), type);
138     }
139
```

##### `formatWeatherOutput` Method

The `formatWeatherOutput` method (lines 141–174) receives the record objects containing the data from the two web-service requests then creates a formatted weather report:

*   Lines 145–146 get the current temperature and convert it from Celsius to Fahrenheit.

*   Lines 149–152 create a `DateTimeFormatter` configured to display the date and time in the format `yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm`.

*   Lines 155–164 use stream processing to convert the first 16 items in the `Fore-castResponse`’s `List<ForecastEntry>` into formatted text containing the date, time, weather description and temperature in both Celsius and Fahrenheit.

*   Lines 166–173 return the result of calling `String` method `formatted` on a format `String` implemented as a text block, inserting the city’s name, the current day’s weather description, the current Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures and the `forecastInfo` from lines 155–164.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0729-02)

```
140     // formats weather output for display
141     private static String formatWeatherOutput(
142        WeatherData weatherData, ForecastResponse forecastResponse) {
143
144        // current temperature
145        double tempC = weatherData.main().temp();
146        double tempF = (tempC * 9 / 5) + 32;
147
148        // date formatter
149        DateTimeFormatter dateFormatter =
150           DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm")
151              .withZone(ZoneId.ofOffset("UTC",
152                 ZoneOffset.ofTotalSeconds(weatherData.timezone())));
153
154        // 7-day forecast of weather descriptions with min/max temperatures
155        String forecastInfo = forecastResponse.list().stream().limit(16)
156           .map(f -> {
157              double tempCForecast = f.main().temp();
158              double tempFForecast = (tempCForecast * 9 / 5) + 32;
159              return String.format(
160                 "%s: %s; temp: %.1f C (%.1f F)",
161                 dateFormatter.format(Instant.ofEpochSecond(f.dt())),
162                 f.weather()[0].main(), tempCForecast, tempFForecast);
163           })
164           .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));
165
166        return """
167           %s Weather: %s
168           Temperature: %.1f C (%.1f F)
169
170           Forecast:
171           %s""".formatted(weatherData.name(),
172              weatherData.weather()[0].description(),
173              tempC, tempF, forecastInfo);
174     }
175  }
```

### 18.9 Thread Synchronization Overview

When multiple threads share an object, and it’s modified by one or more of them, indeterminate results may occur unless access to the shared object is managed correctly:

*   If one thread is updating a shared object and another thread tries to update it at the same time, it’s uncertain which thread’s update takes effect.

*   Similarly, if one thread is updating a shared object and another thread tries to read it at the same time, it’s uncertain whether the reading thread will read the old value that’s no longer valid (known as a **stale value**) or the new one.

In such cases, the program’s behavior cannot be trusted. Sometimes the program will produce the correct results, and sometimes it won’t, and there won’t be any indication that the shared object was manipulated incorrectly.

**The problem can be solved by giving only one thread at a time exclusive access to code that manipulates the shared object.** During that time, other threads desiring to access the object are kept waiting. When the thread with exclusive access finishes manipulating the object, one of the waiting threads can proceed. This process, called **thread synchronization**, coordinates access to shared data by multiple concurrent threads. By synchronizing threads in this manner, you can ensure that each thread accessing a shared object excludes all other threads from doing so simultaneously—this is called **mutual exclusion**.

Java provides extensive mechanisms designed to ensure mutually exclusive access to shared mutable data, from low-level capabilities that enable developers to manage mutual exclusion to high-level ones in which the Java APIs handle mutual exclusion for you. **One of the challenges of multithreaded programming is spotting the errors—they may occur so infrequently and unpredictably that a broken program does not produce incorrect results during testing, creating the illusion that the program is correct.** For this reason, most developers should work with the predefined concurrent collections that handle thread synchronization for you. These collections are designed by Java concurrency experts to work correctly and perform optimally in applications that share mutable data.

##### Immutable Data

Thread synchronization is necessary only for **shared mutable data**—that is, data that may change during its lifetime. With **shared immutable data** that will not change, it’s impossible for a thread to read old or incorrect values due to another thread’s manipulation of that data.

When you share immutable data across threads, declare the corresponding data fields `final` to indicate that the variable’s values will not change after they’re initialized. This prevents accidental modification of the shared data, which could compromise thread safety. **Labeling object references as** **`final`** **indicates that the reference will not change, but it does not guarantee that the referenced object is immutable—this depends entirely on the object’s properties.** But, it’s still good practice to mark references that will not change as `final`.

As a good practice, declare data fields you do not expect to change as `final`. Primitive variables that are declared as `final` can safely be shared across threads. An object reference declared as `final` ensures that the object it refers to will be fully constructed and initialized before it’s used by the program, preventing the reference from pointing to another object.

### 18.10 Producer/Consumer Relationship with `ArrayBlockingQueue`

A common scenario in which multiple threads access shared mutable data is in a **producer/consumer relationship**:

*   The **producer** portion of a program generates data and stores it in a shared object, and

*   the **consumer** portion of the program reads data from the shared object and processes it.

##### Examples of Producer/Consumer Relationship

One example of a producer/consumer relationship is **print spooling**. Although a printer might not be available when you want to print from an application (i.e., the producer), you can still “complete” the print task, as the data is temporarily placed on disk until the printer becomes available. Similarly, when the printer (i.e., a consumer) is available, it doesn’t have to wait until a current user wants to print. The spooled print jobs can print when the printer becomes available. Another example of the producer/consumer relationship is an application that backs up data to a storage device—such as a solid-state drive (SSD)—by placing data in a fixed-size buffer, which is emptied as the storage device writes the data.

#### Generative AI

**1** Prompt genAIs for real-world Java examples of producer/consumer relationships.

#### 18.10.1 Synchronization and State Dependence

In a multithreaded producer/consumer relationship, a **producer thread** generates data and places it in a shared object called a buffer or a queue. A **consumer thread** reads data from the buffer. This relationship requires synchronization to ensure that values are produced and consumed properly to prevent data corruption:

*   Data can be lost or garbled if the producer places new data into the shared buffer before the consumer reads the previous data.

*   Also, data can be incorrectly duplicated if the consumer consumes data again before the producer produces the next value.

Operations on the buffer data shared by a producer and consumer thread are also **state-dependent**. As an example of state dependence, consider an electric vehicle. You can’t drive an electric vehicle if its battery is not charged, and you can’t charge an electric vehicle’s battery more, if it’s already fully charged. Similarly, a producer and consumer should proceed only if the buffer is in the correct state:

*   If the buffer is in a not-full state, the producer may produce.

*   If the buffer is in a not-empty state, the consumer may consume.

All operations that access the buffer must use synchronization to ensure that data is written to the buffer or read from the buffer only if the buffer is in the proper state:

*   If the producer attempts to write a new value into a full buffer, the producer thread must wait until there’s space to write the value.

*   If a consumer thread attempts to read a value from an empty buffer, the consumer must wait for new data to become available.

#### 18.10.2 Class `ArrayBlockingQueue`

A reliable way to synchronize producers and consumers is to use classes that implement the synchronization for you. The `java.util.concurrent` package’s **`ArrayBlockingQueue`** **class** defines a fully implemented, thread-safe buffer class that implements the **interface** **`BlockingQueue`**. Among its methods, this interface declares:

*   **method** **`put`** to place an element at the tail of a `BlockingQueue`, waiting if the queue is full, and

*   **method** **`take`** to remove an element from the head of the `BlockingQueue`, waiting if the queue is empty.

These methods make class `ArrayBlockingQueue` a good choice for implementing a shared buffer. Because method `put` blocks until there’s room in the buffer to write data, and method `take` blocks until there’s new data to read:

*   the producer must produce a value first,

*   the consumer correctly consumes only after the producer writes a value, and

*   the producer correctly produces the next value (after the first) only after the consumer reads the previous (or first) value.

`ArrayBlockingQueue` stores the shared mutable data in an array, the size of which is specified as `ArrayBlockingQueue`’s constructor argument. An `ArrayBlockingQueue` is fixed in size and will not expand to accommodate extra elements.

#### 18.10.3 Overview of the Producer/Consumer Example

Our next example ([Figs. 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig08)–[18.10](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig10)) implements a producer/consumer relationship with proper synchronization provided by a one-element `ArrayBlockingQueue`. The producer thread writes the numbers 1 through 10 into the shared `ArrayBlockingQueue`. The consumer thread reads this data from the shared `ArrayBlockingQueue`. Each value the producer thread writes must be consumed by the consumer thread exactly once. To help confirm this,

*   the producer thread will output each value it writes (produces) and add the values to a running total, and

*   the consumer thread will output each value it reads (consumes) and add the values to a running total.

If the producer writes each value from 1–10 exactly once and the consumer reads each value from 1–10 exactly once, each thread’s total of the values should be 55.

To further emphasize that the `ArrayBlockingQueue` provides the synchronization, the producer and consumer threads each sleep for random intervals of up to 3,000 milliseconds between attempting to write or read a value, respectively. As a result, we do not know when the producer thread will attempt to write a new value into the shared buffer or when the consumer thread will attempt to read what’s in the shared buffer. The program consists of the following interface and classes:

*   interface `Buffer` ([Fig. 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig08)),

*   class `BlockingBuffer` ([Fig. 18.9](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig09)) and

*   class `BlockingBufferTest` ([Fig. 18.10](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig10)).

#### 18.10.4 Interface `Buffer`

Interface `Buffer` ([Fig. 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig08)) declares methods `blockingPut` (line 5) and `blockingGet` (line 8) that our `BlockingBuffer` class implements for a producer thread to place a value in the buffer and a consumer thread to retrieve a value from it, respectively. Methods `blocking-Put` and `blockingGet` will call `ArrayBlockingQueue` methods that throw `InterruptedException`s. They will also output text for pedagogic purposes, which is why this example declares interface `Buffer` rather than calling `ArrayBlockingQueue` methods directly. Interface `Buffer`’s methods list `InterruptedException` in their `throws` clauses so the exceptions can be returned to the producer or consumer threads calling `Buffer`’s methods.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0735-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.8: Buffer.java
 2   // Buffer interface specifies methods called by Producer and Consumer.
 3   public interface Buffer {
 4      // place int value into Buffer
 5      public void blockingPut(int value) throws InterruptedException;
 6
 7      // return int value from Buffer
 8      public int blockingGet() throws InterruptedException;
 9   }
```

**Fig. 18.8** | Buffer interface specifies methods called by `Producer` and `Consumer`.

#### 18.10.5 Class `BlockingBuffer`

Class `BlockingBuffer` ([Fig. 18.9](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig09)) implements the `Buffer` interface and uses an object of class `ArrayBlockingQueue` to store one `Integer` (lines 7–8) and manage mutually exclusive access to it—we’ll say more about an `ArrayBlockingQueue`’s size at the end of this section. Because our `BlockingBuffer` class uses the thread-safe `ArrayBlockingQueue` class to manage all of its shared state (the shared buffer), `BlockingBuffer` is itself thread-safe, even though we have not implemented the synchronization ourselves.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0735-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.9: BlockingBuffer.java
 2   // Creating a synchronized buffer using an ArrayBlockingQueue.
 3   import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue;
 4
 5   public class BlockingBuffer implements Buffer {
 6      // BlockingBuffer uses an ArrayBlockingQueue to manage synchronization
 7      private final ArrayBlockingQueue<Integer> buffer =
 8         new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1);
 9
10      // place value into buffer
11      @Override
12      public void blockingPut(int value) throws InterruptedException {
13         buffer.put(value); // place value in buffer
14         System.out.printf("%s%2d\t%s%d%n", "Producer writes ", value,
15            "Buffer cells occupied: ", buffer.size());
16      }
17
18      // return value from buffer
19      @Override
20      public int blockingGet() throws InterruptedException {
21         int readValue = buffer.take(); // remove value from buffer
22         System.out.printf("%s %2d\t%s%d%n", "Consumer reads ",
23            readValue, "Buffer cells occupied: ", buffer.size());
24
25         return readValue;
26      }
27   }
```

**Fig. 18.9** | Creating a synchronized buffer using an `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

Line 13 in method `blockingPut` calls the `ArrayBlockingQueue` object’s `put` method. If the `ArrayBlockingQueue` is full, the producer thread waits at line 13 until there’s room in the `ArrayBlockingQueue` to write the `value`. Line 21 in method `blockingGet` calls the `ArrayBlockingQueue` object’s `take` method. If the `ArrayBlockingQueue` is empty, the consumer thread waits at line 21 until there’s an element in the `ArrayBlockingQueue` to read. Lines 14–15 and 22–23 use the **`ArrayBlockingQueue size`** **method** to display the `ArrayBlockingQueue`’s current number of elements. In this example, when the size is `1`, the buffer is full, and when it’s `0`, the buffer is empty.

The `ArrayBlockingQueue` approach used in this example demonstrates encapsulated synchronization—**the producer and consumer threads that call** **`blockingPut`** **and** **`blockingGet`** **to access the shared** **`ArrayBlockingQueue`** **(i.e., the buffer) are unaware that their writes and reads are synchronized.** This is handled entirely by the `ArrayBlockingQueue` methods `put` and `take`.

#### 18.10.6 Class `BlockingBufferTest`

Class `BlockingBufferTest`’s `main` method ([Fig. 18.10](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig10)) launches two virtual threads to execute a producer task that writes values into a shared `BlockingBuffer` and a consumer task that reads values from the same `BlockingBuffer`. We split class `BlockingBufferTest` into parts for discussion purposes. The tasks in this example are not CPU-intensive and block if they cannot perform their tasks, so line 10 creates an `ExecutorService` for virtual threads. Line 12 creates the shared `BlockingBuffer` object that both the producer and consumer tasks will access.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0737-01)

```

 2   // Two threads manipulating a blocking buffer that properly
 3   // implements the producer/consumer relationship.
 4   import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
 5   import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
 6
 7   public class BlockingBufferTest {
 8      public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
 9         // virtual-thread-per-task executor
10         try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
11            // create BlockingBuffer to store ints
12            final Buffer buffer = new BlockingBuffer();
13
```

**Fig. 18.10** | Two threads manipulating a blocking buffer that properly implements the producer/consumer relationship.

##### Producer Task

Lines 15–31 define the producer’s `Runnable` task as a lambda expression and launch its execution in a virtual thread. Each iteration of its loop (lines 18–27) invokes `Thread` method `sleep` (line 20) to place the producer’s virtual thread to sleep for a random time interval. When the thread awakens and begins executing again, line 21 passes the control variable `count`’s value to the `buffer` object’s `blockingPut` method to set the shared buffer’s value. Line 22 keeps a total of all the values produced so far so we can output that total when the producer finishes executing. When the loop completes, lines 29–30 output a message indicating that the producer finished executing and the total of all the values produced. The producer virtual thread terminates when the flow of control reaches the end of the lambda that defines its `Runnable`’s `run` method.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0737-02)

```
14            // producer task writes 1-10 into buffer
15            executor.execute(() -> {
16               int sum = 0;
17
18               for (int count = 1; count <= 10; count++) {
19                  try {
20                     Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(3000));
21                     buffer.blockingPut(count); // write value into buffer
22                     sum += count; // keep running total of values written
23                  }
24                  catch (InterruptedException exception) {
25                     Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
26                  }
27               }
28
29               System.out.printf(
30                  "Producer done: Produced values totaling %d%n", sum);
31            });
32
```

##### Consumer Task

Lines 34–49 define the consumer’s `Runnable` task and launch its execution in a virtual thread, enabling it to run concurrently with the producer’s virtual thread. Lines 37–45 iterate 10 times. Each iteration invokes `Thread` method `sleep` (line 39) to put the consumer’s virtual thread to sleep for a random time interval. Next, line 40 calls the `buffer`’s `blockingGet` method to retrieve the value in the shared buffer, then adds the value to variable `sum`. When the loop completes, lines 47–48 indicate that the consumer finished and display the sum of the consumed values, which should match the sum of the values the producer produced. The consumer virtual thread terminates when the flow of control reaches the end of the lambda that defines its `Runnable`’s `run` method. The program terminates once both virtual threads in this program complete their tasks.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0738-01)

```
33            // consumer task reads values from buffer
34            executor.execute(() -> {
35               int sum = 0;
36
37               for (int count = 1; count <= 10; count++) {
38                  try {
39                     Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(3000));
40                     sum += buffer.blockingGet(); // read value from buffer
41                  }
42                  catch (InterruptedException exception) {
43                     Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
44                  }
45               }
46
47               System.out.printf(
48                  "%nConsumer done: Read values totaling %d%n", sum);
49            });
50         }
51      }
52   }

As you execute the program, you’ll notice some pauses between the writes and reads:

*   Sometimes, these are the result of the program’s threads sleeping.

*   Sometimes, they result from the producer or consumer thread having to wait its turn to access the `BlockingBuffer`’s `ArrayBlockingQueue`.

The `ArrayBlockingQueue` is implemented to correctly manage access to its data from concurrent threads, so the program should operate correctly each time with

*   the producer writing each value from 1 to 10 once,

*   the consumer reading each value once and

*   both displaying the same total for the sum of the values from 1 to 10.

Consumer reads    8      Buffer cells occupied: 0
Producer writes   9      Buffer cells occupied: 1
Consumer reads    9      Buffer cells occupied: 0
Producer writes  10      Buffer cells occupied: 1
Producer done:  Produced values totaling 55
Consumer reads   10      Buffer cells occupied: 0

Consumer done: Read values totaling 55
```

##### A Note Regarding `BlockingBuffer`’s Output Statements

There’s no guarantee that the outputs written by `BlockingBuffer` methods `blockingPut` and `blockingGet` will occur immediately after those methods’ corresponding calls to `ArrayBlockingQueue`’s `put` or `take`. So, in some executions, the outputs might appear out of order. Even if the outputs appear out of order, the `ArrayBlockingQueue` object properly synchronizes access to its data, as evidenced by the sums of values written by the producer and read by the consumer.

##### We Call `Thread` Method `sleep` Only for Demonstration Purposes

We call method `sleep` in the producer and consumer `Runnable`s to emphasize that, **in multithreaded programs, it’s unpredictable when each thread will perform its task and for how long it will perform the task when it has a processor**. These thread-scheduling issues are usually beyond the control of Java developers.

**We cannot make assumptions about the relative speeds of concurrent threads**. Interactions that occur with the operating system, the network, the user and other components can cause the threads to operate at different and ever-changing speeds. When this happens, threads wait. When threads wait excessively, programs become less efficient, interactive programs become less responsive, and applications suffer longer delays.

#### 18.10.7 Bounded Buffers

To minimize the waiting time for threads that share resources and operate at the same average speeds, we can implement a **bounded buffer** that provides a fixed number of buffer cells where the producer can place values and the consumer can retrieve those values. In fact, the `ArrayBlockingQueue` class is a bounded buffer.

With a bounded buffer, if the producer temporarily produces values faster than the consumer can consume them, the producer can write additional values into the extra buffer cells if any are available. This capability enables the producer to perform its task even though the consumer is not ready to retrieve the current value being produced. Similarly, if the consumer temporarily consumes faster than the producer produces new values, the consumer can read additional values (if there are any) from the buffer. This enables the consumer to keep busy even though the producer is not ready to produce additional values. An example of the producer/consumer relationship that uses a bounded buffer is video streaming, which we discussed in [Section 18.1](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec1).

Even a bounded buffer is inappropriate if the producer and the consumer operate consistently at different speeds. If the consumer always executes faster than the producer, then a buffer containing one location is enough. If the producer always executes faster, only a buffer with an “infinite” number of locations would be able to absorb the extra production. However, if the producer and consumer execute at about the same average speed, a bounded buffer helps to smooth the effects of any occasional speeding up or slowing down in either thread’s execution.

The key to using a bounded buffer with a producer and consumer that operate at about the same speed is providing the buffer with enough locations to handle the anticipated “extra” production. If, over a period of time, we determine that the producer often produces as many as three more values than the consumer can consume, we can provide a buffer of at least three cells to handle the extra production. Making the buffer too small would cause threads to wait longer.

`ArrayBlockingQueue` can work with multiple producers and multiple consumers, ensuring each stored item is read only once. For example, a factory that produces its product very fast will need to have many more delivery trucks (i.e., consumers) to remove those products quickly from the warehousing area (i.e., the bounded buffer) so that the factory can continue to produce products at full capacity.

**1** Prompt genAIs, asking how the size of a bounded buffer affects performance and how to determine the optimal size of a bounded buffer in a Java application that implements a producer/consumer relationship.

#### 18.10.8 Other Concurrent Collections

In [Chapter 12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12), we introduced various collections from the Java Collections API. The collections from the `java.util.concurrent` package are specifically designed and optimized for sharing collections among multiple threads. A few of the most commonly used are:

*   `ArrayBlockingQueue` ([Fig. 18.9](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig09))—A fixed-size queue that supports the producer/consumer relationship—possibly with many producers and consumers.

*   `ConcurrentHashMap`—A hash-based map (similar to the `HashMap` introduced in [Chapter 12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12)) that allows an arbitrary number of reader and writer threads.

*   `LinkedBlockingQueue`—A blocking queue implemented as a linked list that can optionally be fixed in size.

The concurrent collections provide their own implementations of various stream-like operations. For example, `ConcurrentHashMap` has methods `forEach`, `reduce` and `search`, which are designed and optimized for concurrent collections shared among threads. For more information on the concurrent collections, visit

   util/concurrent/package-summary.html
```

### 18.11 Multithreading in JavaFX

JavaFX apps present unique challenges for multithreaded programming. All JavaFX apps have one **JavaFX application thread** that handles interactions with the app’s controls, such as rendering them or processing user actions with them. All tasks that require interaction with the GUI are placed in an event queue and executed by the JavaFX application thread in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order.

**JavaFX’s scene graph is not thread-safe**—manipulating its nodes from multiple threads can lead to incorrect results that might corrupt the scene graph**.** To ensure thread safety in JavaFX you use a technique called **thread confinement** in which you **ensure that programs manipulate the scene graph from only the JavaFX application thread**, not by using thread synchronization techniques. Allowing just one thread at a time to access non-thread-safe objects eliminates the possibility of corruption due to multiple threads accessing these objects concurrently.

It’s acceptable to perform brief tasks on the JavaFX application thread—like calculating tips and totals in [Chapter 15](#ch15.xhtml_ch15)’s Tip Calculator app. However, lengthy tasks performed in the JavaFX application thread prevent it from rendering controls or responding to events until that task completes, making the GUI unresponsive and leading to a poor user experience. So, it’s preferable to handle long-running tasks in separate threads, freeing the JavaFX application thread to continue managing GUI interactions. Of course, you must update the GUI with the computation’s results from the JavaFX application thread rather than from the worker thread that performed the calculation.

##### `Platform` Method `runLater`

JavaFX provides multiple mechanisms for updating the GUI from other threads. One is to call the **`static`** **method** **`runLater`** **of class** **`Platform`** (package `javafx.application`). This method receives a `Runnable` and schedules it on the JavaFX application thread for execution in the future. Such `Runnable`s should perform only small updates, such as changing the text on a `Label`, so the GUI remains responsive.

##### Class `Task` and Interface `Worker`

Long-running or compute-intensive tasks should be performed on separate worker threads, not the JavaFX application thread. **Package** **`javafx.concurrent`** provides interface `Worker` and classes `Task` and `ScheduledService` for this purpose:

*   The **`Worker`** **interface** is for a task that should execute using one or more separate threads.

*   The **`Task`** **class** provides a `Worker` implementation that enables you to perform a task (such as a long-running computation) in a worker thread and update the GUI from the JavaFX application thread based on the task’s results. `Task` implements several interfaces, including `Runnable`, so a `Task` object can be scheduled to execute in a separate thread. Class `Task` also provides methods that are guaranteed to update its properties in the JavaFX application thread—this enables programs to bind a `Task`’s properties to GUI controls for automatic updates. Once a `Task` completes, it cannot be restarted, so performing it again requires a new `Task` object. We’ll demonstrate `Task`s in the next two examples.

*   The **`ScheduledService`** **class** provides a `Worker` implementation that creates and manages a `Task`. Unlike a `Task`, a `ScheduledService` can be reset and restarted. It can also be configured to automatically restart both after successful completion and if it fails due to an exception.

#### 18.11.1 Performing Computations in a Worker Thread: Fibonacci Numbers

In the next example, the user enters a number *n*, and the program gets the *n*th Fibonacci number in the **Fibonacci series**,

```
0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …
```

which begins with 0 and 1 and has the property that each subsequent value in the series is the sum of the previous two. In this example, we calculate the *n*th Fibonacci number using a CPU-intensive algorithm that we discuss thoroughly in [Section 22.4](#ch22.xhtml_ch22lev1sec4), so we do not present its details here.

The algorithm is particularly time-consuming for large values of *n*, so we use a `Task` object to perform the calculation in a worker thread. The GUI also provides a separate set of components that displays the next Fibonacci number in the sequence each time the user presses (or selects) a `Button`. This set of components performs its short computation directly in the Java FX application thread. The program can produce up to the 92nd Fibonacci number—subsequent values are outside the range that can be represented by a `long`. Recall that you can use class `BigInteger` to represent arbitrarily large integer values.

##### Creating a `Task`

Class `FibonacciTask` ([Fig. 18.11](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig11)) extends `Task<Long>` (line 5) to perform the calculation in a worker thread. The instance variable `n` (line 6) represents the Fibonacci number to calculate. Overridden **`Task`** **method** **`call`** (lines 14–20) computes the *n*th Fibonacci number and returns the result. The `Task`’s type parameter, `Long` (line 5), determines method `call`’s return type (line 15). Inherited **`Task`** **method** **`updateMessage`** (called in lines 16 and 18) updates the `Task`’s `message` property in the JavaFX application thread. In [Fig. 18.12](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig12), we’ll use this to bind a JavaFX control to `FibonacciTask`’s `message` property to display messages while the task is executing.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0743-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.11: FibonacciTask.java
 2   // Task subclass for calculating Fibonacci numbers in the background
 3   import javafx.concurrent.Task;
 4
 5   public class FibonacciTask extends Task<Long> {
 6      private final int n; // Fibonacci number to calculate
 7
 8      // constructor
 9      public FibonacciTask(int n) {
10         this.n = n;
11      }
12
13      // long-running code to be run in a worker thread
14      @Override
15      protected Long call() {
16         updateMessage("Calculating...");
17         long result = fibonacci(n);
18         updateMessage("Done calculating.");
19         return result;
20      }
21
22      // calculates nth Fibonacci number (Section 22.4 explains this method)
23      public long fibonacci(long number) {
24         if (number == 0 || number == 1) {
25            return number;
26         }
27         else {
28            return fibonacci(number - 1) + fibonacci(number - 2);
29         }
30      }
31   }
```

**Fig. 18.11** | `Task` subclass for calculating Fibonacci numbers in the background.

When the worker thread starts running, `FibonacciTask`’s `call` method begins executing. First, line 16 calls the inherited `updateMessage` method to update the `FibonacciTask`’s `message` property, indicating that the task is calculating. Next, line 17 invokes method `fibonacci` (lines 23–30) with instance variable `n`’s value as the argument. When `fibonacci` returns, line 18 updates `FibonacciTask`’s `message` property again to indicate that the calculation completed, then line 19 returns the result to the JavaFX application thread.

##### `FibonacciNumbers` GUI

The following screen captures demonstrate the app. We labeled the app’s GUI (defined in `FibonacciNumbers.fxml`) with its fx:ids in the third screen capture:

![Images](graphics/f0744-01.jpg)

Here, we point out only the key elements and the event-handling methods we’ll implement in class `FibonacciNumbersController` ([Fig. 18.12](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig12)). For the complete layout details, open `FibonacciNumbers.fxml` in Scene Builder. The GUI’s primary layout is a `VBox` containing two `TitledPane`s. The controller class defines two event handlers:

*   `goButtonPressed` is called when the Go `Button` is pressed—this launches the worker thread to calculate a Fibonacci number recursively.

*   `nextNumberButtonPressed` is called when the Next Number `Button` is pressed—this calculates the next Fibonacci number in the sequence. Initially, the app displays the Fibonacci of 0 (which is 0).

We do not present the JavaFX `Application` subclass (located in `FibonacciNumbers.java`) because it performs the same tasks we’ve used previously to load the app’s FXML GUI and initialize the controller.

##### Class `FibonacciNumbersController`

Class `FibonacciNumbersController` ([Fig. 18.12](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig12))—which we’ve split into parts for discussion purposes—handles events from two sets of controls:

*   The "With FibonacciTask" `TitledPane` provides controls that enable the user to enter a Fibonacci number to calculate and launch a `FibonacciTask` in a worker thread. `Label`s in this `TitledPane` display the `FibonacciTask`’s message property value as it’s updated and the final result of the `FibonacciTask` once it’s available.

*   The "Without FibonacciTask" `TitledPane` provides the Next Number `Button` that enables the user to calculate the next Fibonacci number in sequence. `Label`s in this `TitledPane` display the Fibonacci number being calculated (`"Fibonacci of` *n*`"`) and the corresponding Fibonacci value.

Instance variables `n1` and `n2` (lines 20–21) contain the previous two Fibonacci numbers in the sequence and are initialized to `0` and `1`, respectively. Instance variable `number` (initialized to `1` in line 22) keeps track of which Fibonacci value will be calculated and displayed next when the user presses (or selects) the Next Number `Button`. The first time this `Button` is pressed (or selected), the Fibonacci of 1 is displayed.

10   import javafx.scene.control.TextField;
11
12   public class FibonacciNumbersController {

14      @FXML private Button goButton;
15      @FXML private Label messageLabel;
16      @FXML private Label fibonacciLabel;
17      @FXML private Label nthLabel;
18      @FXML private Label nthFibonacciLabel;

**Fig. 18.12** | Using a `Task` to perform a long calculation outside the JavaFX application thread.

##### Method `goButtonPressed`

When the user presses (or selects) the Go `Button`, method `goButtonPressed` (lines 25–59) executes. Line 29 gets the value entered in the `numberTextField` and attempts to parse it as an integer. If this fails, lines 55–57 prompt the user to enter an integer, select the text in the `numberTextField` and give the `numberTextField` the focus so the user can immediately enter a new value in the `numberTextField`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0745-02)

```
24      // starts FibonacciTask to calculate in background
25      @FXML
26      void goButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
27         // get Fibonacci number to calculate
28         try {
29            int input = Integer.parseInt(numberTextField.getText());
30
31            // create, configure and launch FibonacciTask
32            var task = new FibonacciTask(input);
33
34            // display task's messages in messageLabel
35            messageLabel.textProperty().bind(task.messageProperty());
36
37            // clear fibonacciLabel when task starts
38            task.setOnRunning((succeededEvent) -> {
39               goButton.setDisable(true);
40               fibonacciLabel.setText("");
41            });
42
43            // set fibonacciLabel when task completes successfully
44            task.setOnSucceeded((succeededEvent) -> {
45               fibonacciLabel.setText(task.getValue().toString());
46               goButton.setDisable(false);
47            });
48
49            // launch the FibonacciTask
50            var executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1);
51            executor.execute(task); // start the task
52            executor.shutdown(); // prevent more tasks from being scheduled
53         }
54         catch (NumberFormatException e) {
55            numberTextField.setText("Enter an integer");
56            numberTextField.selectAll();
57            numberTextField.requestFocus();
58         }
59      }
60
```

Line 32 creates a new `FibonacciTask` object, passing the constructor the user-entered value. Line 35 binds the `messageLabel`’s `text` property (a `StringProperty`) to the `FibonacciTask`’s `message` property (a `ReadOnlyStringProperty`). When `FibonacciTask` updates this property, the `messageLabel` displays the new value.

All `Worker`s transition through various states. Class `Task`, an implementation of interface `Worker`, enables you to register listeners for several of these states:

*   Lines 38–41 use **`Task`** **method** **`setOnRunning`** to register a listener (implemented as a lambda) that’s invoked when the `Task` begins executing—that is, when the `Task` has been assigned a processor and its `call` method is invoked. In this case, we disable the `goButton` so the user cannot launch another `FibonacciTask` until the current one completes. Then, we clear the `fibonacciLabel` (so an old result is not displayed when a new `FibonacciTask` begins).

*   Lines 44–47 use **`Task`** **method** **`setOnSucceeded`** to register a listener (implemented as a lambda) that’s invoked when the `Task` successfully runs to completion. In this case, we call **`Task`** **method** **`getValue`** (from interface `Worker`) to get the result, which we convert to a `String` then display in the `fibonacciLabel`. Then, we enable the `goButton` so the user can start a new `FibonacciTask`.

You can also register listeners to be notified when a `Task` is canceled, failed to execute correctly or is scheduled for execution.

Finally, lines 50–52 use an `ExecutorService` to launch the `FibonacciTask`, which schedules it for execution in a separate worker thread. Method `execute` does not wait for the `FibonacciTask` to finish executing. It returns immediately, allowing the GUI to continue processing other events while the computation is performed. Line 52 ensures that no other tasks can be scheduled using the `ExecutorService`. We don’t use the `ExecutorSer-vice`’s `AutoCloseable` feature here, because it would block the JavaFX application thread from proceeding as it waits for the task to complete, freezing the GUI.

##### Method `nextNumberButtonPressed`

If the user presses (or selects) the Next Number `Button`, method `nextNumberButtonPressed` (lines 62–71) executes. Lines 65–66 update the `nthLabel` with the `Fibonacci` number, then update `nthFibonacciLabel` to display `n2`’s value. Next, lines 67–70 add the previous two Fibonacci numbers stored in `n1` and `n2` to determine the next number in the sequence (which will be displayed on the next call to `nextNumberButtonPressed`), update `n1` and `n2` to their new values and increment `number`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0747-01)

```
61      // calculates next Fibonacci value
62      @FXML
63      void nextNumberButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
64         // display the next Fibonacci number
65         nthLabel.setText("Fibonacci of " + number + ": ");
66         nthFibonacciLabel.setText(String.valueOf(n2));
67         long temp = n1 + n2;
68         n1 = n2;
69         n2 = temp;
70         ++number;
71      }
72   }
```

The code for these calculations is in method `nextNumberButtonPressed`, so they’re performed on the JavaFX application thread. Handling such short computations in this thread does not cause the GUI to become unresponsive, as with the recursive algorithm for calculating the Fibonacci of a large number. Because the longer Fibonacci computation is performed in a separate worker thread, it’s possible to click the Next Number `Button` to get the next Fibonacci number while the recursive computation is still in progress.

#### 18.11.2 Processing Intermediate Results: Sieve of Eratosthenes

Class `Task` provides additional methods and properties that enable you to update a GUI with a `Task`’s intermediate results as the `Task` continues executing in a `Worker` thread. The next example uses the following `Task` methods and properties:

*   The **`updateProgress`** **method** updates a **`Task`****’s** **`progress`** **property**, which represents the percentage completion.

*   The **`updateValue`** **method** updates a **`Task`****’s** **`value`** **property**, which holds each intermediate value.

Like `updateMessage`, `updateProgress` and `updateValue` are guaranteed to update the corresponding properties in the JavaFX application thread.

##### A `Task` to Find Prime Numbers

[Figure 18.13](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig13) presents class `PrimeCalculatorTask`, which extends `Task<Integer>` to compute the first *n* prime numbers in a worker thread. In the `FindPrimesController` class ([Fig. 18.14](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig14)), we’ll bind this `Task`’s `progress` property to a `ProgressBar` control so the app can indicate the `Task`’s completion percentage. The controller also registers a listener for the `value` property’s changes—we’ll store each prime value in an `ObservableList` that’s bound to a `ListView`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0748-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 18.13: PrimeCalculatorTask.java
 2   // Calculates the first n primes, publishing them as they are found.
 3   import java.util.Arrays;
 4   import javafx.concurrent.Task;
 5
 6   public class PrimeCalculatorTask extends Task<Integer> {
 7      private final boolean[] primes; // boolean array for finding primes
 8
 9      // constructor
10      public PrimeCalculatorTask(int max) {
11         primes = new boolean[max];
12         Arrays.fill(primes, true); // initialize all primes elements to true
13      }
14
15      // long-running code to be run in a worker thread
16      @Override
17      protected Integer call() {
18         int count = 0; // the number of primes found
19
20         // starting at index 2 (the first prime number), cycle through and
21         // set to false elements with indices that are multiples of i
22         for (int i = 2; i < primes.length; i++) {
23            if (isCancelled()) { // if calculation has been canceled
24               updateMessage("Cancelled");
25               return 0;
26            }
27            else {
28               try {
29                  Thread.sleep(10); // slow the thread
30               }
31               catch (InterruptedException ex) {
32                  updateMessage("Interrupted");
33                  return 0;
34               }
35
36               updateProgress(i + 1, primes.length);
37
38               if (primes[i]) { // i is prime
39                  ++count;
40                  updateMessage(String.format("Found %d primes", count));
41                  updateValue(i); // intermediate result
42
43                  // eliminate multiples of i
44                  for (int j = i + i; j < primes.length; j += i) {
45                     primes[j] = false; // i is not prime
46                  }
47               }
48            }
49         }
50
51         return 0;
52      }
53   }
```

**Fig. 18.13** | Calculates the first *n* primes, publishing them as they are found.

##### Constructor

The constructor ([Fig. 18.13](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig13), lines 10–13) receives an `int` for the upper limit of the prime numbers to locate, creates the `boolean` array `primes` and initializes its elements to `true`.

##### Sieve of Eratosthenes

`PrimeCalculatorTask` uses the `primes` array and the **Sieve of Eratosthenes** algorithm to find all primes less than `max`. The Sieve of Eratosthenes takes a list of integers and, beginning with the first prime number, filters out all multiples of that prime. It then moves to the next prime, which will be the next number that’s not yet filtered out, and eliminates all of its multiples. It continues until the end of the list is reached and all non-primes have been filtered out. Algorithmically, we begin with element `2` of the `boolean` array and set the cells corresponding to all values that are multiples of 2 to `false` to indicate that they’re divisible by 2 and thus not prime. We then move to the next array element, check whether it’s `true` and, if so, set all of its multiples to `false` to indicate that they’re divisible by the current index. When the whole array has been traversed in this way, all indices that contain `true` are prime, as they have no divisors.

##### Overridden `Task` Method `call`

`Task` method `call` (lines 16–52) is invoked when the `Task` is executed. The method is `protected` because it’s meant to be overridden by a subclass, not called directly. In method `call`, the control variable `i` for the loop (lines 22–49) represents the current index for implementing the Sieve of Eratosthenes. Line 23 calls the inherited **`Task`** **method** **`isCan-celled`** to determine whether the user has clicked the Cancel button. If so, line 24 updates the `Task`’s `message` property, then line 25 returns `0` to terminate the `Task` immediately.

If the calculation isn’t canceled, line 29 puts the currently executing thread to sleep for 10 milliseconds. We discuss the reason for this shortly. Line 36 calls `Task`’s `update-Progress` method to update the `progress` property in the JavaFX application thread. The percentage completion is determined by dividing the method’s first argument by its second argument.

Next, line 38 tests whether the current `primes` element is `true` (and thus prime). If so, line 39 increments the `count` of prime numbers found so far and line 40 updates the `Task`’s `message` property with a `String` containing the `count`. Then, line 41 passes the index `i` to method `updateValue`, which updates `Task`’s `value` property in the JavaFX application thread—in the controller, we’ll process this intermediate result and display it in the GUI. When the entire array has been traversed, line 51 returns `0`, which we ignore in the controller (line 53 of [Fig. 18.14](#ch18.xhtml_ch18fig14)) because it is not a prime number.

Because the computation progresses quickly, publishing values often, updates can pile up on the JavaFX application thread, causing it to ignore some updates. This is why, for demonstration purposes, we put the worker thread to sleep for 10 milliseconds during each iteration of the loop. The calculation is slowed just enough to allow the JavaFX application thread to keep up with the updates and enable the GUI to remain responsive.
