15   public class FindPrimesController {
16      @FXML private TextField inputTextField;
17      @FXML private Button getPrimesButton;
18      @FXML private ListView<Integer> primesListView;
19      @FXML private Button cancelButton;
20      @FXML private ProgressBar progressBar;
21      @FXML private Label statusLabel;
22
23      // stores the list of primes received from PrimeCalculatorTask
24      private ObservableList<Integer> primes =
25         FXCollections.observableArrayList();
26      private PrimeCalculatorTask task; // finds prime numbers
27
28      // binds primesListView's items to the ObservableList primes
29      @FXML
30      public void initialize() {
31         primesListView.setItems(primes);
32      }
33
```

**Fig. 18.14** | Displaying prime numbers as they’re calculated and updating a `ProgressBar`.

##### Method `getPrimesButtonPressed`

When the user presses (or selects) the Get Primes `Button`, `getPrimesButtonPressed` (lines 35–84) creates a `PrimeCalculatorTask` (line 42) and configures various event listeners:

*   Line 45 binds the `statusLabel`’s `text` property to the task’s `message` property to update the `statusLabel` automatically as new primes are found.

*   Line 48 binds the `progressBar`’s `progress` property to the task’s `progress` property to update the `progressBar` automatically with the percentage of completion.

*   Lines 51–58 register a `ChangeListener` (using a lambda) that responds to the task’s `value` property changes. If the property’s `newValue` is not `0` (indicating the task terminated), line 54 adds it to the `primes ObservableList<Integer>`, which is bound to the `primesListView` to display the list’s elements. Next, lines 55–56 scroll the `ListView` to its last element so the latest prime number is on the screen.

*   Lines 62–72 register listeners for when the task begins running and when the task completes successfully. We use these to enable and disable the app’s `Button`s based on the task’s state.

*   The long-running `PrimeCalculatorTask` sleeps between passing prime values to the JavaFX application thread for display in the `ListView`. Since this task is not CPU-bound, lines 75–77 launch a virtual thread to execute it, potentially enabling better use of your system’s CPU resources. **Note that we do not wait for this thread to complete as we have for all of this chapter’s virtual thread examples. If the app were to wait here, the event handler would not terminate until the task completes, and the GUI would freeze, preventing other user interactions, such as canceling the task.**

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0752-01)

```
34      // start calculating primes in the background
35      @FXML
36      void getPrimesButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
37         primes.clear();
38
39         // get Fibonacci number to calculate
40         try {
41            int input = Integer.parseInt(inputTextField.getText());
42            task = new PrimeCalculatorTask(input); // create task
43
44            // display task's messages in statusLabel
45            statusLabel.textProperty().bind(task.messageProperty());
46
47            // update progressBar based on task's progressProperty
48            progressBar.progressProperty().bind(task.progressProperty());
49
50            // store intermediate results in the ObservableList primes
51            task.valueProperty().addListener(
52               (observable, oldValue, newValue) -> {
53                  if (newValue != 0) { // task returns 0 when it terminates
54                     primes.add(newValue);
55                     primesListView.scrollTo(
56                        primesListView.getItems().size());
57                  }
58               });
59
60            // when task begins,
61            // disable getPrimesButton and enable cancelButton
62            task.setOnRunning((succeededEvent) -> {
63               getPrimesButton.setDisable(true);
64               cancelButton.setDisable(false);
65            });
66
67            // when task completes successfully,
68            // enable getPrimesButton and disable cancelButton
69            task.setOnSucceeded((succeededEvent) -> {
70               getPrimesButton.setDisable(false);
71               cancelButton.setDisable(true);
72            });
73
74            // launch the PrimeCalculatorTask
75            var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
76            executor.execute(task); // start the task
77            executor.shutdown();
78         }
79         catch (NumberFormatException e) {
80            inputTextField.setText("Enter an integer");
81            inputTextField.selectAll();
82            inputTextField.requestFocus();
83         }
84      }
85
```

##### Method `cancelButtonPressed`

When the user presses the Cancel `Button`, method `cancelButtonPressed` calls the `Prime-CalculatorTask`’s inherited **`cancel`** **method** (line 90) to terminate the task, then enables the `getPrimesButton` and disables the `cancelButton`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch18_images.xhtml_f0753-01)

```
86      // cancel task when user presses Cancel Button
87      @FXML
88      void cancelButtonPressed(ActionEvent event) {
89         if (task != null) {
90            task.cancel(); // terminate the task
91            getPrimesButton.setDisable(false);
92            cancelButton.setDisable(true);
93         }
94      }
95   }
```

### 18.12 Wrap-Up

This chapter presented Java’s concurrency capabilities for enhancing performance on multi-core systems. You learned the differences between concurrent and parallel execution. We explained that Java makes concurrency available to you through the language and libraries, and we focused on high-level library features and creating threads to run tasks various ways. You learned that the JVM creates platform threads to run programs and perform housekeeping tasks, such as garbage collection.

We used the `Arrays` class’s `sort` and `parallelSort` methods to demonstrate the benefit of a parallel sorting algorithm on a multi-core processor, timing the operations with the Java Date/Time API. You learned that stream pipelines are easy to parallelize, enabling programs to benefit from enhanced performance on multi-core systems. To obtain a parallel stream, you invoked method `parallel` on an existing sequential stream.

We presented the `Runnable` interface for specifying a task that can execute concurrently with other tasks. This interface’s `run` method is invoked by the thread executing the task. Then we showed how to use the `Executor` interface to manage the execution of `Runnable` objects via a thread pool, which can reuse existing platform threads to eliminate the overhead of creating a new thread for each task and can improve performance by optimizing the number of threads to ensure that the processor stays busy.

We explored Project Loom’s virtual threads, structured concurrency and scoped values—significant enhancements to Java’s concurrency capabilities that address the limitations of traditional platform threads in applications requiring massive numbers of concurrent tasks that spend most of their time blocking. We discussed that virtual threads are lightweight and managed by the JVM rather than the operating system. We compared the initial memory requirements of virtual threads (only a few hundred bytes) and platform threads (one to two megabytes) and presented three ways to create and launch virtual threads. We did detailed performance comparisons, demonstrating how virtual threads significantly outperform platform threads when handling large numbers of concurrent I/O-bound tasks, enabling applications to efficiently manage thousands or millions of concurrent operations. In that example, we discussed the `Callable` and `Future` interfaces, which enable you to execute tasks that return results and obtain those results, respectively.

We discussed structured concurrency and scoped values—preview features at the time of this writing—in the context of a practical weather application example that uses Open-WeatherMap’s web services (introduced in [Section 11.6](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev1sec6)). We demonstrated how these features simplify concurrent programming and resource management while making code easier to read, maintain and debug. We used `StructuredTaskScope` to treat related concurrent tasks as a single unit, enabling concurrent programming with straightforward sequential statements. We also used `ScopedValue` objects to share immutable data between tasks launched from the same structured concurrency scope.

You learned that when multiple threads share an object and one or more of them modify that object, indeterminate results may occur unless access to the shared object is managed properly. In an example of the producer/consumer relationship, we showed how to solve this problem via the built-in class `ArrayBlockingQueue`, which handles all the synchronization details for you.

We discussed the fact that JavaFX GUIs are not thread-safe, so all interactions with and modifications to the GUI must be performed in the JavaFX application thread. We also discussed the problems associated with performing long-running calculations in that thread. Then, we demonstrated how to use class `Task` to perform long-running calculations in worker threads but update the GUI in the JavaFX application thread. You learned how to use a `Task`’s properties to display the results of a `Task` in a GUI when the calculation completes and how to display intermediate results while the calculation is still in process.

In the next chapter, we build API-based Java generative AI applications. You’ll use OpenAI APIs to create apps that summarize text, analyze text for sentiment, create accessible descriptions of images, detect a text’s language and translate text among languages, generate Java code, perform named entity recognition on text and obtain structured JSON outputs, transcribe speech to text, synthesize speech from text, generate closed captions for a video and more.

#### Special Section: Generative AI Exercises

For each of the following questions, try multiple genAIs to determine which performs best. Always verify the results. Keep in mind that they sometimes make mistakes and even hallucinate, creating unreliable information.

**18.1** ***(Best Practices and Common Pitfalls)*** Prompt genAIs for best practices and common pitfalls of Java multithreaded application development.

**18.2** ***(******`ThreadLocal`*** ***Variables vs.*** ***`ScopedValue`******s)*** Prompt genAIs, asking for a detailed comparison of the pros and cons of `ThreadLocal` variables vs. `ScopedValue`s with code examples.

**18.3** ***(Weather App Enhancement)*** Sometimes, a web service may not respond promptly. Prompt genAIs with the code from [Section 18.8](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev1sec8)’s weather app, asking how to make each OpenWeatherMap request stop executing if it has not responded within a specified amount of time (known as “timing out”).

**18.4** ***(Nested*** ***`StructuredTaskScope`******s)*** Prompt genAIs for real-world examples of nested `StructuredTaskScope`s and a simple code example demonstrating how to create them.

**18.5** ***(Exceptions in*** ***`StructuredTaskScope`******s)*** Prompt genAIs for a detailed discussion of how exceptions are handled in `StructuredTaskScope`s.

**18.6** ***(Custom*** ***`StructuredTaskScope`******s)*** You can inherit from `StructuredTaskScope` to customize how their virtual threads are managed. Prompt genAIs to provide code examples demonstrating use-cases for custom `StructuredTaskScope`s.

**18.7** ***(Limiting Concurrent Access By Virtual Threads to a Shared Resource)*** Prompt genAIs, asking how to limit the number of concurrent virtual threads accessing a resource.

**18.8** ***(Java Flight Recorder)*** Prompt genAIs for an overview of Java Flight Recorder and how it can be used to debug multithreaded applications.

**18.9** ***(Fork/Join Framework)*** Prompt genAIs for an overview of Java’s Fork/Join framework and how it’s used in parallel streams and the `Arrays` methods `parallelSort` and `parallelSetAll`.

**18.10** ***(Uncaught Exceptions in Multithreaded Applications)*** Prompt genAIs, asking them to list cases where an uncaught exception does not terminate a Java program.

**18.11** ***(Deadlock, Livelock and Indefinite Postponement)*** Three problems that can occur in systems that allow threads to wait (such as the producer/consumer relationship) are

*   deadlock—in which one or more threads will wait forever for an event that cannot occur,

*   livelock—in which threads remain active but keep retrying or adjusting in a way that prevents completion of their tasks and

*   indefinite postponement—in which one or more threads will be delayed for some unpredictably long time.

Prompt genAIs, asking them to discuss how to avoid deadlock, livelock and indefinite postponement in multithreaded Java programs.

**18.12** ***(Bounded Buffer: A Real-World Example)*** Prompt genAIs to describe how a highway off-ramp onto a local road is a good example of a producer/consumer relationship with a bounded buffer and how the designers might choose the size of the off-ramp.

### 19.1 Introduction

So far, you’ve manually prompted genAIs via their web interfaces and compared and used their results. We did not show these prompts’ results. In this chapter, we program Java API-based genAI applications and show their outputs or play the generated audios and videos.

##### Multimodal GenAIs

When genAI chatbots were introduced, they received a text prompt and generated text or an image. Many are now **multimodal**—they can understand text, code, images, audio and video inputs and use them to generate mixed text, code, images, audio and video outputs.^([1](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_1a),[2](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_2a),[3](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_3a)) For example, you can prompt a genAI with an audio file containing speech and instructions, asking it to transcribe the speech into text, display the transcription, analyze its sentiment, translate it to another spoken language and synthesize speech in that other language.

[1](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_1). “What Is Multimodal AI?” DataCamp. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://www.datacamp.com/blog/what-is-multimodal-ai`](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/what-is-multimodal-ai).

[2](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_2). “What Is Multimodal AI?” IBM. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/multimodal-ai`](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/multimodal-ai).

[3](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_3). “Generative Artificial Intelligence.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence).

Various genAIs allow you to speak to them and receiving spoken responses. In fact, at OpenAI DevDay 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that ChatGPT’s Advanced Voice Mode was so realistic that it made him think he was chatting with another person.^([4](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_4a))

[4](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_4). Zachary Boddy, “Sam Altman Says ChatGPT’s Voice Mode Was the First Time He Was Tricked into Thinking an AI Was a Person,” Windows Central, February 15, 2024\. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://www.windowscentral.com/software-apps/sam-altman-says-chatgpts-voice-mode-was-the-first-time-he-was-tricked-into-thinking-an-ai-was-a-person`](https://www.windowscentral.com/software-apps/sam-altman-says-chatgpts-voice-mode-was-the-first-time-he-was-tricked-into-thinking-an-ai-was-a-person).

#### 19.2.4 OpenAI Developer API Key

You need a developer key to invoke OpenAI’s APIs. Perform the following steps to get one:

1.  Sign into your account at [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/overview`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/overview).

2.  Press (or select) the Start building button in the page’s upper-right corner—after you create your first API key below, this button will change to a settings icon (![Images](graphics/f0762-02.jpg)).

3.  Fill in the Organization name and What best describes you? fields then press (or select) the Create organization button.

4.  In the Invite your team step, you can add email addresses for other team members. Press (or select) Continue.

5.  In the Make your first API call step, specify an API key name and a Project name, then press (or select) the Generate API Key button. (If you create additional API keys in the future, you’ll select API Keys the left column of your account’s settings page.)

6.  Press or select the Copy button to copy the alphanumeric key to the clipboard.

For security, you’ll store your API key in an environment variable on your system rather than embedding it in your code, as discussed below.

##### Storing the API Key in macOS

Perform the following steps to store your API key on macOS:

1.  Open Terminal.

2.  Open `~/.zshrc` using a text editor (e.g., `nano ~/.zshrc`).

3.  Scroll to the end of the file and add the following line, replacing *YourAPIKey* with the lengthy alphanumeric API key you copied previously.

    [Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0762-01)

    ```
    export OPENAI_API_KEY="YourAPIKey"
    ```

4.  Save and close the file.

5.  Run the following command in the Terminal:

    ```
    source ~/.zshrc
    ```

##### Storing the API Key on Windows

Perform the following steps to store your API key on Windows:

1.  In the taskbar’s Search field, enter `SystemPropertiesAdvanced`, and press or select *Enter*.

2.  In the System Properties dialog, press or select the Environment Variables… button.

3.  Under User variables, click New….

4.  Enter the Variable name as `OPENAI_API_KEY` and, for the Variable value, paste in the lengthy alphanumeric API key you copied previously.

5.  Click OK to save the environment variable, then click OK in the System Properties dialog to close it.

### 19.3 Setting Up a Java Environment

OpenAI’s APIs are implemented as web services. We’ll use the following Java library that encapsulates the web-service interactions, making it convenient to use OpenAI’s APIs.

#### 19.3.1 Simple-OpenAI Open Source Library: Connecting to OpenAI from Java

OpenAI does not provide an official Java library, but several third-party options are available. In this chapter, we use Simple-OpenAI—“a Java library to use the OpenAI API in the simplest possible way.”^([21](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_21a)) This library supports most major OpenAI API capabilities, including chat completions, speech synthesis, speech recognition, image generation, image editing, structured outputs, realtime speech-to-speech, and more.^([22](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_22a)) The library provides classes and methods that encapsulate the details of

*   authenticating with OpenAI using your `OPENAI_API_KEY` so you can use their web services,

*   managing files used in your requests,

*   formulating web-service requests that invoke OpenAI’s APIs,

*   handling the responses they return (such as generated text, images and audio), and more.

This enables us to focus on each example’s genAI concepts and present the Simple-OpenAI details later. Class `OpenAIUtilities` also allows us to share code among our applications. When compiling and running this chapter’s apps, you’ll use our custom library file `OpenAIUtilities.jar`, which is located in the `libs` subfolder with this chapter’s examples.

### 19.4 Text Generation Via Chat Completions

In this section, we present fully coded apps that interact with OpenAI’s `"gpt-4o"` model to request chat completions:

*   [Section 19.4.1](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec9) performs **text summarization**—in two OpenAI API requests, we upload a Deitel video transcript and ask the chat API to return a summary abstract paragraph, followed by a list of the transcript’s key points. Text responses like these are known as **chat completions**.

*   [Section 19.4.2](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec11) uses a chat-completion request to perform **sentiment analysis**—determining whether the Deitel video transcript is positive, neutral or negative. We also ask the genAI to explain how it came to its conclusion.

*   [Section 19.4.3](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec12) asks OpenAI to **describe images for accessibility**. This multi-modal application uploads an image and requests a detailed image description. We get detailed descriptions of [Section 4.3](#ch04.xhtml_ch04lev1sec3)’s `for`-loop UML diagram and a scenic Aruba beach photo.

*   [Section 19.4.4](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec13) uses chat-completion requests to **translate text**. OpenAI will auto-detect the text’s source language then translate the text to a specified target language. We translate text from English to Spanish and Japanese then translate the Spanish and Japanese text back to English.

*   [Section 19.4.5](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec15) uses a chat-completion request to **generate Java code** for a simulation that summarizes 600,000,000 six-sided die rolls and displays the results. We then compile and execute the generated code.

*   [Section 19.4.6](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec16) uses a chat-completion request to perform the natural language processing (NLP) task **named-entity recognition (NER)**, which attempts to locate and categorize text mentions like dates, times, quantities, places, people, things, organizations, etc. This example demonstrates OpenAI’s ability to produce **structured output** in your application’s required format. To make the results easier to process, we provide the API with the exact JSON response format we wish to receive, then use the Jackson open-source library ([Chapter 11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11)) to process the result. NER is one of many natural language processing tasks OpenAI’s APIs can perform. [Section 7.7](#ch07.xhtml_ch07lev1sec7) listed many common NLP tasks you could try.

#### 19.4.1 Text Summarization

**Text summarization** is a natural language processing (NLP) task that analyzes a body of text and produces a shorter version containing the key ideas. This is useful for getting quick summaries of items like articles, academic papers, book chapters or sections, lengthy emails, reports, study materials, product reviews and more. [Figure 19.1](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig01) summarizes a presentation transcript as

*   a summary abstract paragraph and

*   a key-points list.

The file `transcript.txt` in the `ch19` examples folder’s `resources` subfolder contains the original presentation transcript. Many of this chapter’s examples use files from this folder, and those that generate audio, images and Java code write their results into files in the `resources` folder’s `outputs` subfolder. Throughout this chapter’s examples, we assume the book’s code is located in your user account’s `Documents` folder in the `examples` subfolder, as discussed in the Before You Begin section. **If you placed them elsewhere, you must update the files paths we specify in the examples.**

##### Requesting a Chat Completion That Produces a Summary Abstract Paragraph

Lines 19–31 call our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `static chat` method (discussed in [Section 19.9.5](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec31)) to request an OpenAI chat completion that produces a summary abstract paragraph for the transcript loaded in line 15\. Our `chat` method uses the Simple-OpenAI library to interact with OpenAI APIs that respond to prompts, similar to when you interact with ChatGPT through its web interface. **When you run this and subsequent examples, keep in mind that the responses returned by genAIs typically change from request to request, even if your prompt is identical.**

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0766-02)

```
17         // get a summary abstract with OpenAI's gpt-4o model
18         System.out.println("CREATE A SUMMARY ABSTRACT OF A TRANSCRIPT");
19         String summaryAbstract = OpenAIUtilities.chat("gpt-4o",
20            List.of(
21               new Message("system", """
22                  Given a transcript of a technical presentation, create a
23                  concise, clear summary abstract in paragraph form, written
24                  in a direct style that avoids prepositional phrases and
25                  uses straightforward sentence structures. Focus on the key
26                  points without referring to the speaker. Capture the key
27                  ideas, so a person can understand it without reading the
28                  full transcript."""),
29               new Message("user", transcript)
30            )
31         );
32         System.out.printf("%s%n%n", summaryAbstract);
33
```

##### Messages Passed to the OpenAI APIs

Many OpenAI API calls require messages consisting of a `role` and `content`. The role is `"user"`, `"system"` or `"assistant"`—discussed momentarily. The `content` is typically

*   a prompt like you’d input via a genAI’s web interface or

*   data the API call will process.

In our code, we defined these messages using our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s nested `record` class `Message` (imported at line 4 and discussed in [Section 19.9.3](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec29)):

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0767-01)

```
public record Message(String role, String content) {}
```

Several of our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s methods, including `chat`, receive `List<Message>` objects. Our `chat` method’s first argument specifies the OpenAI model to use to formulate a response—the **`"gpt-4o"`** **model** was one of OpenAI’s most up-to-date and powerful models at the time of this writing. Each item in the `List<Message>` passed as `chat`’s second argument is a `Message` object containing a `role` and `content`.

##### `"system"` Role

A message with the **`"system" role`**^([25](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_25a)) prompts the model with details to help it perform a task. The corresponding `content` typically explains what you want the model to do.^([26](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_26a)) For example, lines 21–28 define a text block describing how we’d like the model to summarize text. If you were asking the model to write Java code, you might tell it that it’s an expert in Java programming. Instructions like this give the model context to help it provide more relevant results.

[25](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_25). “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles).

[26](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_26). OpenAI recently added `"developer"` messages that are specifically for use with OpenAI’s “reasoning models” (such as `"o1"` or `"o3-mini`). According to [`https://community.openai.com/t/how-is-developer-message-better-than-system-prompt/1062784/2`](https://community.openai.com/t/how-is-developer-message-better-than-system-prompt/1062784/2), if you submit a `"developer"` message to the `"gpt-4o"` model (or another GPT model), it’s converted to a `"system"` message, and if you submit a `"system"` message to reasoning model, it’s converted to a `"developer"` message.

##### `"user"` Role

A message with the **`"user" role`**^([27](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_27a)) provides as its `content` a prompt for a task to perform or data the model requires to perform a task. You can supply multiple `"system"` and `"user"` messages—`"system"` messages are prioritized over `"user"` messages. Line 29 provides the data to summarize (`transcript`). If you’d like the model to generate code, the `content` would indicate what you’d like the code to do.

[27](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_27). “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles).

##### `"assistant"` Role

A message with the **`"assistant" role`**^([28](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_28a)) is typically used to provide examples to the model, such as showing it the exact format you want for a response. Unlike the ChatGPT web interface, the chat-completion API does not have memory, so it does not remember previous chat-completion requests. So, messages with the `"assistant"` role can also be used to supply a previous chat-completion response in a conversation your code is having with the genAI, giving it more context for the current request. For more details on prompt engineering and these roles, visit

[28](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_28). “Messages and Roles.” Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-generation/#messages-and-roles).

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0768-02)

```
https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/prompt-engineering
```

##### Extracting Key Points

To extract key points from the transcript, we use class `OpenAIUtilities`’ `chat` method but lines 36–45 change the `"system"` prompt to ask OpenAI to generate a list of the top five key points from the original audio transcription. In our experience, the resulting key points are sometimes returned as a numbered list and sometimes as a bullet list, so we explicitly asked for a numbered list in this prompt.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0768-01)

```
34         // get key points with OpenAI's gpt-4o model
35         System.out.println("EXTRACT KEY POINTS FROM A TRANSCRIPT");
36         String keyPoints = OpenAIUtilities.chat("gpt-4o",
37            List.of(
38               new Message("system", """
39                  Given a transcript of a technical presentation, identify
40                  the top 5 key points and present them as a numbered list.
41                  For each point, use a concise, direct, clear, and
42                  straightforward sentence. Avoid prepositional phrases."""),
43               new Message("user", transcript)
44            )
45         );
46         System.out.printf("%s%n", keyPoints);
47      }
48   }
```

```
EXTRACT KEY POINTS FROM A TRANSCRIPT
1\. The lesson covers new Java programming features from versions Java 10 to
Java 22 with a preview of Java 23.
2\. Java's recent features include executing source files directly and simpli-
fied main methods for easier coding.
3\. Java 14 introduced switch expressions with powerful pattern matching capa-
bilities.
4\. Java 21's sequenced collections offer unified method naming and reverse
iteration for ease of use.
5\. Sealed classes and interfaces in Java give hierarchy designers complete
control over subclassing and implementation.
```

#### 19.4.2 Sentiment Analysis

[Figure 19.2](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig02) analyzes the sentiment of the text in `transcript.txt`. This example uses our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `chat` method with the `"gpt-4o"` model again, but lines 21–25 change the `"system"` prompt to ask for a chat completion that analyzes the sentiment of the original transcript and explains how the model came to its conclusion. The model’s response indicates that the transcript’s sentiment is neutral. It also broke its conclusion into segments, indicating:

*   the content is “Objective and Informative,”

*   the speaker has a “Lack of Personal Emotional Expression,”

*   the speaker maintains a “Balanced Tone” and

*   the speaker provides “Constructive and Supportive Notes,”

each with explanatory notes.

ANALYZE SENTIMENT
The sentiment of the presentation transcript is **neutral**.

### Analysis:

1\. **Objective and Informative**:
   - The content is highly objective and focused on providing information
about the new features and updates in the upcoming Java course.
   - There is a detailed breakdown of what will be covered in the lesson, in-
cluding the structure and individual topics from fundamentals to high-end
Java concepts.

2\. **Lack of Personal Emotional Expression**:
   - The speaker does not express personal emotions or opinions that would
indicate a positive or negative sentiment.
   - The language is professional and focused on conveying the course de-
tails.

3\. **Balanced Tone**:
   - The transcript maintains a balanced tone throughout, avoiding any emo-
tionally charged language.
   - There are no exclamatory remarks or emotionally connotative words which
could sway the sentiment in either a positive or negative direction.

4\. **Constructive and Supportive Notes**:
   - The speaker provides guidance on how to reach out for any questions and
mentions the availability of updates and support, which is informative but
does not express a particularly strong emotional sentiment.

Conclusively, the presentation's purpose is to inform the audience about the
structure and content of the upcoming Java course updates, rather than to
evoke a particular emotional response. Therefore, it is best categorized as
**neutral**.

##### Markdown-Formatted Responses

The chat completion API often returns responses in **markdown format**, as it did when we ran this example. Markdown is a lightweight formatting language that uses text delimiters to indicate formatting instructions. Various code editors and IDEs can read markdown formatting delimiters and render the text in HTML (web-page) or other formats. The following are examples of markdown formatting that a markdown-enabled tool would format:

*   **```` ``` ````** delimits blocks of program code that should be formatted in a fixed-width code font,

*   **`` ` ``** delimits code words that should be formatted in a code font inside non-code paragraphs,

*   `**` delimits text that should be formatted in bold for emphasis

*   numbers starting from `1`, followed by a period and a space indicate items in a numbered list, and

*   items starting with a `-` followed by a space indicate a bullet in a bullet list.

The website [`markdownguide.org`](http://markdownguide.org) provides a Getting Started guide at

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0770-01)

```
https://www.markdownguide.org/getting-started/
```

and an overview of markdown syntax at

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0770-02)

```
https://www.markdownguide.org/basic-syntax/
```

To experiment with markdown, check out the free online markdown editor with side-by-side live content rendering at [`https://dillinger.io`](https://dillinger.io).

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0772-03)

```
ACCESSIBLE DESCRIPTION OF A DIAGRAM
The image is a highly detailed diagram showing the flow of control within a
logical structure of a Java 'for' loop, using the Unified Modeling Language
(UML) Activity Diagram standards. This diagram visually represents the se-
quence and operations involved in executing a 'for' loop in Java, a common
programming language used for building applications.

### Visual Breakdown:
1\. **Diagram Format:** The activity diagram is structured to use standard UML
elements such as nodes, activities, decision points, transitions, and annota-
tions for depicting the logical flow.

2\. **For Loop Structure:**
   - **Initialization:** The diagram starts with an initial node, indicating
the start of the logical process. This initial node flows into an activity
node representing the 'for' loop's initialization section (e.g., int i = 0).
   - **Condition Checking:** The next activity depicts the condition that
must be met for the loop to execute. This is shown with a diamond-shaped de-
cision node. It checks if the loop condition is true (e.g., i < 10), indicat-
ing whether the loop should continue or terminate.

   - **Loop Body:** From the true branch of the decision node, the flow pro-
ceeds to an activity node representing the loop body where actions (e.g.,
logic or statements) are executed if the condition is satisfied. These ac-
tions are enclosed within a rectangular activity node.
   - **Iteration:** A control flow arrow then typically points from the loop
body back to a small circular node, symbolizing the iterative aspect of the
loop (e.g., i++), where loop control variables are updated.

   - **Re-checking Condition:** After updating, control returns to the deci-
sion node to re-evaluate the condition.

3\. **End of Loop:** If the condition is no longer satisfied, the control flow
follows the false branch from the decision node, leading to a final node.
This terminal node represents the end of the loop operation.

4\. **Annotations:** The diagram may include UML notes or text boxes that pro-
vide additional context or explanations at various stages of the loop for
clarity. These are depicted generally as small rectangles connected to the
relevant part of the diagram by dashed lines.

5\. **Flow Arrows:** The flow of control is indicated with arrows that con-
nect nodes and activities, forming a clear path illustrating the iterative
process of the 'for' loop.

6\. **Styling and Color:** The diagram would use distinct shapes for decision
nodes (diamond), activity nodes (rounded rectangles), and annotations to
avoid confusion and provide a clear visual means to follow the logic.

Overall, this diagram serves as a tool to understand the execution flow of a
'for' loop in Java, detailing the iterative process in a structured graphi-
cal format. Each component is meticulously laid out to ensure the entire
mechanism is visually and logically represented.
```

31   }

#### 19.4.4 Language Detection and Translation

Inter-language translation is a challenging problem in natural language processing and AI. With AI advances in large language models, genAIs can translate between languages instantly. Natural language translation has a wide range of uses, including:^([30](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_30a))

[30](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_30). *ChatGPT* response to “Provide common uses for natural language translation.” December 14, 2024\. [`https://chatgpt.com`](https://chatgpt.com).

*   **Cross-language communication:** Facilitating conversations between people speaking different languages.

*   **Global business operations:** Translating documents, websites and customer communications for international markets.

*   **Tourism:** Helping travelers communicate in foreign countries using.

*   **Education:** Enabling students and researchers to access academic content in different languages.

*   **Healthcare:** Assisting healthcare providers in understanding patients who speak different languages.

*   **Diplomatic relations:** Supporting negotiations and communications between countries, such as at the United Nations.

*   **Entertainment:** Translating subtitles, scripts and media for global audiences.

The program in [Fig. 19.4](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig04) translates text among spoken languages. In the OpenAI APIs, translation is simply a chat request. Our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `translate` method (called in lines 15, 20, 25 and 31; discussed in [Section 19.9.8](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec34)) is similar to the class’s `chat` method ([Section 19.9.5](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec31)), but `translate` sends a `"system"` message to the OpenAI model indicating that

*   it’s an expert in natural language translation, and

*   it should `translate` the text specified in our `translate` method’s second argument to the language specified in the third argument.

For this demonstration, we translate two English sentences to Spanish and Japanese, then translate the Spanish and Japanese versions back to English. Note that the final results had the same first sentence as the original English text, but the second sentences were different (though similar).

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0775-01)

#### 19.4.5 Code Generation

Generative AIs can write code in many programming languages, but their code quality can vary substantially from well-written, functioning code that does what your prompt described to code that does not work. So, thoroughly test and verify any code genAIs provide.

[Figure 19.5](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig05) uses our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `chat` method (lines 20–32) with the `"gpt-4o"` model, a `"system"` message (lines 22–23) telling the model it’s an expert Java programmer and a `"user"` message (lines 24–30) discussing the Java program the model should write. Recall from [Section 19.4.2](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec11) that chat completions often return responses in markdown format, as in this program’s output, which includes Java code with an explanation of how it works. The program the Java code into `RollDie.java` so we can compile and run it later. Lines 38–40 extract the Java code from the response using a regular expression that matches all text between the markdown delimiters ````"```java"````, which begins a Java-code block and ````"```"````, which terminates a code block. The subexpression `"(.*?)"` captures all the text between the delimiters. `Pattern.DOTALL` enables the pattern to match multiple lines of text. Lines 43–48 write the code into `RollDie.java`—line 46 extracts the text that matched the pattern.^([31](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_31a))

[31](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_31). Another approach would be to prompt the model to return only the Java code with no additional formatting so you can write it directly to a file.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0777-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 19.5: CodeGenerationDemo.java
 2   // Generating code for a die-rolling simulation.
 3   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities;
 4   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities.Message;
 5   import java.nio.file.Files;
 6   import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption;
 7   import java.nio.file.Path;
 8   import java.util.List;
 9   import java.util.regex.Matcher;
10   import java.util.regex.Pattern;
11
12   public class CodeGenerationDemo {
13      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
14         // path to store Java source-code that's generated
15         Path codePath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
16            "Documents", "examples", "ch19", "resources", "outputs");
17
18         // generate Java code with OpenAI's gpt-4o model
19         System.out.println("GENERATE DIE ROLLING SIMULATION CODE");
20         String response = OpenAIUtilities.chat("gpt-4o",
21            List.of(
22               new Message("system",
23                  "You are an expert programmer in Java's latest version."),
24               new Message("user", """
25                  Create a Java class named RollDie that simulates rolling
26                  a die 600,000,000 times as quickly as possible. Summarize
27                  the frequencies and display them left-aligned in a
28                  two-column format with the column heads "Face" and
29                  "Frequency". Avoid loops. In the code, use 3-space indents
30                  and restrict each code line to 74 characters or fewer.""")
31            )
32         );
33         System.out.printf("%s%n%n", response);
34
35         // use regex to extract the code and write it to disk;
36         // the Pattern extracts all the text between the delimiters
37         // "```java" and "```"
38         Pattern pattern =
39            Pattern.compile("```java\\s+(.*?)```", Pattern.DOTALL);
40         Matcher matcher = pattern.matcher(response);
41
42         // if there was a match, write it into the file RollDie.java
43         if (matcher.find()) {
44            Files.writeString(
45               Path.of(codePath.toString(), "RollDie.java"),
46               matcher.group(1).trim(),
47               StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING);
48         }
49      }
50   }
```

```
GENERATE DIE ROLLING SIMULATION CODE
To simulate rolling 600,000,000 dice without using loops, we can leverage
Java's streams and parallel computing capabilities to perform the task
efficiently. Below is a basic implementation of your requirements using Java:

```java
import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom;
import java.util.stream.LongStream;
public class RollDie {
   public static void main(String[] args) {
      final int numberOfRolls = 600_000_000;
      final int numberOfSides = 6;

      // Array to hold frequency of each face
      long[] frequencies = new long[numberOfSides];

      // Simulate dice rolls
      LongStream.range(0, numberOfRolls).parallel().forEach(i -> {
         int result = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, numberOfSides);
         synchronized (frequencies) { // Synchronize updates to the array
            frequencies[result]++;
         }
      });

      // Display results
      System.out.printf("%-5s%-10s%n", "Face", "Frequency");

      for (int i = 0; i < numberOfSides; i++) {
         System.out.printf("%-5d%-10d%n", i + 1, frequencies[i]);
      }
   }
}
```

### Explanation:

1\. **Array Initialization**: We create an array `frequencies` to hold the
count of each face result (from 1 to 6).

2\. **Dice Roll Simulation**:
   - We use a `LongStream` to simulate 600 million rolls.
   - With `parallel()`, the stream processes elements in parallel, which can
significantly speed up processing on multi-core processors.
   - For each roll, a random number between 0 and 5 is generated using
`ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, numberOfSides)`, representing the
dice faces (considering array index starts at 0).

3\. **Synchronization**:
   - The updates to the `frequencies` array are synchronized to prevent con-
current modification issues, as multiple threads may attempt to update the
same index simultaneously.

4\. **Result Display**:
   - Finally, the results are printed with a two-column format ("Face" and
"Frequency"), with fields left-aligned.
This approach takes advantage of Java's parallel processing to handle an in-
tensive number of dice rolls efficiently, while avoiding explicit loops by
utilizing parallel streams.
```

##### Other AI Code Capabilities

In addition to writing programs from scratch in various programming languages, many genAIs can also perform coding tasks like:

1.  **Generating code from diagrams/pseudocode**—Convert UML diagrams or flowcharts to code or convert pseudocode to code.

2.  **Improving performance**—Improve speed, reduce memory use and parallelize.

3.  **Debugging**—Locate and fix compilation errors, runtime errors (exceptions) and logic errors.

4.  **Refactoring**—Simplify code, split code into smaller reusable methods and classes, rename code elements and extract repeated code into a method.

5.  **Improving readability**—Rename variables, methods and classes and tune existing comments.

6.  **Code review**—Check code for style, code smells,^([35](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_35a)) adherence to clean code guidelines,^([36](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_36a)) adherence to SOLID principles^([37](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_37a),[38](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_38a)) and adherence to latest idioms.

#### 19.4.6 Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Structured Outputs

You’ve seen that generative AIs can determine what a text is about and summarize information. A key aspect of this is a natural language processing (NLP) task called **named entity recognition (NER)**, which attempts to locate and categorize items like dates, times, quantities, places, people, things, organizations and more. Our next example demonstrates a chat request asking the model to perform NER on a body of text. We ask the model to use the OntoNotes Named Entity Tag Set.^([39](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_39a)) To make the results more convenient to process, we provide the OpenAI API with the exact JSON response format we wish to receive—known as **structured output**.

[39](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_39). Linguistic Data Consortium, OntoNotes Release 5.0, LDC2013T19 (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania, 2013). Accessed March 8, 2024\. [`https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2013T19`](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2013T19).

##### JSON Output for Named Entities

We’d like the chat-completion API to return its response in the JSON format shown below:

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0780-01)

```
{
   "entities": [
      {
         "text": "Tim Berners-Lee",
         "tag: "PERSON"
      },
      {
         "text": "CERN",
         "tag: "ORG"
      },
      ...
   ]
}
```

This has one `"entities"` attribute in which the value is a JSON array of JSON objects. Each JSON object in the array contains

*   a `"text"` attribute representing a named entity identified by the model and

*   a `"tag"` attribute indicating that named entity’s type.

##### Calling Class `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `chatWithStructuredOutput` Method

[Figure 19.6](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig06) uses our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `chatWithStructuredOutput` method ([Section 19.9.9](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec35)) to analyze text in the file `web.txt` containing information about the World Wide Web from [Chapter 1](#ch01.xhtml_ch01). This file is located in the `resources` subfolder with this chapter’s examples. Method `chatWithStructuredOutput` receives as arguments:

*   The OpenAI model to use (`"gpt-4o"` ),

*   a `"system"` message telling the model it’s an expert in named entity recognition and that it should return the results in the specified JSON format,

*   a `"user"` message containing the text in which to identify the named entities and

*   a `Class` object—`OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities.class` (line 29) is used by the compiler to create a `Class<OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities>` object that Simple-OpenAI will use to determine the JSON response format.

The method deserializes the model’s JSON response and returns a `NamedEntities` object containing a `List<NamedEntity>` called `entities`. Lines 37–38 get the `List` then use its `forEach` method to output each `NamedEntity`’s `text` and `tag` attributes. The classes `NamedEntities` and `NamedEntity` (discussed in [Section 19.9.9](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec35)) are nested `record` classes in class `OpenAIUtilities`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0781-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 19.6: NamedEntityRecognitionDemo.java
 2   // Identifying named entities and obtaining them as structured outputs.
 3   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities;
 4   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities.Message;
 5   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities;
 6   import java.nio.file.Files;
 7   import java.nio.file.Path;
 8   import java.util.List;
 9
10   public class NamedEntityRecognitionDemo {
11      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
12         // load web.txt
13         Path transcriptPath = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
14            "Documents", "examples", "ch19", "resources", "web.txt");
15         String text = Files.readString(transcriptPath);
16
17         // create a request to obtain named entities
18         NamedEntities results = OpenAIUtilities.chatWithStructuredOutput(
19            "gpt-4o",
20            List.of(
21               new Message("system", """
22                  You are an expert in named entity recognition (NER) using
23                  the OntoNotes 5.0 NER tag set. Analyze the following text
24                  and return the named entities in the specified structured
25                  JSON format. Do not include any additional information in
26                  your JSON response."""),
27               new Message("user", text)
28            ),
29            OpenAIUtilities.NamedEntities.class
30         );
31
32         // display source text
33         System.out.printf("SOURCE TEXT:%n%s%n%n", text);
34
35         // display named entities
36         System.out.println("ENTITIES:");
37         results.entities().forEach(entity ->
38            System.out.printf("%s: %s%n", entity.text(), entity.tag()));
39      }
40   }
```

### 19.5 Speech Synthesis and Speech Recognition

Let’s demonstrate the OpenAI API’s speech recognition and speech synthesis capabilities, which transcribe speech to text and synthesize speech from text, respectively. The speech-to-text model can transcribe speech in many spoken languages. The text-to-speech models can produce speech in many languages using nine natural-sounding voices.

#### 19.5.1 English Speech-to-Text for Audio Transcription

[Figure 19.7](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig07) performs speech recognition on an audio file, transcribing it to text. Our class `OpenAIUtilities`’ `speechToText` method ([Section 19.9.10](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec36)) uses the Simple-OpenAI library and **OpenAI’s Whisper model** (**`"whisper-1"`**) to transcribe an audio file that’s uploaded to the model. Whisper auto-detects the natural language and returns the transcription. Lines 20–21 pass the model’s name and the audio file’s path to `speechToText`, and line 22 outputs the response. We include a portion of the transcript here, splitting the output into paragraphs for readability. Lines 25–29 write the transcription to the file `WhatsNewInJavaOverview.txt` in the `resources/outputs` subfolder of the chapter’s examples folder. The result was nearly 100% accurate, though it spelled our last name, Deitel, in an email address and URL phonetically as `"dytel"`.

#### 19.5.2 Text-to-Speech

A challenge in natural language processing (NLP) is that there are over 7000 natural languages worldwide.^([40](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_40a)) According to the CIA World Fact Book, the top 11 languages alone account for 44.5% of the world’s population.^([41](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_41a)) **OpenAI’s Audio API** can synthesize speech from text in nine voices (`"alloy"`, `"ash"`, `"coral"`, `"echo"`, `"fable"`, `"onyx"`, `"nova"`, `"sage"` and `"shimmer"`) across 57 languages. OpenAI’s text-to-speech documentation provides audio samples for each voice and lists the supported spoken languages:

[40](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_40). Babbel. “How Many Languages Are There in the World?” Babbel Magazine. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.babbel.com/en/magazine/how-many-languages-are-there-in-the-world`](https://www.babbel.com/en/magazine/how-many-languages-are-there-in-the-world).

[41](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_41). Central Intelligence Agency. “World: People and Society.” The World Factbook. Accessed February 18, 2025\. [`https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/world/#people-and-society`](https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/world/#people-and-society).

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0784-01)

```
https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/text-to-speech
```

The voices are optimized for English but also work for other languages. [Figure 19.8](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig08) uses our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `textToSpeech` method ([Section 19.9.11](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec37)) to synthesize speech using the **OpenAI** **`"tts-1-hd"`** **model**. Our method’s arguments are as follows:

*   The first argument is the model to use—`"tts-1-hd"` returns higher-quality audio than the quicker `"tts-1"` model.

*   The second argument is the text to synthesize into speech.

*   The third argument (`"onyx"`) is the voice to use.

*   The last argument is the filename where the synthesized audio should be stored.

The Audio API returns synthesized speech as an MP3 audio file by default. MP3 is widely supported across platforms and balances file size with audio quality.^([42](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_42a)) The Audio API also supports several other audio formats. We write this example’s synthesized speech files into the `resources/outputs` folder with this chapter’s examples. Simply open the files `english.mp3`, `spanish.mp3` and `japanese.mp3` to listen to the synthesized speech.

[42](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_42). “MP3.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MP3`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MP3).

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0785-01)

### 19.6 Image Generation

[Figure 19.9](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig09) uses the **OpenAI Dall-E API** to generate original images. Lines 18–19, 23–24 and 28–29 call class `OpenAUtilities`’s `image` method ([Figure 19.9](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig09).12), which requires three arguments:

*   the model to use to generate images (**`"dall-e-3"`**),

*   a text prompt describing the image to create and

*   the filename where the program should store the image.

The `"dall-e-3"` model currently supports images in the following resolutions:^([44](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_44a))

[44](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_44). “Image generation.” Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images)`.`

*   1024-by-1024 pixels (the default),

*   1024-by-1792 pixels or

*   1792-by-1024 pixels.

You may request images in standard or high-definition (HD) quality. HD images, which our `image` method requests, provide more detail but take longer to generate. The model returns the image in the **PNG format**, which is widely used on the web for its lossless compression and ability to represent millions of colors.^([45](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_45a)) With **lossless compression**, the image’s original information can be restored from its compressed representation.

[45](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_45). “PNG.” Wikipedia. Wikimedia Foundation. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG).

##### How Does ChatGPT Ensure Images Are Original?

We prompted ChatGPT with “How do you ensure that the images Dall-E creates are original?” ChatGPT responded as follows:^([46](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_46a)) DALL-E generates images using machine learning models trained on large datasets of publicly available images and text, not by copying or manipulating existing images directly. Here's how originality is maintained:

[46](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_46). ChatGPT in response to “How do you ensure that the images Dall-E creates are original?” October 14, 2024, [`https://chatgpt.com/`](https://chatgpt.com/).

1.  **Generative Process**: DALL-E uses a process called “**diffusion**,” where the model starts from random noise and iteratively refines it based on the given text prompt. This ensures that the **output is generated from scratch each time**. The model **doesn’t retrieve or edit existing images** but instead **creates entirely new ones** based on patterns it has learned from its training data.

2.  **No Direct Copying**: DALL-E **doesn’t store specific images from its training data**. It learns to understand relationships between textual descriptions and visual features, but the **outputs are not replicas of any particular image in the dataset**. As a result, the images it creates are novel combinations of visual elements that match the given prompts.

3.  **Ethical Guidelines**: The developers of DALL-E implement safeguards and policies to ensure the model adheres to ethical standards, such as **not creating content that is offensive, harmful, or violates copyright**. Additionally, it’s designed to **avoid creating recognizable likenesses of specific individuals or copyrighted works**, focusing instead on **generating creative, original content**.

4.  **Diversity in Outputs**: The same prompt can result in different images across multiple generations. This variability demonstrates that **the images aren’t pre-generated or stored but are the result of a creative, generative process every time**.

5.  **Training Data**: The model is trained on large, diverse datasets, which include **publicly available images**, but it **doesn’t reproduce them**. Instead, it **learns high-level concepts and relationships between images and text**, which it uses to **create original art in response to new prompts**.

If you’re concerned about originality and copyright, it’s always advisable to **review the specific use cases for the generated images** and consider any legal implications based on how the images will be used (e.g., **commercial vs. personal use**).

### 19.7 Video

This section presents an application that uses multiple OpenAI APIs to create closed captions for a video, demonstrates OpenAI’s Sora video generator and introduces several other powerful video genAIs.

#### 19.7.1 Generating Video Closed Captions

Our next example is a multimodal application (speech, text and video playback) that:

*   uploads a video’s audio track,

*   transcribes it into a JSON format containing timestamps that can be used with the transcribed text to generate **closed captions** (also called **subtitles**), then

*   uses a chat-completion request to generate those closed captions in **VTT (Video Text Track) format**.^([47](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_47a))

[47](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_47). “WebVTT.” Wikipedia. Last modified December 31, 2024\. Accessed February 25, 2025\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebVTT`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WebVTT).

The following screen captures contain a couple of this app’s generated captions overlaid on the original video.

![Images](graphics/f0790-01.jpg)

[Figure 19.10](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig10) call our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `speechToVTT` method (lines 22–23; discussed in [Section 19.9.13](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec39)) to create the VTT captions corresponding to the audio in the file `ImplicitClass.m4a`. Currently, you cannot upload the video file directly to OpenAI to have it generate closed captions. However, you can perform the following steps, which we’ve implemented in the `speechToVTT` method:

1.  Use a tool like QuickTime on macOS or the cross-platform VLC Media Player ([`https://www.videolan.org/`](https://www.videolan.org/)) to save the video’s audio track as an audio file.

2.  Pass the audio file to the `"whisper-1"` model to perform a transcription. In this example, `speechToVTT` explicitly asks the model to produce a verbose JSON formatted response, causing the model to return a collection of transcription segments. Each segment contains a piece of the transcription and the timestamps where that piece starts and ends in the audio file.

3.  Build a `String` containing the segments with their start and end timestamps.

4.  Submit a chat-completion request with the VTT format requirements, asking the chat API to generate captions in the VTT format for video players. We save this to a VTT file.

5.  Open the video in an application that supports closed captions and play it. For this example, we used the cross-platform VLC Media Player, which allows you to indicate where the VTT file is located. Like the other outputs in this chapter, we write the VTT file to the `resources/outputs` subfolder of this chapter’s examples folder.

[Figure 19.10](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig10)’s output contains a portion of the VTT-format closed caption text that was written to the standard output and to the file `ImplicitClass.vtt`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0791-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 19.10: SpeechToVTTDemo.java
 2   // Transcribing the audio track from a video and creating closed captions.
 3   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities;
 4
 5   import java.nio.file.Files;
 6   import java.nio.file.Path;
 7   import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption;
 8
 9   public class SpeechToVTTDemo {
10      public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
11         // get path to resources folder
12         Path resourcesFolder = Path.of(System.getProperty("user.home"),
13            "Documents", "examples", "ch19", "resources");
14
15         // get path to audio file ImplicitClass.m4a
16         Path audioPath =
17            Path.of(resourcesFolder.toString(), "ImplicitClass.m4a");
18
19         // convert speech to closed captions with OpenAI's whisper-1 model
20         System.out.println(
21            "Transcribing audio and creating VTT captions file...");
22         String captions =
23            OpenAIUtilities.speechToVTT("whisper-1", audioPath);
24         System.out.printf("CAPTIONS:%n%s%n", captions);
25
26         // output the captions to a .vtt file
27         var captionsPath = Path.of(resourcesFolder.toString(),
28            "outputs", "ImplicitClass.vtt");
29         Files.writeString(captionsPath, captions.trim(),
30            StandardOpenOption.CREATE,
31            StandardOpenOption.TRUNCATE_EXISTING);
32      }
33   }
```

#### 19.7.2 Sora

In February 2024, OpenAI announced their **Sora video generator**.^([48](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_48a)) Though it was not the first AI video generation tool, Sora sparked a flurry of activity in the genAI video space with many powerful video models released throughout 2024—some free, some with free tiers and some paid. in December 2024, OpenAI released Sora to ChatGPT subscribers^([49](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_49a)) for use at

[48](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_48). “Sora,” OpenAI, February 2024\. Accessed February 27, 2025\. [`https://openai.com/index/sora/`](https://openai.com/index/sora/).

[49](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_49). “Sora Is Here,” OpenAI. December 9, 2024\. Accessed February 27, 2025\. [`https://openai.com/index/sora-is-here/`](https://openai.com/index/sora-is-here/).

```
https://sora.com
```

At the time of this writing, Sora does not have an API. So, you can use it only via its web interface, which supports creating videos by

*   supplying a text-only prompt describing the video to generate,

*   supplying an image or video clip on which to base a generated video, optionally providing additional guidance via a text prompt, or

*   using the Storyboard tool for more precise control over a video’s production.

With the Storyboard, you can place images, video clips and text prompts in individual video frames along a timeline and Sora will use them to guide generation of a video. You also can take a video you generated previously and “re-cut” it. This opens a generated video in the storyboard so you can edit aspects of it.^([50](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_50a))

[50](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_50). “Generating Videos on Sora,” OpenAI Help Center. Accessed February 27, 2025\. [`https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9957612-generating-videos-on-sora`](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9957612-generating-videos-on-sora).

### 19.8 Moderation

The **OpenAI moderation API**^([51](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_51a)) helps developers identify and filter potentially harmful or inappropriate text and image content. The **`"omni-moderation-latest"`** **model** evaluates text and image inputs for harassment, hate speech, violence, self-harm and sexually explicit content—several of these also have more specific subcategories. For each category and sub-category, the response contains:

[51](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_51). OpenAI, “[Moderation](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev1sec8),” OpenAI Platform Documentation. Accessed February 26, 2025\. [`https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation).

*   a `boolean` indicating whether that category was detected and

*   a confidence score from 0 to 1—higher values indicate more offensive content.

For a list of the moderation API’s reporting categories, visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0794-02)

```
https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation
```

Apps can use the results to ensure user safety and comply with ethical guidelines. For information on OpenAI’s usage policies and guidelines, visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0794-03)

```
https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/
```

##### Demonstrating Moderation

[Figure 19.11](#ch19.xhtml_ch19fig11) presents a simple example of using the OpenAI moderation API. The program obtains a prompt from the user, then line 14 calls our `OpenAIUtilities` class’s `static` method `checkPrompt` ([Section 19.9.14](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec40)) to evaluate the prompt for offensive content using the moderation API. Method `checkPrompt` returns a Simple-OpenAI `ModerationResult` object. Line 16 calls its `getFlagged` method to check whether the prompt was flagged. If so, lines 21–46 show the individual moderation categories and their scores. Lines 21–22 get a `ModerationResult.Category` object containing the categories’ `boolean` values and a `ModerationResult.CategoryScore` object containing the categories scores. Both classes provide identically named *get* methods to obtain the `boolean` values and scores (called in lines 32–46).^([52](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_52a))

[52](#ch19.xhtml_fn19_52). At the time of this writing (Simple-OpenAI version 3.18.0), both the `Category` and `CategoryScore` classes contain the misspelled method `getViolencGraphic`, which should be `getViolenceGraphic`. This bug was reported and slated to be fixed in the next Simple-OpenAI release.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0795-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 19.11: ModerationDemo.java
 2   // Using the OpenAI moderation API to check for offensive content.
 3   import deitel.openai.OpenAIUtilities;
 4   import java.util.Scanner;
 5
 6   public class ModerationDemo {
 7      public static void main(String[] args) {
 8         var input = new Scanner(System.in);
 9
10         System.out.print("Enter prompt (or "exit"): ");
11         String prompt = input.nextLine();
12
13         while (!prompt.toLowerCase().equals("exit")) {
14            var result = OpenAIUtilities.checkPrompt(prompt);
15
16            if (!result.getFlagged()) {
17               System.out.println(
18                  "Prompt not flagged for offensive content");
19            }
20            else {
21               var categories = result.getCategories();
22               var scores = result.getCategoryScores();
23
24               // display report
25               System.out.println("Offensive content categories & scores:");
26               System.out.printf("""
27                  harassment: %b %.2f; threatening: %b %.2f
28                  hate: %b %.2f; threatening: %b %.2f
29                  self-harm: %b %.2f; instructions: %b %.2f; intent: %b %.2f
30                  sexual: %b %.2f; minors: %b %.2f
31                  violence: %b %.2f; graphic: %b %.2f%n""",
32                  categories.getHarassment(), scores.getHarassment(),
33                  categories.getHarassmentThreatening(),
34                  scores.getHarassmentThreatening(),
35                  categories.getHate(), scores.getHate(),
36                  categories.getHateThreatening(),
37                  scores.getHateThreatening(),
38                  categories.getSelfHarm(), scores.getSelfHarm(),
39                  categories.getSelfHarmInstructions(),
40                  scores.getSelfHarmInstructions(),
41                  categories.getSelfHarmIntent(), scores.getSelfHarmIntent(),
42                  categories.getSexual(), scores.getSexual(),
43                  categories.getSexualMinors(), scores.getSexualMinors(),
44                  categories.getViolence(), scores.getViolence(),
45                  categories.getViolencGraphic(),
46                  scores.getViolencGraphic());
47            }
48
49            System.out.print("\nEnter prompt (exit to terminate): ");
50            prompt = input.nextLine();
51         }
52      }
53   }
```

hate: false 0.01; threatening: false 0.00

sexual: false 0.00; minors: false 0.00

**Fig. 19.11** | Using the OpenAI moderation API to check for offensive content.

##### Sample Output

To test the moderation API, we began with the statement,

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0796-01)

```
I would die for an ice cream sundae right now.
```

In this sentence, the word `"die"` is used as hyperbole to emphasize the person’s extreme enthusiasm for finding an ice cream sundae immediately.

To cause the moderation API to flag content, we needed a statement that could be interpreted as offensive. We prompted ChatGPT to list some phrases that were not overly offensive but would be likely to be flagged and used the following suggested one:

```
I'm going to make them pay.
```

The moderation API interpreted the statement as offensive, indicating that it tested positive for violence with a score of 0.42.

The output lines containing multiple categories list a main category and subcategories. For example, the output line

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0796-02)

```
harassment: false 0.25; threatening: false 0.33
```

shows the `"harassment"` category and its subcategory "`harassment/threatening"`, which we shorthanded as `"threatening"`. Interestingly, the moderation API gave scores of `0.25` and `0.33` for the categories `"harassment"` and "`harassment/threatening"`, but did not flag those as `true`. Each category has a minimum threshold for which it reports `true` but the exact values are not published in the moderation API’s documentation.

### 19.9 Class `OpenAIUtilities`

In this chapter’s examples, we focused on each application’s genAI concepts, encapsulating the details of using the Simple-OpenAI library to interact with the OpenAI APIs in this section’s `OpenAIUtilities` class. We present this class’s methods and nested types in the order the examples used them. As discussed in [Section 19.3.2](#ch19.xhtml_ch19lev2sec8), the `libs` subfolder with this chapter’s examples contains a JAR file containing the compiled `OpenAIUtilities` class. For those who wish to modify this class, we discuss the IntelliJ IDEA project we used to manage the class and its dependencies in our IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition test-drive at [`https://deitel.com/javafp5`](https://deitel.com/javafp5). We also provide the project with the chapter’s examples.

#### 19.9.1 Builder Design Pattern

[Section 18.6.2](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec13) introduced the builder design pattern—a common technique for constructing complex objects step-by-step via chained method calls. When working with the Simple-OpenAI Library, you’ll use this pattern to

*   create a `SimpleOpenAI` object for performing the interactions with the OpenAI APIs and

*   to formulate the OpenAI API requests.

##### Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Execution

In this chapter’s examples, the programs issue OpenAI API requests and await their entire responses before outputting the results. The Simple-OpenAI library supports asynchronous programming. When you submit a request, Simple-OpenAI returns a **`Completable-Future`**, which is a `Future` ([Section 18.7.1](#ch18.xhtml_ch18lev2sec15)) with additional capabilities. Some features of `CompletableFuture` include:

*   combining multiple asynchronous tasks then handling their results collectively when they become available,

*   providing “callback” methods that are called automatically to process results when a task completes and

*   more control over a task’s lifecycle, such as manually terminating a task.

Each method in our `OpenAIUtilities` class calls a `CompletableFuture`’s `join` method to synchronously await the results. For more information on `CompletableFuture`s, visit:

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0797-01)

```
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs//api/java.base/java/
   util/concurrent/CompletableFuture.html
https://www.baeldung.com/java-completablefuture
https://dzone.com/articles/20-examples-of-using-javas-
   completablefuture
```

This class is defined in its own IntelliJ project as a library that we import into this chapter’s examples. We split the class into parts for discussion purposes. To enable our apps to use class `OpenAIUtilities`, they must be able to import the class from our custom library. For this reason, we placed this class `OpenAIUtilities` in the custom `deitel.openai` package by using a **`package`** **statement** (line 4), which must appear in a Java source-code file before any `import` statements. Lines 7–22 import the Simple-OpenAI library classes—we discuss each as we use it.

#### 19.9.3 Nested `record` Class `Message`

The `record` class `Message` (line 37) groups an OpenAI `role` (`"system"`, `"user"` or `"assistant"`) and its corresponding `content`. We’ll turn each `Message` object into an object of a Simple-OpenAI class that represents a message with the specified role. Simple-OpenAI, in turn, will convert these to messages sent to OpenAI’s web services with our requests.

[Click here to view code image](#ch19_images.xhtml_f0799-01)

```

36      // and corresponding content to this class's chat and translate methods
