exports java.util.zip
exports javax.crypto
exports javax.crypto.interfaces
exports javax.crypto.spec
exports javax.net
exports javax.net.ssl
exports javax.security.auth
exports javax.security.auth.callback
exports javax.security.auth.login
exports javax.security.auth.spi
exports javax.security.auth.x500
exports javax.security.cert
```

The complete output of the preceding command lists lots of additional `java.base` module information. The following presents a portion of the remaining output with sample lines from each category of information.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0878-02)

```
...
uses java.util.spi.CalendarDataProvider
uses java.util.spi.CurrencyNameProvider
...
provides java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider
   with jdk.internal.jrtfs.JrtFileSystemProvider
...
qualified exports com.sun.security.ntlm to java.security.sasl
...
contains jdk.internal
contains jdk.internal.access.foreign
...
```

The `uses` lines like

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0878-03)

```
uses java.util.spi.CalendarDataProvider
```

indicate there are types in the `java.base` module’s packages which use objects that implement various service-provider interfaces. The `provides`…`with`

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0879-01)

```
provides java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider
   with jdk.internal.jrtfs.JrtFileSystemProvider
```

indicates that this module’s `jdk.internal.jrtfs` package contains a service-provider implementation class named `JrtFileSystemProvider` that implements the service-provider interface `FileSystemProvider` from package `java.nio.file.spi`. [Section 21.9](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev1sec9) presents a substantial example demonstrating that service-provider interfaces and implementations create loosely coupled system components for systems that are easier to develop, maintain and evolve than tightly coupled systems.

The `qualified exports`…`to` lines like

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0879-02)

```
qualified exports com.sun.security.ntlm to java.security.sasl
```

indicate that the `java.base` module `exports` a given package (`com.sun.security.ntlm`) only to a specified module (`java.security.sasl`). The `java.base` module has many of these qualified exports. Packages listed in such exports may be read only by the designated modules in the comma-separated list after the `to` keyword. In the JDK, such qualified exports are used for packages containing JDK internal implementations of types that developers should not use.

The `contains` lines like

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0879-03)

```
contains com.sun.crypto.provider
```

specify that the module contains packages that are not exported for use in other modules. Note that `contains` is not a directive like `requires` or `exports` that you can use in your modules. Rather, it’s information inserted by the compiler to indicate that a module contains the specified package. The JVM uses this information to improve performance when it loads classes from those packages at runtime.^([12](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_12a))

[12](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_12). Brian Goetz, e-mail message to authors, March 16, 2017.

#### 21.3.2 Class `Welcome`

[Figure 21.1](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig01)’s `Welcome` app simply displays a `String` at the command line. Types that will be placed in modules must be placed into a package using a **`package`** **statement** (line 3).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0879-04)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.1: Welcome.java
 2   // Welcome class that will be placed in a module
 3   package com.deitel.welcome; // all classes in modules must be packaged
 4
 5   public class Welcome {
 6      public static void main(String[] args) {
 7         // class System is in package java.lang from the java.base module
 8         System.out.println("Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!");
 9      }
10   }
```

**Fig. 21.1** | `Welcome` class that will be placed in a module.

#### 21.3.3 `module-info.java`

[Figure 21.2](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig02) is the module declaration for the `com.deitel.welcome` module, which begins with the `module` keyword followed by the module’s name and braces that enclose the declaration’s body. This module declaration contains a `requires` module directive, indicating that the app depends on types defined in module `java.base`. All modules implicitly depend on `java.base`, so this `requires` directive may be omitted.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0880-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.2: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.welcome module
 3   module com.deitel.welcome {
 4      requires java.base; // implicit in all modules, so can be omitted
 5   }
```

**Fig. 21.2** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.welcome` module.

#### 21.3.4 Module-Dependency Graph

The following diagram is the **module-dependency graph** for `com.deitel.welcome`, indicating that the module reads the standard module `java.base`. This dependency is indicated in the diagram with the arrow from `com.deitel.welcome` to `java.base`.

![Images](graphics/f0880-02.jpg)

A module-dependency graph illustrates dependencies among **observable modules**— standard modules and any additional modules required by a given app or library module.^([13](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_13a)) The graph’s nodes are modules, and their dependencies are represented by directed edges (arrows) that connect the nodes. Some edges represent **explicit dependencies** on modules explicitly specified in a module declaration’s `requires` clauses (as we’ll present in [Fig. 21.6](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig06)). Some edges represent **implicit dependencies** in which one of the required modules, in turn, depends on other modules. The preceding graph was produced using the JDK’s `jdeps` tool and the free Graphviz visualization tool. We discuss how to use these tools to create module dependency graphs in [Section 21.6.3](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec37).

[13](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_13). Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024\. Accessed January 7, 2025. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/261`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/261).

#### 21.3.5 Compiling a Module

The commands to compile modules and run modularized apps using the JDK’s tools are lengthy. Popular IDEs like JetBrains IntelliJ, the Eclipse IDE for Java Developers, Visual Studio Code and NetBeans have build tools that handle these commands for you.

For your convenience, the file `CommandsForCopyPaste.txt` in this chapter’s examples folder contains the commands to compile and run the examples. For readability, we split many commands into multiple lines, using platform-specific line-continuation characters. The commands throughout this chapter are presented in macOS format with the backslash (`\`) line-continuation character. Windows users would replace the backslashes with

*   carets (`^`) in Command Prompt windows or

*   back ticks (`` ` ``) in PowerShell windows.

##### Compiling the Welcome App

To compile the `Welcome` app’s module, open a command window, use the `cd` command to change to this chapter’s `WelcomeApp` folder, then enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0881-01)

```
javac -d mods/com.deitel.welcome \
   src/com.deitel.welcome/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.welcome/com/deitel/welcome/Welcome.java
```

The `-d` option indicates that `javac` should place the compiled code in the specified folder.^([14](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_14a)) This example’s `mods` folder will contain a subfolder named `com.deitel.welcome`, representing the compiled module. The name `mods` is used by convention.

[14](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_14). The “`d`” is short for “directory,” which is another name for a folder.

##### `Welcome` App’s Folder Structure After Compilation

If the code compiles, the `WelcomeApp` folder’s `mods` subfolder structure will be:

![Images](graphics/f0881-02.jpg)

This is known as the **exploded-module folder** because the folders and `.class` files are not in a JAR (Java archive) file. A JAR is a collection of folders and files compressed into a single file, known as an archive. The exploded module’s structure parallels the app’s `src` folder structure described in [Section 21.3.1](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec11). We’ll package the app as a JAR shortly. Exploded module folders and modular JAR files ([Section 21.3.7](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec19)) together are **module artifacts**. These can be placed on the **module path**—a list of module artifact locations— when compiling and executing modularized code.^([15](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_15a),[16](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_16a))

[15](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_15). Reinhold, Mark. “The State of the Module System.” March 8, 2016. Accessed January 7, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/sotms/#module-artifacts`](https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/sotms/#module-artifacts).

[16](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_16). Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024\. Accessed January 7, 2025. [`http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261`](http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261).

##### Listing the `com.deitel.welcome` Module’s Contents

You can use the `java` command’s `--describe-module` option to display information from the `com.deitel.welcome` module descriptor, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0882-01)

```
java --module-path mods --describe-module com.deitel.welcome
```

The resulting output:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0882-02)

```
com.deitel.welcome file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
WelcomeApp/mods/com.deitel.welcome/
requires java.base
contains com.deitel.welcome
```

indicates that the module `requires` the standard module `java.base` and `contains` the package `com.deitel.welcome`. Though the module `contains` this package, it is not exported, so other modules cannot use our module’s contents. This example’s module declaration explicitly required `java.base`, as indicated by the following line in the preceding command’s output:

```
requires java.base
```

If the module declaration had implicitly required `java.base`, the previous command’s output would instead contain

```
requires java.base mandated
```

where `mandated` indicates the implicit dependence on `java.base`.

#### 21.3.6 Running an App from a Module’s Exploded Folders

To run the `Welcome` app from the module’s exploded folders, use the following command (again, from the `WelcomeApp` folder):

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0882-03)

```
java --module-path mods \
   --module com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome
```

The **`--module-path`** option specifies the module path—in this case, the `mods` folder. The **`--module`** option specifies the module name and the fully qualified class name of the app’s entry point—a class containing `main`. The program executes and displays:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0882-04)

```
Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!
```

In the preceding command, `--module-path` can be abbreviated as `-p` and `--module` as `-m`.

**1** Prompt genAIs for the instructions to run modularized apps using your preferred IDE.

#### 21.3.7 Packaging a Module into a Modular JAR File

The **`jar`** **command** can package an exploded module folder as a **modular JAR file**^([17](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_17a)) containing all the module’s files. You specify the JAR file on the module path when you run the app. If a module contains an app’s entry point, you can specify that class with the `jar` command’s **`--main-class`** option, as in:

[17](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_17). Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024\. Accessed January 7, 2025. [`http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261`](http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/261).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0883-01)

```
jar --create --file jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar \
   --main-class com.deitel.welcome.Welcome \
   -C mods/com.deitel.welcome .
```

The options are as follows:

*   `--create` specifies that the command should create a new JAR file.

*   `--file` specifies the name of the JAR file and is followed by the name—in this case, the file `com.deitel.welcome.jar` will be created in the folder named `jars`, which must exist before running the `jar` command.

*   `--main-class` specifies the fully qualified name of the app’s entry point—a class that contains a `main` method.

*   `-C` specifies which folder contains the files that should be included in the JAR file and is followed by the files to include—the dot (`.`) indicates that all files in the folder should be included.

You can simplify the `--create`, `--f`ile and `--main-class` options in the preceding command with the shorthand notation `-cfe`, followed by the JAR file name and main class, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0883-02)

```
jar -cfe jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar \
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome \
   -C mods/com.deitel.welcome .
```

##### Confirming the Contents of a Module’s JAR File

After creating the JAR file, you can verify its contents as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0883-03)

```
jar --describe-module --file jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar
```

which produces the following output for the `com.deitel.welcome` module:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0883-04)

```
com.deitel.welcome jar:file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
   WelcomeApp/jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar!/module-info.class
requires java.base
contains com.deitel.welcome
main-class com.deitel.welcome.Welcome
```

The output includes:

*   the module name (which it obtains from the JAR’s `module-info.class` file),

*   the modular JAR file’s location,

*   what modules this module `requires` (`java.base`),

*   what this module `contains` (the package `com.deitel.welcome`), and

*   the `main-class` that executes when you run the app from this modular JAR file.

#### 21.3.8 Running the `Welcome` App from a Modular JAR File

Once you place an app in a modular JAR file for which you’ve specified the entry point, you can execute the app as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0884-01)

```
java --module-path jars -m com.deitel.welcome
```

or

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0884-02)

```
java -p jars -m com.deitel.welcome
```

The program executes and displays:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0884-03)

```
Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!
```

If you did not specify the entry point when creating the JAR, you may still run the app by specifying the module name and fully qualified class name, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0884-04)

```
java --module-path jars \
   -m com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome
```

or

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0884-05)

```
java -p jars -m com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome
```

#### 21.3.9 Aside: Classpath vs. Module Path

Before Java 9, the compiler and runtime located types via the classpath—a list of folders and library archive files containing compiled Java classes. In early Java versions, the class-path was defined by a combination of a `CLASSPATH` environment variable, extensions placed in a special JRE subfolder and options provided to the `javac` and `java` commands.

Because types could be loaded from several locations, the order in which they were searched resulted in brittle apps. For example, many years ago, one of the authors installed a Java app from a third-party vendor on his system. The app’s installer placed an old version of a Java library into the JRE’s extensions folder. Several Java apps on his system depended on a newer library version with additional types and enhanced versions of the library’s older types. Because classes in the JRE’s extensions folder were loaded before other classes on the classpath,^([18](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_18a)) the apps that depended on the newer library version stopped working, failing at runtime with `NoClassDefFoundError`s and `NoSuchMethodError`s—sometimes long after the apps began executing.

[18](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_18). “Understanding Extension Class Loading.” Accessed December 15, 2024\. [`https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ext/basics/load.html`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ext/basics/load.html).

The reliable configuration provided by modules and module descriptors helps eliminate many such runtime classpath problems. A module’s dependencies are resolved as an app launches. [Section 21.8.4](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec50) presents the steps the JRE’s module resolver performs at launch time.

The module path may contain only one of each module and every package may be defined in only one module. If two or more modules have the same name or export the same packages, the runtime immediately terminates.

#### Generative AI

**1** Prompt genAIs for a discussion of how JPMS and the module path improve upon the classpath’s limitations.

### 21.4 Creating and Using a Custom Module

To demonstrate a module that depends on a custom module, let’s reorganize an earlier, non-modularized example. We’ll declare [Section 8.7](#ch08.xhtml_ch08lev1sec7)’s `Time1` and `Time1Test` classes in separate modules, then use `Time1` from the module containing `Time1Test`. To make `Time1` available to `Time1Test`, we’ll

*   export `Time1`’s package from its custom module and

*   require the module containing `Time1` from the module containing `Time1Test`.

The following diagram contains the `src` folder structure for the app’s two modules.

![Images](graphics/f0885-01.jpg)

#### 21.4.1 Exporting a Package for Use in Other Modules

Every class in a module must be declared in a package. So, we added the `package` statement in line 3 ([Fig. 21.3](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig03)) to [Fig. 8.10](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig10)’s `Time1.java`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0885-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.3: Time1.java
 2   // Class Time1 that will be placed in a module.
 3   package com.deitel.timelibrary;
 4
 5   public class Time1 {
 6      private int hour; // 0 - 23
 7      private int minute; // 0 - 59
 8      private int second; // 0 - 59
 9
10      // set a new time value using universal time; throw an
11      // exception if the hour, minute or second is invalid
12      public void setTime(int hour, int minute, int second) {
13         // validate hour, minute and second
14         if (hour < 0 || hour >= 24 || minute < 0 || minute >= 60 ||
15            second < 0 || second >= 60) {
16            throw new IllegalArgumentException(
17               "hour, minute and/or second was out of range");
18         }
19
20         this.hour = hour;
21         this.minute = minute;
22         this.second = second;
23      }
24
25      // convert to String in universal-time format (HH:MM:SS)
26      public String toUniversalString() {
27         return String.format("%02d:%02d:%02d", hour, minute, second);
28      }
29
30      // convert to String in standard-time format (H:MM:SS AM or PM)
31      public String toString() {
32         return String.format("%d:%02d:%02d %s",
33            ((hour == 0 || hour == 12) ? 12 : hour % 12),
34            minute, second, (hour < 12 ? "AM" : "PM"));
35      }
36   }
```

**Fig. 21.3** | Class `Time1` that will be placed in a module.

##### `com.deitel.timelibrary` Module Declaration

In [Fig. 21.4](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig04)’s module declaration, line 4 `exports` the module’s `com.deitel.timelibrary` package. This package’s `public` class `Time1` (and other public classes, if any) can be used by any module that reads the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module, as long as the module can be found on the module path ([Section 21.4.3](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec26)).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0886-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.4: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.timelibrary module
 3   module com.deitel.timelibrary {
 4      exports com.deitel.timelibrary; // package available to other modules
 5   }
```

**Fig. 21.4** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module.

#### 21.4.2 Using a Class from a Package in Another Module

The app’s entry point—class `Time1Test` (originally declared in [Fig. 8.11](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig11))—also must be packaged for placement in a module (line 3 of [Fig. 21.5](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig05)). In addition, class `Time1Test` manipulates an object of class `Time1`, which is declared in a different package. So, line 5 imports the `com.deitel.timelibrary` package’s `Time1` class.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0887-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.5: Time1Test.java
 2   // Time1 object used in an app.
 3   package com.deitel.timetest;
 4
 5   import com.deitel.timelibrary.Time1;
 6
 7   public class Time1Test {
 8      public static void main(String[] args) {
 9         // create and initialize a Time1 object
10         var time = new Time1(); // invokes Time1 constructor
11
12         // output string representations of the time
13         displayTime("After time object is created", time);
14         System.out.println();
15
16         // change time and output updated time
17         time.setTime(13, 27, 6);
18         displayTime("After calling setTime", time);
19         System.out.println();
20
21         // attempt to set time with invalid values
22         try {
23            time.setTime(99, 99, 99); // all values out of range
24         }
25         catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
26            System.out.printf("Exception: %s%n%n", e.getMessage());
27         }
28
29         // display time after attempt to set invalid values
30         displayTime("After calling setTime with invalid values", time);
31      }
32
33      // displays a Time1 object in 24-hour and 12-hour formats
34      private static void displayTime(String header, Time1 t) {
35         System.out.printf("%s%nUniversal time: %s%nStandard time: %s%n",
36            header, t.toUniversalString(), t.toString());
37      }
38   }
```

**Fig. 21.5** | `Time1` object used in an app.

##### `com.deitel.timetest` Module Declaration

`Time1` is located in a package of the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module, so the module containing class `Time1Test` (`com.deitel.timetest`) must declare its dependency on the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module. The module declaration ([Fig. 21.6](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig06)) indicates this dependency with line 4’s `requires` directive. Due to JPMS’s strong encapsulation and reliable configuration features, this app needs both the `exports` directive in [Fig. 21.4](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig04) and the `requires` directive in [Fig. 21.6](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig06) for class `Time1Test` to import and use class `Time1`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0888-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.6: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.timetest module
 3   module com.deitel.timetest {
 4      requires com.deitel.timelibrary;
 5   }
```

**Fig. 21.6** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.timetest` module.

##### `com.deitel.timetest` Module-dependency Graph

The following `Time1Test` app module-dependency graph indicates that the module `com.deitel.timetest` reads (depend on) the custom module `com.deitel.timelibrary` and the standard module `java.base`.

![Images](graphics/f0888-02.jpg)

#### 21.4.3 Compiling and Running the Example

You must compile both modules before running this app. The `com.deitel.timelibrary` module must be compiled first because `com.deitel.timetest` depends on it. IDEs and other build tools (like Ant, Gradle and Maven) typically can deal with order-of-compilation issues like this for you.

##### Compiling Module `com.deitel.timelibrary`

To compile the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module, open a command window, use the `cd` command to change to this chapter’s `TimeApp` folder on your system, then enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0888-03)

```
javac -d mods/com.deitel.timelibrary \
   src/com.deitel.timelibrary/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.timelibrary/com/deitel/timelibrary/Time1.java
```

##### Compiling Module `com.deitel.timetest`

Next, to compile the `com.deitel.timetest` module, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0888-04)

```
javac --module-path mods -d mods/com.deitel.timetest \
   src/com.deitel.timetest/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.timetest/com/deitel/timetest/Time1Test.java
```

Here, we added the option `--module-path` to indicate that the `mods` folder contains modules on which the `com.deitel.timetest` module depends—in this case, we previously compiled the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module into the `mods` folder.

##### Running the Example

Finally, to run this example, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0889-01)

```
java --module-path mods \
   -m com.deitel.timetest/com.deitel.timetest.Time1Test
```

In this command:

*   the option `--module-path` indicates where the app’s modules are located, and

*   the option `-m` specifies which class should be used as the app’s entry point—that is, a class containing the `main` method that the JVM calls to launch the app.

For the `main` class, note that you must specify its module name followed by a slash and its fully qualified class name because the class is now in a package contained in a module. The program’s output is as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0889-02)

```
After time object is created
Universal time: 00:00:00
Standard time: 12:00:00 AM

After calling setTime
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM

Exception: hour, minute and/or second was out of range

After calling setTime with invalid values
Universal time: 13:27:06
Standard time: 1:27:06 PM
```

#### 21.4.4 Packaging the App into Modular JAR Files

In this section, we’ll package each app into a modular JAR file then run the app. To package `com.deitel.timelibrary` into a modular JAR file, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0889-03)

```
jar --create -f jars/com.deitel.timelibrary.jar \
   -C mods/com.deitel.timelibrary .
```

To package `com.deitel.timetest` into a modular JAR file, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0889-04)

```
jar --create -f jars/com.deitel.timetest.jar \
   --main-class com.deitel.timetest.Time1Test \
   -C mods/com.deitel.timetest .
```

##### Running the App from a Modular JAR File

Once you place an app in a modular JAR file for which you’ve specified the `main` class, you can execute the app as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0889-05)

```
java --module-path jars -m com.deitel.timetest
```

The program executes and displays the same output as in [Section 21.4.3](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec26).

#### 21.4.5 Strong Encapsulation and Accessibility

Before modules, you could use any `public` class you imported into your code. Whether you could access the class’s members was determined by how they were declared—`public`, `protected`, package access or `private` (as described in [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08)). Due to modules’ **strong encapsulation**, `public` types in a module are no longer accessible to your code by default. So, `public` does not necessarily mean “available to all”:

*   If a module exports a package, the `public` types in that package are accessible to any module that reads the package’s module.

*   If a module exports a package to a specific module (via `exports`…`to`), the `public` types in that package are accessible only to the specific module and only if that module reads the package’s module.

*   If a module does not export a package, the `public` types in that package are accessible only within the module itself.

Once you have access to a type in another module, the normal rules of `public`, `protected`, package access and `private` apply.

##### Compilation Error When Attempting to Use an Inaccessible Type

The project `TimeAppMissingExports` in this chapter’s `ExamplesShowingErrors` folder demonstrates that explicitly named modules have strong encapsulation and do not export packages unless you explicitly list them in `exports` directives. In this project, we removed the `exports` directive from the `com.deitel.timelibrary`’s module declaration then recompiled the module. Next, we compiled the `com.deitel.timelibrary` module then tried to recompile the `com.deitel.timetest` module. The compiler produced the following error message, which indicates that the package `com.deitel.timelibrary` is not exported and thus is inaccessible:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0890-01)

```
src/com.deitel.timetest/com/deitel/timetest/Time1Test.java:5: error: package
com.deitel.timelibrary is not visible
import com.deitel.timelibrary.Time1;
          ^
   (package com.deitel.timelibrary is declared in module com.deitel.timeli-
brary, which does not export it)
1 error
```

When a `requires` dependency is not fulfilled by an `exports` clause in another module a compilation error occurs.

### 21.5 Module-Dependency Graphs: A Deeper Look

Let’s continue our discussion of module graphs and present the errors that occur if a module directly or indirectly `requires` itself—known as a cycle.

#### 21.5.1 `java.sql`

Consider the following `modulegraphtest` module that depends on the `java.sql` module:

```
module modulegraphtest {
   requires java.sql;
}
```

The following diagram is the module-dependency graph for `modulegraphtest`:

![Images](graphics/f0891-01.jpg)

The diagram illustrates that `modulegraphtest` depends directly on modules `java.sql` and `java.base`. Modules `java.logging`, `java.transaction.xa` and `java.xml` are included in the graph because `java.sql` depends on them—thus, `modulegraphtest` also depends on them indirectly. The `java.sql` module’s `module-info.java` declares these modules with the following `requires transitive` statements:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0891-02)

```
requires transitive java.logging;
requires transitive java.transaction.xa;
requires transitive java.xml;
```

So, modules that depend on `java.sql` also have access to these modules. Of course, all the modules in the graph point to `java.base` because it’s required by all Java modules.

#### 21.5.2 `java.se`

[Figure 21.7](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig07) presents the significantly more complex **`java.se`** module’s dependency graph. This **aggregator module** specifies via `requires transitive` all the modules necessary to support Java Standard Edition (SE) apps. We rotated the graph 90° for readability.

![Images](graphics/f0892-01.jpg)

**Fig. 21.7** | `java.se` module-dependency graph.

#### 21.5.3 Error: Module Graph with a Cycle

A module is not allowed to directly or indirectly reference itself. Doing so would result in a cycle when computing the module’s dependency graph. A compilation error occurs if a module graph contains a cycle.

##### A Module That (Incorrectly) Requires Itself

Consider the following module declaration in which the module requires itself:

```
module mymodule {
   requires mymodule;
}
```

If you were to compile this declaration, the following error would occur, indicating a cycle in the `module`’s dependencies:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0893-01)

```
module-info.java:2: error: cyclic dependence involving mymodule
   requires mymodule;
            ^
1 error
```

##### Two Modules That (Incorrectly) Require One Another

Similarly, consider the project `CircularDependency` containing two modules—`module1` and `module2`—with the structure in the following diagram:

![Images](graphics/f0893-02.jpg)

If the module declarations for these two modules indicate that each module `requires` the other, as in

```
module module1 {
   exports package1;
   requires module2;
}
```

and

```
module module2 {
   exports package2;
   requires module1;
}
```

then, when you compile these modules

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0894-01)

```
javac --module-source-path src \
   --module-path mods -d mods \
   src/module1/module-info.java \
   src/module1/package1/Class1.java \
   src/module2/module-info.java \
   src/module2/package2/Class2.java
```

the compiler again issues an error indicating a cycle in the module dependencies:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0894-02)

```
src/module1/module-info.java:9: error: cyclic dependence involving module2
   requires module2;
            ^
src/module2/module-info.java:9: error: cyclic dependence involving module1
   requires module1;
            ^
2 errors
```

##### Modules in a Cycle Are Really “One Thing”

Ultimately, all the modules in a cycle are really one module—not separate modules.^([19](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_19a)) When we were writing this chapter for *Java How to Program, 11/e*, a friend who worked for a large organization indicated that the organization had multiple large pre-Java-9 JAR files. Initially they thought they’d make each JAR a separate module. Their JARs were so interdependent that they combined them into a single module. This kind of interdependency is what leads to cycles in your design. Ideally, when you modularize a previously monolithic system, you want to break that system into separate modules that are easier to maintain and secure. This can pose significant refactoring challenges in large code bases.

[19](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_19). Alex Buckley, e-mail message to authors, March 24, 2017.

#### Generative AI

**1** Prompt genAIs for recommendations on how to avoid cyclic dependencies among modules.

### 21.6 Migrating Code to Modules

Many non-modularized apps will run using the modularized JDK. In fact, most programs presented in this book were not modularized and ran without issue. Technically, all programs are compiled and executed using the module system. Java strongly encapsulates types that are not exported by modules, so it’s possible some older apps will fail to compile in Java 9 and beyond because types that were accessible to them before Java 9 no longer are. For example, there are pre-Java-9 **internal APIs** that were meant only for use in the JDK but were used by developers in their apps and libraries. Most of these internal APIs have been replaced with proper publicly accessible capabilities, so the internal APIs are no longer exported and thus are inaccessible.^([20](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_20a))

[20](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_20). Reinhold, Mark. “JEP 260: Encapsulate Most Internal APIs.” Updated April 28, 2024\. Accessed January 7, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/260`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/260).

##### Strong Encapsulation Is Now the Default

As we’ve mentioned, JPMS enables strong encapsulation. Code that is not exported cannot be accessed by other modules. Java versions 9–15 allowed some flexibility with respect to internal APIs to give developers time to migrate their code to JPMS. Since Java 16 and Java 17, strong encapsulation is the default.^([21](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_21a)) If you have older code that uses such internal APIs directly or indirectly, it will fail to compile.

[21](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_21). Buckley, Alex and Mark Reinhold, “JEP 396: Strongly Encapsulate JDK Internals by Default.” Updated April 28, 2024\. Accessed December 17, 2024\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/396`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/396).

##### Checking Your Code’s Dependencies

You can use the `jdeps` tool ([Section 21.6.3](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec37)) to check your code’s dependencies. The `jdeps` option `--jdk-internals` specifically identifies uses of JDK internal APIs in code. For each internal API that `jdeps` locates, it suggests an appropriate replacement.

#### 21.6.1 Unnamed Module

Technically, Java requires all code to be placed in modules. When you execute code that’s not in a module, the code is loaded from the classpath and placed in the **unnamed module**. This is why we can run some non-modularized code in the modularized JDK but without the benefits of strong encapsulation and explicit module dependencies.

The unnamed module:

*   implicitly `exports` all of its packages, and

*   implicitly reads all other modules.

There’s no way to refer to an unnamed module in a `requires` directive from a named module, so a named module cannot depend on an unnamed module.

#### 21.6.2 Automatic Modules

There are enormous numbers of preexisting libraries that you can use in your apps. Some are modularized and some are not. To facilitate migration, you can add any library’s JAR file to an app’s module path then use the packages in that JAR. When you do, the JAR file implicitly becomes an **automatic module** and can be specified in a `module` declaration’s `requires` directives. An automatic module:

*   implicitly `exports` all of its packages—so any module that reads the automatic module (including the unnamed module) has access to the `public` types in the automatic module’s packages.

*   implicitly reads (`requires`) all other modules, including other automatic modules and the unnamed module—so an automatic module has access to all the `public` types exposed by the system’s other modules.

##### Automatic Module Names Derived from JAR File Names

An automatic module’s name is derived from its file name. If the JAR’s file name minus the `.jar` extension is a valid Java identifier, it becomes its automatic module name. Otherwise:

*   Characters that are not allowed in Java identifiers are replaced with dots (`.`).

*   If there are multiple consecutive dots, they are replaced with a single dot.

*   If there are dots at the beginning or end of the remaining name, they’re removed.

#### 21.6.3 `jdeps` Tool for Java Dependency Analysis

Another tool to help you prepare to modularize your code is the **`jdeps`** **command**. It enables you determine a type’s class and package dependencies. Given that 28.8% of Java developers were still using Java 8 in 2024,^([22](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_22a)) a key use of `jdeps` is to help those developers locate dependencies on internal APIs that are now strongly encapsulated. To determine whether a class has any such dependencies, use the following command on your compiled class:

[22](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_22). New Relic, “2024 State of the Java Ecosystem,” April 2024\. Accessed December 15, 2024\. [`https://newrelic.com/resources/report/2024-state-of-the-java-ecosystem`](https://newrelic.com/resources/report/2024-state-of-the-java-ecosystem).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-01)

```
jdeps --jdk-internals YourClassName.class
```

or if you have many compiled classes in a JAR file, use:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-02)

```
jdeps --jdk-internals YourJARName.jar
```

If this command does not produce output, then your class or set of classes does not depend on JDK internal APIs that are no longer accessible.

##### Determining the Modules You Need

A key aspect of modularization is the ability to create more compact Java runtimes that provide only the modules your app requires. When you’re preparing to create custom runtimes, you can use `jdeps` to discover your app’s module dependencies so you know which ones to include in your custom runtime. For example, this chapter’s `Welcome` app depends only on `java.base`. We can confirm that by executing the following command from the `WelcomeApp` folder, which checks the `com.deitel.welcome` module’s dependencies:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-03)

```
jdeps --module-path jars -m com.deitel.welcome
```

This produces the following output containing the packages and modules the app uses— we removed some horizontal spacing in this command’s output to make it more readable:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-04)

```
com.deitel.welcome
 [file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/WelcomeApp/jars/
   com.deitel.welcome.jar]
   requires java.base (@23)
com.deitel.welcome -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.io        java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.lang      java.base
```

The output indicates that our module `com.deitel.welcome` depends on the `java.base` module, and that our module specifically uses types from the `java.base` module’s `java.io` and `java.lang` packages. The preceding command may also be written as

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-05)

```
jdeps jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar
```

In addition, you can use `jdeps` on a specific `.class` file, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0896-06)

```
jdeps mods/com.deitel.welcome/com/deitel/welcome/Welcome.class
```

which produces

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0897-01)

```
Welcome.class -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.io       java.base
   com.deitel.welcome -> java.lang     java.base
```

##### Verbose `jdeps` Output

If you’d like more details, you can specify the `-v` (verbose) option as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0897-02)

```
jdeps -v jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar
```

which produces:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0897-03)

```
com.deitel.welcome
 [file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/WelcomeApp/jars/
   com.deitel.welcome.jar]
   requires java.base (@23)
com.deitel.welcome -> java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.io.PrintStream      java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.Object         java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.String         java.base
   com.deitel.welcome.Welcome -> java.lang.System         java.base
```

This lists precisely which packages, types and modules the app uses. Knowing that the app requires only `java.base`, we can then use `jlink` to create a custom runtime containing only that module, which we’ll do in [Section 21.8](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev1sec8).

##### Using `jdeps` to Produce DOT Files for Graphing Tools

You can use graphing tools—such as Graphviz ([`https://www.graphviz.org/`](https://www.graphviz.org/))—to produce module-dependency graphs using the DOT graph description language,^([23](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_23a)) which specifies a graph’s nodes and edges. The `jdeps` tool can create DOT (`.dot`) files with the `--dot-output` option, as in:

[23](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_23). “DOT (graph description language).” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation. Last modified November 12, 2024\. Accessed December 15, 2024\. [`https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DOT_(graph_description_language)).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0897-04)

```
jdeps --dot-output . jars/com.deitel.welcome.jar
```

This produces two `.dot` files^([24](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_24a)) in the current folder (`.`):

[24](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_24). The `.dot` extension is also used by Microsoft Word document templates. On systems with Microsoft Word installed, open the `jdeps`-produced `.dot` files directly from a text editor.

*   `summary.dot`—the description of module `com.deitel.welcome`’s dependencies.

*   `com.deitel.welcome.dot`—the description of module `com.deitel.welcome`’s specific package dependencies.

After installing Graphviz, we executed the following command to visualize `summary.dot`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0897-05)

```
dot -Tpng summary.dot -Gdpi=600 -Nfontname="Open Sans" \
   -Nshape=box -o WelcomeApp.png
```

*   `-Tpng` specifies the image should be in the popular PNG image format commonly used on the web.

*   `-Gdpi` specifies the image resolution—600 dots-per-inch.

*   `-Nfontname` option enables you to choose a font for the nodes’ text.

*   `-Nshape` specifies the nodes’ shape—`box` produces rectangles rather than the default ovals.

*   `-o` is followed by the image’s filename.

The diagram below illustrates the `com.deitel.welcome` module’s dependencies:

![Images](graphics/f0898-01.jpg)

For a complete list of `jdeps` options, visit

```
https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/23/docs/specs/man/jdeps.html
```

### 21.7 Resources in Modules

When the types in a module require resources—such as images, videos, XML documents and more—those resources should be packaged with the module to ensure that they’re available when the module’s types are used at execution time. This is known as **resource encapsulation**.^([25](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_25a)) In this section, we’ll migrate our non-modularized JavaFX `VideoPlayer` example from [Section 17.6](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec6) into a module that also encapsulates the app’s resources—the FXML file that describes the GUI and its video file that will be loaded and played at execution time. By convention, resources typically are placed in a folder named `res`.

[25](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_25). Mark Reinhold, “Java Platform Module System Requirements.” April 1, 2015. Accessed January 7, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/reqs/#resource-encapsulation`](https://openjdk.org/projects/jigsaw/spec/reqs/#resource-encapsulation).

Recall that the original `VideoPlayer` example consisted of the following files all in [Chapter 17](#ch17.xhtml_ch17)’s `VideoPlayer` folder:

*   `VideoPlayer.xml`—The FXML file that describes the app’s GUI.

*   `VideoPlayer.java`—The `Application` subclass that begins the app’s execution.

*   `VideoPlayerController.java`—The controller class that responds to the GUIs events and loads the video.

*   `A1Launch~medium.mp4`—The NASA video^([26](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_26a)) that the app loads and plays.

    [26](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_26). For NASA’s terms of use, visit [`https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/`](https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/)

*   `controlsfx-11.2.1.jar`—The ControlsFX library containing the dialog class `ExceptionDialog`. We display an `ExceptionDialog` if the `MediaPlayer` encounters any errors.

##### Reorganizing for Modularization

For this example, we reorganized the files into the following folder structure to support modules.

![Images](graphics/f0899-01.jpg)

Notice the following about the structure:

*   The files `VideoPlayer.fxml` and `A1Launch~medium.mp4`, which are not Java source code files, are located in the module directory’s `res` folder. These files will be read from the module’s `res` folder when the app executes.

*   As required for modularization, we placed the `VideoPlayer` and `VideoPlayer-Controller` classes in a package—the folder structure `com/deitel/videoplayer` corresponds to the package `com.deitel.videoplayer`.

*   As required, we created a `module-info.java` file in the module’s root folder.

In addition, we placed `controlsfx-11.2.1.jar` in the `VideoPlayer` folder’s `mods` subfolder.

##### Code Changes for Modularization

We made several code changes to the `VideoPlayer` application for modularization. In `VideoPlayer.fxml`, we modified the controller class’s name to use its fully qualified name

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0899-02)

```
com.deitel.videoplayer.VideoPlayerController
```

so that the `FXMLLoader` can find the controller class. In `VideoPlayer.java`, we changed `"VideoPlayer.fxml"` to `"/res/VideoPlayer.fxml"` to indicate that the FXML file is located in the module’s `res` subfolder. We also added the `package` statement

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0899-03)

```
package com.deitel.videoplayer;
```

In `VideoPlayerController.java`, we changed `"A1Launch~medium.mp4"` to

```
"/res/A1Launch~medium.mp4"
```

to indicate that the video file is located in the module’s `res` folder. We also added the `package` statement

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0899-04)

```
package com.deitel.videoplayer;
```

The rest of the code is identical to what we presented in [Section 17.6](#ch17.xhtml_ch17lev1sec6).

#### 21.7.1 Requiring Multiple Modules

Module `com.deitel.videoplayer`’s declaration ([Fig. 21.8](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig08)) indicates that it requires `javafx.controls`, `javafx.fxml`, `javafx.media` and [`org.controlsfx.controls`](http://org.controlsfx.controls). The module `exports` package `com.deitel.videoplayer` (line 9), because class `VideoPlayer-Controller` is used by class `FXMLLoader` (module `javafx.fxml`) when it creates the controller object and the app’s GUI.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0900-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.8: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.videoplayer module
 3   module com.deitel.videoplayer {
 4      requires javafx.controls;
 5      requires javafx.fxml;
 6      requires javafx.media;
 7      requires org.controlsfx.controls;
 8
 9      exports com.deitel.videoplayer;
10      opens com.deitel.videoplayer to javafx.fxml;
11   }
```

**Fig. 21.8** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.videoplayer` module.

#### 21.7.2 Opening a Module for Reflection

In [Fig. 21.8](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig08), the `opens`…`to` directive (line 10) indicates that the accessible types in the package `com.deitel.videoplayer` should be available via reflection at runtime to types in the `javafx.fxml` module. As we discussed in [Section 21.2.6](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec8), this enables the `FXMLLoader` to locate and load class `VideoPlayerController`. The `FXMLLoader` creates a `VideoPlayer-Controller` object and injects into it references to the GUIs components created from the app’s FXML file. For one module to open a package to another module, that package must first be exported (possibly as a qualified export using `exports`…`to`).

#### 21.7.3 Compiling the Module

To compile the `com.deitel.videoplayer` module, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0900-02)

```
javac --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods \
   -d mods/com.deitel.videoplayer \
   src/com.deitel.videoplayer/module-info.java \
   src/com.deitel.videoplayer/com/deitel/videoplayer/*.java
```

We included the `--module-path` option to specify where the JavaFX modules are (`"$PATH_TO_FX"`) and where `controlsfx-11.2.1.jar` is (`mods`).

##### Copying the Resource Files into the Module

Though some IDEs and build tools will automatically put the module’s resources into the compiled module, the preceding `javac` command does not. Once you’ve compiled the module, copy the `res` folder from this project’s `src/com.deitel.videoplayer` folder into the `mods/com.deitel.videoplayer` folder.

#### 21.7.4 Running a Modularized App

To execute class `VideoPlayer` from the `com.deitel.videoplayer` module, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0901-01)

```
java --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods \
   -m com.deitel.videoplayer/com.deitel.videoplayer.VideoPlayer
```

Here is the app executing on macOS:

![Images](graphics/f0901-02.jpg)

#### 21.7.5 Module-Dependency Graph

The following diagram is the `com.deitel.videoplayer` module-dependency graph:

![Images](graphics/f0901-03.jpg)

We produced this diagram using the following `jdeps` command to create `summary.dot`— the `--recursive` option indicates that jdeps should analyze all the runtime dependencies of the specified module:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0901-04)

```
jdeps --module-path "$PATH_TO_FX":mods --dot-output . \
   --recursive --module com.deitel.videoplayer
```

We then used Graphviz to visualize it:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0901-05)

```
dot -Tpng summary.dot -Gdpi=600 -Nfontname="Open Sans" \
   -Nshape=box -o VideoPlayer.png

### 21.8 Creating Custom Runtimes with `jlink`

Before JPMS, every Java SE program required the entire Java runtime to execute, even if the program used only a small portion of the Java platform’s capabilities. The **`jlink`** **command** enables you to create custom runtime images.^([27](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_27a)) In a custom runtime, you can include only what’s necessary for a given app or set of apps to execute. This is particularly useful for executing large numbers of Java runtimes in cloud-based architectures, where you pay for all the storage, memory and processor resources you use. It’s also useful for smaller capacity devices. If your app requires only packages from the `java.base` module, you can create a runtime containing just that module. In fact, such a runtime can execute most of this book’s text-only, command-line examples.

[27](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_27). Denise, Jean-Francois. “JEP 282: `jlink`: The Java Linker.” Updated May 19, 2017\. Accessed January 7, 2025\. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/282`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/282).

#### 21.8.1 Custom Runtime Containing Only `java.base`

For this example, change to the `WelcomeApp` folder—after creating the custom runtime, you’ll execute the `Welcome` app using it. The following command creates a runtime containing only the module `java.base`:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0902-01)

```
jlink --module-path "$JAVA_HOME/jmods" --add-modules java.base \
   --output javabaseruntime
```

The commands options are as follows:

*   `--module-path` specifies one or more folders in which to locate modules to include in the runtime—in this case, the JDK’s `jmods` folder, which contains the JDK’s modules. Place `"$JAVA_HOME"` in quotes in case the path to the JDK on your system contains spaces.

*   `--add-modules` specifies which modules to include in the runtime—in this case, just `java.base`.

*   `--output` specifies the folder (`javabaseruntime`) in which the runtime’s contents are placed. This folder will be a subfolder of the one in which you execute the preceding command (unless you specify additional path information). If the folder already exists, an error occurs.

This runtime can execute an app that depends only on types from the packages in module `java.base`, including many of this book’s command-line apps.

##### Note Regarding the `JAVA_HOME` Environment Variable

The `JAVA_HOME` environment variable must refer to the JDK’s installation folder on your system. If you installed the JDK using the instructions in our Before You Begin section that follows the preface, the installer set up the `JAVA_HOME` environment variable for you. You may need to set up this environment variable yourself if you used a different Java distribution.

##### Executing the `Welcome` App Using This Custom Runtime

To run the app with the custom runtime, execute:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0903-01)

```
javabaseruntime/bin/java --module-path mods \
   --module com.deitel.welcome/com.deitel.welcome.Welcome
```

The program executes and displays:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0903-02)

```
Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!
```

##### Listing the Modules in a Custom Runtime

Early in this chapter, we listed all the modules in the JDK with the command

```
java --list-modules
```

Once you have a custom runtime, you can use the `java` command from the custom runtime’s `bin` folder to confirm the modules it includes, as in:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0903-03)

```
javabaseruntime/bin/java --list-modules
```

When executing the custom runtime’s `java` command, use `/` to separate folder names on macOS and `\` to separate the folder names on Windows. The preceding command produces the following output:

```
java.base@23
```

Similarly the following command creates a custom runtime containing only the module `java.sql` and any other modules on which it depends:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0903-04)

```
jlink --module-path "$JAVA_HOME/jmods" \
   --add-modules java.sql --output javasqlruntime
```

For this custom runtime, running

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0903-05)

```
javasqlruntime/bin/java --list-modules
```

(again, use forward slashes on macOS and Linux) produces the following output:

```
java.base@23
java.logging@23
java.sql@23
java.transaction.xa@23
java.xml@23
```

#### 21.8.2 Creating a Custom Runtime for the `Welcome` App

To create a custom runtime containing only the modules `com.deitel.welcome` and its dependencies (in this case, `java.base`), change to the `WelcomeApp` folder, then use the following command:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0904-01)

```
jlink --module-path jars:"$JAVA_HOME/jmods" \
   --add-modules com.deitel.welcome --output welcomeruntime
```

This creates a custom runtime in the folder `welcomeruntime`. The preceding command specifies multiple folders—`jars` and `"$JAVA_HOME/jmods"`. On macOS, the path-separator character for lists of folders is a colon (`:`). The Windows version of this command is located in the file `CommandsForCopyPaste.txt` with this chapter’s examples. For the list of modules included in the custom runtime, on macOS use:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0904-02)

```
welcomeruntime/bin/java --list-modules
```

(use backslashes on Windows), which produces the following list of modules:

```
com.deitel.welcome
java.base@23
```

#### 21.8.4 Using the Module Resolver on a Custom Runtime

When you run a modularized app, the JVM’s **module resolver** determines which modules are required at execution time and ensures their dependencies are satisfied—this is known as the **transitive closure** of those modules. To locate modules, the module resolver looks at the **observable modules**—those built into the runtime (like `java.base`) and those located on the module path. The runtime throws a `java.lang.module.FindException` if a required module cannot be found.

For a given app and runtime, you can view the steps the module resolver follows to determine module dependencies and ensure that the required modules are available to the program. To do so, include the **`--show-module-resolution`** **option**^([28](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_28a)) in the `java` command, as in the following command (use backslashes on Windows):

[28](#ch21.xhtml_fn21_28). Bateman, Alan, Alex Buckley, Jonathan Gibbons and Mark Reinhold. “JEP 261: Module System.” Updated August 19, 2024\. Accessed January 7, 2025. [`https://openjdk.org/jeps/261`](https://openjdk.org/jeps/261).

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0904-05)

```
welcomeruntime/bin/java --show-module-resolution -m com.deitel.welcome
```

This uses the custom `welcomeruntime`’s `java` command to display the resolver’s steps for locating modules, followed by the program’s output:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0905-01)

```
root com.deitel.welcome jrt:/com.deitel.welcome
Welcome to the Java Platform Module System!
```

In the `Welcome` app’s module-resolution process, the resolver first locates the app’s **initial module**—`com.deitel.welcome`—containing the app’s entry point. The resolver refers to this as the `root` module—the root node in the module-dependency graph. Then, the resolver looks for other module dependencies. The `Welcome` app’s only other dependency is the `java.base` module. Since all modules depend on this, it’s not listed in the output.

Adding the `--show-module-resolution` option to the `java` command for the `Video-Player` app ([Section 21.7](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev1sec7)) produces a substantial output, a portion of which is shown below:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0905-02)

```
root com.deitel.videoplayer file:///Users/pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/
   VideoPlayer/mods/com.deitel.videoplayer/
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.media file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.media.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.controls file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.controls.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires javafx.fxml file:///Users/pauldeitel/
   Downloads/javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.fxml.jar
com.deitel.videoplayer requires org.controlsfx.controls file:///Users/
   pauldeitel/Documents/examples/ch21/VideoPlayer/mods/controlsfx.jar
javafx.media requires javafx.base file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.base.jar
javafx.media requires javafx.graphics file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.graphics.jar
javafx.controls requires javafx.base file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.base.jar
javafx.controls requires javafx.graphics file:///Users/pauldeitel/Downloads/
   javafx-sdk-23.0.1/lib/javafx.graphics.jar
...
```

After resolving the root module `com.deitel.videoplayer`, the module resolver looks at each module the root requires, then each module those modules require, and so on, essentially building the module graph shown in [Section 21.7.5](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec44). If the module resolver finds all the required modules, the program executes. Otherwise, the module resolver throws a `java.lang.module.FindException` and the program terminates.

### 21.9 Services and `ServiceLoader`

[Section 9.13](#ch09.xhtml_ch09lev1sec13) discussed “programming to an interface, not an implementation” to create loosely coupled objects. In this section, we discuss services and the `ServiceLoader` class, which help you create loosely coupled system components, making large-scale systems easier to develop and maintain.

##### `MathTutor` App

We’ll create a `MathTutor` app consisting of three modules. The app supports various types of randomly generated math problems. Rather than hard-coding these into the app, we’ll load math problems through a service-provider interface that describes how to obtain math problems. We’ll then define two service-provider implementation classes that implement this interface—one for addition problems and one for multiplication problems. We’ll load and use objects of these service-provider implementation classes at runtime. The following diagram contains the completed three-module app structure:

![Images](graphics/f0906-01.jpg)

##### `MathTutor` App’s Modules

Module `com.deitel.mathtutor` aggregates two related packages:

*   `com.deitel.mathtutor`: This package contains class `MathTutor`—a command-line app that displays random math problems to the user, inputs the user’s responses and displays whether each response is correct or incorrect.

*   `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi`: This package contains the service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` and its supporting `abstract` class `Problem`, representing a math problem. `MathTutor` uses `ProblemProvider`s to obtain `Problem` objects.

Module `com.deitel.additionprovider` contains a package of the same name in which we declare class `AdditionProblemProvider`. This implementation of the service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` generates random addition `Problem`s.

Module `com.deitel.multiplicationprovider` contains a package of the same name in which we declare class `MultiplicationProblemProvider`. This implementation of the service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` generates random multiplication `Problem`s.

##### How We’ll Demonstrate the App

We’ll run the `MathTutor` app several times:

*   First, we’ll run it without placing the service-provider implementation modules on the module path to demonstrate what happens when no service providers are found at runtime.

*   Next, we’ll “plug in” the `com.deitel.additionprovider` module on the module path, then re-run the app to demonstrate that we can obtain `Problem`s from an `AdditionProblemProvider`.

*   Finally, we’ll “plug in” both modules `com.deitel.additionprovider` and `com.deitel.multiplicationprovider` on the module path, then re-run the app to demonstrate that we’re able to obtain addition and multiplication `Problem`s from the `AdditionProblemProvider` and the `MultiplicationProblemProvider`.

##### Plug-in Architecture

The `MathTutor` app is easy to extend via this “plug-in” architecture. Simply create a module containing a `ProblemProvider` implementation, then add it to the module path when you run the app. This architecture also makes the app more configurable—you can choose which modules to include on the module path when you execute the app.

##### Reliable Configuration

The mechanisms for creating loosely coupled systems like the `MathTutor` app have been used extensively in Java since its early versions. A key concept in JPMS—which also applies to modules in general—is reliable configuration. For the `MathTutor` app to be able to display `Problem`s to the user, it must be able to locate and load `ProblemProvider` implementations. As you’ll learn, module declarations enable you to specify the service-provider interfaces a module uses and whether a module contains types that implement those interfaces.

#### 21.9.1 Service-Provider Interface

The package `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi` contains the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module’s service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` and the supporting `abstract` class `Problem`. The final component of this package’s name—`spi`—is commonly used in packages that declare one or more service-provider interfaces. The `ProblemProvider` interface ([Fig. 21.9](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig09)) declares the abstract `getProblem` method (line 6), which returns a `Problem`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0907-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.9: ProblemProvider.java
 2   // Service-provider interface for obtaining a Problem
 3   package com.deitel.mathtutor.spi;
 4
 5   public interface ProblemProvider {
 6      public Problem getProblem();
 7   }
```

**Fig. 21.9** | Service-provider interface for obtaining a `Problem`.

The `abstract Problem` class ([Fig. 21.10](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig10)) provides the common features of this exam-ple’s math problems. Each has two `int` operands and an `int` result as well as a `String` representing the operation—the `MathTutor` displays this `String` with each math problem it presents to the user. Class `Problem`’s `abstract` method `getResult` is overridden in each service-provider implementation’s concrete `Problem` subclass.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0908-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.10: Problem.java
 2   // Problem superclass that contains information about a math problem.
 3   package com.deitel.mathtutor.spi;
 4
 5   public abstract class Problem {
 6      private int leftOperand;
 7      private int rightOperand;
 8      private int result;
 9      private String operation;
10
11      // constructor
12      public Problem(int leftOperand, int rightOperand, String operation) {
13         this.leftOperand = leftOperand;
14         this.rightOperand = rightOperand;
15         this.operation = operation;
16      }
17
18      // gets the leftOperand
19      public int getLeftOperand() {return leftOperand;}
20
21      // gets the rightOperand
22      public int getRightOperand() {return rightOperand;}
23
24      // gets the operation
25      public String getOperation() {return operation;}
26
27      // gets the result
28      public abstract int getResult();
29   }
```

**Fig. 21.10** | `Problem` superclass that contains information about a math problem.

#### 21.9.2 Loading and Consuming Service Providers

Class `MathTutor` ([Fig. 21.11](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig11)) is the app’s entry point. It provides the logic to locate and load `ProblemProvider` implementations then use them to generate math problems. We split the `MathTutor` class into parts for discussion purposes.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0908-02)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.11: MathTutor.java
 2   // Math tutoring app using ProblemProviders to display math problems.
 3   package com.deitel.mathtutor;
 4
 5   import java.util.List;
 6   import java.util.Scanner;
 7   import java.util.ServiceLoader;
 8   import java.util.ServiceLoader.Provider;
 9   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
10   import java.util.stream.Collectors;
11   import com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.Problem;
12   import com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.ProblemProvider;
13
14   public class MathTutor {
15      private static Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);
16
17      public static void main(String[] args) {
```

**Fig. 21.11** | Math tutoring app using `ProblemProvider`s to display math problems.

##### Using `ServiceLoader` to Locate Service Providers

Lines 19–20 create a **`ServiceLoader`** (package `java.util`) that loads `ProblemProvider` implementations.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0909-01)

```
18         // get a service loader for ProblemProviders
19         ServiceLoader<ProblemProvider> serviceLoader =
20            ServiceLoader.load(ProblemProvider.class);
21
```

**`ServiceLoader`****’s** **`static load`** **method** receives as its argument the `Class` object representing the service-provider interface’s type—the compiler automatically creates an object of type `Class<ProblemProvider>` from the class literal `ProblemProvider.class`. Method `load` returns a `ServiceLoader<ProblemProvider>` that dynamically discovers and loads `ProblemProvider` implementations available on the module path.

There are several ways to get service-provider implementations from a `Service-Loader`. Lines 23–24 obtain a `List` of the available service-provider implementations using **`ServiceLoader`****’s** **`stream`** **method**.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0909-02)

```
22         // get the list of service providers
23         List<Provider<ProblemProvider>> providersList =
24            serviceLoader.stream().collect(Collectors.toList());
25
26         // check whether there are any providers
27         if (providersList.isEmpty()) {
28            System.out.println(
29               "Terminating MathTutor: No problem providers found.");
30            return;
31         }
32
```

This returns a `Stream<Provider<ProblemProvider>>` representing all available `Problem-Provider` implementations, if any. Interface `Provider` (imported at line 8) is a nested type of class `ServiceLoader`. For each available `ProblemProvider` implementation, the stream contains one `Provider<ProblemProvider>` object. Line 24 uses `Stream`’s `collect` method and the predefined `Collector` defined by `Collectors.toList` to get the `List` containing all the available implementations. If that `List` is empty (line 27) the program displays an appropriate message and terminates.

##### Using a Service-Provider Interface

If the `List` contains any service-provider implementations, lines 36–46 use them to display one math problem at a time to the user. Lines 38–39 randomly select one object from the `providersList`, then invoke that object’s `get` method to obtain its `ProblemProvider`. Line 42 then gets a `Problem` from that `ProblemProvider`. Note the loose coupling. The `MathTutor` app does not explicitly mention the `ProblemProvider` implementation classes `AdditionProblemProvider` and `MultiplicationProblemProvider`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0910-01)

```
33         boolean shouldContinue = true;
34         var random = RandomGenerator.getDefault();
35
36         do {
37            // choose a ProblemProvider at random
38            ProblemProvider provider =
39               providersList.get(random.nextInt(providersList.size())).get();
40
41            // get the Problem
42            Problem problem = provider.getProblem();
43
44            // display the problem to the user
45            showProblem(problem);
46         } while (playAgain());
47      }
48
49      // show the math problem to the user
50      private static void showProblem(Problem problem) {
51         var problemStatement = String.format("%nWhat is %d %s %d? ",
52            problem.getLeftOperand(), problem.getOperation(),
53            problem.getRightOperand());
54
55         // display problem and get answer from user
56         System.out.printf(problemStatement);
57         int answer = input.nextInt();
58
59         while (answer != problem.getResult()) {
60            System.out.println("Incorrect. Please try again.");
61            System.out.printf(problemStatement);
62            answer = input.nextInt();
63         }
64
65         System.out.println("Correct!");
66      }
67
68      // play again?
69      private static boolean playAgain() {
70         System.out.printf("%nTry another? y to continue, n to terminate: ");
71         String response = input.next();
72
73         return response.toLowerCase().startsWith("y");
74      }
75   }
```

#### 21.9.3 `uses` Module Directive and Service Consumers

[Figure 21.12](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig12) contains the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module declaration. This module `exports` the `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi` package containing the service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` and its supporting `Problem` class, enabling modules that implement `ProblemProvider` to access those types. The new feature in this declaration is the `uses` module directive (line 6), indicating that code in the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module uses `ProblemProvider` objects. Such a module is a **service consumer**.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0911-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.12: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.mathtutor module
 3   module com.deitel.mathtutor {
 4      exports com.deitel.mathtutor.spi; // package for provider interface
 5
 6      uses com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.ProblemProvider;
 7   }
```

**Fig. 21.12** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module.

For the `MathTutor` to consume `ProblemProvider`s, the `ServiceLoader` must be able to locate and load their implementations dynamically using Java’s reflection capabilities. When you run this app, the module resolver will note from the module descriptor (the compiled version of `module-info.java`) that this module uses `ProblemProvider` implementations and thus is dependent on such providers. The module resolver will search the modules on the module path looking for any that provide `ProblemProvider` implementations. If it finds any, it will add them to the module-dependency graph.

#### 21.9.4 Running the App with No Service Providers

To compile the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module, enter:

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0911-02)

```

   src/com.deitel.mathtutor/module-info.java \

   src/com.deitel.mathtutor/com/deitel/mathtutor/spi/*.java

```

Terminating MathTutor: No problem providers found.

#### 21.9.5 Implementing a Service Provider

Next, let’s create class `AdditionProblemProvider` ([Fig. 21.13](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig13)), which implements the `ProblemProvider` service-provider interface (line 10). Package `com.deitel.addition-provider` will be placed in module `com.deitel.additionprovider` ([Section 21.9.6](#ch21.xhtml_ch21lev2sec59)). We `import` interface `ProblemProvider` and class `Problem` from the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module’s exported `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi` package (lines 7–8). When `MathTutor` calls an `AdditionProblemProvider`’s `getProblem` method (lines 14–23), the method creates an object of an anonymous inner class ([Section 11.5.2](#ch11.xhtml_ch11lev2sec16)) that’s extends `Problem` (lines 16–22), passing to `Problem`’s constructor two random `int` operands and the `String "+"` to represent the arithmetic operation. Lines 18–21 override `Problem`’s `getResult` method, which adds the left and right operands and returns their sum.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0912-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.13: AdditionProblemProvider.java
 2   // AdditionProblemProvider implementation of interface
 3   // ProblemProvider for the MathTutor app.
 4   package com.deitel.additionprovider;
 5
 6   import java.util.random.RandomGenerator;
 7   import com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.Problem;
 8   import com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.ProblemProvider;
 9
10   public class AdditionProblemProvider implements ProblemProvider {
11      private static RandomGenerator random = RandomGenerator.getDefault();
12
13      // returns a new addition problem
14      @Override
15      public Problem getProblem() {
16         return new Problem(random.nextInt(10), random.nextInt(10), "+") {
17            // override getResult to add the operands
18            @Override
19            public int getResult() {
20               return getLeftOperand() + getRightOperand();
21            }
22         };
23      }
24   }
```

**Fig. 21.13** | `AdditionProblemProvider` implementation of interface `ProblemProvider` for the `MathTutor` app.

#### 21.9.6 `provides`…`with` Module Directive and Declaring a Service Provider

[Figure 21.14](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig14) contains the `com.deitel.additionprovider` module declaration. Note that this module `requires` the module `com.deitel.mathtutor`. Recall from [Fig. 21.12](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig12) that this module `exports` the package `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi` containing the types used in class `AdditionProblemProvider`.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0913-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.14: module-info.java
 2   // Module declaration for the com.deitel.additionprovider module
 3   module com.deitel.additionprovider {
 4      requires com.deitel.mathtutor;
 5
 6      provides com.deitel.mathtutor.spi.ProblemProvider
 7         with com.deitel.additionprovider.AdditionProblemProvider;
 8   }
```

**Fig. 21.14** | Module declaration for the `com.deitel.additionprovider` module.

The new feature in this module declaration is the `provides`…`with` module directive, indicating that the `com.deitel.additionprovider` module is a **service provider**. The `provides` keyword (line 6) is followed by the fully qualified name of an interface or `abstract` class that another module specified in a `uses` module directive. The `with` keyword (line 7) is followed by the name of a concrete class that `implements` the interface or `extends` the `abstract` class. Lines 6–7 specify that this module

*   `provides` an implementation of the `ProblemProvider` interface declared in the `com.deitel.mathtutor` module’s `com.deitel.mathtutor.spi` package

*   `with` the `AdditionProblemProvider` class, which is declared in this module’s `com.deitel.additionprovider` package.

```

#### 21.9.8 Implementing a Second Service Provider

Class `MultiplicationProblemProvider` ([Fig. 21.15](#ch21.xhtml_ch21fig15)) also implements the service-provider interface `ProblemProvider` (line 10). `MultiplicationProblemProvider` is nearly identical to `AdditionProblemProvider`, but line 16 passes the `String "*"` for the `Problem`’s operation, and the overridden `Problem` method `getResult` multiplies the left and right operands, returning their product.

[Click here to view code image](#ch21_images.xhtml_f0914-01)

```
 1   // Fig. 21.15: MultiplicationProblemProvider.java
 2   // MultiplicationProblemProvider implementation of interface
 3   // ProblemProvider for the MathTutor app.
 4   package com.deitel.multiplicationprovider;
