if ($1 > $2) {
   System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
}
100 > 72

jshell>
```

The condition `$1` > `$2` is now `true`, so the `if` statement’s body executes. The list of snippets is now

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0958-04)

```
jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   4 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   5 : $1 = 100
   6 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }

jshell>
```

#### A.2.11 Exiting JShell

To terminate the current JShell session, use the **`/exit`** **command** or enter the keyboard shortcut *Ctrl + d* (or *control + d*).

### A.3 Command-Line Input in JShell

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02), [Intro to Java Programming](#ch02.xhtml_ch02), and the preceding sections in this appendix.]**

In [Chapter 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02), we performed command-line input using a `Scanner` object:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0959-01)

```
Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in);

System.out.print("Enter first integer: ");
int number1 = input.nextInt();
```

We created a `Scanner`, prompted the user for input, then used `Scanner` method `nextInt` to read a value. Recall that the program then waited for you to enter an integer and press (or select) *Enter* before proceeding to the next statement. The on-screen interaction appeared as follows:

```
Enter first integer: 45
```

This section demonstrates what that interaction looks like in JShell.

##### Creating a `Scanner`

Start a new JShell session or `/reset` the current one, then create a `Scanner` object:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0959-02)

```
jshell> Scanner input = new Scanner(System.in)
input ==> java.util.Scanner[delimiters=\p{javaWhitespace}+] ...
\E][infinity string=\Q∞\E]

jshell>
```

You do not need to import `Scanner`. JShell automatically imports the `java.util` package and several others—[Section A.9](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec11) presents the complete list. When you create an object, JShell displays its text representation. The notation to the right of `input ==>` is the `Scanner`’s text representation (which you can simply ignore).

##### Prompting for Input and Reading a Value

Next, prompt the user for input:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0959-03)

```
jshell> System.out.print("Enter first integer: ")
Enter first integer:
jshell>
```

The statement’s output is displayed immediately, followed by the next `jshell>` prompt. Now enter the input statement:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0960-01)

```
jshell> int number1 = input.nextInt()
_
```

At this point, JShell waits for your input. The input cursor is positioned below the `jshell>` prompt and snippet you just entered—indicated by the underscore (`_`) above— rather than next to the prompt `"Enter first integer:"` as it was in [Chapter 2](#ch02.xhtml_ch02). Now enter an integer and press (or select) *Enter* to assign it to `number1`—the last snippet’s execution is now complete, so the next `jshell>` prompt appears.:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0960-02)

```
jshell> int number1 = input.nextInt()
45
number1 ==> 45

jshell>
```

Though you can use `Scanner` for command-line input in JShell, it’s awkward, and in most cases, unnecessary. The goal of the preceding interactions was to store an `int` in the variable `number1`. You can accomplish that in JShell with the simple assignment

```
jshell> int number1 = 45
number1 ==> 45

jshell>
```

So, you’ll typically use assignments, rather than command-line input in JShell.

### A.4 Declaring and Using Classes

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 8](#ch08.xhtml_ch08), [Real-World Modeling with Custom Classes](#ch08.xhtml_ch08).]**

[Section A.2](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec2) demonstrated basic JShell features. Here, we create a class and manipulate an object of a class. We’ll use the version of class `Account` presented in [Fig. 8.1](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig01).

#### A.4.1 Creating a Class in JShell

Start a new JShell session (or `/reset` the current one), then declare class `Account`—we ignored the comments from [Fig. 8.1](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig01):

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0960-03)

```
jshell> public class Account {
   ...>    private String name;
   ...>
   ...>    public void setName(String name) {
   ...>       this.name = name;
   ...>    }
   ...>
   ...>    public String getName() {
   ...>       return name;
   ...>    }
   ...> }
|  created class Account

jshell>
```

JShell recognizes when you enter the class’s closing brace—then displays

```
| created class Account
```

and issues the next `jshell>` prompt. Note that the semicolons throughout class `Account`’s body are required.

To save time, rather than entering a class’s code, you can load an existing source code file into JShell, as we demonstrate in [Section A.4.6](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec19). Though you can specify access modifiers like `public` on your classes (and other types), JShell ignores all access modifiers on the top-level types—that is, types that are not nested in other types.

##### Viewing Declared Classes

To view the names of the classes you’ve declared so far, enter the **`/types`** **command**:^([6](#appa.xhtml_fnappa_6a))

```
jshell> /types
|    class Account

jshell>
```

[6](#appa.xhtml_fnappa_6). `/types` displays all types you declare, including `class`es, `record`s, `interface`s and `enum`s.

#### A.4.2 Explicitly Declaring Reference-Type Variables

The following creates the `Account` variable `account`:

```
jshell> Account account
account ==> null

jshell>
```

The default value of a reference-type variable is `null`.

#### A.4.3 Creating Objects

You can create new objects. The following creates an `Account` variable named `account` and initializes it with a new object:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0961-01)

```
jshell> account = new Account()
account ==> Account@2d928643

jshell>
```

The strange notation

```
Account@2d928643
```

is the default text representation of the new `Account` object. If a class provides a custom `toString` method, the text representation it returns will be output instead. The value after the `@` symbol is the object’s hashcode.

##### Declaring an Implicit `Account` Variable Initialized with an `Account` Object

If you create an object with only the expression `new Account()`, JShell assigns the object to an implicit variable of type `Account`, as in:

```
jshell> new Account()
$4 ==> Account@49993335

jshell>
```

Note that this object’s hashcode (`49993335`) differs from the prior `Account` object’s hash-code (`2d928643`)—these typically are different, but that’s not guaranteed.

##### Viewing Declared Variables

You can view all the variables you’ve declared so far with the JShell **`/vars`** **command**:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0962-01)

```
jshell> /vars
|    Account account = Account@2d928643
|    Account $4 = Account@49993335

jshell>
```

For each variable, JShell outputs the type and variable name followed by an equal sign and the variable’s text representation.

#### A.4.4 Manipulating Objects

Once you have an object, you can call its methods. In fact, you already did this with the `System.out` object by calling its `println`, `print` and `printf` methods in earlier snippets.

The following sets the `account` object’s name:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0962-02)

```
jshell> account.setName("Amanda")

jshell>
```

The method `setName` has the return type `void`, so it does not return a value, and no additional output appears in JShell.

The following gets the account object’s name:

```
jshell> account.getName()
$6 ==> "Amanda"

jshell>
```

Method `getName` returns a `String`. When you invoke a method that returns a value, JShell stores the value in an implicitly declared variable. In this case, `$6`’s type is inferred to be `String`. Of course, you could have assigned the result of the preceding method call to an explicitly declared variable.

##### Using the Return Value of a Method in a Statement

If you invoke a method as part of a larger statement, the return value is used in that statement, rather than stored. For example, the following uses `println` to display the `account` object’s name:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0962-03)

```
jshell> System.out.println(account.getName())
Amanda

jshell>
```

#### A.4.5 Creating a Meaningful Variable Name for an Expression

You can give a meaningful variable name to a value JShell previously assigned to an implicit variable. For example, with the following snippet recalled

```
jshell> account.getName()
```

Enter

```
Shift + Tab, v
```

This notation means you should press (or select) both the *Shift* and *Tab* keys together, then release those keys and press (or select) *v*. JShell infers the expression’s type and begins a variable declaration for you—`account.getName()` returns a `String`, so JShell inserts `String` and an equal sign (`=`) before the expression, as in

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0963-01)

```
jshell> account.getName()
jshell> String _= account.getName()
```

JShell also positions the cursor (indicated by the _ above) immediately before the `=` so you can simply enter the variable name, as in

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0963-02)

```
jshell> String name = account.getName()
name ==> "Amanda"

jshell>
```

When you press (or select) *Enter*, JShell evaluates the new snippet and stores the value in the specified variable.

#### A.4.6 Saving and Opening Code-Snippet Files

You can save a session’s valid code snippets to a file, which you can load into a JShell session as needed.

##### Saving Snippets to a File

To save just the valid snippets, use the **`/save`** **command**, as in:

```
/save filename
```

By default, the file is created in the folder from which you launched JShell. To store the file in a different location, specify the complete path of the file.

##### Loading Snippets from a File

Once you save your snippets, they can be reloaded with the **`/open`** **command**:

```
/open filename
```

which executes each snippet in the file.

##### Using `/open` to Load Java Source-Code Files

You can also open existing Java source code files using `/open`. For example, let’s assume you’d like to experiment with class `Account` from [Fig. 8.1](#ch08.xhtml_ch08fig01) (as you did in [Section A.4.1](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec14)). Rather than entering its code into JShell, you can save time by loading the class from the source file `Account.java`. In a command window, you’d change to the folder containing `Account.java`, execute JShell, then use the following command to load the class declaration into JShell:

```
/open Account.java
```

To load a file from another folder, you can specify the file’s full pathname. [Section A.9](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec11) demonstrates how to use existing compiled classes in JShell.

### A.5 Discovery with JShell Auto-Completion

**[This section may be read after studying [Section 2.8](#ch02.xhtml_ch02lev1sec8).]**

JShell can help you write code. When you partially enter the name of an existing class, variable or method then press (or select) the *Tab* key, JShell does one of the following:

*   If no other name matches what you’ve entered so far, JShell enters the rest of the name for you.

*   If there are multiple names that begin with the same letters, JShell displays a list of those names to help you decide what to enter next—then you can enter the next letter(s) and press (or select) *Tab* again to complete the name.

*   If no names match what you entered so far, JShell does nothing, and your operating system’s alert sound plays as feedback.

Auto-completion is typically an IDE feature, but with JShell, it’s IDE-independent.

#### A.5.1 Auto-Completing Identifiers

Start a new JShell session or reset your current one. Then execute the following snippet to define the `String` variable `greeting` and initialize it to `"hello"`:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0964-00)

```
jshell> String greeting = "hello"
```

The only variable declared so far that begins with lowercase `"g"` is `greeting`—auto-completion is case-sensitive. If you enter `"g"` at the `jshell>` prompt:

```
jshell> g
```

then press (or select) *Tab*, JShell auto-completes the name:

```
jshell> greeting
```

If you then enter a dot:

```
jshell> greeting.
```

then press (or select) *Tab*, JShell does not know what method you want to call, so it displays a list of everything—in this case, all the methods—that can appear to the right of the dot:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0964-01)

```
jshell> greeting.
charAt(                 chars()                 codePointAt(
codePointBefore(        codePointCount(         codePoints()
compareTo(              compareToIgnoreCase(    concat(
contains(               contentEquals(          describeConstable()
endsWith(               equals(                 equalsIgnoreCase(
formatted(              getBytes(               getChars(
getClass()              hashCode()              indent(
indexOf(                intern()                isBlank()
isEmpty()               lastIndexOf(            length()
lines()                 matches(                notify()
notifyAll()             offsetByCodePoints(     regionMatches(
repeat(                 replace(                replaceAll(
replaceFirst(           resolveConstantDesc(    split(
splitWithDelimiters(    startsWith(             strip()
stripIndent()           stripLeading()          stripTrailing()
subSequence(            substring(              toCharArray()
toLowerCase(            toString()              toUpperCase(
transform(              translateEscapes()      trim()
wait(

jshell> greeting.
```

and follows the list with a new jshell> prompt that includes what you’ve entered so far. The list includes the methods declared in class String and several Object methods that all Java classes have (discussed in [Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09)). In the list of method names

*   those followed by "()" are methods that do not require arguments and

*   those followed only by "(" are methods that either require at least one argument or are overloaded methods that can be called with different numbers and/or types of arguments (discussed in [Section 5.7](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec7)).

Let’s assume you want to use String’s endsWith method to check whether greeting starts with "o". There’s only one method that begins with "en", so you can enter en then *Tab* to auto-complete endsWith:

```
jshell> greeting.endsWith(
```

JShell automatically inserts the method call’s opening left parenthesis. Now you can complete the snippet as in:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0965-01)

```
jshell> greeting.endsWith("o")
$2 ==> true

jshell>
```

### A.5.2 Auto-Completing JShell Commands

Auto-completion also works for JShell commands. If you enter `/` then press (or select) *Tab*, JShell displays the list of JShell commands:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0965-02)

```
jshell> /
/!          /?          /drop       /edit     /env       /exit
/help       /history    /imports    /list     /methods   /open
/reload     /reset      /save       /set      /types     /vars

<press tab again to see synopsis>
jshell> /
```

If you then enter `h` and press (or select) *Tab*, JShell displays only the commands that start with `/h`:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0965-03)

```
jshell> /h
/help       /history

<press tab again to see synopsis>
jshell> /h
```

Finally, if you enter `"i"` and press (or select) *Tab*, JShell auto-completes `/history`. Similarly, if you enter `/l` then press (or select) *Tab*, JShell auto-completes the command as `/list` because only that command starts with `/l`.

### A.6 Exploring a Class’s Members and Viewing Documentation

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 5](#ch05.xhtml_ch05), [Methods](#ch05.xhtml_ch05).]**

The preceding section introduced basic auto-completion capabilities. When using JShell for experimentation and discovery, you’ll often want to learn more about a class before using it. In this section, we’ll explore class `Math` to demonstrate how to view:

*   the parameters required by a method so that you can call it correctly

*   the documentation for a method

*   the documentation for a field of a class

*   the documentation for a class, and

*   the list of overloads for a given method.

Start a new JShell session or `/reset` the current one.

#### A.6.1 Listing Class `Math`’s `static` Members

As discussed in [Chapter 5](#ch05.xhtml_ch05), class `Math` contains only `static` members—`static` methods for various mathematical calculations and the `static` constants `PI`, `E` and `TAU`. To view a complete list, start a new JShell session, then enter `"Math."` and press (or select) *Tab*:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0966-01)

```
jshell> Math.
<press tab again to see all possible completions; total possible
completions: 103>
jshell> Math.
```

Because there are so many possible completions, JShell asks you to press *Tab* again to see all possible completions. Once you do, it displays—only 62 of the 103 completions are displayed because many of class `Math`’s methods are overloaded:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0966-02)

```
jshell> Math.
E                  IEEEremainder(     PI                TAU
abs(               absExact(          acos(             addExact(
asin(              atan(              atan2(            cbrt(
ceil(              ceilDiv(           ceilDivExact(     ceilMod(
clamp(             class              copySign(         cos(
cosh(              decrementExact(    divideExact(      exp(
expm1(             floor(             floorDiv(         floorDivExact(
floorMod(          fma(               getExponent(      hypot(
incrementExact(    log(               log10(            log1p(
max(               min(               multiplyExact(    multiplyFull(
multiplyHigh(      negateExact(       nextAfter(        nextDown(
nextUp(            pow(               random()          rint(
round(             scalb(             signum(           sin(
sinh(              sqrt(              subtractExact(    tan(
tanh(              toDegrees(         toIntExact(       toRadians(
ulp(                unsignedMultiplyHigh(
jshell> Math.
```

Again, JShell auto-completion displays everything that can appear to the right of the dot (`.`). Here, we entered a class name and a dot (`.`), so JShell displays only the class’s `static` members. The names that are not followed by any parentheses (`E`, `PI` and `TAU`) are the class’s `static` variables. All the other names are the class’s `static` methods:

*   Any method names followed by `()`—only `random` in this case—do not require arguments.

*   Any method names followed by only an opening left parenthesis, `(`, require at least one argument or are overloaded.

You can easily view the value of constants like `PI` and `E`:

```
jshell> Math.PI
$1 ==> 3.141592653589793

jshell> Math.E
$2 ==> 2.718281828459045

jshell>
```

#### A.6.2 Viewing a Method’s Parameters

Let’s assume you wish to test `Math`’s `pow` method but do not know the required parameters.

You can enter

```
Math.p
```

then press (or select) *Tab* to auto-complete the name `pow`:

```
jshell> Math.pow(
```

No other methods begin with `"pow"`, so JShell inserts the left parenthesis to indicate the beginning of a method call. Next, you can press (or select) *Tab* to view the method’s parameters:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0967-01)

```
jshell> Math.pow(
$1   $2

Signatures:
double Math.pow(double a, double b)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math.pow(
```

JShell displays

*   variables in the current session (`$1` and `$2`) that could be used as `pow`’s arguments,

*   the method’s return type, name and complete parameter list, indicating that the method requires two `double` parameters,

*   `"<press tab again to see documentation>"`, and

*   the next `jshell>` prompt containing what you’ve entered so far.

#### A.6.3 Viewing a Method’s Documentation

JShell integrates the Java API documentation so you can view documentation conveniently in JShell rather than using a separate web browser. Suppose you’d like to learn more about `pow` before completing your code snippet. You can press (or select) *Tab* again to view the method’s Java documentation (known as its javadoc). We cut out some of the documentation text and replaced it with an ellipsis (…) to save space—try the steps in your own JShell session to observe the complete text:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0968-01)

```
jshell> Math.pow(
double Math.pow(double a, double b)
Returns the value of the first argument raised to the power of the
second argument. Special cases:
  * If the second argument is positive or negative zero, then the result
is 1.0.
...
<press tab again to see next page>
jshell> Math.pow(
```

For lengthy documentation, JShell displays part of it followed by the message:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0968-02)

```
<press tab again to see next page>
```

You can press (or select) *Tab* to view the next page of documentation. The next `jshell>` prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

#### A.6.4 Viewing a `public` Field’s Documentation

You can use the *Tab* feature to learn more about a class’s `public` fields. For example, if you enter `Math.PI` followed by *Tab*, JShell displays

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0968-03)

```
jshell> Math.PI
Signatures:
Math.PI:double

<press tab again to see documentation>
```

which includes `Math.PI`’s type and indicates that you can use *Tab* again to view the documentation. Doing so displays:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0968-04)

```
jshell> Math.PI
Math.PI:double
The double value that is closer than any other to pi (π), the ratio of
the circumference of a circle to its diameter.
jshell> Math.PI
```

and the next `jshell>` prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

#### A.6.5 Viewing a Class’s Documentation

You can also enter a class name then *Tab* to view the class’s fully qualified name. For example, entering `Math` then *Tab* outputs:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0968-05)

```
jshell> Math
Math         MathContext

Signatures:
java.lang.Math

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math
```

indicating that class `Math` is in the package `java.lang`. Entering *Tab* again contains the beginning of the class’s documentation:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0969-01)

```
jshell> Math
java.lang.Math
The class Math contains methods for performing basic numeric operations
such as the elementary exponential, logarithm, square root, and
trigonometric functions.
...

<press tab again to see next page>
jshell> Math
```

In this case, there is more documentation to view, so you can press (or select) *Tab* to view it. Whether or not you view the remaining documentation, the `jshell>` prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

#### A.6.6 Viewing Method Overloads

Many classes have overloaded methods. When you press (or select) *Tab* to view an overloaded method’s parameters, JShell displays the complete list of overloads with the parameters for every overload. For example, method `Math.abs` has four overloads:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0969-02)

```
jshell> Math.abs(
$1   $2

Signatures:
int Math.abs(int a)
long Math.abs(long a)
float Math.abs(float a)
double Math.abs(double a)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> Math.abs(
```

When you press (or select) *Tab* again to view the documentation, JShell outputs the first overload’s documentation:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0969-03)

```
jshell> Math.abs(
int Math.abs(int a)
Returns the absolute value of an int value.If the argument is not
negative, the argument is returned. If the argument is negative, the
negation of the argument is returned.
...

<press tab again to see next page>
```

You can then press (or select) *Tab* to view the documentation for the next overload in the list. Again, whether or not you view the remaining documentation, the `jshell>` prompt contains the portion of the snippet you’ve entered so far.

#### A.6.7 Exploring Members of a Specific Object

The exploration features in [Sections A.6.1](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec21)–[A.6.6](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec26) also apply to the members of a specific object. Let’s start a new session then create and explore a `String` object:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0969-04)

```
jshell> String dayName = "Monday"
dayName ==> "Monday"

jshell>
```

To view the `dayName` object’s methods, enter `"dayName."` and press (or select) *Tab*:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0970-01)

```
jshell> dayName.
charAt(                   chars()                codePointAt(
codePointBefore(          codePointCount(        codePoints()
compareTo(                compareToIgnoreCase(   concat(
contains(                 contentEquals(         describeConstable()
endsWith(                 equals(                equalsIgnoreCase(
formatted(                getBytes(              getChars(
getClass()                hashCode()             indent(
indexOf(                  intern()               isBlank()
isEmpty()                 lastIndexOf(           length()
lines()                   matches(               notify()
notifyAll()               offsetByCodePoints(    regionMatches(
repeat(                   replace(               replaceAll(
replaceFirst(             resolveConstantDesc(   split(
splitWithDelimiters(      startsWith(            strip()
stripIndent()             stripLeading()         stripTrailing()
subSequence(              substring(             toCharArray()
toLowerCase(              toString()             toUpperCase(
transform(                translateEscapes()     trim()
wait(

jshell> dayName.
```

##### Exploring `toUpperCase`

Let’s investigate the `toUpperCase` method. Continue by entering `"toU"` and pressing *Tab* to auto-complete its name:

```
jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(
```

Then, enter *Tab* to view the method’s parameters:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0970-02)

```
jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(
Signatures:
String String.toUpperCase(Locale locale)
String String.toUpperCase()

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> dayName.toUpperCase(
```

This method has two overloads. You can now use *Tab* to read about each overload or choose the one you wish to use by specifying the appropriate arguments (if any). In this case, we’ll use the no-argument version to create a new `String` containing `MONDAY`, so we simply enter the closing right parenthesis of the method call and press (or select) *Enter*:

```
jshell> dayName.toUpperCase()
$2 ==> "MONDAY"

jshell>
```

##### Exploring `substring`

Let’s assume you want to create the new `String "DAY"`—a subset of the implicit variable `$2`’s characters. For this purpose, class `String` provides the overloaded method `substring`. First, enter `"$2.subs"` and press (or select) *Tab* to auto-complete the method’s name:

```
jshell> $2.substring(
```

Next, use *Tab* to view the method’s overloads:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0971-01)

```
jshell> $2.substring(
Signatures:
String String.substring(int beginIndex)
String String.substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)

<press tab again to see documentation>
jshell> $2.substring(
```

Next, use *Tab* again to view the first overload’s documentation:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0971-02)

```
jshell> $2.substring(
String String.substring(int beginIndex)
Returns a string that is a substring of this string.The substring begins
with the character at the specified index and extends to the end of this
string.
...
<press tab again to see next page>
```

The documentation indicates that this overload of the method enables you to obtain a substring starting from a specific character index (that is, position) and continuing through the end of the `String`. The first character in the `String` is at index `0`. This is the version of the method we wish to use to obtain `"DAY"` from `"MONDAY"`, so we can return to our code snippet at the `jshell>` prompt:

```
jshell> $2.substring(
```

Finally, we can complete our call to substring and press (or select) *Enter* to view the results:

```
jshell> $2.substring(3)
$3 ==> "DAY"

jshell>
```

### A.7 Declaring Methods

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 5](#ch05.xhtml_ch05), [Methods](#ch05.xhtml_ch05), and the preceding portions of this appendix.]**

You can use JShell to prototype methods. For example, let’s assume we’d like to write code that displays the cubes of the values from 1 through 10\. For the purpose of this discussion, we’re going to define two methods:

*   Method `displayCubes` will iterate 10 times, calling method `cube` each time.

*   Method `cube` will receive one int value and return the cube of that value.

#### A.7.1 Forward Referencing an Undeclared Method—Declaring Method `displayCubes`

Let’s begin with method `displayCubes`. Start a new JShell session or `/reset` the current one, then enter the following method declaration:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0971-03)

```
void displayCubes() {
   for (int i = 1; i <= 10; ++i) {
      System.out.printf("Cube of %d is %d%n", i, cube(i));
   }
}
```

When you complete the method declaration, JShell displays:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0972-01)

```
| created method displayCubes(), however, it cannot be invoked until
method cube(int) is declared

jshell>
```

After you enter the method body’s opening left brace, JShell displays continuation prompts (`...>`) before each subsequent line until you complete the method declaration by entering its closing right brace. Also, although JShell says `"created method display-Cubes()"`, it indicates that you cannot call this method until `"cube(int) is declared"`. This is not fatal in JShell—it recognizes that `displayCubes` depends on an undeclared method (`cube`)—this is known as **forward referencing** an undeclared method. Once you define `cube`, you can call `displayCubes`.

#### A.7.2 Declaring a Previously Undeclared Method

Next, let’s declare method `cube` but purposely make a logic error by returning the square rather than the cube of its argument:

```
jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>    return x * x;
   ...> }
|  created method cube(int)

jshell>
```

At this point, you can use JShell’s **`/methods`** **command** to list the methods declared in the current JShell session:

```
jshell> /methods
|    void displayCubes()
|    int cube(int)

jshell>
```

#### A.7.3 Testing `cube` and Replacing Its Declaration

Now that method `cube` is declared, let’s test it with the argument `2`:

```
jshell> cube(2)
$3 ==> 4

jshell>
```

Based on how the method is currently implemented, it returns the `4` (that is, 2 * 2). However, the method’s purpose was to calculate the cube of its argument, so the result should have been `8` (2 * 2 * 2). You can edit `cube`’s snippet to correct the problem. Let’s edit the snippet directly in JShell rather than in JShell Edit Pad. Use the up arrow three times to redisplay cube’s definition:

```
jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>    return x * x;
   ...> }
```

Then use the arrow keys to move the cursor to the semicolon and edit the statement so the method appears as follows, then press (or select) *Enter*:

```
jshell> int cube(int x) {
   ...>   return x * x * x;
   ...> }
|  modified method cube(int)

jshell>
```

JShell confirms that method `cube` was modified.

#### A.7.4 Testing Updated Method `cube` and Method `displayCubes`

Now that method `cube` is properly declared, let’s test it again with the arguments `2` and `10`:

```
jshell> cube(2)
$5 ==> 8

jshell> cube(10)
$6 ==> 1000

jshell>
```

The method properly returns the cubes of `2` (that is, `8`) and `10` (that is, `1000`) and stores the results in the implicit variables `$5` and `$6`.

Now, let’s test `displayCubes`. If you enter `"di"` and press (or select) *Tab*, JShell auto-completes the name, including the parentheses of the method call, because `displayCubes` receives no parameters. The following contains results of the call:

```
jshell> displayCubes()
Cube of 1 is 1
Cube of 2 is 8
Cube of 3 is 27
Cube of 4 is 64
Cube of 5 is 125
Cube of 6 is 216
Cube of 7 is 343
Cube of 8 is 512
Cube of 9 is 729
Cube of 10 is 1000

jshell>
```

### A.8 Exceptions

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 6](#ch06.xhtml_ch06) and the preceding sections of this appendix.]**

In [Section 6.11](#ch06.xhtml_ch06lev1sec11), we introduced Java’s exception-handling mechanism, demonstrating how to catch an exception that occurred when we attempted to use an out-of-bounds array index. In JShell, catching exceptions is not required—it automatically catches each exception and displays information about it, then displays the next JShell prompt, so you can continue your session. This is particularly important for checked exceptions ([Section 10.5](#ch10.xhtml_ch10lev1sec5)) that must be caught in regular Java programs. As you know, catching an exception requires wrapping the code in a `try`…`catch` statement. By automatically, catching all exceptions, JShell makes it easier for you to experiment with methods that throw checked exceptions.

In the following new JShell session, we declare an array of `int` values then demonstrate both valid and invalid array-access expressions:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0974-01)

```
jshell> int[] values = {10, 20, 30}
values ==> int[3] { 10, 20, 30 }

jshell> values[1]
$2 ==> 20

jshell> values[10]
|  Exception java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 10 out of
bounds for length 3
|        at (#3:1)

jshell>
```

The snippet `values[10]` attempts to access an out-of-bounds element—recall that this results in an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Even though we did not wrap the code in a `try`…`catch`, JShell catches the exception and displays its `String` representation. This includes the exception’s type and an error message (in this case, the invalid index `10`), followed by a stack trace indicating where the problem occurred. The notation

```
|      at (#3:1)
```

indicates that the exception occurred at line 1 of the code snippet with the ID 3\. [Section 5.10](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec10) discussed the method-call stack. A stack trace indicates the methods that were on the method-call stack at the time the exception occurred. A typical stack trace contains several `"at"` lines like the one output here—one per stack frame. After displaying the stack trace, the next `jshell>` prompt appears. [Chapter 10](#ch10.xhtml_ch10) discusses stack traces in detail.

### A.9 Importing Classes and Adding Packages to the `CLASSPATH`

**[This section may be read after studying [Chapter 11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11), [Files, I/O Streams, JSON Serialization & CSV Files](#ch11.xhtml_ch11), and the preceding sections of this appendix.]**

JShell is helpful for experimenting with classes and class libraries before using them in your programs. You can `import` types from Java’s API and third-party libraries that you add to JShell’s classpath and module path. Several packages are so commonly used by Java developers that JShell automatically `import`s them for you. You can change this with JShell’s

```
/set start
```

command, which we present in [Section A.11](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec13).

##### Viewing the Imported Packages

For this section, we assume you started `jshell` from the `ch11` examples folder. The JShell **`/imports`** **command** lists the current session’s `import` declarations. The following packages are auto-imported when you begin a new JShell session:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0975-01)

```
jshell> /imports
|    import java.io.*
|    import java.math.*
|    import java.net.*
|    import java.nio.file.*
|    import java.util.*
|    import java.util.concurrent.*
|    import java.util.function.*
|    import java.util.prefs.*
|    import java.util.regex.*
|    import java.util.stream.*

jshell>
```

The `java.lang` package’s contents are always available in JShell, just as in any Java source-code file.

##### Adding Packages to the Class Path

You can also import your own or third-party packages to experiment with them in JShell. JShell’s **`/env -class-path`** **command** adds packages to JShell’s `CLASSPATH`, which tells JShell where additional packages are located.^([7](#appa.xhtml_fnappa_7a)) You can then use `import` declarations to experiment with the packages’ contents in JShell.

[7](#appa.xhtml_fnappa_7). JShell also provides the options **`-module-path`** and **`-add-modules`** to add modules so you can import packages from them.

##### Using Jackson in JShell

In [Chapter 11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11), we introduced the Jackson open-source library for serializing objects to JSON format. Here, we’ll add it to JShell’s `CLASSPATH`, then serialize an object to a JSON `String` in JShell. If you have an open JShell session, use `/exit` to terminate it. Then, change directories to the `ch11` examples folder and start a new JShell session.

##### Adding the Location of a Package to the `CLASSPATH`

The `ch11` folder’s `libs` subfolder contains the Jackson library components we used in [Chapter 11](#ch11.xhtml_ch11). The following command adds this package to the `CLASSPATH` on Windows—ensure that you type the entire classpath without spaces:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0975-02)

```
jshell> /env -class-path libs/jackson-core-2.18.1.jar;libs/jackson-
databind-2.18.1.jar;libs/jackson-annotations-2.18.1.jar
|  Setting new options and restoring state.

jshell>
```

If you use macOS, replace the semicolons (`;`) with colons (`:`). The `.jar` (Java archive) files are ZIP files containing compiled Jackson library Java code. We use relative paths to the `libs` folder here. You can also specify absolute paths.

##### Importing a Class from the Package

Now, you can import `ObjectMapper` for use in JShell. The following demonstrates importing the `ObjectMapper` class and the complete list of imports in the current session:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0975-03)

```
jshell> import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
jshell> /imports
|    import java.io.*
|    import java.math.*
|    import java.net.*
|    import java.nio.file.*
|    import java.util.*
|    import java.util.concurrent.*
|    import java.util.function.*
|    import java.util.prefs.*
|    import java.util.regex.*
|    import java.util.stream.*
|    import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper

jshell>
```

##### Creating a `List<Account>` to Serialize as JSON

Let’s create a `List<Account>` to serialize in JShell:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0976-01)

```
jshell> record Account(int accountNumber, String name, double balance) {}
|  created record Account

jshell> List<Account> accounts = List.of(
   ...>    new Account(100, "Devi", 24.98),
   ...>    new Account(200, "Taylor", 345.67));
accounts ==> [Account[accountNumber=100, name=Devi, balance=24 ...
e=Taylor, balance=345.67]]

jshell>
```

##### Using the Imported `ObjectMapper` Class

Finally, you can use class `ObjectMapper`. Below, we create an `ObjectMapper` and demonstrate that JShell’s auto-complete capability can display the list of available methods. There are 247 autocomplete options, so we show just a few below and use an ellipsis to indicate there are more:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0976-02)

```
jshell> var mapper = new ObjectMapper();
mapper ==> com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper@7e5afaa6

jshell> mapper.
<press tab again to see all possible completions; total possible
completions: 247>
jshell> mapper.
acceptJsonFormatVisitor(             activateDefaultTyping(
activateDefaultTypingAsProperty(     addHandler(
addMixIn(                            addMixInAnnotations(
...
jshell> mapper.
```

Next, we use **`ObjectMapper`****’s** **`writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter`** **method** to get an `ObjectWriter` that outputs JSON text with indentation for better readability:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0976-03)

```
jshell> var prettyWriter = mapper.writerWithDefaultPrettyPrinter()
prettyWriter ==> com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectWriter@57d7f8ca

jshell>
```

Finally, we use the **`ObjectWriter`****’s** **`writeValueAsString`** **method** to get `accounts`’ JSON representation and display the returned `String`:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0977-01)

```
jshell> System.out.println(prettyWriter.writeValueAsString(accounts))
[ {
  "accountNumber" : 100,
  "name" : "Devi",
  "balance" : 24.98
}, {
  "accountNumber" : 200,
  "name" : "Taylor",
  "balance" : 345.67
} ]

jshell>
```

### A.10 Using an External Editor

[Section A.2.10](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec3) demonstrated JShell Edit Pad for editing code snippets. This tool provides only simple editing functionality. Many programmers prefer to use more powerful text editors. You can specify your preferred text editor using JShell’s **`/set editor`** **command**. For example, the JShell command

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0977-02)

```
jshell> /set editor notepad.exe
|  Editor set to: notepad.exe

jshell>
```

sets `notepad.exe` as the snippet editor for the current JShell session. The `/set editor` command’s argument is operating-system-specific. For example, on macOS, you can use the built-in `nano` text editor with the command

```
/set editor nano
```

##### Editing Snippets with a Custom Text Editor

When you’re using a custom editor, each time you save snippet edits JShell immediately re-evaluates any snippets that have changed and outputs their results (but not the snippets themselves) in the JShell output.

##### Retaining the Editor Setting

You can retain your editor setting for future JShell sessions as follows:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0977-03)

```
/set editor -retain commandToLaunchYourEditor
```

##### Restoring the JShell Edit Pad As the Default Editor

If you do not retain your custom editor, subsequent JShell sessions will use JShell Edit Pad. If you do retain the custom editor, you can restore JShell Edit Pad as the default with

```
/set editor -retain -default
```

### A.11 Summary of JShell Commands

The following table contains the basic JShell commands. Many of these commands have been presented throughout this appendix. Others are discussed in this section.

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `/help` or `/?` | Displays JShell’s list of commands. |
| `/help intro` | Displays a brief introduction to JShell. |
| `/help shortcuts` | Displays a description of several JShell shortcut keys. |
| `/list` | By default, lists the valid snippets you’ve entered in the current session. To list all snippets, use `/list -all`. |
| `/!` | Recalls and re-evaluates the last snippet. |
| `/`*id* | Recalls and re-evaluates the snippet with the specified *id*. You may also specify several individual snippets or snippet ranges, each separated from the next by a space. |
| `/-`*n* | Recalls and re-evaluates a prior snippet—for *n*, `1` is the last snippet, `2` is the second-to-last, etc. |
| `/edit` | By default, opens a JShell Edit Pad window containing the valid snippets you’ve entered in the current session. [Section A.10](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec12) discusses how to configure an external editor. |
| `/save` | Saves the current session’s valid snippets to a specified file. |
| `/open` | Opens a specified file of code snippets, loads the snippets into the current session and evaluates the loaded snippets. |
| `/vars` | Displays the current session’s variables and their corresponding values. |
| `/methods` | Displays the signatures of the current session’s declared methods. |
| `/types` | Displays types declared in the current session. |
| `/imports` | Displays the current session’s `import` declarations. |
| `/exit` | Terminates the current JShell session. |
| `/reset` | Resets the current JShell session, deleting all code snippets. |
| `/reload` | Reloads a JShell session and executes the valid snippets ([Section A.11.3](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec36)). |
| `/drop` | Deletes a specified snippet from the current session ([Section A.11.4](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec37)). |
| `/env` | Makes changes to the JShell environment, such as adding packages or modules so you can use their types in JShell. |
| `/history` | Lists everything you’ve entered in the current JShell session, including all snippets (valid, invalid or overwritten) and JShell commands—the `/list` command outputs only snippets, not JShell commands. |
| `/set` | Sets various JShell configuration options, such as the editor used in response to the `/edit` command, the text used for the JShell prompts, the imports to specify when a session starts, etc. ([Sections A.11.5](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec38)–[A.11.6](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec39)). |

#### A.11.1 Getting Help in JShell

JShell’s help documentation is incorporated directly via the **`/help`** or **`/?`** commands—`/?` is simply a shorthand for `/help`. For a quick introduction to JShell, enter:

```
/help intro
```

To display JShell’s list of commands, enter

```
/help
```

For more information on a given command’s options, enter

```
/help command
```

For example

```
/help /list
```

displays the `/list` command’s more detailed help documentation. Similarly

```
/help /set start
```

displays more detailed help documentation for the `/set` command’s `start` option. For a list of the shortcut key combinations in JShell, enter

```
/help shortcuts
```

#### A.11.2 `/edit` Command: Additional Features

We’ve discussed using `/edit` to load all valid snippets, a snippet with a specified ID or a method with a specified name into JShell Edit Pad. You can specify the identifier for any variable, method or type declaration you’d like to edit. For example, if the current JShell session contains the declaration of a class named `Account`, the following loads that class into JShell Edit Pad:

```
/edit Account
```

#### A.11.3 `/reload` Command

JShell’s **`/reload`** command can re-execute all valid snippets in the current session. Consider the session from [Sections A.2.9](#appa.xhtml_appalev2sec10)–[A.2.10](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec3):

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0979-01)

```
jshell> /list

   1 : 45
   2 : 72
   3 : if ($1 < $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   4 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }
   5 : $1 = 100;
   6 : if ($1 > $2) {
          System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
       }

jshell>
```

The following reloads that session one snippet at a time:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0979-02)

```
jshell> /reload
|  Restarting and restoring state.
-: 45
-: 72
-: if ($1 < $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d < %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
45 < 72
-: if ($1 > $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
-: $1 = 100
-: if ($1 > $2) {
      System.out.printf("%d > %d%n", $1, $2);
   }
100 > 72

jshell>
```

Each reloaded snippet is preceded by `-:` and in the case of the `if` statements, the output (if any) appears immediately following each `if` statement. If you prefer not to list the snippets as they reload, you can use the `/reload` command’s `-quiet` option:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0980-01)

```
jshell> /reload -quiet
|  Restarting and restoring state.
45 < 72
100 > 72

jshell>
```

In this case, only the results of output statements are displayed. Then, you can view the snippets that were reloaded with the `/list` command.

#### A.11.4 `/drop` Command

You can eliminate a snippet from the current session with JShell’s **`/drop`** command followed by a snippet ID or an identifier. The following new JShell session declares a variable `x` and a method `cube`, then drops `x` via its snippet ID and drops `cube` via its identifier:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0980-02)

```
jshell> int x = 10
x ==> 10

jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
|  created method cube(int)

jshell> /list

   1 : int x = 10;
   2 : int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}

jshell> /drop 1
|  dropped variable x

jshell> /drop cube
|  dropped method cube(int)

jshell> /list

jshell>
```

#### A.11.5 Feedback Modes

JShell has several feedback modes that determine what gets displayed after each interaction. To change the feedback mode, use JShell’s **`/set feedback`** command:

```
/set feedback mode
```

where *mode* is `concise`, `normal` (the default), `silent` or `verbose`. All of the prior JShell interactions in this appendix used the `normal` mode.

##### Feedback Mode `verbose`

Below is a new JShell session in which we used `verbose` mode, which developers new to Java might prefer:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0981-01)

```
jshell> /set feedback verbose
|  Feedback mode: verbose

jshell> int x = 10
x ==> 10
|  created variable x : int

jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
|  created method cube(int)

jshell> cube(x)
$3 ==> 1000
|  created scratch variable $3 : int

jshell> x = 5
x ==> 5
|  assigned to x : int

jshell> cube(x)
$5 ==> 125
|  created scratch variable $5 : int

jshell>
```

Notice the additional feedback indicating that

*   variable `x` was created,

*   method `cube` was created,

*   scratch variable `$3` was created on the first call to `cube`,

*   an `int` was assigned to the variable `x`, and

*   scratch variable `$5` was created on the second call to `cube`.

##### Feedback Mode `concise`

Next, we `/reset` the session then set the feedback mode to `concise` and repeat the preceding session:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0981-02)

```
jshell> /set feedback concise
jshell> int x = 10
jshell> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
jshell> cube(x)
$3 ==> 1000
jshell> x = 5
jshell> cube(x)
$5 ==> 125
jshell>
```

Note that the only feedback displayed is the result of each call to `cube`. If an error occurs, its feedback also will be displayed.

##### Feedback Mode `silent`

Finally, we `/reset` the session then set the feedback mode to `silent` and repeat the preceding session:

[Click here to view code image](#appa_images.xhtml_f0982-01)

```
jshell> /set feedback silent
-> int x = 10
-> int cube(int y) {return y * y * y;}
-> cube(x)
-> x = 5
-> cube(x)
-> /set feedback normal
|  Feedback mode: normal

jshell>
```

In this case, the `jshell>` prompt becomes `->` and only error feedback will be displayed. You might use this mode if you’ve copied code from a Java source file and want to paste it into JShell, but do not want feedback for each line.

#### A.11.6 Other JShell Features Configurable with `/set`

So far, we’ve demonstrated the `/set` command’s capabilities for setting an external snippet editor and setting feedback modes. The `/set` command provides extensive capabilities for creating custom feedback modes via the commands:

*   `/set mode`

*   `/set prompt`

*   `/set truncation`

*   `/set format`

The `/set mode` command creates a user-defined custom feedback mode. Then, you can use the other three commands to customize all aspects of JShell’s feedback. The details of these commands are beyond the scope of this appendix. JShell’s help documentation for each of the preceding commands contains more information.

##### Customizing JShell Startup

[Section A.9](#appa.xhtml_appalev1sec11) listed the set of common packages JShell `import`s at the start of each session. Using JShell’s **`/set start`** command

```
/set start filename
```

you can provide a file of Java snippets and JShell commands that will be used in the current session when it restarts due to a `/reset` or `/reload` command. You can also remove all startup snippets with

```
/set start -none
```

or return to the default startup snippets with

```
/set start -default
```

In all three cases, the setting applies only to the current session unless you also include the `-retain` option. For example, the following command indicates that all subsequent JShell sessions should load the specified file of startup snippets and commands:

```
/set start -retain filename
```

You can restore the defaults for future sessions with

```
/set start -retain -default
```

### A.12 Keyboard Shortcuts for Snippet Editing

In addition to the commands in Fig. A.11, JShell supports many keyboard shortcuts for editing code, such as quickly jumping to the beginning or end of a line or jumping between words in a line. The following table contains some of the shortcuts available.

| Shortcut | Description |
| --- | --- |
| *Ctrl + a* | Move cursor to beginning of line. |
| *Ctrl + e* | Move cursor to end of line. |
| *Alt + b* (Windows) or *Option + b* (macOS) | Move the cursor backward by one word. |
| *Alt + f* (Windows) or *Option + f* (macOS) | Move the cursor forward by one word. |
| *Ctrl + r* | Perform a search for the last command or snippet containing the characters you enter after *Ctrl + r*. |
| *Ctrl + t* | Reverse the two characters to the left of the cursor. |
| *Ctrl + k* | Cut everything from the cursor to the end of the line. |
| *Ctrl + u* | Cut everything from the beginning of the line up to, but not including the character at the cursor position. |
| *Ctrl + w* | Cut the word before the cursor. |
| *Alt + d* (Windows) or *Option + d* (macOS) | Cut the word after the cursor. |

### A.13 How JShell Reinterprets Java for Interactive Use

In JShell:

*   A `main` method is not required.

*   Semicolons are not required on standalone statements.

*   Variables do not need to be declared in classes or in methods.

*   Methods do not need to be declared inside a class’s body.

*   Statements do not need to be written inside methods.

*   Redeclaring a variable, method or type drops the prior declaration and replaces it with the new one, whereas the Java compiler typically would report an error.

*   You do not need to catch exceptions, though you can if you need to test exception handling.

*   JShell ignores top-level access modifiers (`public`, `private`, `protected`, `static`, `final`)—only `abstract` ([Chapter 9](#ch09.xhtml_ch09)) is allowed as a class modifier.

*   The `synchronized` keyword ([Chapter 18](#ch18.xhtml_ch18), [Concurrency: Platform Threads to Virtual Threads](#ch18.xhtml_ch18)) is ignored.

*   `package` statements and `module` statements are not allowed.

### A.14 IDE JShell Support

Many Java IDEs include JShell support, including IntelliJ IDEA, the Eclipse IDE for Java Developers, NetBeans and Visual Studio Code. Each handles opening JShell and running code snippets in its own way. Some include code syntax coloring and handle name auto-completion differently.

#### Generative AI

**1** Prompt genAIs for a step-by-step tutorial on using JShell in your preferred IDE. Ask them to explain the key differences between JShell in your IDE vs. JShell at the command line.

### A.15 Wrap-Up

In this appendix, you used JShell—Java’s interactive REPL for exploration, discovery and experimentation. We started a JShell session and worked with various types of code snippets, including statements, variables, expressions, methods and classes—all without having to declare a class containing a `main` method to execute the code.

You listed the valid snippets in the current session, and recalled and executed prior snippets and commands using the up and down arrow keys. You also learned that you can list the current session’s variables, methods, types and `import`s. We cleared the current JShell session to remove all existing snippets and saved snippets to a file then reloaded them.

We demonstrated JShell’s auto-completion capabilities for code and commands, explored a class’s members and displayed documentation directly in JShell. We explored class `Math`, demonstrating how to list its `static` members, how to view a method’s parameters and overloads, view a method’s documentation and view a `public` field’s documentation. We also explored the methods of a `String` object.

You declared methods and forward referenced an undeclared method that you declared later in the session, then learned that you could go back and execute the first method. We also replaced a method declaration with a new method—in fact, you can replace any declaration of a variable, method or type.

We demonstrated that JShell catches all exceptions and simply displays a stack trace followed by the next `jshell>` prompt, so you can continue the session. You imported an existing compiled class from a package, then used that class in a JShell session.

Next, we summarized and demonstrated various other JShell commands. We configured a custom snippet editor, viewed JShell’s help documentation, reloaded a session, dropped snippets from a session, configured feedback modes and more. We listed some additional keyboard shortcuts for editing the current snippet at the `jshell>` prompt. Finally, we discussed how JShell reinterprets Java for interactive use and mentioned IDE support for JShell.

$21 ==> true

jshell> 7 > 9
$22 ==> false

jshell> 7 >= 9
$23 ==> false

jshell>
```

what are the values of `a`, `x`, `y` and `z` after the following statement executes?

a = x = y = z = 10

## B

## Formatted Output

![Images](graphics/common.jpg)

**Objectives**

In this appendix, you’ll:

*   Use `printf` to format outputs.

*   Format decimal, octal and hexadecimal integers.

*   Format floating-point numbers with fixed-point and scientific notations.

*   Format `String`s and characters.

*   Format with field widths and precisions.

*   Use various `printf` formatting flags to align data, display integer bases, pad fields with 0s, display numeric values with their locale-specific thousands separator and display negative values in parentheses.

*   Use argument indexes to specify where to place each argument in a format string.

*   Format `String`s in memory rather than displaying formatted output.

Outline

### B.1 Introduction

This appendix presents formatting features of method `printf` and class `Formatter` (package `java.util`). Class `Formatter` formats data as a `String` in memory by default but also can send formatted output to a specified destination, such as a file. Method `printf` uses a `Formatter` object to send formatted output to the standard output. We’ve discussed many `printf` features throughout the book. Here, we summarize those features and introduce others, such as using argument indexes to position arguments in a format string, and displaying numbers and `String`s with various flags. We briefly introduced date/time formatting in [Section 5.12](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec12), Objects-Natural Case Study: Java Date/Time API. You’ll explore date/time formatting further in Generative AI Exercise B.2.

### B.2 Output with `printf`

Precise output formatting is accomplished with `printf`. Java borrowed (and enhanced) this feature from the C programming language. Method `printf` can perform the following formatting capabilities, each of which is discussed in this appendix:

1.  Rounding floating-point values to an indicated number of decimal places.

2.  Aligning a column of numbers with decimal points appearing one above the other.

3.  Right alignment and left alignment of outputs.

4.  Inserting literal characters at precise locations in a line of output.

5.  Representing floating-point numbers in exponential format.

6.  Representing integers in octal and hexadecimal format.

7.  Displaying all types of data with fixed-size field widths and precisions.

Method `printf` also can display dates and times, but the class `DateTimeFormatter` (introduced in [Section 5.12](#ch05.xhtml_ch05lev1sec12)) is preferred.

Every call to `printf` supplies as the first argument a format string that describes the output format. The format string may consist of fixed text and format specifiers. Fixed text is output by `printf` just as it would be output by `System.out` methods `print` or `println`. Each format specifier is a placeholder for a value and specifies the data type to output. Format specifiers may also include optional formatting information.

In the simplest form, each format specifier begins with a percent sign (`%`), followed by a **conversion character** representing the data type of the value to output. For example, the format specifier `%s` is a placeholder for a `String`, and the format specifier `%d` is a placeholder for an `int` value. The optional formatting information, such as an argument index, flags, field width and precision, is specified between the percent sign and the conversion character. We demonstrate each of these capabilities.

### B.3 Integer Formatting

The following table describes the **integer conversion characters**—[Appendix C](#appc.xhtml_appc) overviews the binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal number systems.

| Conversion character | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **d** | Display a decimal (base 10) integer. |
| **o** | Display an octal (base 8) integer. |
| **x** or **X** Display a hexadecimal (base 16) integer. `X` uses uppercase letters. |  |

[Figure B.1](#appb.xhtml_appbfig01) uses each to print an integer. The plus sign is not displayed by default, but the minus sign is. Later in this appendix ([Fig. B.8](#appb.xhtml_appbfig08)), we’ll see how to force plus signs to print.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1003-02)

```
 1   // Fig. B.1: IntegerConversionTest.java
 2   // Using the integer conversion characters.
 3
 4   public class IntegerConversionTest {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         System.out.printf("%d%n", 26);
 7         System.out.printf("%d%n", +26);
 8         System.out.printf("%d%n", -26);
 9         System.out.printf("%o%n", 26);
10         System.out.printf("%x%n", 26);
11         System.out.printf("%X%n", 26);
12      }
13   }
```

```
26
26
-26
32
1a
1A
```

**Fig. B.1** | Using the integer conversion characters.

The `printf` method has the form

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1003-03)

```
printf(format-string, argument-list);
```

where *format-string* describes the output format and the optional *argument-list* contains the values corresponding to each format specifier in *format-string.* There can be many format specifiers in one format string.

Each format string in lines 6–8 specifies that `printf` should output a decimal integer (`%d`) followed by a newline character. At the format specifier’s position, `printf` substitutes the first argument’s value after the format string. If the format string contains multiple format specifiers, at each subsequent format specifier’s position `printf` substitutes the value of the next argument in the argument list. The `%o` format specifier in line 9 outputs the integer in octal format. The `%x` format specifier in line 10 outputs the integer in hexadecimal format with lowercase letters. The `%X` format specifier in line 11 outputs the integer in hexadecimal format with uppercase letters.

### B.4 Floating-Point Number Formatting

The following table describes the floating-point conversions:

| Conversion character | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `e` or `E` | Display a floating-point value in exponential notation. Conversion character `E` displays the output in uppercase letters. |
| `f` | Display a floating-point value in fixed-point format. |
| `g` or `G` | Display a floating-point value in either the fixed-point format `f` or the exponential format `e` based on the magnitude of the value. If the magnitude is less than 10^(–3) or greater than or equal to 10⁷, the floating-point value is printed with `e` (or `E`). Otherwise, the value is printed in format `f`. The output is displayed in uppercase letters when conversion character `G` is used. |
| `a` or `A` | Display a floating-point number in hexadecimal format. Conversion character `A` displays the output in uppercase letters. |

The **conversion characters `e`** and **`E`** display floating-point values in **computerized scientific notation**, also called **exponential notation**. Exponential notation is the computer equivalent of the scientific notation used in mathematics. For example, the value 150.4582 is represented in scientific notation in mathematics as

```
1.504582 × 102
```

and is represented in exponential notation as

```
1.504582e+02
```

in Java. This notation indicates that 1.504582 is multiplied by 10, raised to the second power `(e+02)`. The e stands for “exponent.”

Values printed with the conversion characters e, `E` and `f` are output with six digits of precision to the right of the decimal point by default (e.g., `1.045921`)—other precisions must be specified explicitly. For values printed with the conversion character `g`, the precision represents the total number of digits displayed, excluding the exponent. The default is six digits (e.g., `12345678.9` is displayed as `1.23457e+07`). **Conversion character `f`** always prints at least one digit to the left of the decimal point. Conversion characters `e` and `E` print lowercase `e` and uppercase `E` preceding the exponent and always print exactly one digit to the left of the decimal point. Rounding occurs if the value being formatted has more significant digits than the precision.

**Conversion character `g`** (or **`G`**) prints in either `e` (`E`) or `f` format, depending on the floating-point value. For example, the values `0.0000875`, `87500000.0`, `8.75`, `87.50` and `875.0` are printed as `8.750000e-05`, `8.750000e+07`, `8.750000`, `87.500000` and `875.000000` with the conversion character `g`. The value `0.0000875` uses `e` notation because the magnitude is less than `10`^(`-3`). The value `87500000.0` uses `e` notation because the magnitude is greater than `10`^(`7`). [Figure B.2](#appb.xhtml_appbfig02) demonstrates the floating-point conversion characters.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1005-01)

```
 1   // Fig. B.2: FloatingNumberTest.java
 2   // Using floating-point conversion characters.
 3
 4   public class FloatingNumberTest {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         System.out.printf("%e%n", 12345678.9);
 7         System.out.printf("%e%n", +12345678.9 );
 8         System.out.printf("%e%n", -12345678.9);
 9         System.out.printf("%E%n", 12345678.9);
10         System.out.printf("%f%n", 12345678.9);
11         System.out.printf("%g%n", 12345678.9);
12         System.out.printf("%G%n", 12345678.9);
13      }
14   }
```

```
1.234568e+07
1.234568e+07
-1.234568e+07
1.234568E+07
12345678.900000
1.23457e+07
1.23457E+07
```

**Fig. B.2** | Using floating-point conversion characters.

### B.5 String and Character Formatting

Conversion characters `c` and `s` print individual characters and `String`s, respectively. **Conversion characters** **`c`** and **`C`** require a `char` argument. **Conversion characters** **`s`** and **`S`** can take a `String` or any `Object` as an argument—any `Object` can be converted to a `String` because they all have `toString` methods. When conversion characters `C` and `S` are used, the output is displayed in uppercase letters. [Figure B.3](#appb.xhtml_appbfig03) displays characters, `String`s and objects with conversion characters `c`, `s` and `S`. Autoboxing occurs at line 7 when an `int` constant is assigned to an `Integer` object. Line 13 outputs an `Integer` argument with the conversion character `s`, which implicitly invokes the `toString` method to get the integer value. You can also output an `Integer` object using the `%d` format specifier. In this case, the `int` value in the `Integer` object will be unboxed and output. Using `%c` to print a `String` causes an `Illegal-FormatConversionException`—a `String` cannot be converted to a character.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1005-02)

```
 1   // Fig. B.3: CharStringConversion.java
 2   // Using character and string conversion characters.
 3   public class CharStringConversion {
 4      public static void main(String[] args) {
 5         char character = 'A'; // initialize char
 6         String string = "This is also a string"; // String object
 7         Integer integer = 1234; // initialize integer (autoboxing)
 8
 9         System.out.printf("%c%n", character);
10         System.out.printf("%s%n", "This is a string");
11         System.out.printf("%s%n", string);
12         System.out.printf("%S%n", string);
13         System.out.printf("%s%n", integer); // implicit call to toString
14      }
15   }
```

```
A
This is a string
This is also a string
THIS IS ALSO A STRING
1234
```

**Fig. B.3** | Using character and `String` conversion characters.

### B.6 Other Conversion Characters

The following table describes the remaining conversion characters—**`b`**, **`B`**, **`h`**, **`H`**, **`%`** and **`n`**:

| Conversion character | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `b` or `B` | Print `"true"` or `"false"` for the value of a `boolean` or `Boolean`. These conversion characters can also format the value of any reference. If the reference is non-`null`, `"true"` is output; otherwise, `"false"`. When conversion character `B` is used, the output is displayed in uppercase letters. |
| `h` or `H` | Print the `String` representation of an object’s hash-code value in hexadecimal format. If the corresponding argument is `null`, `"null"` is printed. When conversion character `H` is used, the output is displayed in uppercase letters. |
| `%` | Print the percent character. |
| `n` | Print the platform-specific line separator (e.g., `\r\n` on Windows or `\n` on macOS/Linux). |

Lines 7–8 of [Fig. B.4](#appb.xhtml_appbfig04) use `%b` to print the value of `boolean` (or `Boolean`) values `false` and `true`. Line 9 associates a `String` to `%b`, which returns `true` because it’s not `null`. Line 10 associates a `null` object to `%B`, which displays `FALSE` because `test` is `null`. Lines 11–12 use `%h` to print the `String` representations of the hash-code values for `String`s `"hello"` and `"Hello"`. These values could be used to store or locate the `String`s in a `HashMap` ([Chapter 12](#ch12.xhtml_ch12), [Generic Collections](#ch12.xhtml_ch12)). The hash-code values for these two `String`s differ because one `String` starts with a lowercase letter and the other with an uppercase letter. Line 13 uses `%H` to print `null` in uppercase letters. The last two `printf` statements (lines 14–15) use `%%` to print the `%` character in a `String` and `%n` to print a platform-specific line separator.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1007-01)

```
 1   // Fig. B.4: OtherConversion.java
 2   // Using the b, B, h, H, % and n conversion characters.
 3
 4   public class OtherConversion {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         Object test = null;
 7         System.out.printf("%b%n", false);
 8         System.out.printf("%b%n", true);
 9         System.out.printf("%b%n", "Test");
10         System.out.printf("%B%n", test);
11         System.out.printf("Hashcode of \"hello\" is %h%n", "hello");
12         System.out.printf("Hashcode of \"Hello\" is %h%n", "Hello");
13         System.out.printf("Hashcode of null is %H%n", test);
14         System.out.printf("Printing a %% in a format string%n");
15         System.out.printf("Printing a new line %nnext line starts here");
16      }
17   }
```

```
false
true
true
FALSE
Hashcode of "hello" is 5e918d2
Hashcode of "Hello" is 42628b2
Hashcode of null is NULL
Printing a % in a format string
Printing a new line
next line starts here
```

**Fig. B.4** | Using the `b`, `B`, `h`, `H`, `%` and `n` conversion characters.

Trying to print a literal percent character using `%` rather than `%%` in the format string might cause a difficult-to-detect logic error. When `%` appears in a format string, it must be followed by a conversion character in the `String`. The single percent could accidentally be followed by a legitimate conversion character, thus causing a logic error.

### B.7 Field Widths and Precisions

The size of a field in which data is printed is specified by a **field width**. If the field width is larger than the data being printed, the data is right aligned in that field by default. We discuss left alignment in [Section B.8](#appb.xhtml_appblev1sec8). You insert an integer representing the field width between the `%` and the conversion character (e.g., `%4d`) in the format specifier. [Figure B.5](#appb.xhtml_appbfig05) prints two groups of five numbers each, right aligning those numbers that contain fewer digits than the field width. The field width is increased to print values wider than the field. The minus sign for a negative value uses one character position in the field. Also, if no field width is specified, the data prints in exactly as many positions as it needs. Field widths can be used with all format specifiers except the line separator (`%n`). Not providing a sufficiently large field width to handle a value to be printed can offset other data being printed and produce confusing outputs. Know your data!

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1008-01)

```
 1   // Fig. B.5: FieldWidthTest.java
 2   // Right aligning integers in fields.
 3
 4   public class FieldWidthTest {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         System.out.printf("%4d%n", 1);
 7         System.out.printf("%4d%n", 12);
 8         System.out.printf("%4d%n", 123);
 9         System.out.printf("%4d%n", 1234);
10         System.out.printf("%4d%n%n", 12345); // data too large
11
12         System.out.printf("%4d%n", -1);
13         System.out.printf("%4d%n", -12);
14         System.out.printf("%4d%n", -123);
15         System.out.printf("%4d%n", -1234); // data too large
16         System.out.printf("%4d%n", -12345); // data too large
17      }
18   }
```

```
 1
  12
 123
1234
12345

  -1
 -12
-123
-1234
-12345
```

**Fig. B.5** | Right aligning integers in fields.

Method `printf` also provides the ability to specify the precision with which data is printed. Precision has different meanings for different types. When used with floating-point conversion characters `e` and `f`, the precision is the number of digits that appear after the decimal point. When used with conversion characters `g`, `a` or `A`, the precision is the maximum number of significant digits to be printed. When used with conversion character `s`, the precision is the maximum number of characters to be written from the `String`. To use precision, place between the percent sign and the conversion specifier a decimal point (`.`) followed by an integer representing the precision. [Figure B.6](#appb.xhtml_appbfig06) demonstrates precision in format strings. When a floating-point value is printed with a precision smaller than the original value’s number of decimal places, the value is rounded. Also, the format specifier `%.3g` indicates that the total number of digits used to display the floating-point value is 3\. Because the value has three digits to the left of the decimal point, it’s rounded to the ones position.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1008-02)

```
 1   // Fig. B.6: PrecisionTest.java
 2   // Using precision for floating-point numbers and strings.
 3   public class PrecisionTest {
 4      public static void main(String[] args) {
 5         double f = 123.94536;
 6         String s = "Happy Birthday";
 7
 8         System.out.printf("Using precision for floating-point numbers%n");
 9         System.out.printf("\t%.3f%n\t%.3e%n\t%.3g%n%n", f, f, f);
10
11         System.out.printf("Using precision for strings%n");
12         System.out.printf("\t%.11s%n", s);
13      }
14   }
```

```
Using precision for floating-point numbers
        123.945
        1.239e+02
        124

Using precision for strings
        Happy Birth
```

**Fig. B.6** | Using precision for floating-point numbers and `String`s.

The field width and the precision can be combined by placing the field width, followed by a decimal point, followed by a precision between the percent sign and the conversion character, as in the statement

```
printf("%9.3f", 123.456789);
```

which displays `123.457` with three digits to the right of the decimal point right aligned in a nine-digit field—this number will be preceded in its field by two blanks.

### B.8 Formatting Flags

Various flags may be used with method `printf` to supplement its output formatting capabilities. The following flags are available for use in format strings:

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **`-`** (minus sign) | Left align the output within the specified field. |
| **`+`** (plus sign) | Display a plus sign preceding positive values and a minus sign preceding negative values. |
| ***space*** | Print a space before a positive value not printed with the `+` flag. |
| **`#`** | When used with the octal conversion character `o`, prefix `0` to the output value. When used with the hexadecimal conversion character `x`, prefix `0x` to the output value. |
| **`0`** (zero) | Pad a field with leading zeros. |
| **`,`** (comma) | Use the locale-specific thousands separator (i.e., `'`,`'` for U.S. locale) to display decimal and floating-point numbers. |
| **`(`** | Enclose negative numbers in parentheses. |

To use a flag in a format string, place it immediately to the right of the percent sign. Several flags may be used in the same format specifier. [Figure B.7](#appb.xhtml_appbfig07) demonstrates right alignment and left alignment of a `String`, an integer, a character and a floating-point number. Line 7 serves as a counting mechanism for the screen output.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1010-01)

```
 1   // Fig. B.7: MinusFlagTest.java
 2   // Right aligning and left aligning values.
 3
 4   public class MinusFlagTest {
 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         System.out.println("Columns:");
 7         System.out.println("0123456789012345678901234567890123456789\n");
 8         System.out.printf("%10s%10d%10c%10f%n%n", "hello", 7, 'a', 1.23);
 9         System.out.printf(
10            "%-10s%-10d%-10c%-10f%n", "hello", 7, 'a', 1.23);
11      }
12   }
```

```
Columns:
0123456789012345678901234567890123456789

     hello         7         a  1.230000

hello     7         a         1.230000
```

**Fig. B.7** | Right aligning and left aligning values.

[Figure B.8](#appb.xhtml_appbfig08) prints a positive and a negative number, each with and without the **`+`** **flag**. The minus sign is displayed in both cases, and the plus sign only when the `+` flag is used.

[Click here to view code image](#appb_images.xhtml_f1010-02)

```

 3

 5      public static void main(String[] args) {
 6         System.out.printf("%d\t%d%n", 786, -786);
 7         System.out.printf("%+d\t%+d%n", 786, -786);
 8   }
 9   }
```
